# Preface

This book is concerned with recent developments in time series and panel data techniques for the analysis of macroeconomic and financial data. It provides a rigorous, nevertheless user-friendly, account of the time series techniques dealing with univariate and multivariate time series models, as well as panel data models. An overview of econometrics asa subject is provided in Pesaran (1987a) and updated in Geweke, Horowitz, and Pesaran (2008).

It is distinct from other time series texts in the sense that it also covers panel data models and attempts at a more coherent integration of time series, multivariate analysis, and panel data models. It builds on the author’s extensive research in the areas of time series and panel data analysis and covers a wide variety of topics in one volume. Different parts of the book can be used as teaching material for a variety of courses in econometrics. It can also be used as a reference manual.

It begins with an overview of basic econometric and statistical techniques and provides an account of stochastic processes, univariate and multivariate time series, tests for unit roots, cointegration, impulse response analysis, autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity models, simultaneous equation models, vector autoregressions, causality, forecasting, multivariate volatility models, panel data models, aggregation and global vector autoregressive models (*GVAR*). The techniques are illustrated using Microfit 5 (Pesaran and Pesaran (2009)) with applications to real output, inflation, interest rates, exchange rates, and stock prices.

The book assumes that the reader has done an introductory econometrics course. It begins with an overview of the basic regression model, which is intended to be accessible to advanced undergraduates, and then deals with more advanced topics which are more demanding and suited to graduate students and other interested scholars.

The book is organized into six parts:

Part I: Chapters 1 to 7 present the classical linear regression model, describe estimation and statistical inference, and discuss the violation of the assumptions underlying the classical linear regression model. This part also includes an introduction to dynamic economic modelling, and ends with a chapter on predictability of asset returns.

Part II: Chapters 8 to 11 deal with asymptotic theory and present the maximum likelihood and generalized method of moments estimation frameworks.

Part III: Chapters 12 and 13 provide an introduction to stochastic processes and spectral density analysis.

Part IV: Chapters 14 to 18 focus on univariate time series models and cover stationary *ARMA* models, unit root processes, trend and cycle decomposition, forecasting and univariate volatility models.

Part V: Chapters 19 to 25 consider a variety of reduced formand structuralmultivariate models, rational expectations models, as well as VARs, vector error corrections, cointegrating *VARs*, *VARX* models, impulse response analysis, and multivariate volatility models.

Part VI: Chapters 26 to 33 considers panel data models both when the time dimension (*T*) of the panels is short, as well as when panels with *N* (the cross-section dimension) and *T* are large. These chapters cover a wide range of panel data models, starting with static panels with homogenous slopes and graduating to dynamic panels with slope heterogeneity, error cross-section dependence, unit roots, and cointegration.

There are also chapters dealing with the aggregation of large dynamic panels and the theory and practice of *GVAR* modelling. This part of the book focuses more on large *N* and *T* panels which are less covered in other texts, and draws heavily on my research in this area over the past 20 years starting with Pesaran and Smith ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-808)).

Appendices [A](#049_BM_appendixGroupa.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1) and [B](#049_BM_appendixGroupb.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2) present background material on matrix algebra, probability and distribution theory, and Appendix [C](#049_BM_appendixGroupc.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3) provides an overview of Bayesian analysis.

This book has evolved over many years of teaching and research and brings together in one place a diverse set of research areas that have interested me. It is hoped that it will also be of interest to others. I have used some of the chapters in my teaching of postgraduate students at Cambridge University, University of Southern California, UCLA, and University of Pennsylvania. Undergraduate students at Cambridge University have also been exposed to some of the introductory material in Part I of the book. It is impossible to name all those who have helped me with the preparation of this volume. But I would like particularly to name two of my Cambridge Ph.D. students, Alexander Chudik and Elisa Tosetti, for their extensive help, particularly with the material in Part VI of the book.

The book draws heavily from my published and unpublished research. In particular: [Chapter 7](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7) is based on Pesaran ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-777)).

[Chapter 25](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25) draws from Pesaran and Pesaran ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-777)).

[Chapter 32](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32) is based on Pesaran ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-772)) and Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) where additional technical details and proofs are provided.

[Chapter 31](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31) is based on Breitung and Pesaran (2008) and provides some updates and extensions. [Chapter 33](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33) is based on Chudik and Pesaran ([2015b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-224)).

I would also like to acknowledge all my coauthors whose work has been reviewed in this volume. In particular, I would like to acknowledge Ron Smith, Bahram Pesaran, Allan Timmermann, Kevin Lee, Yongcheol Shin, Vanessa Smith, Cheng Hsiao, Michael Binder, Richard Smith, Alexander Chudik, Takashi Yamagata, Tony Garratt, Til Schermann, Filippo di Mauro, Stéphane Dées, Alessandro Rebucci, Adrian Pagan, Aman Ullah, and Martin Weale. It goes without saying that none of them is responsible for the material presented in this volume.

Finally, I would like to acknowledge the helpful and constructive comments and suggestions from two anonymous referees which provided me with further impetus to extend the coverage of the material included in the book and to improve its exposition over the past six months. Ron Smith has also provided me with detailed comments and suggestions over a number of successive drafts. I am indebted to him for helping me to see the wood from the trees over the many years that we have collaborated with each other.

Hashem Pesaran

*Cambridge and Los Angeles*

*January 2015*

# 1.1 Introduction

There are a number of ways that a regression between two or more variables can be motivated. It can, for example, arise because we know *a priori* that there exists an exact linear relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0001.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0002.gif), with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0003.gif) being observed with measurement errors. Alternatively, it could arise if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0004.gif) have bivariate distribution and we are interested in the conditional expectations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0005.gif) given ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0006.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0007.gif), which will be a linear function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0008.gif) either if the underlying relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0009.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0010.gif) is linear, or if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0011.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0012.gif) have a bivariate normal distribution. A regression line can also be considered without any underlying statistical model, just as a method of fitting a line to a scatter of points in a two-dimensional space.

# 1.2 The curve fitting approach

We first consider the problem of regression purely as an act of fitting a line to a scatter diagram. Suppose that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0013.gif) pairs of observations on the variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0014.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0015.gif), given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0016.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0017.gif), are available. We are interested in obtaining the equation of a straight line such that, for each observation ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0018.gif), the corresponding value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0019.gif) on a straight line in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0020.gif) plane is as ‘close’ as possible to the observed values ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0021.gif).

Immediately, different criteria of ‘closeness’ or ‘fit’ present themselves. Two basic issues are involved:

**A:** How to define and measure the *distance* of the points in the scatter diagram from the fitted line. There are three plausible ways to measure the distance of a point from the fitted line:

(i) perpendicular to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0022.gif) -axis

(ii) perpendicular to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0023.gif) -axis

(iii) perpendicular to the fitted line.

**B:** How to *add up* all such distances of the sampled observations. Possible weighting (adding-up) schemes are:

(i) simple average of the square of distances

(ii) simple average of the absolute value of distances

(iii) weighted averages either of squared distance measure or absolute distance measures.

The simplest is the combination **A**(i) and **B**(i), which gives the ordinary least squares (*OLS*) estimates of the regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0024.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0025.gif). The method of ordinary least squares will be extensively treated in the rest of this Chapter and in [Chapter 2](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2). The difference between **A**(i) and **A**(ii) can also be characterized as to which of the two variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0026.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0027.gif), is represented on the horizontal axis. The combination **A**(ii) and **B**(i) is also referred to as the ‘reverse regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0028.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0029.gif)’. Other combinations of distance/weighting schemes can also be considered. For example **A**(iii) and **B**(i) is called orthogonal regression, **A**(i) and **B**(ii) yields the absolute minimum distance regression. **A**(i) and **B**(iii) gives the weighted (or absolute distance) least squares (or absolute distance) regression.

# 1.4 Correlation coeffcients between *Y* and *X*

There are many measures of quantifying the strength of correlation between two variables. The most popular one is the product moment correlation coeffcient which was developed by Karl Pearson and builds on an earlier contribution by Francis Galton. Other measures of correlations include the Spearman rank correlation and Kendall’s ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0056.gif) correlation. We now consider each of these measures in turn and discuss their uses and relationships.

## 1.4.1 Pearson correlation coeffcient

## 1.4.2 Rank correlation coeffcients

Rank correlation is often used in situations where the available observations are in the form of cardinal numbers, or if they are not suffciently precise. Rank correlations are also used to avoid undue influences from outlier (extreme tail) observations on the correlation analysis. A number of different rank correlations have been proposed in the literature. In what follows we focus on the two most prominent of these, namely Spearman’s rank correlation and Kendall’s ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0087.gif) correlation coeffcient. A classic treatment of the subject can be found in Kendall and Gibbons ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-587)).

The alternative estimators, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0141.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0142.gif) are likely to have some merit over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0143.gif) in small samples in cases where the population distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0144.gif) differs from bivariate normal and/or when the observations are subject to measurement errors.

Tests based on the different correlation measures are discussed in Section [3.4](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3-div1-31).

# 1.6 Linear statistical models

So far we have viewed the regression equation as a line fitted to a scatter of points in a two-dimensional space. As such it is purely a descriptive scheme that attempts to summarize the scatter of points by a single regression line. An alternative procedure would be to adopt a statistical model where the regression disturbances, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0171.gif) ’s, are characterized by a probability distribution. Under this framework there are two important statistical models that are used in the literature:

**A:** Classical linear regression model. This model assumes that the relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0172.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0173.gif) is a linear one:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0174.gif)(1.14)

and that the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0175.gif)s satisfy the following assumptions:

(i) *Zero mean*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0176.gif) have zero means, i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0177.gif)

(ii) *Homoskedasticity:* conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0178.gif) the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0179.gif) have constant conditional variance. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0180.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0181.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0182.gif).

(iii) *Non-autocorrelated error*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0183.gif) are serially uncorrelated. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0184.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0185.gif).

(iv) *Orthogonality:* the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0186.gif) and the regressor ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0187.gif) are uncorrelated, or conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0188.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0189.gif) has a zero mean (namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0190.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0191.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0192.gif) ).

Assumption (i) ensures that the unconditional mean of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0193.gif) is correctly specified by the regression equation. The other assumptions can be relaxed and are introduced to provide a simple model that can be used as a benchmark in econometric analysis.

**B:** Another way of motivating the linear regression model is to focus on the *joint* distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0194.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0195.gif), and assume that this distribution is normal with constant means, variances and covariances. In cases where the number of moment conditions exceed the number of unknown parameters, the method of moments is generalized to take account of the additional moment conditions in an effcient manner. The resultant estimator is then referred to as the generalized method of moments (*GMM*), which will be discussed in some detail in [Chapter 10](#021_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-10).

# 1.8 The likelihood approach for the bivariate regression model

An alternative estimation approach developed by R. A. Fisher over the period 1912–22 (building on the early contributions of Gauss, Laplace, and Edgeworth) is to estimate the unknown parameters by maximizing their likelihood. The likelihood function is then given by the joint probability distribution of the observations. # 1.9 Properties of the *OLS* estimators

Under the classical assumptions (i)–(iv) in Section [1.6](#011_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-1-div1-6) above, the *OLS* estimators of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0292.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0293.gif) possess the following properties:

# 2.1 Introduction

This chapter considers the extension of the bivariate regression discussed in [Chapter 1](#011_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-1) to the case where more than one variable is available to explain/predict ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0524.gif), the dependent variable. The topic is known as multiple regression analysis, although only one relationship is in fact considered between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0525.gif) and the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0526.gif) explanatory variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0527.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0528.gif). The problem of multiple regressions where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0529.gif) sets of dependent (or endogenous) variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0530.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0531.gif) are explained in terms of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0532.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0533.gif) will be considered in [Chapter 19](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19) and is known as multivariate analysis and includes topics such as canonical correlation and factor analysis. This chapter covers standard techniques such as ordinary least squares (*OLS*) and examines the properties of *OLS* estimators under classical assumption, discusses the Gauss–Markov theorem, multiple correlation coefficient, the multicollinearity problem, partitioned regression, introduces regressions that are nonlinear in variables and discusses the interpretation of coefficients.

Consider the general linear regression model

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0535.gif) are the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0536.gif) observation on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0537.gif) regressors. If the regression contains an intercept, then one of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0538.gif) regressors, say the first one ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0539.gif), is set equal to unity for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0540.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0541.gif). The parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0542.gif) assumed to be fixed (i.e., time invariant) are the regression coefficients, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0543.gif) are the ‘disturbances’ or the ‘errors’ of the regression equation. The regression equation can also be written more compactly as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0544.gif)(2.2)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0545.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0546.gif). Stacking the equations for all the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0547.gif) observation and using matrix notations, ([2.1](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-displayMaths-104)) or ([2.2](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-displayMaths-105)) can be written as (see Appendix [A](#049_BM_appendixGroupa.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1) for an introduction to matrices and matrix operations)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0548.gif)(2.3)

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0549.gif)

The disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0550.gif) (or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0551.gif) ) satisfy the following assumptions:

Assumption A1: *Zero mean*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0552.gif) have zero means

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0553.gif)

Assumption A2: *Homoskedasticity*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0554.gif) have constant conditional variances

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0555.gif)

Assumption A3: *Non-autocorrelated errors*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0556.gif) are serially uncorrelated

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0557.gif)

Assumption A4: *Orthogonality*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0558.gif) and the regressors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0559.gif) are uncorrelated

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0560.gif)

Assumption A5: *Normality*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0561.gif) are normally distributed.

Assumption A2 implies that the variances of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0562.gif) s are constant also unconditionally, since,[¹](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-note-3)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0563.gif)

given that, under A4, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0564.gif). The assumption of constant conditional and unconditional error variances is likely to be violated when dealing with cross-sectional regressions, while that of constant conditional error variances is often violated in analysis of financial and macro-economic times series, such as exchange rates, stock returns and interest rates. However, it is possible for errors to be unconditionally constant (time-invariant) but conditionally time varying. Examples include stationary autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic (ARCH) models developed by Engle ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-330)) and discussed in detail in [Chapters 18](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18) and [25](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25).

In time series analysis the critical assumptions are A3 and A4. Assumption A3 is particularly important when the regression equation contains lagged values of the dependent variable, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0565.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0566.gif). However, even if lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0567.gif) are not included among the regressors, the breakdown of assumption A3 can lead to misleading inferences, a problem recognized as early as 1920s by Yule ([1926](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-993)), and known in the econometrics time series literature as the spurious regression problem.[²](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-note-4) The orthogonality assumption, A4, allows the empirical analysis of the relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0568.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0569.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0570.gif),…,![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0571.gif) to be carried out without fully specifying the stochastic processes generating the regressors, also known as ‘forcing’ variables. We notice that assumption A1 is implied by A4, if a vector of ones is included among the regressors. It is therefore important that an intercept is always included in the regression model, unless it is found to be statistically insignificant.

As they stand, assumptions A2, A3, and A4 require the regressors to be strictly exogenous, in the sense that the first- and second-order moments of the errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0572.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0573.gif) are uncorrelated with the current, past *and* future values of the regressors (see Section [9.3](#020_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-9-div1-100) for a discussion of strict and weak exogeneity, and their impact on the properties of estimators). This assumption is too restrictive for many applications in economics and in effect treats the regressors as given which is more suitable to outcomes of experimental designs rather than economic observations that are based on survey data of transaction prices and quantities. The strict exogeneity assumption also rules out the inclusion of lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0574.gif) amongst the regressors. However, it is possible to relax these assumptions somewhat so that it is only required that the first- and second-order moments of the errors are uncorrelated with current and past values of the regressors, but allowing for the errors to be correlated with the future values of the regressors. In this less restrictive setting, assumptions A2–A4 need to be replaced by the following assumptions:

Assumption A2(i) *Homoskedasticity*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0575.gif) have constant conditional variances

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0576.gif)

Assumption A3(i) *Non-autocorrelated errors*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0577.gif) are serially uncorrelated

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0578.gif)

Assumption A4(i) *Orthogonality*: the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0579.gif) and the regressors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0580.gif) are uncorrelated

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0581.gif)

Under these assumptions the regressors are said to be *weakly exogenous*, and allow for lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0582.gif) to be included in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0583.gif).

Adding assumption A5 to the classical model yields the classical linear normal regression model. This model can also be derived using the *joint* distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0584.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0585.gif), and by assuming that this distribution is a multivariate *normal* with constant means, variances and covariances. In this setting, the regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0586.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0587.gif) defined as the mathematical expectation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0588.gif) conditional on the realized values of the regressors, will be linear in the regressors. The linearity of the regression equation follows from the joint normality assumption and need not hold if this assumption is relaxed. To be more precise suppose that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0589.gif)(2.4)

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0590.gif)

Then using known results from theory of multivariate normal distributions (see Appendix [B](#049_BM_appendixGroupb.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2) for a summary and references) we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0591.gif)

Under this setting, assuming that ([2.2](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-displayMaths-105)) includes an intercept, the regression coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0592.gif) will be given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0593.gif). It is also easily seen that the regression errors associated with ([2.4](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-displayMaths-116)) are given by

Both of the above interpretations of the classical normal regression model have been used in the literature (see, e.g., Spanos ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-921))). We remark that the normality assumption A5 may be important in small samples, but is not generally required when the sample under consideration is large enough.

All the various departures from the classical normal regression model mentioned here will be analysed in [Chapters 3 to 6](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3).

The criterion function in this general case will be

The likelihood approach also forms the basis of the Bayesian inference where the likelihood is combined with prior distributions on the unknown parameters to obtain posterior probability distributions which is then used for estimation and inference: see Section [C.6](#049_BM_appendixGroupc.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3-div1-417) in Appendix C.

These properties of *OLS* residuals lie at the core of some of the difficulties encountered in practice in developing tests of the classical assumptions based on *OLS* residuals, that perform well in small samples. Fortunately, the serial correlation and heteroskedasticity properties of *OLS* residuals tend to disappear in ‘large enough’ samples.

# 2.8 Mean square error of an estimator and the bias-variance trade-off

The Gauss–Markov theorem states that, under the classical assumptions, it is not possible to find linear unbiased estimators of regression coefficients which have smaller variances than the *OLS* estimator, ([2.8](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2-displayMaths-126)). However, as shown by James and Stein ([1961](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-543)), it is possible to find other estimators that are biased but have a lower variance than the *OLS* estimator. In applied econometrics, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0880.gif) is often used as a criterion of model selection. However, its use can be justified when the regression models under consideration are non-nested, in the sense that none of the models under consideration can be obtained from the others by means of some suitable parametric restrictions. In the case where the models are nested, a more suitable procedure would be to apply classical hypotheses testing procedures and test the models against one another by means of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0881.gif) - or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0882.gif) -tests. (See [Chapter 3](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3) on hypotheses testing in linear regression models.)

This property is known as the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, first introduced by Frisch and Waugh ([1933](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-372)), and then by Lovell ([1963](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-648)). For further details see also Davidson and MacKinnon ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-265)).

The partitioned and the unpartitioned regressions also yield the same results for the variance matrix of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0957.gif). It is, therefore, possible to estimate the coefficients of the ‘focus’ regressors in two ways. The partitioned method first ‘filters’ the observations by allowing for the effect of ‘non-focus’ variables by running regressions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0958.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0959.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0960.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0961.gif) and then computes estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0962.gif) by regression of the filtered variables. In the case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0963.gif) contains seasonal dummies, the residuals from regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0964.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0965.gif) represent seasonally adjusted ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0966.gif), and similarly the residuals from regressions of the columns of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0967.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0968.gif) represent seasonally adjusted ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0969.gif). Hence, regression of seasonally adjusted variables yields the same coefficient estimates as running a regression of seasonally unadjusted variables so long as the same seasonal dummies used to adjust ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0970.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0971.gif) are also included in the unseasonally adjusted regression. The same results also hold for the regressions of detrended and non-detrended variables.

Special care should be exercised when using the above results from partitioned regressions. Firstly, the results do not apply when the seasonal adjustments or detrending are carried out over a time period that differs from the period over which the regression of focus variables are run. Neither do they apply if the seasonal adjustments are carried out by government agencies who often use their own in-house methods. Secondly, the computer results based on regression of seasonally adjusted variables do not generally take account of the loss in degrees of freedom associated with the estimation of seasonal or trend effects. In view of these pitfalls, it is often advisable to base estimation and hypothesis testing on the unpartitioned regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0972.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0973.gif). The use of partitioned regressions is helpful primarily for pedagogic purposes.

# 2.12 How to interpret multiple regression coefficients

The issue of how to interpret the regressions coefficients in a multiple regression model has been recently discussed in Pesaran and Smith ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-810)). Suppose we are interested in measuring the effects of a unit change in the regressor ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0977.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0978.gif). The standard procedure is to use the estimated coefficient of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0979.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0980.gif), on the assumption that the hypothetical change in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0981.gif) does not affect ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0982.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0983.gif) namely it assumes that the hypothetical change in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-0984.gif) is accompanied with holding the other regressors constant, the so called *ceteris paribus* assumption. But in almost all economic applications we are not able to control the inputs and the counterfactual exercise by which all other regressors can be held constant might not be relevant. Pesaran and Smith ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-810)) argue that in time series analysis, rather than focussing on the signs of individual coefficients in multiple regressions holding the other variables constant, we should measure a total impact effect which allows for direct and indirect induced changes that arise due to the historical correlations amongst the regressors. The limitation of the usual *ceteris paribus* approach lies in the fact that it ignores the stochastic interdependence of the regressors which we need to allow for in time series economic applications. Similar issues arise in the derivation of impulse response functions for the analysis of dynamic models and have been discussed by Koop, Pesaran, and Potter ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-608)) and Pesaran and Shin ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-796)) and will be addressed in [Chapter 24](#038_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-24).

To illustrate Pesaran and Smith ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-810))’s argument consider the following simple classical linear regression model with two regressors:

# 2.13 Implications of misspecification for the *OLS* estimators

The unbiasedness property of the *OLS* estimators in the classical linear regression model crucially depends on the validity of the classical assumptions and the correct specification of the regression equation. Here we consider the effects of misspecification, that results from adding or omitting a regressor in error, on the *OLS* estimators. In [Chapter 3](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3) we consider the implications of such misspecifications for inference on the regression coefficients.

# 2.15 Further reading

Further reading on multiple regression and on the properties of *OLS* estimator can be found in Wooldridge ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-983)) and in Greene ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-431)) (see [Chapters 2–4](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2)). An interesting geometric interpretation of linear regression, shedding light on the numerical properties of *OLS*, is presented in Davidson and MacKinnon ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-265)). The latter also provides an in-depth discussion on the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, and partitioned regression.

# 3.1 Introduction

Statistical hypothesis testing is at the core of the classical theory of statistical inference. Although it is closely related to the problem of estimation, it can be considered almost independently of it. In this chapter, we introduce some key concepts of statistical inference, and show their use to investigate the statistical significance of the (linear) relationships modelled through regression analysis, or to investigate the validity of the classical assumptions in simple and multiple linear regression.

# 3.2 Statistical hypothesis and statistical testing

A *statistical hypothesis* is an assertion about the distribution of one or more random variables. If the hypothesis completely specifies the probability distribution, it is called a *simple* hypothesis, otherwise it is called a *composite* hypothesis. For example, suppose ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1193.gif) are drawn from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1194.gif). Then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1195.gif) is a simple hypothesis, while ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1196.gif) is a composite hypothesis. If one hypothesis can be derived as a limiting sequence of another, we say the two hypotheses are *nested*. If neither hypothesis can be obtained from the other as a limiting process, then we call the hypotheses under consideration *non-nested*. For example, suppose ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1197.gif) are drawn from log-normal distribution under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1198.gif), while under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1199.gif) they are drawn from an exponential distribution. Then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1200.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1201.gif) are non-nested hypotheses. We refer to [Chapter 11](#022_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-11) for a review of tests for non-nested hypotheses.

## 3.2.1 Hypothesis testing

A test of a statistical hypothesis ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1202.gif) is a rule for *rejecting* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1203.gif). If the sample space is denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1204.gif), a test procedure decomposes ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1205.gif) into two regions. If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1206.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1207.gif) is called the critical or *rejection region* of the test, then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1208.gif) is rejected, otherwise ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1209.gif) is not rejected. In practice we often map ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1210.gif) into a test statistic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1211.gif) and consider whether ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1212.gif) or not.

The hypothesis being tested (i.e. the maintained hypothesis) is usually denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1213.gif) and is called the *null* hypothesis. The hypothesis against which ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1214.gif) is tested is called the *alternative* hypothesis and is usually denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1215.gif).

## 3.2.2 Types of error and the size of the test

The decision rule yields two types of error:

• The *type I error* is the error involved in rejecting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1216.gif) when it is true

• The *type II error* is the error involved in not rejecting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1217.gif) when it is false

The probability of a type I error is called the *size of the test* and, often denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1218.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1219.gif) per cent, is also called the *significance level* of the test. The probability of the type II error is called the *size of the type II error* and is often denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1220.gif). Ideally, we would like both errors to be as small as possible. However, there is a trade-off between the two, and by reducing the probability of a type I error, we must increase the probability of a type II error.

The *power* of a test is defined as 1 minus the size of the type II error, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1221.gif). For a given significance level, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1222.gif), we would like the power of the test, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1223.gif) to be as large as possible.

# 3.7 Joint tests of linear restrictions

So far we have considered testing a *single* linear restriction on the regression coefficients. Suppose now that we are interested in testing two or more linear restrictions, jointly. One simple example is the joint test of zero restrictions on the regression coefficients:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1586.gif)

Note that this joint hypothesis is different from testing the following two hypotheses separately.

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1587.gif)

The latter tests are known as separate induced tests and could lead to test outcomes that differ from the outcome of a joint test.

The general procedure for testing joint hypotheses in regression contexts is to construct the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1588.gif) -statistic that compares the sum of squares of residuals (SSR) of the regression under the restrictions (i.e., under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1589.gif) ) with the SSR under the alternative hypothesis, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1590.gif), when the parameter restrictions are not applied. This procedure is valid for a two-sided test. Carrying out one sided tests in the case of joint hypotheses is more complicated and will not be addressed here.

# 3.11 The multicollinearity problem

Multicollinearity is commonly attributed to situations where there is a high degree of intercorrelations among the explanatory variables in a multivariate regression equation. Multicollinearity is particularly prevalent in the case of time series data where there often exists the same common trend in two or more regressors in the regression equation. As a simple example consider the model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1708.gif)(3.31)

and assume for simplicity that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1709.gif) have a bivariate distribution with the correlation coefficient, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1710.gif). That is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1711.gif)

It is clear that as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1712.gif) approaches unity *separate* estimation of the slope coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1713.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1714.gif) becomes more and more problematic. Multicollinearity (namely a value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1715.gif) near unity in the context of the present example) will be a problem if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1716.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1717.gif) are jointly statistically significant but neither is statistically significant when taken individually. Put differently, multicollinearity will be a problem when the hypothesis ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1718.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1719.gif) can not be rejected when tested separately, while the joint hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1720.gif) is rejected. This clearly happens when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1721.gif) (or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1722.gif) ) is an exact linear function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1723.gif) (or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1724.gif) ). In this case ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1725.gif) and ([3.31](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3-displayMaths-346)) reduces to the simple regression equation

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1726.gif)

and it is only possible to estimate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1727.gif). Neither ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1728.gif) nor ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1729.gif) can be estimated (or tested) separately. This is the case of ‘perfect multicollinearity’ and arises out of faulty specification of the regression equation. One important example is when four seasonal dummies are included in a quarterly regression model that already contains an intercept term. In general the multicollinearity problem is likely to arise when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1730.gif) is close to 1.

The multicollinearity problem is also closely related to the problem of low power when testing hypotheses concerning the values of the regression coefficients separately. It is worth noting that no matter how large the correlation coefficient between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1731.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1732.gif), so long as it is not exactly equal to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1733.gif), a test of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1734.gif) (or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1735.gif) ) will have the correct size. The high degree of correlation between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1736.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1737.gif) causes the power of the test to be rather low and as a result we may end up not rejecting the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1738.gif) even if it is false.

The above example considers the simple case of a regression model with two explanatory variables. In case of regression models with more than two regressors the detection of the multicollinearity problem becomes more complicated. For example, when there are three regressors with the coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1806.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1807.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1808.gif), we need to consider all the possible combinations of the coefficients, namely testing them separately: ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1809.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1810.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1811.gif) ; in pairs: ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1812.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1813.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1814.gif) ; and jointly: ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1815.gif). Only in the case where the results of separate induced tests, the ‘pairs’ tests and the joint test are free from contradictions can we be confident that multicollinearity is not a problem.

There exist a number of measures in the literature that purport to detect and measure the seriousness of the multicollinearity problem. One commonly used diagnostic is the *condition number* defined as the square root of the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1816.gif), where the columns of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1817.gif) have been re-scaled to length 1 (namely, the elements of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1818.gif) column of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1819.gif) have been divided by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1820.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1821.gif) ). The condition number detects whether the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1822.gif) has a small determinant, namely if it is *ill-conditioned*. The larger the condition number, the more ill-conditioned is the matrix, and difficulties can be encountered in calculations involving ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1823.gif). Values of condition number higher than 30 are suggested as indicative of a problem (see Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-97)) for details). Another diagnostic used to detect multicollinearity is the *variance-inflation factor (VIF)*, defined as *VIF*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1824.gif), for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1825.gif) regressor, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1826.gif) is the squared multiple correlation coefficient of the regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1827.gif) on all other variables in the regression. A high value of *VIF*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1828.gif) suggests that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1829.gif) is in some collinear relationship with the other regressors. As a rule of thumb, for scaled data, a *VIF*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1830.gif) higher than ten indicates severe collinearity (see Kennedy ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-589))). We remark that these measures only examine the inter-correlation between the regressors, and at best give a partial picture of the multicollinearity problem, and can often ‘lead’ to misleading conclusions.

A useful rule of thumb which goes beyond regressor correlations is to compare the squared multiple correlation coefficient of the regression equation, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1831.gif), with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1832.gif). Klein ([1962](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-602)) suggests that collinearity is likely to be a problem and could lead to imprecise estimates if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1833.gif), for some ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1834.gif).

**Example 8** *To illustrate the problem return to the simulation exercise, and use the first 500 observations (instead of the first 50 observations) in computing the regression of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1835.gif) *on* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1836.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1837.gif). *The results are*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1838.gif)

*As compared with the estimates based on the first 50 observations \[see* ([*3.32*](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3-displayMaths-351)) *and* ([*3.33*](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3-displayMaths-352))\], *these estimates have much smaller standard errors and using the 95 percent significance level we arrive at similar conclusions whether we test* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1839.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1840.gif) *separately or jointly. Yet the sample correlation coefficient between* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1841.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1842.gif) *estimated over the first 500 observations is equal to 0.9895 which is only marginally smaller than the estimate obtained for the first 50 observations. By increasing the sample size from 50 to 500 we have increased the precision with which* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1843.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1844.gif) *are estimated and the power of testing* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1845.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1846.gif) *both separately and jointly*.

The above illustration also points to the fact that the main cause of the multicollinearity problem is lack of adequate observations (or information), and hence the imprecision with which the parameters of interest are estimated. Assuming the regression model under consideration is correctly specified, the only valid solution to the problem is to increase the information on the basis of which the regression is estimated. The new information could be either in the form of additional observations on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1847.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1848.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1849.gif), or it could be some *a priori* information concerning the parameters. The latter fits well with the Bayesian approach, but is difficult to accommodate within the classical framework. There are also other approaches suggested in the literature such as the ridge regression, and the principle component regression to deal with the multicollinearity problem. For a Bayesian treatment of the regression analysis see Section [C.6](#049_BM_appendixGroupc.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3-div1-417) in Appendix C. However, in using Bayesian techniques to deal with the multicollinearity problem it is important to bear in mind that the posterior means of the regression coefficients are well defined in small samples even if the regressors are highly multicollinear and even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1850.gif) is rank deficient. But in such cases the posterior mean of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1851.gif) can be very sensitive to the choice of the priors, and unless ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1852.gif) tends to a positive definite matrix the Bayes estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1853.gif) could become unstable as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1854.gif).

**Example 9** *As an example consider the following Fisher type explanation of nominal interests estimated on US quarterly data over the period 1948(1)–1990(4) using the file USGNP.FIT provided in Microfit 5:*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1855.gif)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1856.gif)

*where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1857.gif) *= nominal rate of interest*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1858.gif) *= the growth of money supply (*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1859.gif) *definition). In this regression, the coefficients of the lagged interest rate variables are all significant, but neither of the two coefficients of the lagged monetary growth variable is statistically significant. The* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1860.gif) *-ratios for the coefficients of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1861.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1862.gif) *are equal to 1.23 and 1.01, respectively, while the 95 percent critical value of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1863.gif) *-distribution with 165 (namely* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1864.gif)) *degrees of freedom is equal to 1.97. As we have seen above, it would be a mistake to necessarily conclude from this result that monetary growth has no significant impact on the nominal interest rates in the US. The statistical insignificance of the coefficients of DM*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1865.gif) *and DM*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1866.gif), *when tested separately may be due to the high intercorrelation between the regressors. Also we are not interested in testing the statistical significance of individual coefficients of the past monetary growth rates. What is of interest is the sum of the two coefficients of the lagged monetary growth rates, and not the individual coefficients, separately. *To compute the estimate of the standard error of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-1873.gif) *we recall that*

Therefore, we strongly reject the hypothesis that monetary growth has no effect on the nominal interest in the US. We also note that for every one percent increase in the growth of money supply there is around 0.24 of one percent increase in nominal interest within the space of two quarters. The long-run impact of money supply growth on nominal interest is much larger and depends on the magnitude of the lagged coefficients of the nominal interest rates*.

# 3.17 Non-parametric estimation of the density function

Suppose ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2013.gif) denotes the density function of a variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2014.gif) at point ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2015.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2016.gif) are observations drawn from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2017.gif). Two general approaches have been proposed to estimate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2018.gif). The first is a parametric method, which assumes that the form for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2019.gif) is known (e.g., normal), except for the few parameters that need to be estimated consistently from data (e.g., the mean and variance). In contrast, the non-parametric approach tries to estimate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2020.gif) directly, without strong assumptions on its form. One simple example of such an estimator is the histogram, although it has the drawback of being discontinuous, and not applicable for estimating the distribution of two or more variables. The non-parametric density estimator takes the following general form

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2021.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2022.gif) is called kernel function, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2023.gif) is the window width, also called the *smoothing* parameter or *bandwidth*. The kernel function needs to satisfy some regularity conditions typical of probability density functions, for example, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2024.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2025.gif). There exists a vast literature on the choice of this function. One popular choice is the Gaussian kernel, namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2026.gif)

Another common choice is the *Epanechnikov* kernel

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2027.gif)

As also pointed by Pagan and Ullah ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-747)), the choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2028.gif) is not critical to the analysis, and the optimal kernel in most cases will only yield modest improvements in the performance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2029.gif), over selections such as the Gaussian kernel.

When implementing density estimates, the choice of the window width, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2030.gif), plays an essential role. One crude way of choosing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2031.gif) is by a trial-and-error approach, consisting of looking at several different plots of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2032.gif) against ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2033.gif), when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2034.gif) is computed for different values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2035.gif). Other more objective and automatic methods for selecting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2036.gif) have been proposed in the literature. One popular choice is the *Silverman rule of thumb*, according to which

# 3.18 Further reading

Further material on statistical inference and its application to econometrics can be found in Rao ([1973](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-856)) and Bierens ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-114)). See also Appendix [B](#049_BM_appendixGroupb.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2) for a review of key concepts from probability theory and statistics useful for this chapter. For what concerns non-parametric density estimators, further discussion can be found in Horowitz ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-520)), which contains a treatment of non-parametric methods within econometrics.
