# 4.1 Introduction

Two important assumptions of the classical linear regression model are that the disturbances of the regression equation have constant variances across statistical units and that they are uncorrelated. These assumptions are needed to prove the Gauss–Markov theorem and to show that the least squares estimator is asymptotically efficient. In this chapter, we consider an important extension of the classical model introduced in [Chapter 2](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2) by allowing the disturbances, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2164.gif), to have variances differing across different values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2165.gif), namely to be heteroskedastic. [Chapter 5](#015_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-5) will consider the case of autocorrelated disturbances.

The heteroskedasticity problem frequently arises in cross-section regressions, while it is less common in time-series regressions. Important examples of regressions with heteroskedastic errors include cross-section regressions of household consumption expenditure on household income, cross-country growth regressions, and the cross-section regression of labour productivity on output growth across firms or industries. Heteroskedasticity also arises if regression coefficients vary randomly across observations or when observations on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2166.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2167.gif) are average estimates based on stratified sampling where the average estimates are based on different sample sizes. In time series regressions heteroskedasticity can arise either because of structural change or omission of relevant variables from the regression.

Therefore, the presence of heteroskedastic errors biases the estimates of the variances of the *OLS* estimators and hence invalidates the application of the usual ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2191.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2192.gif) tests to the parameters. This result readily generalizes to the multivariate case.

The direction of the bias in the *OLS* variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2193.gif) depends on the pattern of the heteroskedasticity. In the case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2194.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2195.gif) are positively correlated, the *OLS* formula underestimates the true variance ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2196.gif) given by ([4.5](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-displayMaths-436)), and its use can thus result in invalid inferences.

There are two general ways of dealing with the heteroskedasticity problem. One possibility is to specify the form of the heteroskedasticity and estimate the regression coefficients and the standard errors of their estimates by taking explicit account of the assumed pattern of heteroskedasticity. An alternative approach is to continue using the *OLS* estimators (i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2197.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2198.gif) ), but adjust the variances of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2199.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2200.gif) for the presence of heteroskedasticity. This latter procedure is particularly of interest when the exact form of the heteroskedasticity (namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2201.gif) ; ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2202.gif) ) is not known. In these circumstances, consistent estimators of the variances and covariances of the *OLS* estimators of the regression coefficients have been suggested in the literature, and are known as heteroskedasticity-consistent estimators (HCV) (see Eicker ([1963](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-316)), Eicker, LeCam, and Neyman ([1967](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-317)), Rao ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-855)), and White ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-971))). In the case of the simple regression the heteroskedasticity-consistent estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2203.gif) is given by

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2205.gif) are the *OLS* residuals. # 4.3 Efficient estimation of the regression coefficients in the presence of heteroskedasticity

The above procedure popularized in econometrics by Halbert White deals with the inconsistency of the *OLS* standard errors when heteroskedasticity is present, but does not deal with the inefficiency of the *OLS* estimators. 2. The *additive* specification:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2253.gif)(4.12)

defined over values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2254.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2255.gif) such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2256.gif).

3. The *mean-variance* specification:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2257.gif)

or for the simple regression model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2258.gif)(4.13)

This model postulates a nonlinear relation between the conditional mean and the conditional variance of the dependent variable and can be justified on theoretical grounds. For example, in the case of risk-adverse investors, mean return is related to volatility of stock returns measured by conditional variance of returns.

The estimation of the regression model under any of the above specifications of the heteroskedasticity can be carried out by the maximum likelihood (*ML*) method as illustrated in [Chapter 9](#020_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-9). However, in many cases estimation involves using some iterative numerical algorithm, as in the following example.

# 4.5 Diagnostic checks and tests of homoskedasticity

There exist three general methods that can be used to check the validity of the homoskedasticity assumption:

(i) Graphical methods

(ii) General non-parametric methods, such as the Goldfeld–Quandt test

(iii) Parametric tests.

## 4.5.1 Graphical methods

The graphical approach simply involves plotting the squares of the *OLS* residuals against the square of fitted values (i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2324.gif) ), or against other variables thought to be important in explaining heteroskedasticity of the error variances. Identification of systematic patterns in such graphical displays can be viewed as casual evidence of heteroskedasticity.

## 4.5.2 The Goldfeld–Quandt test

This test involves grouping the observations into ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2325.gif) (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2326.gif) ) categories and then testing the hypothesis that error variances are equal across these ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2327.gif) groups. The test assumes that the error variances, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2328.gif), are homoskedastic within each observation group. In practice, the observations are placed into three categories and the test of the equality of error-variances is carried out across the first and the third category, thus ignoring the observations in the middle category. This is done to reduce the possibility of dependence between the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2329.gif) over the first group of observations and over the third group of observations. Application of the Goldfeld–Quandt test to the simple regression model comprises the following steps.

**Step I:** Split the sample of observations into three groups, so that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2330.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2331.gif).

**Step II:** Run the *OLS* regressions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2332.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2333.gif) for the first and the third groups separately. Obtain the sums of squares of residuals for these two regressions, and denote them by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2334.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2335.gif), respectively.

**Step III:** Construct the statistic

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2336.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2337.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2338.gif) are the unbiased estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2339.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2340.gif), computed using the observations in groups I and III, respectively. It is convenient to compute the above ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2341.gif) statistic such that it is larger than unity (by putting the larger estimate of the variance in the numerator), so that the test statistic is more directly comparable to the critical values in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2342.gif) Tables.

Under the null hypothesis of homoskedasticity, the above ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2343.gif) -statistic has an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2344.gif) -distribution with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2345.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2346.gif) degrees of freedom. Large values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2347.gif) are associated with the rejection of the homoskedasticity assumption, and possible evidence of the heteroskedasticity. The Goldfeld–Quandt test readily generalizes to multivariate regressions and to more than three observation groups.

## 4.5.3 Parametric tests of homoskedasticity

The starting point of these tests is a parametric formulation of the heteroskedasticity, such as those specified by ([4.11](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-displayMaths-445)), ([4.12](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-displayMaths-446)), and ([4.13](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-displayMaths-448)). In the case of these specifications, the homoskedasticity hypothesis can be formulated in terms of the following null hypotheses:

1. Multiplicative specification:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2348.gif)

2. Additive specification:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2349.gif)

3. Mean-variance specification:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2350.gif)

Any one of the three likelihood-based approaches discussed in Section [9.7](#020_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-9-div1-104) can be used to implement the tests. The simplest procedure to compute is the Lagrange multiplier (*LM*) method, since this method does not require the estimation of the regression model under heteroskedasticity. One popular *LM* procedure for testing the homoskedasticity assumption is based on an additive version of the mean-variance model, ([4.13](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-displayMaths-448)). The *LM* statistic is computed as the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2351.gif) -ratio of the slope coefficient in the regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2352.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2353.gif) (including an intercept), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2354.gif) are the *OLS* residuals and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2355.gif) are the fitted values. Under the null hypothesis of homoskedastic variances, this ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2356.gif) -ratio is asymptotically distributed as a standard normal variable. In small samples, however, it is more advisable to use critical values from the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2357.gif) -distribution rather than the critical values from the normal distribution.

# 4.6 Further reading

Further reading on heteroskedasticity-robust inference and testing for heteroskedasticity can be found in Wooldridge ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-983), ch. 9), Wooldridge ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-986), chs 4 and 5), and Greene ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-431), ch. 11). Robust inference under heteroskedasticity in two-stage least squares is treated in Wooldridge ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-986), ch. 5). See also [Chapter 18](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18), which introduces various autoregressive models for the conditional variance of disturbance terms, in a time series framework.

# 5.1 Introduction

This chapter considers extensions of multiple regression analysis to the case where regression disturbances are serially correlated. Serial correlation, or autocorrelation, arises when the regression errors are not independently distributed either due to persistent of observations over time or over space. Our focus in this chapter is on time series observations; the problem of spatial dependence is addressed in [Chapter 30](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30). Serially correlated errors may also arise when the dynamics of the interactions between the dependent variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2413.gif), and the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2414.gif), are not adequately taken into account, or if the regression model is misspecified due to the omission of persistent regressors.

## 5.4.1 Feasible generalized least squares

The *GLS* estimator, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2480.gif), assumes ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2481.gif) is known. But in general ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2482.gif) is not known, and for this reason ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2483.gif) is known as the ‘infeasible’ *GLS* estimator. A ‘feasible’ *GLS* estimator can be obtained by replacing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2484.gif) with a consistent estimator. However, in cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2485.gif) is unrestricted, there are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2486.gif) additional unknown parameters to be estimated from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2487.gif) observations and this is clearly not feasible. Then, under certain regularity conditions, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2492.gif) will be a consistent estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2493.gif). # 5.6 Cochrane–Orcutt iterative method

This estimation method employs the Cochrane and Orcutt ([1949](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-243)) iterative procedure to compute *ML* estimators of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2671.gif) under the assumption that the disturbances, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2672.gif), follow the *AR*(![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2673.gif) ) process

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2674.gif)(5.43)

with ‘fixed initial’ values. The fixed initial value assumption is the same as treating the values, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2675.gif) as given or non-stochastic. This procedure in effect ignores the possible contribution of the distribution of the initial values to the overall log-likelihood function of the model. Once again the primary justification of treating initial values as fixed is asymptotic and is plausible only when ([5.43](#015_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-5-displayMaths-552)) is stationary and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2676.gif) is reasonably large (see Pesaran and Slater ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-802), Section [3.2](#013_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-3-div1-29)), and Judge et al. ([1985](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-558)) for further discussion).

The log-likelihood function for this case is defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2677.gif)(5.44)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2678.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2679.gif). Notice that the constant term ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2680.gif) in ([5.44](#015_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-5-displayMaths-553)) is undefined, and is usually set equal to zero. The Cochrane–Orcutt (C-O) method maximizes ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2681.gif) or equivalently minimizes ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2682.gif) with respect to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2683.gif) by the iterative method of ‘successive substitution’. Each iteration involves two steps: in the first step, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2684.gif) is maximized with respect to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2685.gif) taking ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2686.gif) as given. In the second step, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2687.gif) is taken as given and the log-likelihood function is maximized with respect to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2688.gif). # 5.7 *ML/AR* estimators by the Gauss–Newton method

This method provides an alternative numerical procedure for the maximization of the log-likelihood function ([5.44](#015_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-5-displayMaths-553)). In cases where this log-likelihood function has a unique maximum, the Gauss–Newton and the *CO* iterative methods should converge to nearly identical results. But in general this need not be the case. However, the Gauss–Newton method is likely to perform better than the *CO* method when the regression equation contains lagged dependent variables.

The computations using the Gauss–Newton procedure are based on the following iterative relations (also see Section [A.16](#049_BM_appendixGroupa.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1-div1-395) in Appendix A for further details):

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2764.gif)(5.56)

# 5.9 Newey–West robust variance estimator

When errors are heteroskedastic and/or autocorrelated, provided that the other standard regularity conditions of the regression model are satisfied, particularly the orthogonality condition ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2836.gif), then the *OLS* estimator of the regression parameters remains consistent and asymptotically normal. However, the standard statistical tests such as the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2837.gif) - or the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2838.gif) tests are no longer valid and inference based on them can be misleading. One possible way of dealing with this problem is to base the computation of the test statistics on the Newey and West ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-728)) robust standard errors. The Newey–West (*NW* ) heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (*HAC*) variance matrix is a direct generalization of White’s estimators described in Section [4.2](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-div1-48). The *NW* variance matrix is computed according to the following formula:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2839.gif)(5.64)

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2840.gif)(5.65)

in which

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2841.gif)

and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2842.gif) is the kernel or lag window, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2843.gif) is the ‘bandwidth’ or the ‘window size’. White’s heteroskedasticity-consistent estimators considered in Section [4.2](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-div1-48) can be computed using the Newey-West estimator by setting the window size, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2844.gif), equal to zero. In applied work the following are popular choices for the kernel:

• *Uniform (or rectangular) kernel*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2845.gif)

• *Bartlett kernel*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2846.gif)

• *Parzen kernel*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2847.gif)

In their paper, Newey and West ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-728)) adopted the Bartlett kernel. The uniform kernel is appropriate when estimating a regression model with moving average errors of known order. This type of model arises in testing the market efficiency hypothesis where the forecast horizon exceeds the sampling interval (see, e.g., Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770), Section [7.6](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-div1-81))). In other cases, a Parzen lag window may be preferable. Note that the positive semi-definiteness of the Newey-West variance matrix is only ensured in the case of the Bartlett and Parzen kernels. The choice of the uniform kernel can result in a negative-definite variance matrix, especially if a large value for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2848.gif) is chosen relative to the number of available observations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2849.gif). See the discussion in Andrews ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-33)), and Andrews and Monahan ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-37)).

The choice of the window size or bandwidth, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2850.gif), is even more critical for the properties of the *NW* estimator. The maximum lag ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2851.gif) must be determined in advance to be sufficiently large so that the correlation between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2852.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2853.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2854.gif) is essentially zero. Current practice is to use the smallest integer greater than or equal to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2855.gif), or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2856.gif). Automatic bandwidth selection procedures that asymptotically minimize estimation errors have also been proposed in the literature. See, for example, Newey and West ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-729)) and Sun, Phillips, and Jin ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-935)).

One major problem in the use of tests based on the *NW* estimator is the tendency to over-reject the null hypothesis in finite samples. This problem has been documented in several studies; see, among others, Andrews and Monahan ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-37)) and den Haan and Levin ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-284)). To deal with this issue, as discussed below, a number of authors have proposed a stochastic transformation of *OLS* estimates so that the asymptotic distribution of the transformed estimates does not depend on nuisance parameters.

# 5.10 Robust hypothesis testing in models with serially correlated/heteroskedastic errors

Kiefer, Vogelsang, and Bunzel ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-594)) proposed an alternative approach which uses a data transformation to deal with the error serial correlation problem and which does not explicitly require a *NW* type variance matrix estimator. The procedure consists of applying a nonsingular stochastic transformation to the *OLS* estimates, so that the asymptotic distribution of the transformed estimates does not depend on nuisance parameters. However, the distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2870.gif) is non-standard, although it only depends on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2871.gif), the number of regression coefficients being estimated. Critical values have been computed by simulation by Kiefer, Vogelsang, and Bunzel ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-594)). The main advantage of this approach compared with standard approaches is that estimates of the variance-covariance matrix are not explicitly required to construct the tests. Further, Kiefer, Vogelsang, and Bunzel ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-594)) show that tests constructed using their procedure can have better finite sample size properties than tests based on consistent *NW* estimates.

Kiefer and Vogelsang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-592)) showed that the above approach is exactly equivalent to using *NW* standard errors with Bartlett kernel, and without truncation (namely, setting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2872.gif) in ([5.65](#015_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-5-displayMaths-582))). This result suggests that valid tests can be constructed using kernel based estimators with bandwidth ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2873.gif).

Kiefer and Vogelsang ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-593)) studied the limiting distribution of robust tests based on the *NW* estimators setting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2874.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2875.gif) is a constant, labelling the asymptotics obtained under this framework as ‘fixed-![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2876.gif) asymptotics’. The authors showed that the limiting distribution of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2877.gif) - and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2878.gif) -statistics based on such *NW* variance estimator are non-standard, and that they depend on the choice of the kernel and on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2879.gif). Kiefer and Vogelsang ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-593)) have also analysed the properties of these test statistics *via* a simulation study. Their results indicate a trade-off between size distortions and power with regard to choice of the bandwidth. Smaller bandwidths lead to tests with higher power but at the cost of greater size distortions, whereas larger bandwidths lead to tests with smaller size distortions but lower power. They also found that, among a group of common choice kernels, the Bartlett kernel leads to tests with highest power in their fixed-![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2880.gif) framework.

Phillips, Sun, and Jin ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-842)) suggested a new class of kernel functions obtained by exponentiating a ‘mother’ kernel (such as the Bartlett or Parzen lag window), but without using lag truncation. When the exponent parameter is not too large, the absence of lag truncation influences the variability of the estimate because of the presence of autocovariances at long lags. Such effects can have the advantage of better reflecting finite sample behavior in test statistics that employ *NW* estimates, and leading to some improvement in test size, as also reported in a simulation study by Phillips, Sun, and Jin ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-842)).

While this approach works well, Kapetanios and Psaradakis ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-571)) note that it does not exploit information on the structure of the dependence in the regression errors. However, such information may be used to improve the properties of robust inference procedures. Hence, the authors suggest to employ a feasible *GLS* estimator where the stochastic process generating disturbances is approximated by an autoregessive model with an order that grows at a slower rate than the sample size (see also Amemiya ([1973](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-14)) on such approximation). Specifically, let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2881.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2882.gif) is an initial consistent estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2883.gif). One drawback of *NW* -type estimators is that they cannot be employed to obtain valid tests of the significance of *OLS* estimates when there are lagged dependent variables in the regressors, and errors are serially correlated. The problem is that these procedures require the *OLS* estimator to be consistent. However, as formally proved in Section [14.6](#027_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-14-div1-147), in general *OLS* estimators will be inconsistent when errors are autocorrelated and there are lagged values of the dependent variable among the regressors. One possible way of dealing with this problem would be to use an instrumental variables (*IV* ) approach for estimating consistently the parameters of the regression model, and then obtain *IV* -based robust tests. As an alternative, Godfrey ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-405)) suggested a joint test for misspecification and autocorrelation using the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2900.gif) -test approach by Davidson and MacKinnon ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-263)) and introduced in [Chapter 11](#022_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-11) (see Section [11.6](#022_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-11-div1-122)). The author suggested a heteroskedasticity-robust joint test of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2907.gif) restrictions ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2908.gif), in the ‘artificial’ ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-2909.gif) regression

To overcome this problem, Davidson and MacKinnon ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-263)) suggested a bootstrap implementation of the above test, using the wild bootstrap method.

# 5.11 Further reading

Further reading on multiple regression analysis under autocorrelated disturbances can be found in Wooldridge ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-983), ch. 14), and Greene ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-431), chs. 10 and 12). A brief review of the literature on robust variance estimators and robust testing can be found in the introduction of the paper by Kiefer and Vogelsang ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-593)).

# 6.1 Introduction

Dynamic economic models typically arise as a characterization of the path of the economy around its long-run equilibrium (steady state), and involve modelling expectations, learning and adjustment costs. There exist a variety of dynamic specifications used in applied time series econometrics. This chapter reviews a number of single-equation specifications suggested by econometric literature to represent dynamics in regression models. It provides a preliminary introduction to distributed lag models, autoregressive distributed lag models, partial adjustment models, error-correction models, and adaptive and rational expectations models. More general multi-equation dynamic systems will be considered in the second part of the book, where vector autoregressive models with and without weakly exogenous variables and multivariate rational expectations are discussed.

# 6.2 Distributed lag models

Most linear distributed lag models discussed in the literature belong to the class of rational distributed lag models. Early examples of this type of models include the polynomial and geometric distributed lag models. The rational distributed lag model can also be written in the form of the autoregressive distributed lag (*ARDL*) models.

# 6.8 Rational expectations models

Rational expectations (*RE*) models assume that economic agents (e.g., firms, consumers, etc.) are influenced by their expectations on the unknown, future behaviour of a variable of interest. Under the rational hypothesis (*REH*), originally advanced by Muth ([1961](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-715)), expectations are formed by mathematical expectations of variables, conditional on all the available information at the time.

# 6.9 Further reading

Further discussion on autoregressive distributed lag models can be found in Hamilton ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-465), ch. 1). A review of non-stochastic difference equations is provided in Appendix [A](#049_BM_appendixGroupa.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1), while a formal treatment of stochastic processes is given in [Chapter 12](#024_part3_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-12). More details on univariate rational expectations models are provided in Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770)) and Gouriéroux, Monfort, and Gallo ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-414)).

| [7](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7) | [Predictability of Asset Returns and the Efficient Market Hypothesis](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7) |

# 7.1 Introduction

Economists have long been fascinated by the nature and sources of variations in the stock market. By the early 1970s, a consensus had emerged among financial economists suggesting that stock prices could be well approximated by a random walk model and that changes in stock prices were basically unpredictable. Fama ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-344)) provides an early, definitive statement of this position. Historically, the ‘random walk’ theory of stock prices was preceded by theories relating movements in the financial markets to the business cycle. A prominent example is the interest shown by Keynes in the variation in stock returns over the business cycle.

The efficient market hypothesis (EMH) evolved in the 1960s from the random walk theory of asset prices advanced by Samuelson ([1965](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-880)). Samuelson showed that, in an informationally efficient market, price changes must be unforecastable. Kendall ([1953](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-585)), Cowles ([1960](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-252)), Osborne ([1959](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-743), [1962](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-744)), and many others had already provided statistical evidence on the random nature of equity price changes. Samuelson’s contribution was, however, instrumental in providing academic respectability for the hypothesis, despite the fact that the random walk model had been around for many years, having been originally discovered by Louis Bachelier, a French statistician, back in 1900.

Although a number of studies found some statistical evidence against the random walk hypothesis, these were dismissed as economically unimportant (they could not generate profitable trading rules in the presence of transaction costs) and statistically suspect (they could be due to data mining). For example, Fama ([1965](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-343)) concluded that ‘there is no evidence of important dependence from either an investment or a statistical point of view’. Despite its apparent empirical success, the random walk model was still a statistical statement and not a coherent theory of asset prices. For example, it need not hold in markets populated by risk-averse traders, even under market efficiency.

There now exist many different versions of the EMH, and one of the aims of this chapter is to provide a simple framework where alternative versions of the EMH can be articulated and discussed. We begin with an overview of the statistical properties of asset returns at different frequencies (daily, weekly, and monthly), and consider the evidence on return predictability, risk aversion, and market efficiency. We then focus on the theoretical foundation of the EMH, and show that market efficiency could co-exist with heterogeneous beliefs and individual ‘irrationality’, so long as individual errors are cross-sectionally weakly dependent in the sense defined by Chudik, Pesaran, and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-225)). But at times of market euphoria or gloom these individual errors are likely to become cross sectionally strongly dependent and the collective outcome could display significant departures from market efficiency. Market efficiency could be the norm, but most likely it will be punctuated by episodes of bubbles and crashes. To test for such episodes we argue in favour of compiling survey data on individual expectations of price changes that are combined with information on whether such expectations are compatible with market equilibrium. A trader who believes that asset prices are too high (low) might still expect further price rises (falls). Periods of bubbles and crashes could result if there are sufficiently large numbers of such traders that are prepared to act on the basis of their beliefs. The chapter also considers if periods of market inefficiency can be exploited for profit.

## 7.2.2 Multi-period returns

Single-period price changes (returns) can be used to compute multi-period price changes or returns. Denote the return over the most recent ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3294.gif) periods by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3295.gif) then (abstracting from dividends)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3296.gif)

or

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3297.gif)

and

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3298.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3299.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3300.gif) are the single-period returns. For example, weekly returns are defined by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3301.gif). Similarly, since there are 25 business days in one month, then the 1-month return can be computed as the sum of the last 25 1-day returns, or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3302.gif).

## 7.2.3 Overlapping returns

Note that multi-period returns have overlapping daily observations. In the case of weekly returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3303.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3304.gif) have the four daily returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3305.gif) in common. As a result the multi-period returns will be serially correlated even if the underlying daily returns are not serially correlated. One way of avoiding the overlap problem would be to sample the multi-period returns ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3306.gif) periods apart. But this is likely to be inefficient as it does not make use of all available observations. A more appropriate strategy would be to use the overlapping returns but allow for the fact that this will induce serial correlations. For further details see Pesaran, Pick, and Timmermann ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-785)).

A large part of financial econometrics is concerned with alternative ways of modelling the conditional mean (mean returns), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3343.gif), the conditional variance (asset return volatility), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3344.gif), and the cumulative probability distribution of the errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3345.gif). A number of issues need to be addressed in order to choose an adequate model. In particular:

– Is the distribution of returns normal?

– Is the distribution of returns constant over time?

– Are returns statistically independent over time?

– Are squares or absolute values of returns independently distributed over time?

– What are the cross correlation of returns on different instruments?

The above modelling issues can be readily extended to the case where we are concerned with a vector of asset returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3346.gif). In this case we also need to model the pair-wise conditional correlations of asset returns, namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3347.gif)

Typically the conditional variances and correlations are modelled using exponential smoothing procedures or the multivariate generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic models developed in the econometric literature. See [Chapters 18](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18) and [25](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25) for further details.

# 7.4 Empirical evidence: statistical properties of returns

[Table 7.1](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-tableGroup-6) gives a number of statistics for daily returns (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3388.gif) ) on four main equity index futures, namely S&P 500 (SP), FTSE 100 (FTSE), German DAX (DAX), and Nikkei 225 (NK), over the period 3 Jan 2010–31 Aug 2009 (for a total of 2,519 observations).[²](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-note-23)

The kurtosis coefficients are particularly large for all four equity futures and exceed the benchmark value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3389.gif) for the normal distribution. There is some evidence of positive skewness, but it is of second order importance as compared to the magnitude of excess kurtosis coefficient given by, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3390.gif). The large values of excess kurtosis are reflected in the huge values of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3391.gif) statistics reported in 7.1. Under the assumption that returns are normally distributed, we would have expected the maximum and minimum of daily returns to fall (with 99 per cent confidence) in the region of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3392.gif) 2.33![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3393.gif) S. D., which is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3394.gif) for S&P 500, as compared to the observed values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3395.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3396.gif). See also [Figure 7.1](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-figureGroup-2).

The departure from normality is particularly pronounced over the past decade where markets have been subject to two important episodes of financial crises: the collapse of markets in 2000 after the dot-com bubble and the stock market crash of 2008 after the 2007 credit crunch (see [Figure 7.2](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-figureGroup-3)).

However, the evidence of departure from normality can be seen in daily returns even before 2000. For example, over the period 3 Jan 1994–31 Dec 1999 (1565 daily observations) kurtosis coefficient of returns on S&P 500 was 9.5, which is still well above the benchmark value of 3. The recent financial crisis has accentuated the situation but cannot be viewed as the cause of the observed excess kurtosis of equity returns.

Similar results are also obtained if we consider weekly returns. The kurtosis coefficients estimated using weekly returns over the period Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009 (504 weeks) were 12.4, 15.07, 8.9, and 15.2 for S&P 500, FTSE, DAX, and Nikkei, respectively. These are somewhat lower than the estimates obtained using daily observations for S&P 500 and Nikkei, but are quite a bit higher for FTSE. For DAX daily and weekly observations yield a very similar estimate of the kurtosis coefficient.

The kurtosis coefficient of returns for currencies (measured in terms of the US dollar) varies from 4.5 for the euro to 13.8 for the Australian dollar. The estimates computed using daily observations over the period 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009 are summarized in [Table 7.2](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-tableGroup-7). The currencies considered are the British pound (GBP), euro (EU), Japanese yen (JPY), Swiss franc (CHF), Canadian dollar (CAD), and Australian dollar (AD), all measured in terms of the US dollar.

## 7.4.1 Other stylized facts about asset returns

Asset returns are typically uncorrelated over time, are difficult to predict and, as we have seen, tend to have distributions that are fat-tailed. In contrast, the absolute or squares of asset returns (that measure risk), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3417.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3418.gif), are serially correlated and tend to be predictable. It is interesting to note that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3419.gif) can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3420.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3421.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3422.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3423.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3424.gif). Since ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3425.gif) is predictable, it is, there- fore, the non-predictability of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3426.gif), or the direction of the market, which lies behind the difficulty of predicting returns.

The extent to which returns are predictable depends on the forecast horizon, the degree of market volatility, and the state of the business cycle. Predictability tends to rise during crisis periods. Similar considerations also apply to the degree of fat-tailedness of the underlying distribution and the cross-correlations of asset returns. The return distributions become less fat-tailed as the horizon is increased, and cross-correlations of asset returns become more predictable with the horizon. Cross-correlation of returns also tends to increase with market volatility. The analysis of time variations in the cross correlation of asset returns is discussed in [Chapter 25](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25).

In the case of daily returns, equity returns tend to be negatively serially correlated. During normal times they are small and only marginally significant statistically, but they become relatively large and attain a high level of statistical significance during crisis periods. These properties are illustrated in the following empirical application.

The first- and second-order serial correlation coefficients of daily returns on S&P 500 over the period 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2007 are —0.015 (0.0224) and —0.0458 (0.0224), respectively, but increase to —0.068 (0.0199) and —0.092 (0.0200) once the sample is extended to the end of August 2009, which covers the 2008 global financial crisis.[³](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-note-24) Similar patterns are also observed for other equity indices. For currencies the evidence is more mixed. In the case of major currencies such as euro and yen, there is little evidence of serial correlation in returns and this outcome does not seem much affected by whether one considers normal or crisis periods. For other currencies there is some evidence of negative serial correlation, particularly at times of crisis. For example, over the period 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009 the first-order serial correlation of daily returns on Australian dollar amounts to —0.056 (0.0199) ), but becomes statistically insignificant if we exclude the crisis period. There is also very little evidence of serial correlation in daily returns on the four major government bonds that we have been considering. This outcome does not depend on whether the crisis period is included in the sample. Irrespective of whether the underlying returns are serially correlated, their absolute values (or their squares) are highly serially correlated, often over many periods. For example, over the 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009 period the first- and second-order serial correlation coefficients of absolute return on S&P 500 are 0.2644(0.0199), 0.3644(0.0204); for euro they are 0.0483(0.0199) and 0.1125(0.0200), and for US 10Y bond they are 0.0991(0.0199) and 0.1317(0.0201). The serial correlation in absolute returns tends to decay very slowly and continues to be statistically significant event after 120 trading days (see [Figure 7.3](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-figureGroup-4)).

It is also interesting to note that there is little correlation between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3443.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3444.gif). Based on the full sample ending in August 2009, this correlation is —.0003 for S&P 500, 0.025 for euro, and 0.009 for the US 10Y bond.

## 7.4.2 Monthly stock market returns

Many of the regularities and patterns documented for returns using daily or weekly observations can also be seen in monthly observations, once a sufficiently long period is considered. For the US stock market long historical monthly data on prices and dividends are compiled by Shiller and can be downloaded from his homepage.[⁴](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-note-25) An earlier version of this data set has been analysed in Shiller ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-903)). Monthly returns on S&P 500 (inclusive of dividends) is computed as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3448.gif)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-graphic-006.gif)

**Figure 7.3** Autocorrelation function of the absolute values of returns on S&P 500 (over the period 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009).

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3449.gif) is the monthly spot price index of S&P 500 and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3450.gif) denotes the associated dividends on the S&P 500 index. Over the period 1871m1 to 2009m9 (a total of 1,664 monthly observations) the coefficient of skewness and kurtosis of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3451.gif) amounted to 1.07 and 23.5 per cents, respectively. The excess kurtosis coefficient of 20.5 is much higher than the figure of 11.3 obtained for the daily observations on SP over the period 3 Jan 2000–31 Aug 2009. Also as before the skewness coefficient is relatively small. However, the monthly returns show a much higher degree of serial correlation and a lower degree of volatility as compared to daily or weekly returns. The correlation coefficients of RSP are 0.346 (0.0245) and 0.077 (0.027), and the serial correlation coefficients continue to be statistically significant up to the lag order of 12 months. Also, the pattern of serial correlations in absolute monthly returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3457.gif), is not that different from that of the serial correlation in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3458.gif), which suggests a lower degree of return volatility (as compared with the volatility of daily or weekly returns) once the effects of mean returns are taken into account.

Similar, but less pronounced, results are obtained if we exclude the 1929 stock market crash and focus on the post-Second World War period. The coefficients of skewness and kurtosis of monthly returns over the period 1948m1 to 2009m9 (741 observations) are –0.49 and 5.2, respectively. The first- and second-order serial correlation coefficients of returns are 0.361 (0.0367) and 0.165 (0.041), respectively. The main difference between these sub-sample estimates and those obtained for the full sample is the much lower estimate for the kurtosis coefficient. But even the lower post 1948 estimates suggest a significant degree of fat-tailedness in the monthly returns.

# 7.6 Market efficiency and stock market predictability

It is often argued that if stock markets are efficient then it should not be possible to predict stock returns, namely that none of the variables in the stock market regression ([7.4](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-732)) should be statistically significant. Some writers have even gone so far as to equate stock market efficiency with the non-predictability property. But this line of argument is not satisfactory and does not help in furthering our understanding of how markets operate. The concept of market efficiency needs to be defined separately from predictability. In fact, it is easily seen that stock market returns will be non-predictable only if market efficiency is combined with risk neutrality.

There are, however, three different types of empirical evidence that shed doubt on the empirical validity of the present value model under risk neutrality.

1. The model predicts a constant price-dividend ratio for a large class of the dividend processes, two prominent examples being the linear and the geometric random walk models, ([7.10](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-746)) and ([7.14](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-752)), discussed above. For more general dividend processes the price-dividend ratio, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3546.gif) could be time varying, but it must be mean-reverting, in the sense that shocks to prices and dividends must eventually cancel out. In reality, the price-dividend ratio varies considerably over time, shows a high degree of persistent, and in general it is not possible to reject the hypothesis that the processes for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3547.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3548.gif) contain a unit root. For the Shiller data discussed in ([7.4.2](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-div2-54) the autocorrelation coefficient of the log dividend to price ratio computed over the period 1871m1 to 2009m9 is 0.994 (0.024) and falls very gradually as its order is increased and amounts to 0.879 (0.111) at the lag order 12. Formal tests of unit root hypothesis are discussed in [Chapter 15](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15).

2. We have already established that under risk neutrality excess returns must not be predictable (see equation ([7.8](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-741))). Yet there is ample evidence of excess return predictability at least in periods of high market volatility. For example, it is possible to explain 15 per cent of the variations in monthly excess returns on S&P 500 over the period 1872m2–2009m9 by running a linear regression of the excess return on a constant and its 12 lagged values—namely by a univariate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3554.gif) process. This figure rises to 19 per cent if we exclude the 1929 stock market crash and focus on the post 1948 period. See also the references cited in Section [7.7.1](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-div2-59). Formal tests of unit root hypothesis are discussed in [Chapter 15](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15).

3. To derive the geometric random walk model of asset prices, ([7.16](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-756)), from the present value model under risk neutrality, we have assumed that innovations to the dividend process are normally distributed. This implies that innovations to asset returns must also be normally distributed. But the empirical evidence discussed in Section [7.4](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-div1-79) above clearly shows that innovations to asset returns tend to be fat-tailed, and often significantly depart from normality. This anomaly between the theory and the evidence is also difficult to reconcile. Under the present value model prices will have fat-tailed innovations only if the dividends that drive asset prices are also fat-tailed. But under the geometric random walk model for dividends ([7.14](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-732)), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3555.gif) need not exist if the dividend innovations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3556.gif), are fat-tailed. One important example arises when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3557.gif) has the Student ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3558.gif) -distribution as defined by ([7.3](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-displayMaths-720)). For the derivation of the present value expression in this case we need ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3559.gif), which is the moment generating function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3560.gif) evaluated at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3561.gif). But the Student ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3562.gif) -distribution does not have a moment generating function, and hence the present value formula cannot be computed when innovations to the dividends are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3563.gif) distributed.

## 7.6.2 Risk-averse investors

In addition to the above documented empirical shortcomings, it is also important to note that risk neutrality is a behavioural assumption and need not hold even if all market information is processed efficiently by all the market participants. A more reasonable way to proceed is to allow some or all of the investors to be risk averse. In this more general case the certain pay out, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3564.gif), and the expectations of the uncertain pay out, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3565.gif), will not be the same and differ by a (possibly) time varying risk premium which could also vary with the level of the initial capital, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3566.gif). More specifically, we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3567.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3568.gif) is the premium per \$ of invested capital required (expected) by the investor. It is now easily seen that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3569.gif)

and it is no longer necessarily true that under market efficiency excess returns are non-predictable. The extent to which excess returns can be predicted will depend on the existence of a historically stable relationship between the risk premium, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3570.gif) and the macro and business cycle indicators such as changes in interest rates, dividends and various business cycle indicators.

In the context of the consumption capital asset pricing model, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3571.gif) is determined by the ex ante correlation of excess returns and changes in the marginal utility of consumption. In the case of a representative consumer with the single period utility function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3572.gif), the first-order inter-temporal optimization condition (the Euler equation) is given by

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3574.gif) denotes the consumer’s real consumption in period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3575.gif). Using the above condition it is now easily seen that[⁵](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-note-26)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3576.gif)

For a power utility function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3577.gif), we have ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3578.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3579.gif) is the coefficient of relative risk aversion. In this case ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-3580.gif) is given by
