|----------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [12](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-12) | [ Introduction to Stochastic Processes](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-12) |

# 12.1 Introduction

Any ordered series may be regarded as a time series. The temporal, immutable order imposed on the observations is the critical and distinguishing feature of time series. As a result, time series techniques cannot be generally applied to cross-section observations (such as those over different individuals, firms, countries, or regions) where they cannot be ordered in an immutable (time-invariant) fashion. The origin of modern time series analysis dates back to the pioneering work of Slutsky ([1937](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-911)) and Yule ([1926](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-993), [1927](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-994)), on the analysis of the linear combinations of purely random numbers. There are two main approaches to the analysis of time series; the *time* domain and the *spectral* (or frequency domain) approaches. Time domain techniques are prevalent in econometrics, whilst in engineering and oceanography the frequency domain approach dominates. Until 1980s, the analysis of time series has been confined to stationary processes, or processes that can be transformed to stationarity. But important developments have taken place, particularly in the area of non-stationary and nonlinear times series analysis.

# 12.2 Stationary processes

The notion of stationarity has played an important role in the theory of stochastic processes and time series analysis. Broadly speaking, a process is said to be stationary if its probability distribution remains unchanged as time progresses. This concept is relevant to stochastic processes for which the underlying data generation process is not changing over time, and is more suited to the study of natural rather than social phenomena. Khintchine ([1934](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-591)) was apparently the first to formalize the concept of stationarity for continuous-time processes, and Wold ([1938](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-981)) developed similar ideas in the context of a discrete-time stochastic process.

For a formal definition of stationarity, consider a stochastic process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6482.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6483.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6484.gif) represents time and belongs to a linear index set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6485.gif) . An index set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6486.gif) is said to be *linear* if for any ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6487.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6488.gif) belonging to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6489.gif), their sum ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6490.gif) also belongs to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6491.gif). The index set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6492.gif) could be discrete or continuous, one-sided or two-sided. Examples of index sets for a discrete-time stochastic process is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6493.gif), while for a continuous-time process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6494.gif) .

**Definition 14 (Strict stationarity of order s)** *The stochastic process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6495.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6496.gif) *is said to be strictly stationary of order* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6497.gif), *if the joint distribution functions of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6498.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6499.gif) *are identical for all values of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6500.gif), *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6501.gif), *and all positive integers* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6502.gif).

**Definition 15 (Strict stationarity)** *The stochastic process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6503.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6504.gif) *is said to be strictly stationary if it is strictly stationary of order* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6505.gif) *for any positive integer* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6506.gif).

In effect, under strict stationarity the process is in ‘stochastic equilibrium’ and realizations of the process obtained over different time intervals would be similar. This is a counterpart of the concept of static equilibrium in the theory of deterministic processes. One important implication of strict stationarity is that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6507.gif) will have the same distribution for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6508.gif). The importance of the stationarity property for empirical analysis is closely tied up with the ergodicity property which, loosely speaking, ensures consistent estimation of the unknown parameters of the process from time-averages. For a rigorous account of the ergodicity property and the conditions under which it holds see, for example, Hannan ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-467)), and Karlin and Taylor ([1975](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-574)). It is clear that if a process is strictly stationary and has second-order moments, then its mean and variance will be time invariant, namely they do not depend on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6509.gif).

Another important concept is *weak stationarity* (or, simply, stationarity).

**Definition 16 (Weak stationarity)** *A stochastic process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6510.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6511.gif) *is said to be weakly stationary if it has a constant mean and variance and its covariance function*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6512.gif) *defined by*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6513.gif)

*depends only on the absolute difference* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6514.gif), *namely* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6515.gif).

Therefore, for a weakly stationary process the covariance between any two observations depends only on the length of time separating the observations. A weakly stationary process is also referred to as ‘covariance stationary’, or ‘wide-sense stationary’. This definition is, however, too restrictive for most economic time series that are trended. A related concept which allows for deterministic trends is the *trend-stationary process*.

**Definition 17** *The process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6516.gif) *is said to be trend stationary if* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6517.gif) *is covariance stationary, where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6518.gif) *is the perfectly predictable component of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6519.gif).

Examples of purely deterministic processes include time trends, seasonal dummies and sinusoid functions, such as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6520.gif) for odd (even) value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6521.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6522.gif), or more generally ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6523.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6524.gif) is a deterministic function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6525.gif).

Finally, note that a strictly stationary process with finite second-order moments is weakly stationary, but a weakly stationary process need not be strictly stationary. It is also worth noting that it is possible for a strictly stationary process not to be weakly stationary. This happens when the strictly stationary process does not have a second-order moment.

The simplest form of a covariance (or weakly) stationary process is the ‘white noise process’.

**Definition 18** *The process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6526.gif) *is said to be a white noise process if it has mean zero, a constant variance, and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6527.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6528.gif) *are uncorrelated for all* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6529.gif).

More general stationary processes can be specified by considering linear combinations of white noise processes at different lags or leads.

# 12.5 Classical decomposition of time series

One important aim of time series analysis is to decompose a series into a number of components that can be associated with different types of temporal variations. Time series are often governed by the following four main components:

– long term *trend*

– *seasonal* component

– *cyclical* component

– *residual* component.

These four components are usually combined together using either an additive or a multiplicative model. The latter is often transformed into an additive structure using the log-transformation. Most statistical procedures are concerned with modelling of the cyclical component and usually take trend and seasonal patterns as given or specified *a priori* by the investigator. Further discussion can be found in Mills ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-691), [2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-692)).

The meaning and the importance of stationarity can be appreciated in the context of the famous decomposition theorem due to Wold ([1938](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-981)). Wold proved that any stationary process can be decomposed into the sum of a deterministic (perfectly predictable) and a purely non-deterministic (stochastic) component. More formally

**Theorem 42** (Wold’s decomposition) *Any trend-stationary process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6650.gif) *can be represented in the form of*

*where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6652.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6653.gif) *. The term* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6654.gif) *is a deterministic component, while* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6655.gif) *is a serially uncorrelated process defined by innovations in* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6656.gif)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6657.gif)

In the above decomposition, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6659.gif) is the error in the one step ahead forecast of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6660.gif), and is also known as the ‘innovation error’. Further discussion on Wold’s decomposition theorem can be found in Nerlove, Grether, and Carvalo ([1979](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-726)) and in Brockwell and Davis ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-161)).

Stationary ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6781.gif) processes have been used extensively in the time series literature. An important reference in this literature is the book by Box and Jenkins ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-141)) that contains a unified treatment of the estimation and the model selection problems associated with univariate stationary ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6782.gif) processes. Other important references are Whittle ([1963](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-977)), Rozanov ([1967](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-873)), Hannan ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-467)), Anderson ([1971](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-27)), Granger and Newbold ([1977](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-425)), Nerlove, Grether, and Carvalo ([1979](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-726)), Priestley ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-850)), Brockwell and Davis ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-161)), Hannan and Deistler ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-468)), and Harvey ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-483)). More introductory expositions can be found in Chatfield ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-205)), Hamilton ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-465)), and Davidson ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-260)).

# 12.7 Further reading

Further discussion on stationary processes can be found in Mills ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-691)), Hamilton ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-465)), Davidson ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-260)), and Chatfield ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-205)). Estimation of stationary processes is considered in [Chapter 14](#027_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-14), while the problem of forecasting is discussed in [Chapter 17](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17).

# 13.1 Introduction

Spectral analysis provides an alternative to the time domain approach to time series analysis. This approach views a stochastic process as a weighted sum of the periodic functions sin![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6837.gif) and cos![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6838.gif) with different frequencies, namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6839.gif)(13.1)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6840.gif) denotes *frequency*in the range ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6841.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6842.gif) denotes a particular realization of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6843.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6844.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6845.gif) are the weights attached to different sine and cosine waves, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6846.gif) is the window size. The above specification explicitly models ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6847.gif) as a weighted average of sine and cosine functions rather than lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6848.gif). Any covariance stationary process has both a time domain and a frequency domain representation, and any feature of the data that can be described by one representation can equally be described by the other. The frequency domain approach, or spectral analysis, is concerned with determining the importance of cycles of different frequencies for the variations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6849.gif) over time.

Since ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6991.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6992.gif) absolutely summable implies ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6993.gif), we get ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6994.gif) This shows that if the input is a stationary stochastic process, then the output process is also stationary. On the other hand, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6995.gif) shows the degree and direction of the changes in memory through the filter. If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6996.gif) the filter increases the memory of the output process, the larger the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6997.gif), the more persistent will be the output process. If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-6999.gif) the filter does not affect the memory of the output process.

# 14.1 Introduction

We start with the problem of estimating the mean and autocovariances of a stationary process and then consider the estimation of autoregressive and moving average processes as well as the estimation of spectral density functions. We also relate the analysis of this section to the standard *OLS* regression models and show that when the errors are serially correlated, the *OLS* estimators of models with lagged dependent variables are inconsistent, and derive an asymptotic expression for the bias.

# 14.2 Estimation of mean and autocovariances

We first briefly discuss the estimation of mean, autocovariances and spectral density of a stationary process.

# 14.5 Small sample bias-corrected estimators of

Although the least squares estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7378.gif), defined by (14.34), has desirable asymptotic properties, it is nevertheless biased in small samples. The bias is due to the fact that the regressors in the *AR* regressions are not strictly exogenous. For a regressor to be strictly exogenous it should be uncorrelated with past and future errors. But it is easily seen that in the case of *AR* regressions, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7379.gif) is uncorrelated with current and future values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7380.gif), but not with its past values; namely, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7381.gif) is not strictly exogenous and the standard regression assumptions do not apply to time series regressions.[⁶](#027_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-14-note-57) The fact that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7382.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7383.gif) can be easily established for the *AR*(1) model, noting that when the process is stationary

Both bias-corrected estimators work well in reducing the bias, but impact the variances of the bias-corrected estimators differently. Specification of *kernel* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7554.gif) can equivalently be described in terms of a weighting sequence ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7555.gif). One important problem is the choice of the bandwidth parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7556.gif). As a practical guide, it is often recommended to plot an estimate of the spectrum using several different bandwidths and then rely on subjective judgement to choose the bandwidth that produces the most plausible estimate. More formal statistical procedures for the choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7557.gif) have been proposed, among others, by Andrews ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-33)), and Andrews and Monahan ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-37)).

For an introductory text on the estimation of the spectrum see [Chapter 7](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7) in Chatfield ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-205)). For more advanced treatments of the subject see Priestley ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-850), Ch. 6), and Brockwell and Davis ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-161), Ch. 10).

# 15.1 Introduction

Within the class of stochastic linear processes discussed in the earlier chapters, the case where one of the roots of the autoregressive representation of the underlying process is unity plays an important role in the analysis of macroeconomic and financial data. In this chapter we compare the properties of unit root processes with the stationary processes and consider alternative ways of testing for unit roots.

# 15.2 Difference stationary processes

A process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7633.gif) is said to be difference stationary if it is not covariance stationary, but can be transformed into a covariance stationary process by first differencing. A difference stationary process is also known as an *integrated* process. The number of times one needs to difference a process, say ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7634.gif), before it is made into a stationary process is called the order of the integration of the process, and written as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7635.gif). A simple example of a difference stationary process is the random walk model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7636.gif)(15.1)

with a given (fixed or stochastic) initial value, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7637.gif). The parameter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7638.gif) is known as the ‘drift’ parameter. Solving for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7639.gif) in terms of its initial value we obtain

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7640.gif)

and it readily follows that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7641.gif)

Clearly, the random walk model is not covariance stationary, even if we set the drift term ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7642.gif) equal to zero. The coefficients of the innovations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7643.gif), are not square summable, and the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7644.gif) is trended. But it is easily seen that the first difference of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7645.gif) namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7646.gif), is covariance stationary. For this reason the random walk model is also called the first-difference stationary process. Pictorial examples of random walk models are given in [Figures 15.1](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-figureGroup-6) and [15.2](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-figureGroup-7).

# 15.3 Unit root and other related processes

A unit root process is a generalization of the random walk model, where the innovations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7648.gif), in the random walk model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7649.gif)(15.2)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7650.gif)(15.3)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7651.gif) is mean zero, serially uncorrelated process. Therefore, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7652.gif) is an integrated process of order 1, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7653.gif). Similarly, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7654.gif) is also referred to as an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7655.gif) process.

The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7656.gif) process in (15.2) is a unit root process without a drift, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7657.gif). A unit root process with a non-zero drift is defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7658.gif)(15.4)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7659.gif), is the drift parameter of the process. Under (15.4), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7660.gif) is still an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7661.gif) process, but with a drift. **Definition 24** *Let* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7698.gif) *be a sequence of random variables, and let* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7699.gif) *denote information available at date* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7700.gif) *which at least contains* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7701.gif). *If* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7702.gif), *then* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7703.gif) *is a martingale difference process with respect to* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7704.gif).

A martingale difference process is serially uncorrelated. To see this, since ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7705.gif), we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7706.gif)

But ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7707.gif), by definition. Hence, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7708.gif). Similarly, it follows that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7709.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7710.gif).

Note that the zero correlation property of martingale difference processes does not necessarily imply that the underlying processes are independently distributed. Further distributional assumptions are needed. For example, zero correlation implies independence if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7711.gif) is also assumed to be normally distributed. However, in many applications in economics and finance the normality assumption does not hold and martingale difference processes are more generally applicable.

## 15.3.3 -mixingales

The one-step ahead unpredictability property of martingale differences is often unrealistic in a time series context. A more general class of processes, known as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7713.gif) -mixingales introduced by McLeish ([1975b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-684)) and Andrews ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-32)), provide an important generalization of martingale differences to situations where the process is asymptotically unpredictable in the sense formalized in Definition 25.

**Definition 25** *Let* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7714.gif) *be a sequence of random variables with* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7715.gif), *and let* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7716.gif) *be the information set available at time* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7717.gif) *. The sequence is said to follow an* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7718.gif) *-mixingale with respect to* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7719.gif) *if we can find a sequence of deterministic constants* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7720.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7721.gif) *such that* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7722.gif) *as* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7723.gif) *and*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7724.gif)

*for all* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7725.gif), *and for all* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7726.gif).

The mixingale is said to be of size ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7727.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7728.gif), for some ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7729.gif). The size of the mixingale is a useful summary measure of the degree of its dependence. The higher the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7730.gif) the less dependent the process. A martingale difference process is a mixingale having ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7731.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7732.gif).

# 15.4 Trend-stationary versus first difference stationary processes

If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7733.gif) is trend stationary then

1. It will have a finite variance.

2. A shock will have only a *temporary* effect on the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7734.gif)

3. The spectrum of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7735.gif) exists and will be finite at *zero* frequency.

4. The expected length of time between crossings of the trend of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7736.gif) is finite.

5. The autocorrelation coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7737.gif), decrease steadily in magnitude in large enough ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7738.gif).

None of the above properties holds for a model with a unit root. In the case of the *simple* random walk process *without* a drift

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7739.gif)

we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7740.gif)

The trend and difference stationary processes have both played a very important role in the empirical analysis of economic data, with the latter being used particularly in the analysis of financial data. The importance of difference stationary processes for the analysis of economic time series was first emphasized by Nelson and Plosser ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-721)), who argued that in the case of a majority of aggregate time series such as output, employment, prices and interest rates they are best characterized by a first difference stationary process, rather than by a stationary process round a deterministic trend. The issue of whether economic time series are trend stationary or first difference stationary (also known as the ‘unit root’ problem) has been the subject of intensive research and controversy.

This follows since as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7985.gif) the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7986.gif) component dominates the augmentation part, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7987.gif) which is a stationary process, and hence its effect diminishes and can be ignored as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7988.gif). When using the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7989.gif) tests the following points are worth bearing in mind:

1. The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7990.gif) test is not very powerful in finite samples for alternatives ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7991.gif) when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7992.gif) is near unity.

2. There is a size-power trade-off depending on the order of augmentation used in dealing with the problem of residual serial correlation. Therefore, it is often crucial that an appropriate value is chosen for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7993.gif), the order of augmentation of the test.

Appropriate (asymptotic) critical values of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-7994.gif) test have been tabulated by Fuller ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-375)) and by MacKinnon ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-658)). In the following, we describe how critical values can be obtained.

Other unit root tests have been proposed in the literature. In Section [15.7](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-div1-158), we review unit root tests proposed by Phillips and Perron ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-839)), Elliott, Rothenberg, and Stock ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-325)), Park and Fuller ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-751)), and Leybourne ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-633)). We also describe a test of stationarity developed by Kwiatkowski et al. ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-612)).

## 15.7.3 The weighted symmetric tests of unit root

The Weighted Symmetric ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8106.gif) (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8107.gif) -![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8108.gif) ) has been proposed by Park and Fuller ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-751)) and analyzed further by the means of Monte Carlo simulations by Pantula, Gonzalez-Farias, and Fuller ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-750)). A detailed discussion is also provided by Fuller ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-375), Section 10.1.3).

## 15.7.5 Testing for stationarity

# 15.8 Long memory processes

Long memory processes lie somewhere between covariance stationary and unit root processes. Covariance stationary processes have absolutely summable autocovariances and fall in the class of *short memory* processes, in the sense that their autocovariances decay relatively fast. The unit root processes stand at the other extreme and, as we have seen, their autocovariances do not decay at all. But, in the case of many time series in economics and finance, the effects of a shock might not be permanent and could take a very long time to vanish. In such cases autocovariances could fail to be absolutely summable. Such covariance stationary processes whose autocovariances are not absolute summable are known as long memory processes.

As a simple example, consider the linear process

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8177.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8178.gif) is a white noise process. It is easily seen that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8179.gif) has mean zero, a finite constant variance, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8180.gif), and

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8181.gif)

But these autocovariances are not absolutely summable. This is because

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8182.gif)

since all the elements are positive and for each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8183.gif) we have ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8184.gif)

The above four definitions of long memory are not necessarily equivalent, unless further restrictions are imposed. But all point to a decay in the dependence of the series on their past which is slower than the exponential decay, but with the decay being sufficiently fast to ensure that the series have a finite variance. Under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8228.gif), the above model displays long memory, and can be used to characterise a wide range of long-term patterns. Estimation techniques for fractionally integrated processes include semi-parametric estimators of their spectral density function, such as the methods proposed by Robinson ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-865)) and Velasco ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-952)), or parametric methods based on approximation of the likelihood function (see, for example, Fox and Taqqu ([1986](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-369))). Further details of long memory processes can be found in Robinson ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-864)) and Baillie ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-66)).

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8262.gif) . It is easily seen that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8263.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8264.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8265.gif) are serially uncorrelated with zero means and finite variances. Therefore, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8266.gif) has a moving average representation with coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8267.gif) . The rate of decay of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8268.gif) over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8269.gif) depends on the distribution ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8270.gif). For example, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8271.gif) are random draws from a uniform distribution over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8272.gif) we have ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8273.gif), and the coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8274.gif) are not absolute summable, and therefore ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8275.gif) is a long memory process. Similar results follow if it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8276.gif) are draws from beta distribution with support that covers unity. Granger ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-416)) was the first to obtain this result, albeit under a more restrictive set of assumptions. Granger also showed that when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8277.gif) is type II beta distributed with parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8278.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8279.gif), the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8280.gif) -order autocovariance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8281.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8282.gif), and therefore the aggregate variable behaves as a fractionally integrated process of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8284.gif). For a generalization to multivariate models see Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) and [Chapter 32](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32).

Finally, it is important to note that the long memory property of the aggregate, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8285.gif), critically depends on whether the support of the distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8286.gif) covers unity. For example, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8287.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8288.gif), are draws from uniform distribution over the range ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8289.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8290.gif), the moving average coefficients are given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8291.gif) and we have[⁶](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-note-67)

Hence, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8293.gif) is an absolute summable sequence and the aggregate variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8294.gif), will no longer be a long memory process.

# 15.9 Further reading

See Hall and Heyde ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-460)) for further discussion and results on martingale processes, and Davidson ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-259), Ch. 16) for a general discussion of the properties of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8297.gif) -mixingales. The properties of unit root processes, as well as testing for unit root are broadly reviewed in Hamilton ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-465)). For further discussions of the time series properties of cross-section aggregates see [Chapter 32](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32) and Robinson ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-863)), Granger ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-416)), Pesaran ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-772)), Zaffaroni ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-995)), and Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)).

# 16.1 Introduction

In this chapter we consider alternative approaches proposed in the literature for the decomposition of time series into trend and cyclical components. We focus on univariate techniques, and consider Hodrick–Prescott and band-pass filters, structural time series techniques, and the Beveridge–Nelson decomposition technique specifically designed for the unit root processes. A multivariate version of the Beveridge–Nelson decomposition is considered in Section [22.15](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22-div1-246), where the role of long run economic theory in such decomposition is also discussed.

# 16.2 The Hodrick–Prescott filter

The Hodrick–Prescott (*HP*) filter is a curve fitting procedure proposed by Hodrick and Prescott ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-512)) to estimate the trend path of a series. More specifically, suppose an observed time series, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8403.gif) is composed of a trend component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8404.gif) and a cyclical component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8405.gif), as follows

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8406.gif)

Hodrick and Prescott ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-512)) suggested a way to isolate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8407.gif) from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8408.gif) by the following minimization problem

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8409.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8410.gif) is a penalty parameter. The first term in the loss function penalizes the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8411.gif), while the second term penalizes the lack of smoothness in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8412.gif), with the parameter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8413.gif) regulating the trade-off between the two sources of variations. Putting it differently, the *HP* filter identifies the cyclical component ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8414.gif) from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8415.gif) by trading-off the extent to which the trend component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8416.gif), keeps track of the original series, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8417.gif) (goodness of fit) whilst maintaining a desired degree of smoothness in the trend component. Note that as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8418.gif) approaches ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8419.gif), the trend component becomes equivalent to the original series, while as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8420.gif) diverge to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8421.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8422.gif) becomes a linear trend, since for sufficiently large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8423.gif) it is optimal to set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8424.gif), which yields, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8425.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8426.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8427.gif) are fixed constants.

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-graphic-010.gif)

**Figure 16.1** Logarithm of UK output and its Hodrick–Prescott filter using ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8433.gif).

The ‘smoothing’ parameter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8428.gif) is usually chosen by trial and error, and for quarterly observations it is set to 1,600. A discussion on the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8429.gif) for different observation frequencies can be found in Ravn and Uhlig ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-857)) and Maravall and Rio ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-669)).

Figure*[*16.2*](#029_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-16-figureGroup-9) *reports the detrended series, computed using Microfit 5.0. The HP detrending procedure in this exercise is quite sensitive to the choice of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8431.gif), *giving much more pronounced cyclical fluctuations for smaller values of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8432.gif).

For a discussion of the statistical properties of the *HP* filter, see, for example, Cogley ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-246)), Sderlind ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-919)), and Harvey and Jaeger ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-485)) who show that the use of the *HP* filter can generate spurious cyclical patterns.

# 16.3 Band-pass filter

The *HP* filter can be seen as a high-pass filter, in that it removes low frequencies and passes through only higher frequencies. In contrast, the filter advanced by Baxter and King ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-95)) is a band-pass filter, since it allows suppression of both very slow-moving (trend) components and very high-frequency (irregular) components while retaining intermediate (business-cycle) components. Baxter and King ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-95)) argue that the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) definition of a business cycle (see Burns and Mitchell ([1946](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-169))) requires a two-sided, or band-pass approach, that passes through components of the time series with periodic fluctuations, for example, between six and 32 quarters, while removing components at higher and lower frequencies.

Specifically, the band-pass filter proposed by Baxter and King takes the form of a two-sided moving average

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8435.gif)(16.1)

The weights can be derived from the inverse Fourier transform of the frequency response function (see Priestley ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-850))). Baxter and King adjust the band-pass filter with a constraint that the sum of the coefficients in (16.1) must be zero. Under this condition, the authors show that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8436.gif) can be factorized as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8437.gif)

with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8438.gif) being a symmetric moving average with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8439.gif) leads and lags. It follows that the moving average has the characteristic of rendering stationary series that contain quadratic deterministic trends.

When applied to quarterly data, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8440.gif) in the band-pass filter is usually set at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8441.gif), and as a result 24 data points (12 at the start and 12 at the end of the sample) are sacrificed, seriously limiting the usefulness of the filter for the analysis of the current state of the economy. The use of two-sided filters also creates difficulties in forecasting. To avoid some of these difficulties two-sided filters must be applied recursively, rather than to the full sample. Further details are provided in the papers by Baxter and King ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-95)) and Christiano and Fitzgerald ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-216)).

# 16.4 The structural time series approach

In macroeconomic research a crucial step is establishing some ‘stylized facts’ associated with a set of time series variables. For such facts to be useful, they should be consistent with the stochastic properties of the data and present meaningful information. However, as also pointed out by Harvey and Jaeger ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-485)), many stylized facts reported in the literature do not fulfil these criteria. Information based on mechanically detrended series can easily lead the researcher to report spurious cyclical behaviours; analysis based on *ARIMA* models can also be misleading if such models are chosen primarily on grounds of parsimony.

Structural time series models which are linear and time invariant all have a corresponding reduced form *ARIMA* representation which is equivalent in the sense that it will give identical forecasts to the structural form.[¹](#029_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-16-note-68) For example, consider the local trend model,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8442.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8443.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8444.gif) are uncorrelated white noise disturbances. Taking first differences yields

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8445.gif)

which is equivalent to an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8446.gif) process with a non-positive autocorrelation at lag one. By equating autocorrelations at lag one it is possible to derive the relationship between the moving average parameter and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8447.gif), the ratio of the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8448.gif) to that of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8449.gif) In more complex models, there may not be a simple correspondence between the structural and reduced form parameters. The key to handling structural time series models is the state space form, with the state of the system representing the various unobserved components such as trends and seasonals. See Harvey and Shephard ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-486)) for a detailed analysis of structural time series models.

# 16.5 State space models and the Kalman filter

State space models were originally developed by control engineers in aerospace-related research, and have been used extensively in time series analysis. State space models consist of two sets of linear equations that define how observable and unobservable components evolve over time. In the general state space form, the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8450.gif) -dimensional vector of observable variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8451.gif), is related to an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8452.gif) -dimensional vector of (partly) unobservable state variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8453.gif), through the measurement equation

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8454.gif)(16.2)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8455.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8456.gif) matrix and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8457.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8458.gif) -dimensional vector of serially uncorrelated disturbances with mean zero and the covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8459.gif) ; that is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8460.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8461.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8462.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8463.gif). The state variables are generated by a transition equation

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8464.gif)(16.3)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8465.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8466.gif) are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8467.gif) coefficient matrices, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8468.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8469.gif) -dimensional vector of serially uncorrelated disturbances with mean zero and the covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8470.gif), that is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8471.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8472.gif). Kalman ([1960](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-561)) showed that the calculations needed for estimating a state space model could be set out in a recursive form which has proved very convenient computationally. Since then, the so-called Kalman filter has been almost universally adopted in modern control and system theory, and has been useful in handling time series models (Harvey ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-483)), Durbin and Koopman ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-308))). The method based on the Kalman filter has many practical advantages among which are its applicability to cases where there are missing observations, measurement errors and variables which are observed at different frequencies. # 16.6 Trend-cycle decomposition of unit root processes

Recall that every trend stationary process can be decomposed into a deterministic trend and a stationary component according to Wold’s decomposition (see Section [12.5](#024_part3_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-12-div1-132)). However, this method is not applicable for non-stationary time series.

## 16.6.1 Beveridge–Nelson decomposition

Beveridge and Nelson ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-110)) proposed to decompose unit root processes into a permanent and a transitory component allowing both components to be stochastic. Consider the first difference process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8531.gif) with

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8532.gif)(16.10)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8533.gif) is a drift coefficient and the coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8534.gif) are absolutely summable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8535.gif). We can decompose the non-stationary process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8536.gif) as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8537.gif)(16.11)

with

# 17.1 Introduction

This chapter provides an introduction to the theory of forecasting and presents some applications to forecasting univariate processes. It begins with a discussion of alternative criteria of forecast optimality. It distinguishes between point and probability forecasts, one-step and multi-step ahead forecasts, conditional and *ex ante* forecasts. Using a quadratic loss function, point and probability forecasts are derived for univariate time series processes that are optimal in the mean squared forecast error sense. Also, the problem of parameter and model uncertainty in forecasting is discussed, and an overview of the techniques for forecast evaluation is provided.

# 17.2 Losses associated with point forecasts and forecast optimality

Since errors in forecasts invariably entail costs (or losses), a specification of how costly different mistakes are is needed to guide our procedure. The loss function describes in relative terms how costly any forecast error is given the outcome and possibly other observed data (Elliott and Timmermann ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-327))). The most commonly used loss function is the quadratic loss, also known as the mean squared forecast error (*MSFE*) loss.

# 17.3 Probability event forecasts

In the context of decision-making, forecasting methods are employed in order to produce better decisions. In this case, point forecasts are usually not sufficient and the full conditional probability distribution of the variables entering the decision problem is required.

As a simple example, consider a situation where there are two ‘states’ of the world, say ‘Bad’ and ‘Good’. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8783.gif) denote the forecast probability made at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8784.gif) that the Bad event will occur on day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8785.gif). Thus the forecast probability of the Good event is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8786.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8787.gif), while ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8788.gif) is an estimate of the probability of the Bad event occurring in day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8789.gif), denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8790.gif). This case of two states with predicted probabilities of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8791.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8792.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8793.gif) is the simplest possible example of forecasting a probability distribution (or *predictive distribution*). Consider the variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8794.gif) if the Bad event occurs and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8795.gif), otherwise. As an alternative to the probability forecasts, a point forecast of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8796.gif), is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8797.gif) if the Bad state is forecast to occur or otherwise ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8798.gif). In this case, the probability (event) forecast, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8799.gif), can be converted to the point forecast, using a ‘rule of thumb’ which gives ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8800.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8801.gif) exceeds some specified probability threshold, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8802.gif).

Hence, the economic forecaster has two alternative forms of forecast to announce, either ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8803.gif) which takes some value in the region ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8804.gif), and represents a probability forecast; or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8805.gif) which is an event forecast. The relationship between probability and event forecasts can also be written as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8806.gif), where the indicator function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8807.gif), is defined by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8808.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8809.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8810.gif), otherwise. For further discussion see Pesaran and Granger ([2000a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-426), [2000b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-427)). Two-states decision problems typically arise when the focus of the analysis is correct prediction of the direction of change in the variable under consideration (up, down) (see Pesaran and Timmermann ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-813)) on this, and also Section [17.12](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-div1-181) below).

More generally, let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8811.gif) be a variable of interest, and suppose that we are interested in forecasting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8812.gif) at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8813.gif), having available an information set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8814.gif). Probability event forecast refers to the probability of a particular event taking place, say the probability that the event ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8815.gif) occurs. For example, the probability of inflation (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8816.gif)) conditional on the information at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8817.gif) falling in the range ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8818.gif), or the probability of a recession defined as two successive negative growth rates (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8819.gif))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8820.gif)

or the joint probability of the inflation rate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8821.gif) falling within a target range and a positive output growth

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8822.gif)

Probability forecasts also play an important role in the Value-at-Risk (*VaR*) analysis in insurance and finance (see [Chapter 7](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7)). For example, it is often required that return on a given portfolio, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8823.gif) (or insurance claim) satisfies the following *VaR* probability constraint

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8824.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8825.gif) denotes the maximum permitted loss over the period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8826.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8827.gif).

A density forecast of the realization of a random variable at some future time is an estimate of the probability distribution of the possible future values of that variable. Thus, density forecasting is concerned with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8828.gif) for all feasible values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8829.gif), or equivalently with its probability distribution function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8830.gif) for all feasible values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8831.gif). It thus provides a complete description of the uncertainty associated with a forecast, and stands in contrast to a point forecast, which by itself contains no description of the associated uncertainty. Notice that probability forecasts can be seen as a special case of density forecasting, since we have
