This could be done with respect to a probability threshold, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8835.gif), often taken to be 1/2 in practice. In the case of the above example we have

# 17.5 Multi-step ahead forecasting

Economists are commonly asked to forecast uncertain events multiple periods ahead in time. For example, in a recession state a policy maker may want to know when the economy will recover and so is interested in forecasts of output growth for, say, horizons of 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 months. Similarly, fixed-income investors are interested in comparing forecasts of spot rates multiple periods ahead against current long-term interest rates in order to arrive at an optimal investment strategy. More formally, multi-step ahead forecasting consists of forecasting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8858.gif) based on information up to period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8859.gif), given that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8860.gif) observations ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8861.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-8862.gif), are available for model estimation. Marcellino, Stock, and Watson ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-670)) compared the performance of iterated and direct approaches by applying simulated out-of-sample methods to 170 US macroeconomic time series spanning 1959–2002. They found that iterated forecasts outperform direct forecasts, particularly if the models can select long lag specifications. Along similar lines, Pesaran, Pick, and Timmermann ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-785)) conducted a broad-based comparison of iterated and direct multi-period forecasting approaches applied to both univariate and multivariate models in the form of parsimonious factor-augmented vector autoregressions. These authors also accounted for the serial correlation in the residuals of the multi-period direct forecasting models by considering SURE-based estimation methods, and proposed modified Akaike information criteria for model selection. Using the data set studied by Marcellino, Stock, and Watson ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-670)), Pesaran, Pick, and Timmermann ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-785)) further show that information in factors helps improve forecasting performance for most types of economic variables, although it can also lead to larger biases. They also show that SURE estimation and finite-sample modifications to the Akaike information criterion can improve the performance of the direct multi-period forecasts.

# 17.8 Combining forecasts

In many cases, multiple forecasts are available for the same variable of interest. These forecasts may differ because they are based on different information sets, or because the individual models underlying each forecast are different or are subject to misspecification bias (Bates and Granger ([1969](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-93))). Forecast combination, also known as forecast pooling, refers to a procedure by which two or more individual forecasts are combined from a set of forecasts to produce a single, ‘pooled’ forecast (Elliott, Granger, and Timmermann ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-943))). Empirical literature has shown that forecast combination often produces better forecasts than methods based on individual forecasting models. Indeed, the forecast resulting from a combination of several forecasts may be more robust against misspecification bias and measurement errors in the data sets underlying individual forecasts.

Consider the problem of forecasting at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9023.gif) the future value of a target variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9024.gif), after ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9025.gif) periods, whose realization is denoted ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9026.gif). Suppose we have an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9027.gif) -dimensional vector of alternative forecasts of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9028.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9029.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9030.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9031.gif) forecast of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9032.gif) formed on the basis of information available at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9033.gif). Forecast combination consists of aggregating or pooling the forecasts so that the information in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9034.gif) components of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9035.gif) is reduced to a single combined or pooled point forecast,

These weights are typically constrained to be positive and add up to unity, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9040.gif), with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9041.gif). Other possible choices of weights involve the use of shrinking methods, which shrink the weights towards a value imposed *a priori*.

Also see Sections [17.9](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-div1-178), and Section [C.4 in Appendix C](#049_BM_appendixGroupc.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3-div1-415) on a Bayesian approach to forecast combination.

# 17.9 Sources of forecast uncertainty

Forecast uncertainty reflects the variability of possible outcomes relative to the forecast being made. Clements and Hendry ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-232)) identify five sources of uncertainties for model-based forecasts:

\- Mis-measurement of the data used for forecasting

\- Misspecification of the model (or model uncertainty, including policy uncertainty)

\- Future changes in the underlying structure of the economy

\- The cumulation of future errors, or shocks, to the economy (or future uncertainty)

\- Inaccuracies in the estimates of the parameters of a given model (or parameter uncertainty).

Measurement uncertainty and future changes in the underlying structure of the economy pose special problems of their own and will not be addressed in this chapter. We refer to Hendry and Ericsson ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-501)) for further discussion on these sources of forecast uncertainty. Model uncertainty concerns the ‘structural’ assumptions underlying a statistical model for the variable of interest. Further details on the problem of model uncertainty can be found in Draper ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-297)). Future uncertainty refers to the effects of unobserved future shocks on forecasts, while parameter uncertainty is concerned with the robustness of forecasts to the choice of parameter values, assuming a given forecasting model. In the following, we focus on future and parameter uncertainty and consider alternative ways that these types of uncertainty can be taken into account.

The standard textbook approach to taking account of future and parameter uncertainties is through the construction of forecast intervals. For the purpose of exposition, initially we abstract from parameter uncertainty and consider the following simple linear regression model

# 17.10 A decision-based forecast evaluation framework

As Whittle ([1979](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-978), p. 177) notes, ‘Prediction is not an end in itself, but only a means of optimizing current actions against the prospect of an uncertain future.’ To make better decisions we need better forecasts, and to evaluate forecasts we need to know how and by whom forecasts are used. From a user’s perspective, the criteria for forecast evaluation must depend on the decision environment.

Consider a single period decision problem faced by an individual with a globally convex cost function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9147.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9148.gif) is a state variable of relevance to the decision with the conditional probability distribution function

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9149.gif)(17.23)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9150.gif) is the decision variable to be chosen by the decision maker, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9151.gif) is the information set containing at least observations on current and past values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9152.gif). To simplify the analysis, we assume that the choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9153.gif) does not affect ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9154.gif), although clearly changes in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9155.gif) will influence the decisions. In general, the cost and the probability distribution functions, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9156.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9157.gif), also depend on a number of parameters characterizing the degree of risk aversion of the decision maker and his/her (subjective) specification of the future uncertainty characterized by the curvature of the conditional distribution function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9158.gif).

Suppose now that, at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9159.gif), a forecaster provides the decision maker with the predictive distribution ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9160.gif) being an estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9161.gif), and we are interested in computing the value of this forecast to the decision maker. Under the traditional approach, the forecasts ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9162.gif) are evaluated using statistical criteria which are based on the degree of closeness of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9163.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9164.gif) at different realizations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9165.gif). This could involve the first- or higher-order conditional moments of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9166.gif), the probability that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9167.gif) falls in a particular range, or other event forecasts of interest. However, such evaluation criteria need not be directly relevant to the decision maker. A more appropriate criterion would be the loss function that underlies the decision problem. As we shall see, such decision-based evaluation criteria simplify to the familiar *MSFE* criterion only in special cases.

Under the decision-based approach, we first need to solve for the decision variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9168.gif) based on the predictive distribution function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9169.gif). ## 17.10.1 Quadratic cost functions and the *MSFE* criteria

Only in the univariate *LQ* case can the implied evaluation criterion be cast in terms of a purely statistical criterion function.

The dependence of the evaluation criterion in the multivariate case on the parameters of the cost (or utility) function of the underlying decision model has direct bearing on the non-invariance critique of *MSFE*s to scale-preserving linear transformations discussed by Clements and Hendry ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-231)). In multivariate forecasting problems, the choice of the evaluation criterion is not as clear cut as in the univariate case even if we confine our attention to *MSFE* type criteria. One possible procedure, commonly adopted, is to use ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9223.gif), or equivalently the trace of the *MSFE* matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9224.gif). Alternatively, the determinant of the *MSFE* matrix has also been suggested. In the context of the *LQ* decision problem, both of these purely statistical criteria are inappropriate. The trace *MSFE* criterion is justified only when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9225.gif) is proportional to an identity matrix of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9226.gif).

## 17.10.2 Negative exponential utility: a finance application

The link between purely statistical and decision-based forecast evaluation criteria becomes even more tenuous for non-quadratic cost or utility functions. One important example is the negative exponential utility function often used in finance for the determination of optimal portfolio weights in asset allocation problems. Consider a risk-averse speculator with a negative exponential utility function who wishes to decide on his/her long ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9227.gif), and short positions ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9228.gif), in a given security.[⁴](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-note-80) To simplify the exposition we abstract from transaction costs. # 17.11 Test statistics of forecast accuracy based on loss differential

One possible approach to measure forecast accuracy is to consider statistics that make a comparison between competing forecasts rather than seek absolute standards of forecast accuracy. Suppose that we have two competing forecasting models, that produce the forecasts ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9258.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9259.gif), respectively. To determine which model produces better forecasts, we may test the null hypothesis

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9260.gif)(17.34)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9261.gif) is a given loss function, against the alternative

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9262.gif)(17.35)

Hence, under (17.34) the two forecast models are equally accurate on average, according to a given loss function. If the null hypothesis is rejected, one would choose the model yielding the lower loss. where

Expression (17.38) is used for the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9270.gif) because the sample of loss differentials, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9271.gif), is serially correlated for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9272.gif). Under the null of equal predictive ability, and under a set of regularity conditions, it is possible to show that as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9273.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9274.gif) Notice that this result holds for a wide class of loss functions (see McCracken and West ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-682))). A number of modifications and extensions of the above test have been suggested in the literature. West ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-962)) has extended the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9275.gif) test to deal with the case in which forecasts and forecast errors depend on estimated regression parameters. Harvey, Leybourne, and Newbold ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-487)) have proposed two modifications of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9276.gif) test. Since the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9277.gif) test could be seriously oversized for moderate numbers of samples observations,[⁸](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-note-75) the authors suggests the use of the following modified statistic

A further modification of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9279.gif) test proposed by Harvey, Leybourne, and Newbold ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-487)) is to compare the statistic with critical values from the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9280.gif) -distribution with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9281.gif) degrees of freedom, rather than the standard normal. Monte Carlo experiments provided by these authors show substantially better size properties for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9282.gif) test when compared to the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9283.gif) test in moderate samples (see also Harvey, Leybourne, and Newbold ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-488))).

The statistic (17.36) is based on unconditional expectations of forecasts and forecast errors, and therefore can be seen as a test of unconditional out-of-sample predictive ability. More recently, Giacomini and White ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-399)) (GW) have focused on a test for the null hypothesis of equal conditional predictive ability, namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9284.gif)(17.39)

Notice that, in the above expression expectations are conditional on the information set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9285.gif) available at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9286.gif), and the losses depend on the parameter estimates at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9287.gif). One important advantage of the GW test is that it captures the effect of estimation uncertainty together with model uncertainty, and can be used to study forecasts produced by general estimation methods. These advantages come at the cost of having to specify a test function, which helps to predict the loss from a forecast.

# 17.12 Directional forecast evaluation criteria

Directional evaluation criteria can be used in the context of two-state decision problems discussed in Section [17.3](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-div1-172), where the focus of the analysis is correct prediction of the direction of change in the variable under consideration (e.g., up, down). These criteria can be formulated using information from a contingency table in realizations and forecasts, like that reproduced in [Table 17.1](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-tableGroup-26). The states are denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9288.gif) taking the value of unity if the ‘Up’ state materializes and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9289.gif) otherwise.

## 17.12.4 A generalized *PT* test for serially dependent outcomes

One shortcoming of directional evaluation criteria described above is the assumption that under the null hypothesis the outcome (and the underlying data generating process) are serially independent. This assumption is clearly restrictive and unlikely to hold for many economic and financial time series. This could be due to the construction of the data—a single isolated quarter with negative GDP growth is usually not viewed as a recession, nor is the emergence of a short period with negative stock returns sufficient to constitute a bear market—or may reflect the serial dependence properties of the underlying data generating process. For example, the presence of regimes whose dynamics are determined by a Markov process as in Hamilton ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-464)) might give rise to persistence in output growth. Serial correlation in such variables is likely to generate serial dependence in the qualitative outcomes and could cause distortions in the size of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9372.gif) test, typically in the form of over-rejection of the null hypothesis.

In the context of the regression based test (17.47), the serial dependence in outcomes under the null hypothesis translates into serial dependence in the errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9373.gif). Due to the discrete nature of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9374.gif) series, the pattern of serial dependence in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9375.gif) could differ from that of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9376.gif) and additionally ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9377.gif) could be conditionally heteroskedastic even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9378.gif) is not and *vice versa*.

In testing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9379.gif) in (17.46), serial dependence in the errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9380.gif), can be dealt with either parametrically or by using Bartlett weights recommended by Newey and West ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-728)) in the construction of the test statistic. Consider the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9381.gif) -ratio

# 17.13 Tests of predictability for multi-category variables

The above approach can be extended to the case of multi-category variables, possibly serially correlated. A number of applications require generalizing the setup to allow for an arbitrary (but countably finite) number of categories. For example, in the evaluation of predictive performance when interest lies in testing whether one sequence of discrete random variables (‘outcomes’, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9394.gif) ) is predicted by another sequence of discrete random variables (‘forecasts’, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9395.gif) ). # 17.14 Evaluation of density forecasts

Statistical techniques for the evaluation of density forecasts have been advanced by Dawid ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-267)) and further elaborated by Diebold, Gunther, and Tay ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-290)) in the case of univariate predictive densities, and by Diebold, Hahn, and Tay ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-291)) and Clements and Smith ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-233)) for the evaluation of multivariate density forecasts. These techniques are based on the idea of the probability integral transform that originates in the work of Rosenblatt ([1952](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-871)). Suppose that we have the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9568.gif) consecutive pairs ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9569.gif) of the realizations and density forecasts. The probability integral transform for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9570.gif) sequence is (see Diebold, Gunther, and Tay ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-290)))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9571.gif)(17.61)

Hence, the probability integral transform ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9572.gif) is the cumulative density function corresponding to the density, evaluated at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9573.gif). Under the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9574.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9575.gif) coincide, the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9576.gif) are independent uniform ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9577.gif) random variables. Deviations from uniform ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9578.gif) will indicate that the forecasts have failed to capture some aspect of the underlying data generating process. Non uniformity may indicate improper distributional assumptions, while the presence of serial correlation in the series ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9579.gif) may indicate that the dynamics are not adequately captured by the forecast model. Hence, the statistical adequacy of the predictive distributions, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9580.gif), can be assessed by testing whether ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9581.gif) forms an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9582.gif) sequence. (see Diebold, Gunther, and Tay ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-290))). This test can be carried out using a number of familiar statistical procedures. The uniformity of the distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9583.gif) over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9584.gif) can be evaluated by adopting graphical methods, for example by visually comparing the estimated density (by simple histograms) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9585.gif). Formal tests of goodness of fit can also be employed, such as the Kolmogorov test, which measures the maximum absolute difference between the empirical distribution function and the uniform distribution. The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9586.gif) property again can be visually evaluated, by examining the correlogram of the series ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9587.gif). It is important to note that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9588.gif) uniform property is a necessary but not a sufficient condition for the optimality of the underlying predictive distribution. For example, expanding the information set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9589.gif) will lead to a different predictive distribution, but ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9590.gif) continues to satisfy the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9591.gif) uniform property.

In practice, there will be discrepancies between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9592.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9593.gif) that could be more serious for some ranges of the state variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9594.gif), and for some decisions as compared with other ranges or decisions. For example, in risk management the extreme values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9595.gif) (viewed as portfolio returns) are of interest, while in macroeconomic management values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9596.gif) (inflation or output growth) the middle of the distribution may be of concern. In general, the forecast density function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9597.gif) can at best provide an approximation to the true density and from a decision perspective its evaluation is best carried out following the approach advanced in Section [17.10](#030_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-17-div1-179). Consider the forecast distribution function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9598.gif) over the period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9599.gif) The sample counterpart of (17.25), namely

# 17.15 Further reading

# 18.1 Introduction

Volatility as a measure of uncertainty has been used extensively in the theoretical and empirical literature. But ‘volatility’ as such is not directly observable and like many other economic concepts, such as expectations, demand and supply, it is usually treated as a latent variable and measured indirectly using a number of different proxies. Initially, volatility was measured by standard deviations of price changes computed over time, typically using a rolling window. But it was realized that such an historical measure tends to underestimate sudden changes in volatility and is only suitable when the underlying volatility is relatively stable.

To allow for time variations in volatility, Engle ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-330)) developed the autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic (*ARCH*) model that relates the (unobserved) volatility to squares of past innovations in price (or output) changes. Such a model-based approach only partly overcomes the deficiency of the historical measure and continues to respond very slowly when volatility undergoes rapid changes, as has been the case during the recent financial crisis. (See, e.g., Hansen, Huang, and Shek ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-475))). The use of *ARCH*, or its various generalization (*GARCH*), in macro-econometric modelling is further complicated by the temporal aggregation of daily *GARCH* models for use in quarterly models.

In finance literature, the focus of the volatility measurement has shifted to market-based implied volatility obtained from option prices, and realized measures based on summation of intra-period higher-frequency squared returns. The use of implied volatility in macro-econo- metric modelling is limited both by availability of option price data and the fact that we still need to aggregate daily implied volatilities to a quarterly measure. By contrast, the idea of realized volatility can be easily adapted for use in macro-econometric models by summing squares of daily returns within a given quarter to construct a quarterly measure of market volatility. The approach can be extended to include intra-daily return observations when available, but this could contaminate the quarterly realized volatility measures with measurement errors of intra-daily returns due to market micro-structure and jumps in intra-daily returns. In addition, intra-daily returns are not available for all markets, and when available tend to cover a relatively short period.

# 18.2 Realized volatility

Realized volatility (*RV* ) can be computed for any given time interval. In finance, the most popular time interval is a trading day. To construct measures of daily *RV*, we need information on intra-day price movements. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9694.gif) be the price of a given asset at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9695.gif) during day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9696.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9697.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9698.gif) is the number of times that prices are measured during day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9699.gif). Then daily *RV* associated with intra-day price changes is computed as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9700.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9701.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9702.gif) is the average intra-daily price changes over the day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9703.gif). In practice, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9704.gif) is very small and is set to zero. The key issue is the appropriate number of price changes to be included in the computation of *RV* measures and the implications of large price changes (jumps) for the measurement of volatility. For further details see Andersen et al. ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-24)) and Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-89)).

The same idea can be applied to measuring quarterly *RV* based on daily price changes. In this case, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9705.gif) would refer to price changes in day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9706.gif) of quarter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9707.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9708.gif) will be the number of trading days within the quarter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9709.gif). # 18.3 Models of conditional variance

In contrast to realized volatility, which is purely data-based, (conditional) volatility is defined as conditional variance, and denoted by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9715.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9716.gif) is the variable under consideration (such as asset returns, inflation rate or output growth), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9717.gif) is the information set at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9718.gif). Volatility can arise due to a number of factors: over-reaction to news, incomplete learning, parameter variations, and abrupt switches in policy regimes. Econometric analysis of volatility usually focuses on daily, weekly or monthly observations. This chapter provides the technical details of the econometric methods that underlie models of asset return volatility.

# 18.4 Econometric approaches

Consider the regression model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9742.gif)

Under the classical normal assumptions (A1 to A5) set out in [Chapter 2](#012_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-2), the disturbances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9743.gif), in the above regression model have a constant variance both *unconditionally* and *conditionally*. However, in many applications in macroeconomics and finance, the assumption that the conditional variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9744.gif) is constant over time is not valid. One possible model capturing such variations over time is the autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (*ARCH*) model, where volatility depends on the variability of past observations. In financial econometrics, *ARCH* is a fundamental tool for analyzing the time-variation of conditional variance. The *ARCH* model was introduced into the econometric literature by Engle ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-330)), and was subsequently generalized by Bollerslev ([1986](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-131)), who proposed the generalized *ARCH* (or *GARCH*) model. Other related models where the conditional variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9745.gif) is used as one of the regressors explaining the conditional mean of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9746.gif) have also been suggested in the literature, and are known as *ARCH*-in-mean and *GARCH*-in-mean (or *GARCH-M*) models.

# 18.5 Testing for *ARCH/GARCH* effects

The simplest way to test for an *ARCH*(q) effect is to use the Lagrange multiplier test procedure proposed by Engle. The test involves two steps. In the first step, the *OLS* residuals, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9837.gif), from the regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9838.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9839.gif) are computed. In the second step, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9840.gif) is regressed on a constant and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9841.gif) of its own lagged values

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9842.gif)

A test of the *ARCH*(![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9843.gif) ) effect can now be carried out by testing the statistical significance of the slope coefficients

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9844.gif)

in the above *OLS* regression.

Several points need to be kept in mind when we use *GARCH* model:

1. *GARCH* models are not closed under cross-sectional aggregation. This means that if every individual process follows ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9858.gif), there is no guarantee that the average of those processes is also ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9859.gif).

2. *GARCH* models need restrictions on their coefficients to make sure that the variance is positive.

3. In order to price options, one needs to know how volatile the price is. To achieve this, one has to match the *GARCH* model to some diffusion process. However, *GARCH* models do not fit diffusion processes.

The unconditional variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9928.gif) in the case of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9929.gif) model does not have a simple analytical form.

The absolute ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9930.gif) model can also be estimated for different error distributions. The log-likelihood functions for the cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9931.gif) has a standard normal distribution and when it has a standardized Student ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9932.gif) -distribution are given by (18.18) and (18.19), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9933.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9934.gif) are now specified by (18.11) and (18.12), respectively.

**Example 36** (The volatility of asset returns) *In this example, we provide ML estimates of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9935.gif) *models for* 22 *main industry indices of the Standard & Poor’s* 500. *The source of our data is Datastream, which provides 24 S&P 500 industry price indices according to the Global Industry Classification Standard. To ensure a sufficiently long span of daily prices, we exclude the ‘Semiconductors & Semiconductor Equipment’ and ‘Real Estates’ from our analysis. The list of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9938.gif) *industries included in the analysis is given in Table*[*18.1*](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18-tableGroup-28)*. The data set covers the industry indices from 2 Jan. 1995 to 13 October 2003 (*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9939.gif) *observation). Daily returns are computed as* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9940.gif), *where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9941.gif) *is the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9942.gif) *price index. The realized returns* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9943.gif) *exhibit all the familiar stylized features over our sample period. They are highly cross-correlated, with an average pair-wise cross-correlation coefficient of* 0.5. *A standard factor analysis yields that the two largest estimated eigenvalues are equal to* 11.5 *and* 1.7, *with the remaining being all smaller than unity. The unconditional daily volatility differs significantly across industries and lies in range of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9947.gif) *(Food, Beverage & Tobacco) to* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9948.gif) *(Technology Hardware & Equipment). See Table*[*18.2*](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18-tableGroup-29)*. The first-order autocorrelation coefficients of the individual returns are quantitatively very small (ranging from* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9949.gif) *to* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9950.gif) *) and are statistically significant only in the case of four out of the 22 industries (Automobiles & Components, Health Care Equipment & Services, Diversified Financial, and Utilities). Estimates of univariate* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9951.gif) *models for the returns are summarized in Table*[*18.3*](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18-tableGroup-30), *and support the use of a Student t-distribution with a low degree of freedom for the conditional distribution of the asset returns. The degrees of freedom estimated for the different assets lie in the relatively narrow range of (*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-9953.gif) *) with an average estimate of* 7.3, *and a mid-point value of* 8.5.

# 18.11 Further reading

See Gardner Jr ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-379)) for a review of the research on exponential smoothing. For a useful survey of the literature on *ARCH*/*GARCH* modelling see Bollerslev, Chou, and Kroner ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-133)) and Engle, Lillien, and Robins ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-336)), while textbook treatments can be found in Hamilton ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-465)), Satchell and Knight ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-891)), Campbell, Lo, and MacKinlay ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-176)), and Engle ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-331)). Shephard ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-902)) provides selected readings of the literature on stochastic volatility. For an extension of volatility models to the multivariate case see [Chapter 25](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25).

# 19.1 Introduction

This chapter reviews techniques for the analysis of multivariate systems. It begins with a discussion of the system of regression equations both when the regressors are strictly exogenous (the so called *SURE* model) and when one or more of the regressors are endogenously determined (the classical simultaneous equation system). It provides an overview of two and three stage least squares, and iterated instrumental variables estimators for systems of equations containing endogenous variables. It then considers other statistical techniques for the analysis of multivariate systems and gives an account of principal components analysis and factor models that are useful when introducing econometric techniques for panel data with error cross-sectional dependence (see [Chapter 29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29)). We end the chapter with canonical correlation analysis and reduced rank regressions where a sub-set of matrix coefficients in a *SURE* model is assumed to be rank deficient. Such analyses form the basis of cointegration analysis that will be considered in [Chapter 22](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22).

## 19.2.4 Testing linear/nonlinear restrictions

Under fairly general conditions (for a fixed ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10249.gif) and as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10250.gif) ), the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10251.gif) estimators, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10252.gif), are asymptotically normally distributed with mean ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10177.gif) and the covariance matrix given by (19.19). It is therefore possible to test linear or nonlinear restrictions on the elements of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10254.gif) using the Wald procedure. Notice that the restrictions to be tested could involve coefficients from different equations (i.e., they could be cross-equation restrictions). ## 19.3.2 Iterated instrumental variables estimator

A special case occurs when the number of exogenous variables (or potential instruments) exceeds the number of available observations, namely, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10418.gif). # 19.4 Principal components

Principal components (*PC*) analysis is a technique for reducing the dimensionality of a data set consisting of a number of interrelated variables, whilst simultaneously preserving as much of the variation present in the data as possible. This is achieved by transforming the original variables to a fewer number of uncorrelated variables, known as the principal components, which are ordered so that the first few retain most of the variation present in all of the original variables.

Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10462.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10463.gif) be the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10464.gif) matrix of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10465.gif) observations on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10466.gif) variables, and assume that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10467.gif). The simplest and most popular procedures are the Kaiser ([1960](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-560)) criterion and the scree test. To use the Kaiser criterion the observations are standardized so that the variables have unit variances (in sample), and hence ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10543.gif) (when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10544.gif) ). According to this criterion one would then retain only factors with eigenvalues greater than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10545.gif). In effect only factors that explain as much as the equivalent of one original variable are retained.

The scree test is based on a graphical method, first proposed by Cattell ([1966](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-191)). A simple line plot of the eigenvalues is used to identify a visual break in this plot. There is no formal method for identifying the threshold, and a certain degree of personal judgement is required.

For comprehensive treatments of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10546.gif) literature see [Chapter 11](#022_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-11) of Anderson ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-28)), and Jolliffe ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-554)).

# 19.5 Common factor models

The common factor model was originally developed in the psychometric literature to measure cognitive abilities on the basis of observation on a large number of individual characteristics (Spearman ([1904](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-922)); Garnett ([1920](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-380))). Instead of directly shrinking the observations, as is done under PC analysis, the factor modelling approach reduces the number of parameters to be estimated by relating the observations to a fewer number of unobserved latent variables, known as factors. A static factor model is defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10550.gif)(19.43)

where the variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10551.gif), observed over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10552.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10553.gif), is explained in terms of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10554.gif) unobserved common factors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10555.gif). The variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10556.gif) could measure cognitive ability of type ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10557.gif) for an individual ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10558.gif), or could represent an activity variable of type ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10559.gif) measured at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10560.gif), or interest rates on bonds of different maturity ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10561.gif) observed at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10562.gif).

The factors influence the individual units through the parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10563.gif), known as factor loadings. The factors are assumed to be pervasive (or strong) in the sense that almost all units are affected by variations in the factors. To ensure that the factors are pervasive, it is typically assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10564.gif) is a positive definite matrix for any ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10565.gif) and as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10566.gif). The remainder (error) terms, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10567.gif), are assumed to be independently distributed over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10568.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10569.gif), with zero mean and variance ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10570.gif), as well as being independently distributed of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10571.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10572.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10573.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10574.gif). Such a factor model is known as the exact factor model to be distinguished from the approximate factor model where the idiosyncratic errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10575.gif), are allowed to be weakly cross-sectionally correlated. Analysis of the approximate factor model requires both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10576.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10577.gif) to be large. In a Monte Carlo exercise, Onatski ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-739)) shows that Bai and Ng ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-57)) information criteria perform rather poorly, unless ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10912.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10913.gif) are quite large. Further, the performance of these criteria deteriorates considerably as the variances of the idiosyncratic components increase, or when such components are cross-sectionally (weakly) correlated. In particular, Onatski observes an overestimation of the number of factors when the idiosyncratic errors are contemporaneously correlated. One explanation for this result is that, in this case, some linear combinations of the idiosyncratic errors may have a non-trivial effect on a sizeable portion of the data. Hence, the explanatory power of such linear combination rises and Bai and Ng ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-57)) criteria have difficulty in distinguishing these linear combinations from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-10914.gif).

Onatski ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-739)) proposes an estimator of the number of factors based on the empirical distribution of eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix. # 19.8 Further reading

A general account of principal components and canonical correlation analysis can be found in Anderson ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-28)), while textbook treatments of system estimation are available in Judge et al. ([1985](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-558)) and in Greene ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-431)).

# 20.1 Introduction

All economic and financial decisions are subject to major uncertainties. How to model uncertainty and expectations has been controversial, although since the pioneering contributions of Muth, Lucas, and Sargent, the rational expectations hypothesis (*REH*) has come to dominate economics and finance as the favoured approach to expectations formation. According to the *REH*, subjective characterization of uncertainty as conditional probability distributions will coincide (through learning) with the associated objective outcomes. The *REH* is mathematically elegant and allows model-consistent solutions, and fits nicely within the equilibrium economic theory. Almost all dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (*DSGE*) models used in macroeconomics and finance are solved under the *REH*. It is with this in mind that we devote this chapter to the solution, identification, and estimation of rational expectations models. But readers should be aware of the limitations of the *REH*, as set out in Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770)).

We begin with an overview of solution techniques, distinguishing between *RE* models with and without feedbacks from the decision (or target) variables to the state variables. We also consider models with and without lagged values of the decision variables. In the case of *RE* models with feedbacks we argue that it is best to cast the *RE* models as a closed dynamic system before solving them. We then consider identification of structural parameters of *DSGE* models and estimation of *RE* models in general.

# 20.2 Rational expectations models with future expectations

## 20.2.2 Method of undetermined coefficients

Under the above conditions the unique solution can also be obtained by the method of undetermined coefficients. # 20.6 A ‘finite-horizon’ *RE* model

One important special case occurs when economic agents face only a finite horizon. Finite-horizon *RE* models have widespread applicability in economics including, for example, the finite-lifetime life-cycle model of consumption, asset pricing models and models involving non-linear adjustment costs such as the Hayashi ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-495)) formulation of the neoclassical model of investment.

A general formulation for a model with finite and shifting planning horizon and fixed terminal point is:

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11629.gif)(20.34)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11630.gif) is defined for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11631.gif). Binder and Pesaran ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-122)) have presented efficient methods for the solution of model (20.34), and showed that this is linked to the problem of solving sparse linear equations systems with a block tridiagonal coefficients matrix structure.

See Binder and Pesaran ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-122)) and Gilli and Pauletto ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-401)).

# 20.7 Other solution methods

In this section we review a number of other methods that have been advanced in the literature for solution of *RE* models.

## 20.7.1 Blanchard and Kahn method

Early work by Blanchard and Kahn ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-125)) considers solutions for a model of the type

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11661.gif)(20.38)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11662.gif) is a vector of endogenous variables, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11663.gif) is a vector of strictly exogenous variables. Their procedure consists of partitioning ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11664.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11665.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11666.gif) vector of non-predetermined variables, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11667.gif) is a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11668.gif) vector of predetermined variables. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11840.gif)(20.55)

Solutions to the *RE* model (20.7) can thus be computed by finding the martingale difference processes, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11841.gif), that satisfy (20.55), and then solving the corresponding difference equation systems (20.53) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11842.gif) in terms of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11843.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11844.gif) . Generally there will be an infinite number of bounded solutions, and the number of martingale difference processes that can be chosen arbitrarily may be derived using the restrictions implied by (20.55). For further details see Broze, Gouriéroux, and Szafarz ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-164)).

**Remark 5** *The choice amongst the alternative solution methods depends on the nature of the RE model and the type of solution sought. For example, the undetermined coefficients method is appropriate when it is known that the solution is unique. The Blanchard and Kahn method only applies when the coefficients of the future expectations are nonsingular which could be highly restrictive in practice. The King and Watson solution strategy relaxes the restrictive nature of the Blanchard and Kahn’s approach but does not allow characterizations of all the possible solutions in the general case. The same also applies to Sims’ method. In contrast, QDE and the martingale difference methods can be used to develop all the solutions of the RE models in a transparent manner. In the case where a unique solution exists, the numerical accuracy and speed of alternative solution methods are compared by* *Anderson (*[*2008*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-25)*)*.

# 20.8 Rational expectations *DSGE* models

## 20.8.1 A general framework

Most macroeconomic *DSGE* models are constructed by linearizing an underlying nonlinear rational expectations, *RE*, model around its steady state. A typical log-linearized *RE* model can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11845.gif)(20.56)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11846.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11847.gif) vector of deviations from the steady states, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11848.gif) is a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11849.gif) vector of observed exogenous variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11850.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11851.gif) vector of unobserved variables, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11852.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11853.gif) vector of structural shocks, assumed to be serially uncorrelated with mean zero and the covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11854.gif) . For Bayesian or maximum likelihood estimation, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11855.gif) is also typically assumed to be normally distributed. The expectations ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11856.gif) are assumed to be rationally formed with respect to the information set, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11857.gif). To simplify the exposition it is assumed that both the exogenous and unobserved variables follow *VAR*(1) processes. The parameters of interest are the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11858.gif) vector of structural parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11859.gif), and the remaining (reduced form) parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11860.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11861.gif) are assumed as given. It is also assumed that there are no feedbacks from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11862.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11863.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11864.gif) To identify the structural shocks it is common in the literature to assume that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11865.gif)

If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11866.gif) is nonsingular, then (20.56) can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11867.gif)(20.57)

The solution of this model is discussed in Section [20.3](#034_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-20-div1-209), and assuming that the solution is unique it takes the form

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11868.gif)(20.58)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11869.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11870.gif) The matrices ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11871.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11872.gif) can be obtained using the method of undetermined coefficients. Notice that the coefficient matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11873.gif), for the lagged dependent variable vector is just a function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11874.gif) and does not depend on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11875.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11876.gif) .

If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11877.gif) this is just a *VAR* with exogenous variables and the likelihood function for the reduced form parameters is easily obtained. In the general case where the unobserved components of the model are serially correlated, the rational expectations solution will involve moving average components and it is more convenient to write the model as a state space model where Kalman filtering techniques can be used to evaluate the likelihood function. In such cases the reduced form parameters may not be identified.

Notice that (20.63) provides us with a likelihood function which does not depend on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11889.gif) and, therefore, the parameters that are unique to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11890.gif) (i.e., the coefficients that are specific to the forward variables) are not identified. Since what can be estimated from the data, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11891.gif) is not a function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11892.gif), all possible choices of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11893.gif) are observationally equivalent in the sense that they lead to the same observed data covariance matrix. Although the coefficients in the forward solution (20.61) are functions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11894.gif) this does not identify them because ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11895.gif) Elements of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11896.gif) could be identified by certain sorts of *a priori* restrictions, but these are likely to be rather special, rather limited in number and cannot be tested.

If the parameters of the *DSGE* model were thought to be known *a priori* from calibration, there would be no identification problem and the structural errors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11897.gif) could be recovered and used, for instance, in calculating impulse response functions, IRFs (see [Chapter 24](#038_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-24)). However, suppose someone else believed that the true model was just a set of random errors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11898.gif) with different IRFs. There is no information in the data that a proponent of the *DSGE* could use to persuade another person that the *DSGE* model was correct relative to the random error model.

The above result generalizes to higher-order *RE* models. Consider, for example, the model
