## 20.8.3 *DSGE* models with lags

In order to reproduce the dynamics that are typically observed with macroeconomic data, most empirical *DSGE* models include lagged values of endogenous or exogenous (observed or unobserved) variables. For instance Clarida, Gali, and Gertler ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-230)) assume that the errors in the IS and Phillips curve equations follow *AR*(1) processes and derive an optimal feedback policy for the interest rate based on the forecasts from these autoregressions. In this case, there is a predictable component in expected inflation because of the serial correlation in the equation errors.

Consider the special case of (20.56), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11942.gif) so that the model only contains lagged endogenous variables

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11943.gif)(20.69)

In this case the unique solution is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11944.gif)(20.70)

where, as shown in Section [20.3.1](#034_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-20-div2-192), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11945.gif) solves the quadratic matrix equation ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11946.gif). The solution is unique and stationary if all the eigenvalues of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11947.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11948.gif) lie strictly inside the unit circle. Therefore, the *RE* solution is observationally equivalent to the non-*RE* simultaneous equations model (*SEM*)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11949.gif)

where, in the case of the *SEM*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11950.gif)

Again whereas the order condition for identification of the *SEM* requires ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11951.gif) restrictions, the *RE* model requires ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11952.gif) restrictions. Not only is the *RE* model observationally equivalent to a purely backward looking *SEM*, it is observationally equivalent (in the sense of having the same reduced form), to any other model of expectations formation where in (20.69) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11953.gif) is replaced by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11954.gif). More specifically, knowing the form of the solution, (20.70), does not, on its own, provide information on the cross-equation parametric restrictions. In either case, the identifying cross-equation restrictions are lost.

Thus, in models with lags, the same problem of observational equivalence between *RE* and other models recurs. One may be able to distinguish the reduced forms of particular *RE* models from other observationally equivalent models, because the *RE* models impose particular types of cross-equation restriction on the reduced form, which arise from the nature of the rational expectations. But such restrictions are subject to the objection made by Sims ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-906)), who criticized identification by ‘incredible’ dynamic restrictions on the coefficients and lag lengths. *RE* models, which depend on restrictions on the form of the dynamics, such as *AR*(1) errors, are equally vulnerable to such objections.

# 20.9 Identification of *RE* models: a general treatment

In order to consistently estimate the parameters of a *RE* model from the time series observations, these must be identified. Therefore, identification is fundamental to the empirical analysis of structural models, and must be addressed before estimation and hypothesis testing.

Suppose that the purpose of modelling is to explain the observations ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11995.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11996.gif), on the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11997.gif) -dimensional vector of endogenous variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11998.gif) conditional on the occurrence of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-11999.gif) -dimensional exogenous variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12000.gif). The model for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12001.gif) is defined by the joint probability distribution function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12002.gif), conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12003.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12004.gif), for all admissible values of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12005.gif) -dimensional unknown parameter vector, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12006.gif) . We assume that the probability distribution function is known to the researcher except for the parameter vector, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12007.gif) . The set of admissible values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12008.gif), namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12009.gif), is known as the parameter space.

In the context of the model ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12010.gif), two parameter points ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12011.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12012.gif) are said to be observationally equivalent if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12013.gif) for all values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12014.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12015.gif). The parameter vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12016.gif) is said to be identified at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12017.gif) if and only if for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12018.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12019.gif) implies ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12020.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12021.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12022.gif). If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12023.gif) is identified for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12024.gif) then it is said that it is globally identified. Equivalently, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12025.gif) is said to be globally identified at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12026.gif), if there is no other ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12027.gif) which is observationally equivalent to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12028.gif) . It is often difficult to establish global identification. A weaker notion, known as local identification, is also used. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12029.gif) is said to be locally identified at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12030.gif) if there exists an open neighbourhood of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12031.gif) containing no other ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12032.gif) which is observationally equivalent to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12033.gif) . The identification problem consists of finding conditions on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12034.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12035.gif) that are necessary and sufficient for the identification of the parameters in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12036.gif). Rothenberg ([1971](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-872)) proved that, under some regularity conditions, local identification of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12037.gif) for a given model occurs if and only if the information matrix evaluated at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12038.gif) is nonsingular (see Sections [4.2](#014_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-4-div1-48) and [9.4](#020_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-9-div1-101) for details on Fisher’s information matrix). Rothenberg ([1971](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-872)) also provided some criteria for local identification of parameters when these satisfy a set of constraints, and when reduced form parameters help to establish the identification of structural parameters.

Early work on identification of multivariate *RE* models have been carried out by Wallis ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-958)), Pesaran ([1981b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-766)), Wegge and Feldman ([1983](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-961)), and Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770)). Most of these studies focused on models containing exogenous variables in the system, and current expectations (namely, including the term ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12039.gif) ). In particular, Wallis ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-958)) first provided sufficient conditions for global identification of a simultaneous equations system with current expectations, given in terms of rank conditions on the reduced form matrices. Pesaran ([1981b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-766)) and Wegge and Feldman ([1983](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-961)) extended this work by allowing for more general identification restrictions, and for models with lagged exogenous variables. Further, they presented a rank condition for identification of a simultaneous equations system, expressed in terms of the structural parameters, rather then of the reduced form parameters, as in Wallis ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-958)). Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770)) provided a rank condition for identification of a single equation in a system with future expectations. A central issue in the early literature was the problem of observational equivalence between two distinct models, namely, when two distinct models generate exactly the same probability distribution and likelihood function for the data (see also Sargent ([1976](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-889)) on this). Identification conditions were given by determining when the mapping from reduced-form to structural parameters is unique.

The focus of the more recent discussion on identification of *RE* models has been on closed systems with no exogenous variables. Specifically, consider the following structural *RE* model with lagged values:

## 20.9.1 Calibration and identification

During the 1990s interest in identification waned, partly because of the shift in focus to calibration, where it is assumed that the parameters are known *a priori*, perhaps from microeconometric evidence. Kydland and Prescott ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-613)) argue that the task of computational experiments of the sort they conduct is to derive the quantitative implications of the theory rather than to measure economic parameters, one of the primary objects of econometric analysis. Calibration is generally based on estimates from microeconomic studies, or cross-country estimates. As pointed out by Canova and Sala ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-182)), if the calibrated parameters do not enter in the solution of the model (and therefore do not appear in the likelihood function), then estimates of the remaining parameters will be unaffected.

Over the past ten years it has become more common to estimate, rather than calibrate, dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (*DSGE*) models, often using Bayesian techniques (see, among many others, De Jong, Ingram, and Whiteman ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-268)), Smets and Wouters ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-913)), Smets and Wouters ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-914)) and An and Schorfheide ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-20)) ). In this context, the issue of identification has attracted renewed attention. Questions have been raised about the identification of particular equations of the standard new Keynesian *DSGE* model, such as the Phillips curve (Mavroeidis ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-679)), Nason and Smith ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-718)), Kleibergen and Mavroeidis ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-601)), Dées, di Mauro, Pesaran, and Smith (2009), and others), or the Taylor rule, Cochrane ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-244)). There have also been questions about the identification of *DSGE* systems as a whole. Canova and Sala ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-182), p. 448) conclude: ‘it appears that a large class of popular *DSGE* structures are only very weakly identified’. Iskrev ([2010a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-540)), concludes ‘the results indicate that the parameters of the Smets and Wouters ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-914)) model are quite poorly identified in most of the parameter space’. Other recent papers which consider determining the identification of *DSGE* systems are Iskrev ([2010b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-541)), Iskrev and Ratto ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-542)), who provide rank and order conditions for local identification based on the spectral density matrix.

Whereas papers like Iskrev ([2010b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-541)) and Iskrev ([2010a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-540)) and Komunjer and Ng ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-605)) provide classical procedures for determining identification based on the rank of particular matrices, Koop, Pesaran, and Smith ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-609)) propose Bayesian indicators. A Bayesian approach to identification is useful both because the *DSGE* models are usually estimated by Bayesian methods and since the issues raised by identification are rather different in a Bayesian context. Given an informative choice of the prior, such that a well-behaved marginal prior exists for the parameter of interest, then there is a well-defined posterior distribution, whether or not the parameter is identified. In a Bayesian context lack of identification manifests itself in rendering the Bayesian inference sensitive to the choice of the priors even for sufficiently large sample sizes. If the parameter is not identified, one cannot learn about the parameter directly from the data and, even with an infinite sample of data, the posterior would be determined by the priors.

Within a Bayesian context, learning is interpreted as a changing posterior distribution, and a common practice in *DSGE* estimation is to judge identification by a comparison of the prior and posterior distributions for a parameter. Among many others, Smets and Wouters ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-914), p. 594) compare prior and posteriors and note that the mean of the posterior distribution is typically quite close to the mean of the prior distribution and later note that ‘It appears that the data are quite informative on the behavioral parameters, as indicated by the lower variance of the posterior distribution relative to the prior distribution.’

As we discuss, not only can the posterior distribution differ from the prior even when the parameter is unidentified, but in addition a changing posterior need not be informative about identification. This can happen because, for instance, the requirement for a determinate solution of a *DSGE* model puts restrictions on the joint parameter space, which may create dependence between identified and unidentified parameters, even if their priors are independent. What proves to be informative in a Bayesian context is the rate at which learning takes place (posterior precision increases) as more data become available.

Koop, Pesaran, and Smith ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-609)) suggest two Bayesian indicators of identification. The first, like the classical procedures, indicates non-identification while the second, which is likely to be more useful in practice, indicates either non-identification or weak identification. Like most of the literature the analysis is local in the sense that identification at a given point in the feasible parameter space is investigated. Although these indicators can be applied to any point in the parameter space, in the Bayesian context prior means seem a natural starting point. If the parameters are identified at their prior means then other points could be investigated.

The first indicator, referred to as the ‘Bayesian comparison indicator’, is based on Proposition 2 of Poirier ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-847)) and considers identification of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12063.gif) vector of parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12064.gif), assuming that the remaining ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12065.gif) vector of parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12066.gif), is identified. It compares the posterior distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12067.gif) with the posterior expectation of its prior distribution conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12068.gif), and concludes that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12069.gif) is unidentified if the two distributions coincide. This contrasts with the direct comparison of the prior of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12070.gif) with its posterior, which could differ even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12071.gif) is unidentified. Like the classical indicators based on the rank of a matrix, this Bayesian indicator provides a yes/no answer, though in practice the comparison will depend on the numerical accuracy of the MCMC procedures used to compute the posterior distributions.

The application of the Bayesian comparison indicator to *DSGE* models can be problematic, since it is often difficult to suitably partition the parameters of the model such that there exists a sub-set which is known to be identified. Furthermore, in many applications the main empirical issue of interest is not a yes/no response to an identification question, but whether a parameter of the model is weakly identified, in the sense discussed, for example, by Stock, Wright, and Yogo ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-928)), and Andrews and Cheng ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-36)), in the classical literature. Accordingly, Koop, Pesaran, and Smith ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-609)) also propose a second indicator, which they refer to as the ‘Bayesian learning rate indicator’, that examines the rate at which the posterior precision of a given parameter gets updated with the sample size, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12072.gif), using simulated data. For identified parameters the posterior precision increases at the rate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12073.gif). But for parameters that are either not identified or weakly identified the posterior precision may be updated but its rate of update will be slower than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12074.gif). Implementation of this procedure requires simulating samples of increasing size and does not require the size of the available realized data to be large. In a recent paper Caglar, Chadha, and Shibayama ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-173)) apply the learning rate indicator to examine the identification of the parameters of the Bayesian *DSGE* model of Smets and Wouters ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-914)), and find that many parameters of this widely used model do not appear to be well identified.

We shall return to Bayesian estimation of *RE* models below. But first we consider estimation of *RE* models by *ML* and *GMM* approaches.

# 20.10 Maximum likelihood estimation of *RE* models

*ML* estimation of rational expectations models can be carried out by full information or limited information methods. The goal of full information methods is to estimate the entire model by exploiting all its cross-equation restrictions. This estimation method is efficient and produces estimates for all the parameters in the model. These methods are maximum likelihood and its Bayesian counterparts. To apply these methods, the econometrician needs to specify the entire structure of the model, including the distribution of shocks. Consider the structural *RE* model defined by (20.75) which we reproduce here for convenience

It is therefore important that identification of the parameters is adequately investigated before estimation.

# 20.11 *GMM* estimation of *RE* models

The parameters of the *RE* model can also be estimated by the *GMM* method discussed in [Chapter 10](#021_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-10). The starting point of the *GMM* approach is to replace the unobserved expectations with their actual future values minus the expectational errors, in a similar way to the martingale difference solution procedure discussed in Section [20.7.4](#034_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-20-div2-201). For example, to apply the *GMM* procedure to (20.75)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12113.gif)

Also considering that the structural errors are serially uncorrelated, it follows that the composite errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12117.gif) are also uncorrelated with past observations. Hence, the *GMM* procedure can be based on the following moment conditions

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12119.gif) denotes the number of lagged variables used in the construction of the moment conditions. The choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12120.gif) is determined by the number of unknown parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12121.gif), but otherwise is arbitrary. The orthogonality condition (20.82) suggests that a consistent estimate of the parameters can be obtained by applying the IV method using ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12122.gif) (as well as current and past values of any exogenous variables present in the model) as instruments. However, the validity of the *GMM* procedure critically depends on whether the parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12123.gif) are identified. This aspect is clearly illustrated in Example 47.

See also the discussion in Pesaran (*[*1987c*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770), *Ch. 7)*.

The *GMM* method is particularly convenient for estimation of unknown parameters of the nonlinear rational expectations equations obtained as first-order conditions of intertemporal optimization problems encountered by agents and firms. However, such applications can be problematic since in practice it might not be possible to ascertain whether the underlying parameters are identifiable. Example 47 clearly illustrates the danger of indiscriminate application of *GMM* method to *RE* models. This example illustrates that prior to estimation, identification of the parameters should be checked.

A textbook treatment of *GMM* can be found in Hall ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-457)), where *GMM* inference techniques are also illustrated through some empirical examples from macroeconomics (see, in particular, Ch. 9).

# 20.12 Bayesian analysis of *RE* models

Given the difficulties associated with the *ML* and *GMM* estimation of *RE* models and recent advances in computing technology, *DSGE* models are increasingly estimated and analysed using Bayesian techniques, where prior information is used to compensate for the weak nature of identification of *DSGE* models or the flat nature of the likelihood function over important part of the parameter space.

In Bayesian analysis the likelihood function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12147.gif), given by (20.77), is combined with the prior probability distribution, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12148.gif), to obtain the posterior distribution

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12149.gif)

When the structural parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12150.gif), are identified, the posterior probability distribution, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12151.gif), will become dominated by the likelihood function and the posterior mean will converge in probability to the *ML* estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12152.gif) . In cases where one or more elements of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12153.gif) are not identified, or are only weakly identified, this convergence need not take place or might require ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12154.gif) to be very large, which is not the case in most empirical macro economic applications. In such cases the Bayesian inference could be quite sensitive to the choice of the priors and it is important that the robustness of the results to the choice of priors are investigated.

In the context of *DSGE* models, the errors are typically assumed to be Gaussian and the log-likelihood is given by (20.77), or by (20.81) if the errors are serially correlated. For the priors many specifications have been considered in the literature including improper priors, conjugate priors, Minnesota priors (Litterman ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-639), [1986](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-640)) and Doan, Litterman, and Sims ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-294))), and priors more recently proposed by Sims and Zha ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-909)) that are intended to simplify the computations of the posterior distribution in the case of structural *VAR*s. Since the *DSGE* model can be viewed as a restricted *VAR* model, the prior specification must also satisfy the *DSGE* parameter restrictions. To this end Markov chain Monte Carlo (*MCMC*) methods are employed to generate random samples for the purpose of numerical evaluation of the posterior distributions that are otherwise impossible to evaluate analytically or by standard quadrature or Monte Carlo methods. An introduction to the *MCMC* algorithm is provided in Chib ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-208)). Empirical applications of Bayesian *DSGE* models can be carried out using standard software packages such as Dynare (\<<http://www.dynare.org/>\>).

An overview of Bayesian analysis is provided in Appendix [C](#049_BM_appendixGroupc.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3).

# 20.13 Concluding remarks

In this chapter we have provided a review of how multivariate *RE* models are solved. The issues of identification and estimation of these models are also discussed briefly, distinguishing between *ML*, *GMM*, and Bayesian procedures. But it is important to recognize that, although less demanding than the perfect foresight assumption, the *REH* still requires economic agents to know or fully learn the ‘true’ conditional probability distributions of the state variables they encounter in their decision-making process. This could be a demanding requirement, particularly in applications where the source of uncertainty is behavioural or arises from strategic considerations, namely where agents need to guess about the motives and actions of others, first articulated in economics by Keynes in his famous beauty contest example (see, also Pesaran ([1987c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-770))). In such cases, other forms of expectations formation models, such as adaptive schemes, might be more appropriate.

# 20.14 Further reading

Solution techniques for multivariate rational expectations models are reviewed and discussed in Binder and Pesaran ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-119), [1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-120)). Del Negro and Schorfheide ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-282)) provide a review of the Bayesian analysis of *DSGE* models.

# 21.1 Introduction

This chapter provides an overview of vector autoregressive (*VAR*) models, with a particular focus on estimation and hypothesis testing.

# 21.2 Vector autoregressive models

The simplest multivariate system is the vector autoregressive model of order 1, also known as *VAR*(1) The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12266.gif) vector of random variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12267.gif), is said to follow a *VAR*(1) process with the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12268.gif) coefficients matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12269.gif), if

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12270.gif)

Assumption B1: ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12273.gif), for all![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12274.gif)

A straightforward generalization of the *VAR*(1) model is given by the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12280.gif) specification defined as

**Example 49** *We now consider the problem of selecting the order of a trivariate*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12435.gif)*model in the output growths of USA, Japan and Germany, estimated over the period 1964(3)-1992(4).Table*[*21.1*](#035_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-21-tableGroup-36)*reports the log-likelihood, Akaike and the Schwarz criteria, the LR and adjusted LR statistics for the seven VAR models VAR(p)*, *for*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12436.gif). *As expected, the maximized values of the log-likelihood function given under the column headed*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12437.gif)*increase with*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12438.gif). *However, the Akaike and the Schwarz criteria select the orders 1 and 0, respectively. The log-likelihood ratio statistics reject order 0, but do not reject a*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12439.gif) *of order 1. In the light of these results we choose the VAR(1) model. Note that it is quite usual for the SBC to select a lower order VAR as compared with the AIC. Having chosen the order of the VAR it is prudent to examine the residuals of individual equations for serial* *correlation. Tables* [*21.2*](#035_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-21-tableGroup-37)*to*[*21.4*](#035_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-21-tableGroup-39)*show the regression results for the US, Japan, and Germany, respectively. There is no evidence of residual serial correlation in the case of the US and Germany’s output equations, but there is statistically significant evidence of residual serial correlation in the case of Japan’s output equation. There is also important evidence of departures from normality in the case of output equations for the US and Japan. A closer examination of the residuals of these equations suggests considerable volatility during the early 1970s as a result of the abandonment of the Bretton Wood system and the quadrupling increase in oil prices. It is therefore likely that the remaining serial correlation in the residuals of Japan’s output equation may be due to these unusual events. Such a possibility can be handled by introducing a dummy variable for the oil shock in the*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12440.gif)*model.*

# 21.6 Granger causality

The concept of Granger causality is based on the idea that the cause occurs before the effect, hence if an event *X* is the cause of another event *Y*, then *X* should proceed *Y* (Granger ([1969](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-415))). More specifically, a variable *X* is said to ‘Granger-cause’ a variable *Y* if past and present values of *X* contain information that helps predict future values of *Y* better than using the information contained in past and present values of *Y* alone.

There are other notions of ‘cause’ and ‘effect’ discussed in philosophy and statistics that we shall not be considering here. But even if we confine our analysis to the causality in Granger’s sense, we need to be careful that all proximate third-party channels that influence the interactions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12471.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12472.gif) are taken into account. The most obvious case arises when there exists a third variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12473.gif) which influences both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12474.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12475.gif), but with differential time delays. As an example, suppose that changes in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12476.gif) affect ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12477.gif) before affecting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12478.gif). Then in the absence of an *a priori* knowledge of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12479.gif), it might be falsely concluded that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12480.gif) is the cause of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12481.gif). In practice, the presence ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12482.gif) (not known to the investigator) might not be an issue if the profiles of the effects of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12483.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12484.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12485.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12486.gif) are stable over time. But the situation could be very different if (for some reason unknown to the investigator) the time delays in the way ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12487.gif) affects ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12488.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12489.gif) change.

Other examples arise in situations where economic agents possess forecasting skills. Consider an individual who decides to take an umbrella when leaving home depending on whether the forecast is rain or shine. Suppose further that this individual is reasonably good at predicting the weather over the course of a day. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12490.gif) be an indicator variable that takes the value of 1 if the individual carries an umbrella and zero otherwise, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12491.gif) takes the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12492.gif) if it rains and zero otherwise. Then it is clear that a crude application of the Granger causality test to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12493.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12494.gif), can lead to the misleading conclusion that the decision to take the umbrella causes rain! However, if a third variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12495.gif), which captures the forecasting skill of the individual, is included in the analysis, we will soon learn that the correlation between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12496.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12497.gif) represents the extent to which the individual is good at forecasting the weather.

In short, we need to consider all possible variables that interact to bring about an outcome before making any definite conclusions about causality from the application of Granger non-causality tests. In what follows we discuss a useful generalization that allows for additional factors in the application of the Granger test. But the fundamental problem remains that no matter how exhaustive we are in our analysis of Granger non-causality, we still need to be aware of other possible casual links that we might have inadvertently overlooked.

As can be seen from the summary statistics, the size of the forecast errors and the in-sample residuals are very similar. A similar picture also emerges by plotting in-sample fitted values and out-of-sample forecasts* (see *Figure*[*21.1*](#035_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-21-figureGroup-11)). *It is, however, important to note that the US growth experience in 1993 may not have been a stringent enough test of the forecast performance of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12574.gif), *as the US output growth has been positive in all four quarters. A good test of forecast performance is to see whether the*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12575.gif)*model predicts the turning points of the output movements. Similarly, forecasts of output growths for Japan and Germany can also be computed. For Japan the root mean sum of squares of the forecast errors over the 1993(1)–1993(4) period turned out to be 1.48 per cent, which is slightly higher than the value of 1.02 per cent obtained for the root mean sum of squares of residuals over the estimation period. It is also worth noting that the growth forecasts for Japan miss the two negative quarterly output growths that occurred in the second and fourth quarters of 1993. A similar conclusion is also reached in the case of output growth forecasts for Germany.*

# 22.1 Introduction

In this chapter we provide an overview of the econometric methods used in long-run structural macroeconometric modelling. In what follows we first introduce the concept of cointegration for a set of time series variables. We then turn our attention to cointegration within a *VAR* framework and review the literature on identification, estimation and hypothesis testing in cointegrated systems. We discuss estimation of cointegrating relations under general linear restrictions, and review tests of the over-identifying restrictions on the cointegrating vectors. We also comment on the small sample properties of some of the test statistics discussed in the chapter, and discuss a bootstrap approach for obtaining critical values. We conclude the chapter by reviewing the multivariate version of the Beveridge-Nelson decomposition, extended to include possible restrictions on the intercepts and/or trend coefficients, as well as the existence of long-run relationships.

# 22.2 Cointegration

The concept of cointegration was first introduced by Granger ([1986](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-417)) and more formally developed in Engle and Granger ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-333)). Two or more variables are said to be cointegrated if they are individually integrated (or have a random walk component), but there exist linear combinations of them which are stationary. More formally, consider ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12662.gif) time series variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12663.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12664.gif) *known* to be non-stationary with unit roots, integrated of order one, namely (see Section [15.2](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-div1-153))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12665.gif)

The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12666.gif) vector time series ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12667.gif) is said to be cointegrated if there exists an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12668.gif) matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12669.gif) such that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12670.gif)

where the integer ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12671.gif) denotes the number of cointegrating vectors, also known as dimension of the cointegration space. Cointegration means that, although each individual series is I(1), there exist some relations linking the individual series together, represented by the linear combinations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12672.gif), which are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12673.gif). The cointegrating relations summarized in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12674.gif) vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12675.gif) are also known as *long-run relations* (Johansen ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-548))).

**Example 52** *Many examples of cointegrating relations exist in the literature. In finance, under the expectations hypothesis, interest rates of different maturities are cointegrated. In macroeconomics examples of cointegration include the purchasing power parity hypothesis, the Fisher equation (that relates nominal interest rate to the expected rate of inflation), and the uncovered interest parity. For further details see* *Garratt et al. (*[*2003b*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)*)*. *Here we derive the cointegrating relationship that exists between equity prices and dividends in a simple model where equity prices are assumed to be determined by the discounted stream of dividends that are expected to occur to the equity*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12676.gif)

*where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12677.gif) *is the information set, and assuming that* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12678.gif) *is constant over time. To model* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12679.gif) *we first need to model the dividend process,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12680.gif) *. If* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12681.gif) *is a unit root process, then* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12682.gif) *will also be a unit root process. A bilinear version of the above model is*

# 22.3 Testing for cointegration: single equation approaches

### Engle and Granger residual-based tests

Engle and Granger ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-333)) suggest a two-step method to test for cointegration. In the first step, residuals from an *OLS* regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12704.gif) on the rest of the variables, namely, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12705.gif), are computed. In the second step Dickey–Fuller and augmented Dickey–Fuller statistics are applied to these residuals, assuming no intercept and no linear trend. If the null of a unit root in the residuals is rejected, the test outcome is interpreted as evidence in favour of cointegration. Note that other standard unit root tests, such as those described in [Chapter 15](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15), can also be used in the second step.

Because unit root tests are applied to residuals from regressions that are spurious under the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12706.gif) are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12707.gif), the asymptotic distribution of the *ADF* test based on the residuals will be different from that in the standard unit root case. Hence, the associated critical values used to interpret the unit root statistic differ from those used in the standard unit root tests, employed in [Chapter 15](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15). Engle and Yoo ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-338)) provide the asymptotic distribution of *DF* and ADF statistics under the null hypothesis that the data follow a vector random walk driven by *IID* random innovations. Phillips and Ouliaris ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-838)) relax the independence assumption and compute the asymptotic null distribution of the DF tests and other residuals-based tests. Critical values for a set of residual-based statistics can be found in MacKinnon ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-659)). Since residuals from regressing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12708.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12709.gif), are not the same as residuals from regressing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12710.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12711.gif), the test can be repeated re-ordering the variables and running *OLS* regressions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12712.gif) (say) on the rest of the variables. For large enough samples, the results should not depend on such re-ordering of the variables, but in practice the situation may be very different.

Residual-based tests have a number of shortcomings. First, in small samples the test results crucially depend on the choice of the left-hand side variable in the first step. Tests for cointegration that are invariant to the ordering of variables based on the full information maximum likelihood have been proposed by Johansen ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-548)) (see Section [22.10](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22-div1-241)). Another shortcoming of residual-based tests is that they do not allow for more than one cointegrating relation. Further, these tests do not make the best use of available data, and have generally low power. We refer to Pesavento ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-827)) for a comparison of residuals-based tests under a set of local alternatives.

## 22.3.1 Bounds testing approaches to the analysis of long-run relationships

Another important difficulty with residual-based tests of cointegration lies in the fact that the investigator must know with certainty that the underlying regressors in the model are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12713.gif). However, given the generally low power of unit root tests, testing whether the underlying variables are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12714.gif) may introduce an additional degree of uncertainty into the analysis. One approach that overcomes this problem has been suggested by Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-801)), and consists of estimating an error correction form of an autoregressive distributed lag (*ARDL*) model in the variables under consideration. Suppose we are interested in testing the existence of a long-run relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12715.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12716.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12717.gif) and we are not sure whether these variables are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12718.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12719.gif). The Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-801)) approach consists of the following steps

Step 1: Estimate the error correction model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12720.gif)(22.1)

Step 2: Compute the usual Wald or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12721.gif) -statistics for testing the null hypothesis

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12722.gif)

The distribution of this test statistic is non-standard, and the relevant critical value bounds have been tabulated by Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-801)). The critical values differ depending on whether the regression equation has a trend or not.

Step 3: Compare the Wald or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12723.gif) -statistic computed in Step 2 with the upper and lower critical value bounds for a given significance level, denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12724.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12725.gif). Then:

– If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12726.gif), then reject ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12727.gif), and hence conclude that potentially there exists a long-run relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12728.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12729.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12730.gif).

– If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12731.gif), then conclude that a long-run relationship between the variables does not seem to exist.

– If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12732.gif), then the inference is inconclusive.

Hence, if the computed Wald or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12733.gif) -statistics fall outside the critical value bounds, a conclusive decision results without needing to know the order of the integration of the underlying variables. If, however, the Wald or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12734.gif) -statistics fall within these bounds, inference would be inconclusive. In such circumstances, more needs to be found out about the order of integration of the underlying variables.

It is also possible to carry out a bounds ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12735.gif) -test only on the coefficient of the lagged dependent variable, namely testing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12736.gif), against ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12737.gif) in the error correction model (22.1). Such test is also non-standard, and the appropriate critical values are tabulated in Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-801)). Once it is established that the linear relationship between the variables is not ‘spurious’ the parameters of the long-run relationship can be estimated using the *ARDL* procedure, discussed in [Chapter 6](#016_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-6) (see, in particular, Section [6.5](#016_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-6-div1-70)). Pesaran and Shin ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-797)) show that the *ARDL* approach to estimation of long-run relations continues to be applicable even if the variables under consideration are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-12738.gif) and cointegrated. They also provide Monte Carlo evidence on the comparative small sample performance of the *ARDL* and the fully modified *OLS* (*FM-OLS*) approach proposed by Phillips and Hansen ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-836)), showing that in general the former performs better than the latter. For proofs and further details see Pesaran and Shin ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-797)). In what follows we provide a brief account of the *FM-OLS* approach for completeness.

# 22.10 Testing for cointegration in *VAR* models

## 22.10.1 Maximum eigenvalue statistic

# 22.11 Long-run structural modelling

As we have seen, the estimation of the *VECM* (22.54) subject to rank restrictions on the long-run multiplier matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13234.gif), does not generally lead to a unique choice for the cointegrating relations. The identification of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13235.gif) (in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13236.gif) ) requires at least ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13237.gif) restrictions per each of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13238.gif) cointegrating relations. In the simple case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13239.gif), the one restriction needed to identify the cointegrating relation can be viewed as a ‘normalizing’ restriction which could be applied to the coefficient of any one of the integrated variables that enter the cointegrating relation, so long as it is *a priori* known that the coefficient which is being normalized is not zero. Therefore, the choice of the normalization is not innocuous and is itself based on the *a priori* identifying information that the variable associated with the coefficient being normalized belongs to the cointegrating relation. However, in the more general case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13240.gif), the number of such ‘normalizing’ restrictions is just equal to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13241.gif) which needs to be supplemented with further ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13242.gif) *a priori* restrictions; preferably obtained from a suitable long-run economic theory.

Identification schemes have been proposed by Johansen ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-548)), Phillips ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-832)), Phillips ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-834)), and Pesaran and Shin ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-798)). In what follows, we introduce a framework for identification of cointegrated systems when the cointegrating coefficients are subject to restrictions obtained from economic theory or other relevant *a priori* information. See Pesaran and Shin ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-798)) for further details.

The above testing procedure is also applicable when interest is on testing restrictions on a single cointegrating vector of a subset of cointegrating vectors. For this purpose, one simply needs to impose just-identifying restrictions on all the vectors except for the vector (s) that are to be subject to the over-identifying restrictions. See Pesaran and Shin ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-798)).

# 22.12 Small sample properties of test statistics

The distributions of the maximal eigenvalue and trace statistics ((22.61) and (22.62)) and the log-likelihood ratio tests of the over-identifying restrictions ((22.76)) are appropriate only asymptotically. Moreover, Monte Carlo results show that these asymptotic tests are valid only when *T* is reasonably large, and *m* and *p* relatively small. This suggests that in practice care should be exercised in interpreting the test statistics obtained.

In some cases, it is advisable to use bootstrapped critical values instead of the asymptotic ones. Suppose that the *VEC* model of (22.16) has been estimated subject to the just- or over-identifying restrictions suggested by economic theory. Using the observed initial values for each variable, it is possible to generate *S* new samples of data (of the same size as the original) under the hypothesis that the estimated version of (22.16) is the true data generating process. For each of the *S* replications of the data, the tests of the cointegrating rank and of the over-identifying restrictions can be carried out and, hence, distributions of the test statistics are obtained which take into account the small sample of data available when calculating the statistics. Working at the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13349.gif) per cent level of significance, critical values which take into account the small sample properties of the tests can be obtained from the simulated distribution of the bootstrapped test statistics, by ordering them and then selecting the appropriate critical value that match the desired ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13350.gif) per cent level.

More specifically, suppose that the model in (22.16) has been estimated under the exact- or over-identifying restrictions given by (22.65). We therefore have estimates of the cointegrating vectors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13351.gif), of the short-run parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13352.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13353.gif), and the elements of the covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13354.gif). Taking the *p* lagged values of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13355.gif) observed just prior to the sample as fixed, for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13356.gif) replication, we can recursively simulate the values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13357.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13358.gif), using

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13359.gif)(22.77)

The simulated errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13360.gif) can be obtained in two alternative ways, so that the contemporaneous correlations that exist across the errors in the different equations of the *VAR* model are taken into account and maintained. The first is a *parametric* method where the errors are drawn from an assumed probability distribution function. Alternatively, one could employ a *non-parametric* procedure. The latter is slightly more complicated and is based on re-sampling techniques in which the simulated errors are obtained by a random draw from the in-sample estimated residuals (e.g., Hall ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-459))).

## 22.12.1 Parametric approach

Under the parametric approach the errors are drawn, for example, from a multivariate distribution with zero means and the covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13361.gif).
