In the absence of parameter uncertainty, we obtain ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13372.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13373.gif) is the lower triangular Choleski factor of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13374.gif).

## 22.12.2 Non-parametric approach

The most obvious non-parametric approach to generating the simulated errors, which we denote ‘Method 1’, is simply to take *h* random draws with replacements from the in-sample residual vectors. The simulated errors thus obtained clearly have the same distribution and covariance structure as that observed in the original sample. However, this procedure is subject to the criticism that it could introduce dependence across the different random samples since the pseudo-random draws are made from the same set of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13375.gif) -dimensional vector of residuals. An alternative non-parametric method for generating simulated errors, ‘Method 2’, makes use of the Choleski decomposition of the estimated covariance employed in the parametric approach. For a given choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13376.gif) a set of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13377.gif) transformed error terms ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13378.gif) are computed such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13379.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13380.gif). The *mT* individual error terms are uncorrelated with each other, but retain the distributional information contained in the original observed errors. A set of *mh* simulated errors is then obtained by drawing with replacement from these transformed residuals, denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13381.gif) these are then used to obtain ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13382.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13383.gif).

Given that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13384.gif) matrix is used to generate the simulated errors, it is clear that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13385.gif) has the same covariance structure as the original estimated errors. Being based on errors drawn at random from the transformed residuals, these simulated errors will display the same distributional features. Further, given that the re-sampling occurs from the *mT* transformed error terms, Method 2 also has the advantage over Method 1 that the dependence introduced through sampling with replacement is likely to be less problematic.

The two non-parametric approaches described above have the advantage over the parametric approach in that they make no distributional assumptions on the error terms, and are better able to capture the uncertainties arising from (possibly rare) extreme observations. However, they suffer from the fact that they require random sampling with replacement, which inevitably introduces dependence across the simulated errors.

Having generated the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13386.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13387.gif) and making use of the observed ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13388.gif), it is straightforward to estimate the *VEC* of (22.16) subject to just-identifying restrictions and then subject to the over-identifying restrictions of (22.65) to obtain a sequence of log-likelihood ratio test statistics, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13389.gif) each testing the validity of the over-identifying restrictions in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13390.gif) simulated dataset, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13391.gif). These statistics can be sorted in an ascending order and the critical value associated with the desired level of significance obtained. Since the simulated data has been generated under (22.16) which incorporates the over-identifying restrictions, then the use of the simulated critical values is likely to be more appropriate than the asymptotic critical values for testing the over-identifying restrictions. Hence, for example, the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13392.gif) which exceeds 95 per cent of the observed statistics represents the appropriate 95 per cent critical value for the test of the validity of the over-identifying restrictions.

Finally, it is worth bearing in mind that the maximum likelihood estimation of the *VECM* can be time-consuming, especially if one is to be sure that all of the estimates relate to global and not local maxima of the underlying likelihood function. In practice, the choice of an optimization algorithm is likely to be important in this exercise, and the simulated annealing algorithm discussed in Goffe, Ferrier, and Rogers ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-408)) can prove useful in this respect.

# 22.13 Estimation of the short-run parameters of the *VEC* model

Having computed the *ML* estimates of the cointegrating vectors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13393.gif), obtained under the exact and/or over-identifying restrictions given by (23.28), the *ML* estimates of the short-run parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13394.gif) in (22.39) can be computed by the *OLS* regressions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13395.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13396.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13397.gif) is the *ML* estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13398.gif). Notice that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13399.gif) is super-consistent (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13400.gif)-consistent), while the *ML* estimators of the short-run parameters are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13401.gif) -consistent.

It is worth emphasizing that, having established the form of the long-run relations, then standard *OLS* regression methods and standard testing procedures can be applied. All the right-hand side variables in the error correction regression models are stationary and are the same across all the equations in the *VECM*. In these circumstances, *OLS* is the appropriate estimation procedure and diagnostic statistics for residual serial correlation, normality, heteroskedasticity and functional form misspecifications can be readily computed, based on these *OLS* regressions, in the usual manner. Further discussion of the validity of standard diagnostic test procedures when different estimation procedures are adopted in models involving unit roots and cointegrating relations is provided in Gerrard and Godfrey ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-392)). This is an important observation because it simplifies estimation and diagnostic testing procedures. Moreover, it makes clear that the modelling procedure is robust to uncertainties surrounding the order of integration of particular variables. It is often difficult to establish the order of integration of particular variables using the techniques and samples of data which are available, and it would be problematic if the modelling procedure required all the variables in the model to be integrated of a particular order. However, the observations above indicate that, so long as the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13402.gif) cointegrating relations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13403.gif) are stationary, the conditional *VEC* model, estimated and interpreted in the usual manner, will be valid even if it turns out that some or all of the variables in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13404.gif) are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13405.gif) and not ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13406.gif) after all.

# 22.14 Analysis of stability of the cointegrated system

Having estimated the system of equations in the cointegrating *VAR*, we will typically need to check on the stability of the system as a whole, and more particularly to check that the disequilibria from the cointegrating relations are in fact mean-reverting. Although such a mean-reverting property is intrinsic to the modelling framework when the cointegration restrictions are not rejected, it is possible that the estimated model does not display this property in practice or that, if it does, the speed with which the system reverts back to its equilibrium is very slow. Summary statistics that shed light on the convergence property of the error correction terms, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13407.gif), will therefore be of some interest.

In the empirical applications of cointegration analysis where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13408.gif) the rate of convergence of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13409.gif) to its equilibrium is ascertained from the signs of the estimates of the error correction coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13410.gif). # 22.15 Beveridge–Nelson decomposition in *VAR*s

The Beveridge–Nelson trend/cycle decomposition allows partitioning a vector of random variables in the sum of a stationary process, called transitory or cyclical component, and a permanent component, which may be further sub-divided into a deterministic (trend) and a stochastic part (Evans and Reichlin ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-341)), Mills ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-692)), Robertson, Garratt, and Wright ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-860)), and Garratt et al. ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-385))). In this section we consider a modification of the multivariate Beveridge–Nelson decomposition (see Beveridge and Nelson ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-110)) and Engle and Granger ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-333))), and extend it to include possible restrictions in the intercept and/or trend, as well as the existence of long-run relationships in the variables under consideration. The univariate Beveridge–Nelson decomposition is already discussed in Section 16.6.

Consider an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13464.gif) vector of random variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13465.gif), partitioned into a permanent, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13466.gif), and a cyclical component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13467.gif). # 22.17 Further reading

An excellent survey of the early developments in the literature on cointegration can be found in Banerjee et al. ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-86)), and Watson ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-960)). For more recent developments and further references to the literature on long-run structural modelling see Lütkepohl ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-652)), Pesaran and Smith ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-809)), Lütkepohl and Kratzig ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-653)), and Juselius ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-559)).

# 23.1 Introduction

This chapter generalizes the cointegration analysis of [Chapter 22](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22) and provides a brief account of the econometric issues involved in the modelling approach advanced by Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-800)). We start by describing a general ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13730.gif) model, which allows for the possibility of distinguishing between endogenous and weakly exogenous I(1) variables, and consider its efficient estimation. In this framework, we also prove that weak exogeneity is sufficient for consistent estimation of the long-run parameters of interest that enter the conditional model. We then turn our attention to the analysis of cointegrating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13731.gif) models, present cointegrating rank tests, derive their asymptotic distribution, and discuss testing the over-identifying restrictions on the cointegrating vectors. We also consider the problem of forecasting using a *VARX* model, and conclude with an empirical application to the UK economy as discussed in Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)). The methods discussed in this chapter are used to estimate country-specific modules in the *GVAR* approach outlined in [Chapter 33](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33).

In other words, one needs to take into account the possibility that changes in one variable may have an impact on the weakly exogenous variables and that these effects will continue and interact over time.

# 23.4 Testing weak exogeneity

The main assumption underlying the estimation of *VARX* models is the weak exogeneity of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-13934.gif) with respect to the long-run parameters of the conditional model. ## 23.5.3 Testing in the presence of *I*(0) weakly exogenous regressors

The (log-) likelihood ratio tests described above require that the process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14051.gif) is integrated of order one as noted below (23.11), and the weak exogeneity restriction, (23.4), is satisfied. However, many applications will include current and lagged values of weakly exogenous regressors which are integrated of order zero as explanatory variables in (23.6). In such circumstances, the above results are no longer applicable, and the limiting distributions of the (log-) likelihood ratio tests for cointegration will now depend on nuisance parameters. However, the above analysis may easily be adapted to deal with this difficulty.

Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14052.gif) denote a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14053.gif) -vector process of weakly exogenous explanatory variables which is integrated of order zero. Therefore, the partial sum vector process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14054.gif) is integrated of order one. Defining ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14055.gif) as a sub-vector of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14056.gif) with the corresponding sub-vector of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14057.gif) as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14058.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14059.gif), allows the above analysis to proceed unaltered. With these re-definitions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14060.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14061.gif) to include ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14062.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14063.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14064.gif), respectively, the partial sum ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14065.gif) will now appear in the cointegrating relations (22.53) and the lagged level term ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14066.gif) in (23.6) although economic theory may indicate its absence; that is, the corresponding ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14067.gif) block of the cointegrating matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14068.gif) is null. This constraint on the cointegrating matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14069.gif) is straightforwardly tested using a likelihood ratio statistic which will possess a limiting chi-squared distribution with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14070.gif) degrees of freedom under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14071.gif). See Rahbek and Mosconi ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-854)) for further discussion.

The asymptotic critical values for the (log-) likelihood ratio cointegration rank statistics (23.24) and (23.27) are available in Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-800)). However, as also explained in Section 22.10, these distributions are appropriate only asymptotically. When the sample is small or when the order of the *VARX* or the number of variables in the *VARX* is large, it is advisable to compute critical values by the bootstrap approach, as outlined in Section 22.12.

# 23.6 Identifying long-run relationships in a cointegrating *VARX*

Typically, the applied econometrician will be interested not only in the number of cointegrating relations that might exist among the variables but also the specification of the identifying (and possibly over-identifying) restrictions on the cointegrating relations. We have already seen that Johansen ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-547), [1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-548)) have provided procedures for estimating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14072.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14073.gif) using ‘statistical’ over-identifying restrictions. The more satisfactory approach promoted in Pesaran and Shin ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-798)) is to estimate the cointegrating relations under a general set of structural long-run restrictions provided by *a priori* economic theory. This approach, described in Section 22.11, can be employed also in the context of the *VARX* model (23.1). # 23.7 Forecasting using *VARX* models

Forecasting with a *VARX* model of the type given by (23.10) requires the specification of the processes driving the weakly exogenous variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14106.gif). Indeed, one needs to take into account the possibility of feedbacks from changes in one or more of the endogenous variables to the weakly exogenous variables, which in turn affect the current and future values of the endogenous variables. This last point is worth emphasizing and applies to any analysis involving counterfactuals such as impulse response analysis and forecasting exercises. Macro-modellers frequently consider the dynamic response of a system to a change in an exogenous variable by considering the effects of a once-and-for-all increase in that variable. This (implicitly) imposes restrictions on the processes generating the exogenous variable, assuming that there is no serial correlation in the variable and that a shock to one exogenous variable can be considered without having to take account of changes in other exogenous variables. These counter-factual exercises might be of interest. But, generally speaking, one needs to take into account the possibility that changes in one exogenous variable will have an impact on other exogenous variables and that these effects might continue and interact over time. This requires an explicit analysis of the dynamic processes driving the exogenous variables, as captured by the marginal model in (33.3). For this, we require the full-system ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14107.gif), obtained by augmenting the conditional model for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14108.gif), (23.10), with the marginal model for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14109.gif), (23.11). The combined model can be written as (See also (23.13)).

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14110.gif)(23.30)

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14111.gif)(23.31)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14114.gif) , ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14115.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14116.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14117.gif).

The above reduced form equation can now be used for forecasting or impulse response analyses. The forecasts can be evaluated in terms of their root mean squared forecast error (*RMSFE*), which constitutes a widely used loss function. See Section 17.2 for a discussion on loss functions. # 23.8 An empirical application: a long-run structural model for the UK

In this section we discuss the empirical application in Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)), and consider a small macroeconomic model for the UK economy, show how this can be cast in the form of (23.10), and provide *ML* estimation using quarterly time series data. The model comprises six domestic variables whose developments are widely regarded as essential to a basic understanding of the behaviour of the UK macroeconomy; namely, aggregate output, the ratio of domestic to foreign price level, the rate of domestic inflation, the nominal short-term interest rate, the exchange rate, and the real money balances. The model also contains foreign output, foreign short-term interest rate, and oil prices. For estimation and testing purposes, we use quarterly data over the period 1965q1–1999q4, the data set used by Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)).

The long-run relationships of the core model (adopting a log-linear approximation) take the following form

The variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14145.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14146.gif) are the domestic and foreign price indices, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14147.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14148.gif) are per-capita domestic and foreign outputs, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14149.gif) is the nominal interest rate on domestic assets held from the beginning to the end of period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14150.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14151.gif) is the nominal interest rate paid on foreign assets during period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14152.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14153.gif) is the effective exchange rate, defined as the domestic price of a unit of foreign currency at the beginning of period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14154.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14155.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14156.gif) the stock of high-powered money.

Equations (23.34), (23.35) and (23.38) describe a set of arbitrage conditions, included in many macroeconomic models in one form or another. These are the (relative) purchasing power parity ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14157.gif), the uncovered interest parity ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14158.gif), and the Fisher inflation parity ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14159.gif) relationships. Equation (23.36) is an output gap relation, while (23.37) is a long-run condition that is derived from the solvency constraints to which the economy is subject (see Garratt et al. (2003b) for details).

We have allowed for intercept and trend terms (when appropriate) in order to ensure that (long-run) reduced form disturbances, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14160.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14161.gif) have zero means.

In modelling the short-run dynamics, we follow Sims ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-906)) and others and assume that departures from the long-run relations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14166.gif) can be approximated by a linear function of a *finite* number of past changes in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14167.gif). For estimation purposes we also partition ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14168.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14169.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14170.gif) . Here, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14171.gif) is considered to be a ‘long-run forcing’ variable for the determination of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14172.gif), in the sense that changes in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14173.gif) have a direct influence on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14174.gif), but changes in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14175.gif) are not affected by the presence of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14176.gif) , which measures the extent of disequilibria in the UK economy. The treatment of oil prices as ‘long-run forcing’ represents a generalization of the approach to modelling oil price effects in some previous applications of cointegrating *VAR* analyses (e.g., Johansen and Juselius ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-552))), where the oil price change is treated as a strictly exogenous ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14177.gif) variable. The approach taken in the previous literature excludes the possibility that there might exist cointegrating relationships which involve the oil price level, while the approach taken here allows the validity of the hypothesized restriction to be tested, and for the restriction to be imposed if it is not rejected. Note that foreign output and interest rates are treated as endogenous, to allow for the possibility of feedbacks. This involves loss of efficiency in estimation if they were in fact long-run forcing or strictly exogenous.

where

However, specification of an oil price equation is required for the analysis of the short-run dynamics. We shall adopt the following general specification for the evolution of oil prices

These assumptions are weaker than the requirement of ‘Granger non-causality’ often invoked in the literature.

Assuming that the variables in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14183.gif) are difference-stationary, our modelling strategy is now to embody ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14184.gif) in an otherwise unrestricted ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14185.gif) in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14186.gif). Using equation (23.39), we now have

The above specification embodies the economic theory’s long-run predictions by construction, in contrast to the more usual approach where the starting point is an unrestricted *VAR* model, with some vague priors about the nature of the long-run relations.

Estimation of the parameters of the core model, (23.44), can be carried out using the long-run structural modelling approach described in Sections 23.3 and 23.5. With this approach, having selected the order of the underlying *VAR* model (using model selection criteria such as the Akaike information criterion ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14205.gif) or the Schwarz Bayesian criterion ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14206.gif), we test for the number of cointegrating relations among the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14207.gif) variables in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14208.gif). When performing this task, and in all subsequent empirical analyses, we work with a *VARX* model with unrestricted intercepts and restricted trend coefficients (Case IV). In terms of (23.44), we allow the intercepts to be freely estimated but restrict the trend coefficients so that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14209.gif) , where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14210.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14211.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14212.gif) vector of unknown coefficients. We then compute ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14213.gif) estimates of the model parameters subject to exact and over-identifying restrictions on the long-run coefficients. Assuming that there is empirical support for the existence of five long-run relationships, as suggested by theory, exact identification in our model requires five restrictions on each of the five cointegrating vectors (each row of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14214.gif) ), or a total of 25 restrictions on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14215.gif) . These represent only a subset of the restrictions suggested by economic theory, as characterized in **(**23.41). Estimation of the model subject to all the (exact- and over-identifying) restrictions given in **(**23.41) enables a test of the validity of the over-identifying restrictions, and hence the long-run implications of the economic theory, to be carried out.

## 23.8.1 Estimation and testing of the model

We assume our variables are I(1), and refer to Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)) for a detailed analysis of the non-stationarity properties of these variables. The first stage of our modelling sequence is to select the order of the underlying *VAR* in these variables. Here we find that a *VAR* of order two appears to be appropriate when using the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14216.gif) as the model selection criterion, but that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14217.gif) favours a *VAR* of order one. We proceed with the cointegration analysis using a *VARX*(2,2), on the grounds that the consequences of over-estimation of the order of the *VAR* is much less serious than under-estimating it (see Kilian ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-595))).

Using a *VARX*(2,2) model with unrestricted intercepts and restricted trend coefficients, and treating the oil price variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14218.gif), as weakly exogenous for the long-run parameters, we computed Johansen’s ‘trace’ and ‘maximal eigenvalue’ statistics. These statistics, together with their associated 90 per cent and 95 per cent critical values, are reported in [Table 23.1](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-tableGroup-41).

The maximal eigenvalue statistic indicates the presence of just two cointegrating relationships at the 95 per cent significance level, which does not support our *a priori* expectations of five cointegrating vectors. However, as shown by Cheung and Lai ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-207)), the maximum eigenvalue test is generally less robust to the presence of skewness and excess kurtosis in the errors than the trace test. Given that we have evidence of non-normality in the residuals of the *VAR* model used to compute the test statistics, we therefore believe it is more appropriate to base our cointegration tests on the trace statistics. As it happens, the trace statistics reject the null hypotheses that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14219.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14220.gif) at the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14221.gif) per cent level of significance but cannot reject the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14222.gif). This is in line with our *a priori* expectations based on the long-run theory discussed above. Hence we proceed under the assumption that there are five cointegrating vectors.

With five cointegrating relations we require five restrictions on each of the five relationships to exactly identify them. In view of the underlying long-run theory (see Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)) for description of the derivation of long-run, steady state relations of the UK core macroeconomic model) we impose the following 25 exact-identifying restrictions on the cointegrating matrix that corresponds to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14224.gif) . The first vector (the first row of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14225.gif) relates to the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14226.gif) relationship defined by (23.34) and is normalized on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14227.gif) ; the second relates to the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14228.gif) relationship defined by (23.35) and is normalized on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14229.gif) ; the third relates to the ‘output gap’ relationship defined by (23.36) and is normalized on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14230.gif) ;[²](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-note-124) the fourth is the money market equilibrium condition defined by (23.37) and is normalised on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14231.gif).; and the fifth is the real interest rate relationship defined by (23.38), normalised on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14232.gif)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14223.gif)(23.45)

**Table 23.1**: Cointegration rank statistics for the UK model

![Table_Image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-table-41.jpg)

Having exactly identified the long-run relations, we then test the over-identifying restrictions predicted by the long-run theory. There are 20 unrestricted parameters in (23.45), and two in (23.41), yielding a total of 18 over-identifying restrictions. In addition, working with a cointegrating *VAR* with restricted trend coefficients, there are potentially five further parameters on the trend terms in the five cointegrating relationships. The imposition of zeros on the trend coefficients in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14233.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14234.gif) or output gap relationships provides a further three over-identifying restrictions. The absence of a trend in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14235.gif) relationship is also consistent with the theory, as is the restriction that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14236.gif) (so that equation (23.37) is effectively a relationship explaining the velocity of circulation of money). These final two restrictions, together with those which are intrinsic to the theory, mean that there are just two parameters to be freely estimated in the cointegrating relationships and provide a total of 23 over-identifying restrictions on which the core model is based and with which the validity of the economic theory can be tested.

The log-likelihood ratio ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14237.gif) statistic for jointly testing the 23 over-identifying restrictions takes the value ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14238.gif). In view of the relatively large dimension of the underlying *VAR* model, the number of restrictions considered and the available sample size, we proceed to test the significance of this statistic using critical values which are computed by means of bootstrap techniques. (See Section 22.12 for a discussion of bootstrap techniques applied to cointegrating *VAR* models.) In the present application, the bootstrap exercise is based on 3,000 replications of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14239.gif) statistic testing the 23 restrictions. For each replication, an artificial data set is generated (of the same length as the original data set) on the assumption that the estimated version of the core model is the true data-generating process, using the observed initial values of each variable, the estimated model, and a set of random innovations.[³](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-note-125) The test of the over-identifying restrictions is carried out on each of the replicated data sets and the empirical distribution of the test statistic is derived across all replications. This shows that the relevant critical values for the joint tests of the 23 over-identifying restrictions are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14240.gif) at the 10 per cent significance level and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14241.gif) at the 5 per cent level. Therefore, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14242.gif) statistic of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14243.gif) is not sufficiently large to justify the rejection of the over-identifying restrictions implied by the long-run theory.

*ML* estimation of the five error correction terms yields

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14245.gif)(23.47)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14246.gif)(23.48)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14247.gif)(23.49)

The bracketed figures are asymptotic standard errors. The first equation, (23.46), describes the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14249.gif) relationship and the failure to reject this in the context of our core model provides an interesting empirical finding. Of course, there has been considerable interest in the literature examining the co-movements of exchange rates and relative prices, and the empirical evidence on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14250.gif) appears to be sensitive to the data set used and the way in which the analysis is conducted. For example, the evidence of a unit root in the real exchange rate found by Darby ([1983](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-257)) and Huizinga ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-533)) contradicts ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14251.gif) as a long-run relationship, while Grilli and Kaminsky ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-439)) and Lothian and Taylor ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-647)) have obtained evidence in favour of rejecting the unit root hypothesis in real exchange rates using longer annual series.

The second cointegrating relation, defined by (23.47), is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14252.gif) condition. This includes an intercept, which can be interpreted as the deterministic component of the risk premia associated with bonds and foreign exchange uncertainties. Its value is estimated at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14253.gif) implying a risk premium of approximately ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14254.gif) per cent per annum. The empirical support we find for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14255.gif) condition, namely that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14256.gif) is in accordance with the results obtained in the literature, and is compatible with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14257.gif), defined by (23.35). However, under the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14258.gif) hypothesis it is also required that a regression of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14259.gif) on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14260.gif) has a unit coefficient, but this is not supported by the data.

The third long-run relationship, given by (23.48), is the output gap ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14261.gif) ) relationship with per capita domestic and foreign output (measured by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) total output) levels moving in tandem in the long run. It is noteworthy that the co-trending hypothesis cannot be rejected; that is, the coefficient of the deterministic trend in the output gap equation is zero. This suggests that average long-run growth rate for the UK is the same as that in the rest of the OECD. This finding seems, in the first instance, to contradict some of the results obtained in the literature on the cointegrating properties of real output across countries. Campbell and Mankiw ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-178)), and Cogley ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-245)), for example, consider cointegration among international output series and find little evidence that outputs of different *pairs* of countries are cointegrated. However, our empirical analysis, being based on a single foreign output index, does not necessarily contradict this literature, which focuses on pair-wise cointegration of output levels. The hypothesis advanced here, that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14262.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14263.gif) are cointegrated, is much less restrictive than the hypothesis considered in the literature that *all* pairs of output variables in the OECD are cointegrated.

For the money market equilibrium ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14264.gif) ) condition, given by (23.49), we could not reject the hypothesis that the elasticity of real money balances with respect to real output is equal to unity, and therefore (23.49) in fact represents an M0 velocity equation. The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14265.gif) condition, however, contains a deterministic downward trend, representing the steady decline in the money–income ratio in the UK over most of the period 1965–99, arising primarily from the technological innovations in financial inter-mediation. There is also strong statistical evidence of a negative interest rate effect on real money balances. This long-run specification is comparable with the recent research on the determinants of the UK narrow money velocity reported in, for example, Breedon and Fisher ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-144)).

Finally, the fifth equation, (23.50), defines the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14266.gif) relationship, where the estimated constant implies an annual real rate of return of approximately ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14267.gif) per cent. While the presence of this relationship might appear relatively non-contentious, there is empirical work in which the relationship appears not to hold; see, for example MacDonald and Murphy ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-656)) and Mishkin ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-693)). The results support the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14268.gif) relationship and again highlight the important role played by the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14269.gif) relationship in a model of the macroeconomy which can incorporate interactions between variables omitted from more partial analyses.

The estimates of the long-run relations and short-run dynamics of the model are provided in [Table 23.2](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-tableGroup-42). The estimates of the error correction coefficients (also known as the loading coefficients) show that the long-run relations make an important contribution in most equations and that the error correction terms provide for a complex and statistically significant set of interactions and feedbacks across commodity, money and foreign exchange markets. The results in [Table 23.2](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-tableGroup-42) also show that the core model fits the data well and has satisfactory diagnostic statistics.

# 24.1 Introduction

We first introduce impulse response analysis and forecast error variance decomposition for unrestricted *VAR* models, and discuss the orthogonalized and generalized impulse response functions. We then consider the identification problem of short-run effects in a structural *VAR* model. We review Sims’ approach, and then investigate the identification problem of a structural model when one or more of the structural shocks have permanent effects.

# 24.2 Impulse response analysis

An impulse response function measures the time profile of the effect of shocks at a given point in time on the (expected) future values of the variables. The best way to think of an impulse response function is to view it as the outcome of a *conceptual* experiment, whereby interest is on the effect of shock(s) hitting the economy at time *t* on the future state of the economy at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14505.gif), given the history of the economy, and the types of shocks that are likely to hit the economy in the future (at the interim times ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14506.gif) ).

The main issues are:

1. What types of shocks hit the system at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14507.gif) ?

2. What was the state of the system at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14508.gif), before the shocks hit?

3. What types of shocks are expected to hit the system from time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14509.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14510.gif) ?

# 24.5 Generalized impulse response function (*GIRF*)

The main idea behind the generalized *IR* function is to circumvent the problem of the dependence of the orthogonalized impulse responses to the ordering of the variables in the *VAR*. The concept of the generalized impulse response function, advanced in Koop, Pesaran, and Potter ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-608)) was originally intended to deal with the problem of impulse response analysis in the case of nonlinear dynamic systems, but it can also be readily applied to multivariate time series models such as *VAR*.

The generalized *IR* analysis deals explicitly with three main issues that arise in impulse response analysis:

1. How was the dynamical system hit by shocks at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14624.gif) ? Was it hit by a variable-specific shock or system-wide shocks?

2. What was the state of the system at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14625.gif), before the system was hit by shocks? Was the trajectory of the system in an upward or in a downward phase?

3. How would one expect the system to be shocked in the future, namely over the interim period from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14626.gif), to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14627.gif) ?

In the context of the *VAR* model, the *GIRF* for a *system-wide shock*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14628.gif), is defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14629.gif)(24.11)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14630.gif) is the conditional mathematical expectation taken with respect to the *VAR* model, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14631.gif) is a particular historical realization of the process at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14632.gif). In the case of the *VAR* model having the infinite moving average representation (24.3) we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14633.gif)(24.12)

which is independent of the ‘history’ of the process. This history invariance property of the impulse response function (also shared by the traditional methods of impulse response analysis) is, however, specific to linear systems and does not carry over to nonlinear dynamic models.

In practice, the choice of the vector of shocks, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14634.gif), is arbitrary; one possibility would be to consider a large number of likely shocks and then examine the empirical distribution function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14635.gif) for all these shocks. # 24.7 Forecast error variance decompositions

The forecast error variance decomposition provides a decomposition of the variance of the forecast errors of the variables in the *VAR* at different horizons.

## 24.7.1 Orthogonalized forecast error variance decomposition

While the impulse responses show the effect of a shock to a particular variable, the persistence profile, as developed by Lee and Pesaran ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-617)) and Pesaran and Shin ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-795)), shows the effects of system-wide shocks on the cointegrating relations. In the case of the cointegrating relations the effects of the shocks (irrespective of their sources) will eventually disappear. Therefore, the shape of the persistence profiles provides valuable information on the speed of convergence of the cointegrating relations towards equilibrium. ## 24.8.2 Persistence profiles for cointegrating relations

Pesaran and Shin ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-795)) suggest using the persistence profiles to measure the speed of convergence of the cointegrating relations to equilibrium (see also Section 22.14 on this). The (unscaled) persistence profile of the cointegrating relations is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14856.gif)

The profiles tend to zero as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14857.gif), and provide a useful graphical representation of the extent to which the cointegrating (equilibrium) relations adjust to system-wide shocks. The persistence profiles are uniquely determined.

Therefore, in total we have ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14945.gif)![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14946.gif) restrictions, as required for just (or exact) identification of the structural parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14947.gif).

The above identification scheme, in addition to requiring structural shocks to be orthogonal (which is a questionable requirement), also imposes a recursive casual ordering on the variables in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14948.gif). For example, different structural models will result from different ordering of the variables in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14949.gif). It is in fact the same as the recursive ordering proposed by Wold whereby the first structural shock, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14950.gif), is assumed to be proportional to the first reduced-form error ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14951.gif), the second structural shock, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14952.gif), is related linearly to the first two reduced form errors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14953.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14954.gif) the third structural error, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14955.gif) is linearly related to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14956.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14957.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-14958.gif), and so on. As Wold showed, the parameters of these linear relations can be estimated consistently in a recursive manner.

Other identification schemes have followed the work by Sims ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-906)). One prominent example is the identification scheme developed in Blanchard and Quah ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-126)), who distinguished between permanent and transitory shocks and attempted to identify the structural models through long-run restrictions. For example, Blanchard and Quah argued that the effect of a demand shock on real output should be temporary (namely it should have a zero long-run impact), whilst a supply shock should have a permanent effect. This approach is known as ‘structural *VAR*’ (*SVAR*) and has been used extensively in the literature.

# 24.11 Structural systems with permanent and transitory shocks

We now consider the identification problem of a structural model when one or more of the structural shocks are permanent.[²](#038_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-24-note-129) We first introduce a simple structural model and then explore the implications for the identification of the structural shocks provided by a permanent/transitory decomposition.

# 24.12 Some applications

## 24.12.1 Blanchard and Quah (1989) model

We now consider an application of the above framework to the model analysed by Blanchard and Quah ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-126)). Blanchard and Quah ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-126)) consider a two equation system in GNP (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15040.gif) ) and unemployment rate (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15041.gif) ), which are assumed to be ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15042.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15043.gif), respectively. They further assume that there is one permanent (supply) and one transitory (demand) shock. These are denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15044.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15045.gif), respectively. Although there is no cointegration in this case, our methodological approach can be applied by treating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15046.gif), the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15047.gif) variable as if it ‘cointegrates’ with itself.

Let us set up a pseudo cointegrating vector of the form ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15048.gif) which produces the lagged ‘EC term’ given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15049.gif) According to the above results, the equation with the permanent shock will have the form (normalizing on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15050.gif) )

and the second equation (normalizing on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15052.gif) ) will be

It is clear that in this setup ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15054.gif) does not enter the first equation and can therefore be used as an instrument for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15055.gif) in it. So long as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15056.gif), the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15057.gif) does not matter as the instrumental variable estimator is invariant to it. However, unlike the cointegration case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15058.gif) could be estimated super-consistently, this is not possible when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15059.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15060.gif) so that we would need to treat ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15061.gif) as a regressor in the second equation. But the residuals from the first equation form a suitable instrument. This instrumental variable interpretation of Blanchard and Quah is due to Shapiro and Watson ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-900)). The problem with this procedure is that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15064.gif) is often a very poor instrument for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15065.gif) and this can lead to highly non-normal densities for the instrumental variables estimator. Using the same data as Blanchard and Quah this is shown in Fry and Pagan ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-373)).

## 24.12.2 Gali’s *IS-LM* model

Gali ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-377)) presents a model in four ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15066.gif) variables: log of GNP (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15067.gif) ), inflation rate (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15068.gif) ), growth rate of the money supply (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15069.gif) ) and nominal interest rate (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15070.gif) ). The implied *SVAR* for the first equation has the form

It is clear that we can use ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15078.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15079.gif) as instruments for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15080.gif). But still we need another instrument for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15081.gif). To this end Gali assumes that the long-run effect of the second permanent shock upon ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15082.gif) is zero, which yields the restriction ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15083.gif) and so the equation for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15084.gif) can be re-expressed in terms of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15085.gif) allowing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15086.gif) to be used as an instrument.

The second equation has the form

We can still use the lagged ECM terms as instruments. Assuming that the shocks are uncorrelated, we can also use the residuals from the first equation as instruments. Gali adopts the latter but not the former as instruments.

# 24.13 Identification of monetary policy shocks

We now discuss the problem of identification of the monetary policy shocks within a model for the UK macroeconomy, described in Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)), and link it to impulse response analysis of the monetary policy shocks. The model proposed in Garratt et al. ([2003b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-382)) comprises six domestic variables whose developments are widely regarded as essential to a basic understanding of the behaviour of the UK macroeconomy; namely, aggregate output, the ratio of domestic to foreign price levels, inflation, the nominal interest rate, the exchange rate, and real money balances. The model also contains foreign output, foreign interest rates and oil prices (see Section 23.8 for further details). For identification of the monetary policy shocks, we need to formally articulate the decision problem of the monetary authorities.

Assume monetary authorities try to influence the market interest rate, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15088.gif), by setting the base rate, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15089.gif) that they control. # 25.1 Introduction

Modelling of conditional volatilities and correlations across asset returns is part of portfolio decision making and risk management. In risk management the Value at Risk (*VaR*) of a given portfolio can be computed using univariate volatility models, but a multivariate model is needed for portfolio decisions.[¹](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-note-131) Even in risk management the use of a multivariate model would be desirable when a number of alternative portfolios of the same universe of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15192.gif) assets are under consideration. By using the same multivariate volatility model marginal contributions of different assets towards the overall portfolio risk can be computed in a consistent manner. Multivariate volatility models are also needed for determination of hedge ratios and leverage factors.

There exists a growing literature on multivariate volatility modelling. A general class of such models is the multivariate generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedastic (*MGARCH*) specification (Engle and Kroner ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-335))). However, the number of unknown parameters in the unrestricted *MGARCH* model rises exponentially with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15193.gif) and its estimation will not be possible even for a modest number of assets. To deal with the curse of dimensionality the dynamic conditional correlations (*DCC*) model is proposed by Engle ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-332)) which generalizes an earlier specification in Bollerslev ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-132)) by allowing for time variations in the correlation matrix. This is achieved parsimoniously by separating the specification of the conditional volatilities from that of the conditional correlations. The latter are then modelled in terms of a small number of unknown parameters, which avoids the curse of the dimensionality. *DCC* is an attractive estimation procedure which is reasonably flexible in modeling individual volatilities and can be applied to portfolios with a large number of assets. Pesaran and Pesaran ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-761)) propose a *DCC* model combined with a multivariate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15194.gif) -distribution assumption on the distribution of asset returns. Indeed, in many applications in finance the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15195.gif) -distribution seems more appropriate to capture the fat-tailed nature of the distribution of asset returns. The authors suggest a simultaneous approach for estimating the parameters, including the degree-of-freedom parameter of the multivariate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15196.gif) -distribution, of a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15197.gif) -*DCC* model.

## 25.2.2 Two parameters exponential-weighted moving average

Practitioners and academics have often pointed out that the effects of shocks on conditional variances and conditional correlations could decay at different rates, with correlations typically responding at a slower pace than volatilities. This suggests using two different parameter values for the decay coefficients, one for volatilities and the other for correlations. This yields the two-parameter Exponential-Weighted Moving Average, EWMA (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15228.gif) ). Therefore, the diagonal elements of (25.1) define conditional variances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15229.gif), the square-roots of which form the diagonal matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15230.gif). The covariances are based on the same recursion as (25.1) but using a smoothing parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15231.gif), generally different from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15232.gif) yielding

We assume that the same window size, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15235.gif), applies to variance and covariance recursions. The ratio

represents the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15237.gif) entry of the correlation matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15238.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15239.gif). The parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15240.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15241.gif) are not estimated but calibrated *a priori*, as for the one-parameter EWMA model.

## 25.2.4 Generalized exponential-weighted moving average (*EWMA*(n,p,q, ))

This is a generalization of the two-parameter EWMA. In the first stage ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15248.gif) different univariate *GARCH*(![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15249.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15250.gif), volatility models are estimated for each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15251.gif) by *QMLE* (see [Chapter 18](#031_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-18)). The conditional covariances are then obtained using the Riskmetrics filter (25.1), with the parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15252.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15253.gif) fixed *a priori*. The results are then normalized using (25.2), with the resultant variances and correlations recombined according to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15254.gif).

The above multivariate volatility models are either *ad hoc* or are formed by combining the univaraite volatility specification with some *ad hoc* specification of the correlations across the different asset returns. We now turn to system approaches to modelling the multivariate nature of interactions across different returns using the maximum likelihood framework. To deal with the curse of dimensionality, specification of the volatility of individual returns is separated from modelling of the correlations which are specified to depend on only a small number of unknown parameters.

In practice, the hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15295.gif) needs to be tested.

Returns in (25.6) are standardized to achieve normality. Transformation to Gaussianity is important since the use of correlation as a measure of dependence can be misleading in the case of (conditionally) non-Gaussian returns (see Embrechts, Hoing, and Juri ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-329)) on this). Engle ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-332)) proposes the following standardization for returns
