An alternative way of standardizing returns is to use a measure of realized volatility (Pesaran and Pesaran ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-761)))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15298.gif)(25.8)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15299.gif) is a proxy for the realized volatility of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15300.gif) return during day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15301.gif). The use of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15302.gif) is data intensive and requires intra-daily observations. Although intra-daily observations are becoming increasingly available across a large number of assets, it would still be desirable to work with a version of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15303.gif) that does not require intra-daily observations, but is nevertheless capable of rendering the devolatized returns approximately Gaussian. One of the main reasons for the non-Gaussian behavior of daily returns is the presence of jumps in the return process as documented for a number of markets in the literature (see, e.g., Barndorff Nielsen and Shephard ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-89))). The standardized return (25.7) does not deal with such jumps, since the jump process that affects the numerator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15304.gif) in day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15305.gif) does not enter the denominator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15306.gif) which is based on past returns and excludes the day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15307.gif) return, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15308.gif). The problem is accentuated due to the fact that jumps are typically independently distributed over time. The use of realized volatility ensures that the numerator and the denominator of the devolatized returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15309.gif), are both affected by the same jumps in day ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15310.gif).

Pesaran and Pesaran ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-761)) have suggested the following approximation for the realized volatility

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15311.gif)(25.9)

The lag-order, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15312.gif), needs to be chosen carefully. We refer to returns (25.8) where the realized volatility is estimated using (25.9) as ‘devolatized returns’. In a series of papers Andersen, Bollerslev and Diebold show that daily returns on foreign exchange and stock returns standardized by realized volatility are approximately Gaussian (see, e.g., Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold, and Ebens ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-22)), and Andersen et al. ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-22))).

Note that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15313.gif) is not the same as the rolling historical estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15314.gif) defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15315.gif)

Specifically,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15316.gif)

It is the inclusion of the current squared returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15317.gif), in the estimation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15318.gif) that seems to be critical in the transformation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15319.gif) (which is non-Gaussian) into ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15320.gif) which seems to be approximately Gaussian.

# 25.5 Maximum likelihood estimation of *DCC* model

*ML* estimation of the *DCC* model can be carried out under two different assumptions concerning the conditional distribution of assets returns, the multivariate Gaussian distribution and the multivariate Student’s ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15344.gif) -distribution.

In its most general formulation (the mean reverting specifications given by (25.4) and (25.6)) the *DCC* model contains ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15345.gif) unknown parameters; ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15346.gif) coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15347.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15348.gif) that enter the individual asset returns volatilities, and the coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15349.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15350.gif) that enter the conditional correlations. In the case of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15351.gif) -distributed returns, a further parameter, the degrees of freedom of the multivariate Student ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15352.gif) -distribution, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15353.gif), needs to be estimated.

The intercepts ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15354.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15355.gif) in (25.4) and (25.6) refer to the unconditional volatilities and return correlations and can be estimated as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15356.gif)(25.10)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15357.gif)(25.11)

In the non-mean reverting case these intercept coefficients disappear, but for initialization of the recursive relations (25.4) and (25.6) it is still advisable to use unconditional estimates of the correlation matrix and asset returns volatilities.

## 25.5.1 *ML* estimation with Gaussian returns

Denote the unknown coefficients by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15358.gif). Based on a sample of observations on returns, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15359.gif), available at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15360.gif), the time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15361.gif) log-likelihood function based on the decomposition (25.3) is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15362.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15363.gif) is the start date of the estimation window and

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15364.gif)

with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15365.gif). For estimation of the unknown parameters, Engle ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-332)) shows that the log-likelihood function of the *DCC* model can be maximized using a two-step procedure. In the first step, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15366.gif) univariate *GARCH* models are estimated separately. In the second step using standardized residuals, computed from the estimated volatilities from the first stage, the parameters of the conditional correlations are then estimated. The two-step procedure can then be iterated if desired for full maximum likelihood estimation. Note that under Engle’s specification ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15367.gif) depends on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15368.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15369.gif) as well as on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15370.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15371.gif).

This procedure has two main drawbacks. First, the Gaussian assumption in general does not hold for daily returns (see [Chapter 7](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7)) and its use can under-estimate the portfolio risk. Second, the two-stage approach is likely to be inefficient even under Gaussianity.

For further details on *ML* estimation using Gaussian returns, see Engle ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-332)).

# 25.8 An application: volatilities and conditional correlations in weekly returns

We estimate alternative versions of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15518.gif) -*DCC* model for a portfolio composed of weekly returns on:

• 6 currencies: British pound (GBP), euro (EU), Japanese yen (JPY), Swiss franc (CHF), Canadian dollar (CAD), and Australian dollar (AD).

• 4 government bonds: US T-Note 10Y (BU), Europe euro bund 10Y (BE), Japan government bond 10Y (JGB), and UK long gilts 8.75-13Y (BG).

• 7 equity index futures S&P 500 (SP), FTSE 100 (FTSE), German DAX (DAX), French CAC40 (CAC), Swiss Market Index (SM), Australia SPI200 (AUS), Nikkei 225 (NK).

The weekly returns are computed from daily prices obtained from Datastream and cover the period from 7 Jan 94 to 30 Oct 2009.

## 25.8.1 Devolatized returns and their properties

[Table 25.1](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-tableGroup-43) provides summary statistics for the weekly returns (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15519.gif), in percent) and the devolatized weekly returns ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15520.gif), where in the absence of intra-daily observations ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15521.gif) is defined by (25.9), with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15522.gif) weeks. The choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15523.gif) was guided by some experimentation with the aim of transforming ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15524.gif) into an approximately Gaussian process. A choice of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15525.gif) well above ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15526.gif) does not allow the (possible) jumps in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15527.gif) to become adequately reflected in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15528.gif), and a value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15529.gif) well below ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15530.gif) transforms ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15531.gif) to an indicator looking function. In the extreme case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15532.gif) we have ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15533.gif), if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15534.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15535.gif), if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15536.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15537.gif), if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15538.gif). We did not experiment with other values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15539.gif) for the sample under consideration and set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15540.gif) for all 17 assets.

For the non-devolatized returns, the results are as to be expected from previous studies. The returns seem to be symmetrically distributed with kurtosis in some cases well in excess of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15541.gif) (the value for the Gaussian distribution). The excess kurtosis is particularly large for equities, mostly around 5 or more. For currencies, the kurtosis coefficient is particularly large for yen, British pound, and Singapore dollar. By comparison the weekly returns on government bonds are less fat-tailed with kurtosis coefficients only marginally above 3. In contrast, none of the 17 devolatized returns shows any evidence of excess kurtosis. For example, for equities the excess kurtosis of weekly returns on SP, FTSE and Nikkei falls from 8.01, 10.40, 9.65 to –0.124, –0.132 and –0.147, respectively after the returns are devolatized. For currencies. the excess kurtosis of the weekly returns on AD, BP, and JY falls from 7.89, 5.35, and 9.46 to –0.112, –0.020, and 0.139, respectively. Out of the four ten year government bonds only the weekly returns on Japanese government bond show some degree of excess kurtosis which is eliminated once the returns are devolatized. It is also interesting to note that the standard deviations of the devolatized returns are now all very close to unity, that allows for a more direct comparison of the devolatized returns across assets.

## 25.8.2 *ML* estimation

It is well established that daily or weekly returns are approximately mean zero serially uncorrelated processes and for the purpose of risk analysis it is reasonable to assume that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15542.gif). Using the *ML* procedure described above, initially we estimate a number of *DCC* models on the 17 weekly returns over the period 27 May 1994 to 28 Dec 2007 (710 observations). We then use the post estimation sample observations from 4 January, 2008 to 30 October, 2009 for the evaluation of the estimated volatility models using the *VaR* and distribution free diagnostics.[⁶](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-note-137) We also provide *separate* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15543.gif) -*DCC* models for currencies, bonds and equities for purposes of comparison.

We begin with the unrestricted version of the *DCC*(1,1) model with asset-specific volatility parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15544.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15545.gif), and common conditional correlation parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15546.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15547.gif), and the degrees-of-freedom parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15548.gif), under conditionally ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15549.gif) distributed returns (note that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15550.gif). We did not encounter any convergence problems, and obtained the same *ML* estimates when starting from different initial parameter values. But to achieve convergence in some applications we had to experiment with different initial values. In particular we found the initial values ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15551.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15552.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15553.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15554.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15555.gif) to work relatively well. Also the sum of unrestricted estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15556.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15557.gif) for the Canadian dollar exceeded ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15558.gif), and to ensure a non-explosive outcome we estimated its volatility equation subject to the restriction ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15559.gif).

To evaluate the statistical significance of the multivariate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15560.gif) -distribution for the analysis of return volatilities, in [Table 25.2](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-tableGroup-44) we first provide the maximized log-likelihood values under multivariate normal and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15561.gif) -distributions for currencies, bonds and equities separately, as well as for all the 17 assets jointly. These results are reported for both the standardized and devolatized returns. It is firstly clear from these results that the normal-*DCC* specifications are strongly rejected relative to the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15562.gif) -*DCC* models for all asset categories. The maximized log-likelihood values for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15563.gif) -*DCC* models are significantly larger than the ones for the normal-*DCC* models. The estimated degrees of freedom of the multivariate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15564.gif) -distribution for different asset classes are quite close and range from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15565.gif) (for equities) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15566.gif) (for bonds), all well below the value of 30 and above what one would expect for a multivariate normal distribution. For the full set of 17 assets the estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15567.gif) is closer to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15568.gif). There seems to be a tendency for the estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15569.gif) to rise as more assets are included in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15570.gif) -*DCC* model.

**Table 25.2**: Maximized log-likelihood values of *DCC* models estimated with weekly returns over 27 May 1994 to 28 December 2007

![Table_Image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-table-44.jpg)

The above conclusions are robust to the way returns are scaled for computation of cross asset return correlations. The maximized log-likelihoods for the standardized and devolatized returns are very close although, due to the non-nested nature of the two return transformations, no definite conclusions can be reached as to their relative merits. The specifications where the returns are standardized by the conditional volatilities tend to fit better (give higher log-likelihood values). But this is to be expected since the maximization of the log-likelihood function in this case is carried out with respect to the parameters of the scaling factor, unlike the case where scaling is carried out with respect to the realized volatilities which do not depend on the unknown parameters of the likelihood function. In what follows we base our correlation analysis on the devolatized returns on the grounds of their approximate Gaussianity, as argued in Section 25.3.

## 25.8.3 Asset-specific estimates

[Table 25.3](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-tableGroup-45) presents the *ML* estimates of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15571.gif) -*DCC* model including all the 17 assets computed over the period 27 May 94–28 Dec 07 (710 weekly returns). The asset-specific estimates of the volatility decay parameters are all highly significant, with the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15572.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15573.gif) falling in the range of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15574.gif) (for Japanese government bond) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15575.gif) (for Canadian dollar).[⁷](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-note-138) The average estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15576.gif) across assets is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15577.gif) which is somewhat smaller than the values in the range of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15578.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15579.gif) recommended by Riskmetrics for computation of *daily* volatilities using their exponential smoothing procedure. This is not surprising, since one would expect the exponential smoothing parameter for computing the volatility of weekly returns to be smaller than the one used for computing the volatility of daily returns.

There are, however, notable differences across asset groups with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15580.gif) estimated to be larger for currencies as compared to the estimates for equities and bonds. The average estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15581.gif) across currencies is 0.95 as compared to 0.93 for equities and 0.88 for bonds. The correlation parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15582.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15583.gif), are very precisely estimated and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15584.gif), which suggest very slow but statistically significant mean reverting conditional correlations.

The sum of the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15585.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15586.gif) is very close to unity, but the hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15587.gif) (the integrated *GARCH* hypothesis) against the one-sided alternative ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15588.gif) is rejected for 10 out of the 17 assets at the 5 per cent significance level; the exceptions being British pound, Swiss franc, Nikkei, S&P 500, and Australian SPI200. In order to ensure a non-explosive outcome for Canadian dollar, as noted earlier, estimation is carried out subject to the restriction ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15589.gif). If the test is carried out at the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15590.gif) per cent significance level, the integrated *GARCH* hypothesis is rejected only in the case of the *JGB* (Japanese government bond).

The integrated *GARCH* (*IGARCH*) hypothesis is implicit in the approach advocated by Riskmetrics, but as shown by Zaffaroni ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-996)), this can lead to inconsistent estimates. However, in the present applications, the unrestricted parameter estimates and those obtained under *IGARCH* are very close and one can view the restrictions ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15591.gif) as a first-order approximation that avoids explosive outcomes. We also note that the diagnostic test results, to be reported in Section 25.8.5, are not qualitatively affected by the imposition of the restrictions, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15592.gif).

## 25.8.4 Post estimation evaluation of the *t-DCC* model

The evaluation sample, 04 Jan 08–30 Oct 09, covers the recent periods of financial crisis and includes ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15605.gif) weeks of post estimation sample of portfolio returns. The parameter values are estimated using the sample 27 May 04–28 Dec 07 and then fixed throughout the evaluation sample. To evaluate the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15606.gif) -*DCC* model we first consider the tests based on probability integral transforms (PIT), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15607.gif), defined by (25.20). We have already seen that under the null hypothesis the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15608.gif) -*DCC* model is correctly specified, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15609.gif) ’s are serially uncorrelated and uniformly distributed over the range ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15610.gif). To compute ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15611.gif) we consider an equal-weighted portfolio, with all elements of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15612.gif) in (25.15) set to 1/17, and use the risk tolerance probability of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15613.gif), which is the value typically assumed in practice. We consider two versions of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15614.gif) -*DCC* model: a version with no restrictions on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15615.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15616.gif) (except for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15617.gif) ), and an integrated version where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15618.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15619.gif).

Using the Lagrange multiplier statistic to test the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15620.gif) ’s are serially uncorrelated, we obtained the values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15621.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15622.gif) for the unrestricted and the restricted ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15623.gif) -*DCC* specifications. These statistics are computed assuming a maximum lag order of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15624.gif), and are asymptotically distributed as chi-squared variates with twelve degrees of freedom. It is clear that both specifications of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15625.gif) -*DCC* model pass this test.

Next we apply the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15626.gif) ’s to test the null hypothesis that the PIT values are draws from a uniform distribution. The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15627.gif) statistics for the unrestricted and the restricted versions amount to 0.0646 and 0.0454, respectively. Both these statistics are well below the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15628.gif) critical value of 0.1388 (at the 5 per cent level).[⁸](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-note-140) Therefore, the null hypothesis that the sample *CDF* of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15629.gif) ’s is similar to the hypothesized uniform *CDF* cannot be rejected.

It is interesting that neither of the tests based on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15630.gif) ’s are capable of detecting the effects of the financial turmoil that occured in 2008. A test based on the violations of the *VaR* constraint is likely to be more discriminating, since it focusses on the tail properties of the return distributions. For a tolerance probability of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15631.gif), we would expect only one violation of the *VaR* constraint in 100 observations (our evaluation sample contains 96 observations). The unrestricted specification results in three violations of the *VaR* constraint, and the restricted specification in four violations. Both specifications violate the *VaR* constraint in the weeks starting on 5 Sep 08, 3 Oct 08, and 10 Oct 08. The restricted version also violates the *VaR* in the week starting in 18 Jan 08. The test statistics associated with these violations are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15632.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15633.gif) which are normally distributed. Thus both specifications are rejected by the *VaR* violation test.[⁹](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-note-141) Not surprisingly, the rejection of the test is due to the unprecedented market volatility during the weeks in September and October of 2008. This period covers the Fed’s take over of FannieMae \<<http://www.fanniemae.com/portal/index.html>\> and Freddie Mac \<<http://www.freddiemac.com/>\>, the collapse of Lehman Brothers, and the downgrading of the AIG’s credit rating. In fact, during the two weeks starting on 3 Oct 08, the S&P 500 dropped by 29.92 per cent, which is larger than the 20 per cent market decline experienced during the October Crash of 1987.

## 25.8.5 Recursive estimates and the *VaR* diagnostics

We now consider whether the excess *VaR* violations documented above could have been avoided if the parameter estimates of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15638.gif) -*DCC* model were updated at regular intervals. To simplify the computations we focused on the *IGARCH* version of the model and re-estimated all its parameters (including the degree-of-freedom parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15639.gif) ) every 13 weeks ( or four times in a year). Using the recursive estimates of the PIT, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15640.gif) and the *VaR* indicator ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15641.gif) we obtained similar results for the post 2007 period. The *KS* statistic for the recursive estimates is 0.0518 as compared with the 5 per cent critical value of 0.1381 and does not reject the null hypothesis that the the recursive *PIT* values are draws from a uniform distribution. We also could not find any evidence of serial correlation in the *PIT* values. But as before, the violations of the *VaR* constraint were statistically significant with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15642.gif). The violations occur exactly on the same dates as when the parameters were fixed at the end of 2007. Updating the parameter estimates of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15643.gif) -*DCC* model seem to have little impact on the diagnostic test outcomes.

## 25.8.6 Changing volatilities and correlations

The time series plots of volatilities are displayed in [Figures 25.1](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-figureGroup-12)–[25.3](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-figureGroup-14) for returns on currencies, bonds and equities, respectively. Conditional correlations of the euro with other currencies, US 10 year bond futures with other bond futures, and S&P futures with other equity future indices are shown in [Figures 25.4](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-figureGroup-15) to [25.6](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-figureGroup-17), respectively. To reduce the impact of the initialization on the plots of volatilities and conditional correlations, initial estimates for 1994 are not shown. These figures clearly show the declining trends in volatilities over the 2003–06 period just before the financial crisis which led to an unprecedented rise in volatilities, particularly in the currency and equity markets. It is, however, interesting to note that return correlations have been rising historically and seem to be only marginally accentuated by the recent crisis. This trend could reflect the advent of the euro and a closer integration of the world economy, particularly in the euro area. Return correlations across asset types have also been rising, although to a lesser extent. An overall measure of the extent of the correlations across all the 17 assets under consideration is given by the maximum eigenvalue of the 17 by 17 matrix of asset return correlations. [Figure 25.7](#039_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-25-figureGroup-18) displays the conditional estimates of this eigenvalue over time and clearly shows the sharp rise in asset return correlations particularly over the years 2008 and 2009.

# [ Panel Data Econometrics](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-part-6)

|----------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| [26](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-26) | [Panel Data Models with Strictly Exogenous Regressors](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-26) |

# 26.1 Introduction

Panel data consist of observations on many individual economic units over two or more periods of time. The individual units are usually referred to as cross-sectional units, and in economic and finance applications are typically represented by single individuals, firms, returns on individual securities, industries, regions, or countries.

In recent years, panel data sets have become widely available to empirical researchers. Examples of such data sets in the US include the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), collected by the Institute for Social Research at the University of Michigan, and the National Longitudinal Surveys of Labor Market Experience (NLS), from the Center for Human Resource Research at Ohio State University. The PSID began in 1968 by collecting of annual economic information from a representative national sample of about 6,000 families and 15,000 individuals. The NLS started in the mid 1960s, and contains five separate annual surveys covering various segments of the labour force. In Europe, many countries have their national annual surveys such as the Netherlands Socioeconomic Panel, the German Social Economics Panel, and the British Household Panel Survey. At aggregated level, the published statistics of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) contain numerous series of economic aggregates observed yearly for many countries. New data sources are also emerging through Google search engine and retail scanner datasets. Examples are Google Flu Trends (\<<http://www.google.org/flutrends/>\>), Nielson Datasets for consumer marketing (\<[http://research.chicagobooth.edu/nielsen/](http://www.research.chicagobooth.edu/nielsen/)\>). This increasing availability of panel data sets, while opening up new possibilities for analysis, has also raised a number of new and interesting econometric issues.

Panel data offer several important advantages over data sets with only a temporal or longitudinal dimension. A major motivation for using panel data is the ability to control for possibly correlated, time-invariant heterogeneity without actually observing it. One may be able to identify and measure effects that are otherwise not detectable, as well as to account for latent individual heterogeneity. An additional advantage of panel data, compared to time series data, is the reduction in collinearity among explanatory variables and the increase in efficiency of econometric estimators. Finally, the cross-sectional dimension may also alleviate problems of aggregation. These benefits do come at a cost. Important difficulties arise when explanatory variables in panel data regression models cannot be assumed strictly exogenous. As we shall see in [Chapter 27](#042_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27), standard panel estimators are inconsistent when panel data regression models have weakly exogenous regressors, and their treatment poses a number of methodological challenges. A further complication arises when regression errors attached to different cross-section units are dependent, even after conditioning on variables that are specific to cross-sectional units. In the presence of cross-section dependence, conventional panel estimators can result in misleading inference and even inconsistent estimators (see [Chapter 29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29) on this). Finally, important econometric issues arise when panel data sets involves non-responses and measurement errors.

The literature on panel data can be broadly divided into three categories, depending on their assumptions about the relative magnitudes of the number of cross-sectional units (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15691.gif) ) and the number of time periods (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15692.gif) ). First, there exists a ‘small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15693.gif), large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15694.gif) ’ time series literature which closely follows the SURE procedure, due to Zellner ([1962](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-997)) and described in [Chapter 19](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19). The main attraction of the SURE approach is that it allows the contemporaneous error covariances to be freely estimated. But this is possible only when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15695.gif) is reasonably small relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15696.gif), while the SURE procedure is not feasible when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15697.gif) is of the same order of magnitude as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15698.gif). Also the SURE approach assumes that the regressors are uncorrelated with the errors which rules out the error correlation being due to the presence of unobserved common factors. The general problem of error cross-sectional correlation will be discussed in [Chapter 29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29). Second, there is the ‘small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15699.gif), large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15700.gif) ’ panel literature. The set of econometric models and techniques suggested to carry inference on this type of panel data sets, assuming strictly exogenous regressors, will be the object of this chapter. Next chapter relaxes the exogeneity assumption and allows the regressors to be weakly exogenous. The analysis of ‘large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15701.gif), large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15702.gif) ’ panels will be covered in Chapters 28 and 31.

# 26.4 Fixed-effects specification

Under the fixed-effects (FE) specification, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15853.gif) are treated as free parameters which are incidental to the analysis, with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15854.gif) being the focus of interest. Typically, the only restriction imposed on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15855.gif) is boundedness, namely that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15856.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15857.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15858.gif) is a fixed positive constant. Otherwise, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15859.gif) is allowed to have any degree of dependence on the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15860.gif) or the error term, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15861.gif). This setup does not rule out the possibility that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15862.gif) are random draws from a given distribution. In general, one can think of the fixed-effects as draws from a joint probability distribution function over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15863.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15864.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15865.gif), where the number of parameters characterizing this distribution is allowed to increase at the same rate as the number of cross-sectional observations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15866.gif). For further discussion see Mundlak ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-711)) and Hausman and Taylor ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-492)).

Under the FE specification, we assume that conditional on the individual effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15867.gif), the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15868.gif), are strictly exogenous, but do not impose any restrictions on the fixed-effects. More formally, we continue to maintain Assumptions P1, P4 and P5 , but replace Assumptions P2 and P3 with the following:

The above results show that the *FE* estimator is fairly robust to temporal dependence and cross-sectional heteroskedasticity. But it is important to note that the robustness of the *FE* estimator to possible correlations between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15991.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15992.gif) comes at a cost. Using the *FE* approach we can only estimate the effects of time varying regressors. The effects of non-time varying regressors (such as sex or race) will be unidentified under the within or the *FE* transformation. But with additional assumptions the time-invariant effects can be estimated using time averages of the residuals from fixed-effects regressions. For further details see Section 26.10.

Another important point to bear in mind is that the consistency of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15993.gif) crucially depends on the assumption of strict exogeneity of the explanatory variables. As we shall see in [Chapter 27](#042_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27), in the presence of weakly exogenous regressors, since the time averages ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15994.gif) in (26.15), contain the values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15995.gif) at all time periods, the demeaning operation would introduce a correlation of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15996.gif) between the regressors and the error term in the transformed equation (26.16) that renders ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15997.gif) biased in small samples. Finally, the *FE* is often not fully efficient since it ignores variation across individuals in the sample (see Hausman and Taylor ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-492))).

## 26.4.1 The relationship between *FE* and least squares dummy variable estimators

The *FE* estimator can also be computed by stacking all the observations for all the cross-sectional units and then adding dummy variables for each unit in the resultant stacked regression. Stacking the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15998.gif) regressions in (26.3) we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-15999.gif)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16000.gif)

which can be written more compactly as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16001.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16002.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16003.gif) vector of a dummy variable with all its elements zero except for the elements associated with the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16004.gif) cross-sectional unit which are set to unity. It is easily seen that the *OLS* estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16005.gif) in this regression is the same as the *FE* estimator. For this reason the *FE* estimator is also known as the least squares dummy variable (*LSDV* ) estimator. However, when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16006.gif) is relatively large it is not computationally efficient as compared to using the pooled formula given by (26.17). Also, especial care needs to be exercised when the *LSDV* approach is used, since the standard errors obtained from such regressions are only valid under the strong assumptions that the errors are homoskedastic and serially uncorrelated. In general it is more appropriate to use (26.17) to compute the *FE* estimator and then compute robust standard errors as set out in Section 26.7.

# 26.5 Random effects specification

The random effects (*RE*) approach assumes that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16030.gif) are realizations from a probability distribution function with a fixed number of parameters, distributed independently of the regressors. More formally, under this specification it is assumed that:

Assumption *RE*.1: (a) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16031.gif). (b) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16032.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16033.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16034.gif).

Assumption *RE*.2: (a) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16035.gif). (b) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16036.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16037.gif).

As in the *FE* specification, Assumption *RE*.1(a) implies strict exogeneity of explanatory variables conditional on the individual effects. Assumptions *RE*.1(b) and *RE*.2(b) imply that each group effect, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16038.gif), is a random draw that enters in the regression identically in each time period, and is independent of the explanatory variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16039.gif), at all time periods.

Contrary to the *FE* approach, under the random effects formulation, inference pertains to the population from which the sample was randomly drawn.

If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16097.gif) is close to 1 (which implies ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16098.gif) close to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16099.gif) ), the random effects and fixed-effects estimates tend to be close.

The above discussion also shows that, similar to FE estimation, the consistency of the RE estimator crucially depends on the assumption of strict exogeneity of the explanatory variables. In the presence of weakly exogenous regressors, the transformation (26.34) to eliminate the individual effects would render the transformed regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16100.gif), correlated with the new error term, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16101.gif), thus inducing a small sample bias in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16102.gif).

There are a number of advantages in using an RE specification. First, it allows the derivation of efficient estimators which, as seen above, make use of both within- and between-group variations. Further, contrary to the FE specification, with an RE specification it is possible to estimate the impact of time-invariant variables. However, the disadvantage is that one has to specify a conditional density of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16103.gif) given ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16104.gif), which needs to be independent of the explanatory variables. If such an independence assumption does not hold, then the RE estimator would be inconsistent. For further discussion, see Mundlak ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-711)).

## 26.6.1 Relation between pooled *OLS* and *RE* estimators

We begin with a comparison of pooled *OLS* and *RE* estimators. Although pooled *OLS* is estimated under the assumption that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16168.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16169.gif), it can also be rationalized under the random effects specification. To see this, note that the *RE* model can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16170.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16171.gif). Since under *RE* specification ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16172.gif), then Assumption P1 of the pooled *OLS* estimator is satisfied. Also Assumptions P2 and P3 are satisfied under the RE model. Furthermore, Assumption P5 clearly applies to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16173.gif), as they allow for the errors of the pooled *OLS* regression to be serially correlated. Finally, Assumption P4, the cross-sectional independence of the errors, is assumed to hold for both pooled *OLS* and *RE* estimators. Therefore, pooled *OLS* continues to be consistent under *RE* specification, although it will be inefficient under the *RE* specification that maintains ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16174.gif) to be serially uncorrelated and homoskedastic. But these assumptions are likely to be quite restrictive in practice, and pooled *OLS* with robust standard errors might be preferable. For estimation of robust standard errors for the pooled *OLS* estimator in the presence of general forms of residual serial correlation and cross-sectional heteroskedasticity see Section 26.7.

## 26.6.3 Fixed-effects versus random effects

When ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16198.gif) is large, whether to treat the group effects as fixed or random makes no difference, because, as seen above, the FE and the RE estimators become identical. When ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16199.gif) is finite and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16200.gif) is large, whether to use a fixed-effects or a random effects specification depends on a number of factors, such as the context of the data, the way in which the data were gathered, and the purposes of the analysis. For instance, suppose we are interested in studying the consumption behaviour of a group of people. If an experiment involves hundreds of individuals who are considered a random sample from some larger population, then random effects are more appropriate. Conversely, a fixed-effects specification would be more appropriate if we want to assess differences between specific individuals. As pointed out by Mundlak ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-711)), the key issue to take into consideration is the degree to which individual effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16201.gif), are likely to be correlated to the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16202.gif).

# 26.7 Estimation of the *variance* of pooled *OLS, FE*, and *RE* estimators of robust to heteroskedasticity and serial correlation

In the case of serially correlated and cross-sectionally heteroskedastic errors, the standard variance formulae that assume serially uncorrelated and homoskedastic errors will be inappropriate and their use can result in spurious inference. In a simulation study, Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-107)) found that panel data inference procedures which fail to account for within individual serial correlation may be severely size distorted. Arellano ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-46)) suggests a simple method for obtaining robust estimates of the standard errors for the FE estimator, that allow for a general covariance matrix of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16204.gif), as in White ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-971)). **Example 58** *In an interesting study, Lillard and Weiss (*[*1979*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-635)*) investigate the sources of variation in the earnings of American scientists reported by a panel of PhDs every two years, and over the decade 1960–1970. The sample is composed of six fields: biology, chemistry, earth sciences, mathematics, physics, and psychology. The earning function has the form*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16307.gif)

*where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16308.gif) *are year dummies,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16309.gif) *is a dummy variable equal to 1 if the scientist is a male and 0 otherwise,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16310.gif) *is a set of schooling related variables, and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16311.gif) *is a set of experience related variables. The residual earnings variation in* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16312.gif) *is decomposed into a random effect individual variance component in the level of earnings, a random effect individual component in earnings growth, and a serially correlated transitory component. Specifically, it is assumed that (see also Exercise 5 below)*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16313.gif)(26.50)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16314.gif), *and*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16315.gif)

*where*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16316.gif)

*The individual-specific term,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16317.gif), *represents the effect of unmeasured characteristics such as ability and work-related preferences, on the relative earnings of scientists, while* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16318.gif) *represents the effect of omitted variables which influence the growth in earnings such as individual learning ability. It is not unreasonable to expect some of the same unobserved variables to affect both* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16319.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16320.gif), *in which case they will be correlated. The serial correlation coefficient,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16321.gif), *represents the rate of deterioration of the effects of random shocks,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16322.gif), *which persist for more than a year. The model is estimated by maximum likelihood. One interesting finding is that, during the sample period, divergent patterns in earnings are observed for individuals with similar characteristics. In particular, individuals with greater mean earnings also had greater earnings growth. Further, it is observed that a substantial increase in the variance of individual mean earnings with increased experience, while the variance of the growth component remains constant. These patterns suggest that a substantial amount of inequality is sustained even if one adopts measures of earnings which are based on longer periods, such as a* *lifetime or permanent income. See Lillard and Weiss (*[*1979*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-635)*) for further details.*

## 26.9.1 Hausman’s misspecification test

The Hausman principle can be applied to hypothesis testing problems in which two estimators are available, one of which is known to be *consistent and efficient* under the null hypothesis, and inconsistent under the alternative, while the other estimator is consistent under both hypotheses without necessarily being efficient. The idea is to construct a test statistic based on the difference between the two estimators.

Denote the efficient estimator by subscript ‘e’ and the inefficient but consistent estimator (under the alternative hypothesis) by the subscript ‘c’. We then have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16343.gif)(26.52)

This is the result used by Hausman ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-491)) where it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16344.gif) is asymptotically the *most* efficient estimator. However, it is easily shown that (26.52) holds under a weaker requirement, namely when the (asymptotic) efficiency of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16345.gif) cannot be enhanced by the information contained in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16346.gif). In this section we shall assume there are time-invariant regressors in (26.1), namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16419.gif)(26.61)

where

# 26.11 Nonlinear unobserved effects panel data models

A prominent example of a nonlinear panel data model is the binary choice model where the variable to be explained, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16756.gif), is a random variable taking one of two different outcomes, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16757.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16758.gif), observed for a random sample of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16759.gif) individuals over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16760.gif) time periods. As in the single cross-section case, the discrete outcomes can be viewed as the observed counterpart of a latent continuous random variable crossing a threshold. Consider the following function for the continuous latent random variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16761.gif),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16762.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16763.gif) is a vector of exogenous explanatory variables, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16764.gif) could be treated as fixed or random. Instead of observing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16765.gif), we observe ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16766.gif), where

In the probit specification, the identification condition that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16770.gif) is imposed.

If the individual-specific effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16771.gif), are assumed to be fixed, then both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16772.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16773.gif) are unknown parameters to be estimated for the model ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16774.gif). However, when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16775.gif) is small, we have again the incidental-parameter problem (Neyman and Scott ([1948](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-730))). Contrary to the linear-regression case where individual effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16776.gif), can be eliminated by taking a linear transformation, in general there is no simple transformation of data to eliminate the incidental parameters from a nonlinear model. Further, the *MLE*s for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16777.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16778.gif) are not independent of each other for the discrete-choice models, and when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16779.gif) is fixed, the inconsistency of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16780.gif) is transmitted into the *MLE* for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16781.gif). Hence, even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16782.gif) tends to infinity, the *MLE* of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16783.gif) remains inconsistent, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16784.gif) is fixed.

In the case of the logit model with strictly exogenous regressors, an estimator for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16785.gif) can be obtained by adopting a conditional likelihood approach, which consists of finding the joint distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16786.gif) conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16787.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16788.gif) and the statistic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16789.gif). The function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16790.gif) is a minimum sufficient statistic for the incidental parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16791.gif). It turns out that such conditional joint distribution does not depend on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16792.gif), and the estimator obtained by maximizing it, the so called fixed-effects logit estimator, is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16793.gif) -consistent and asymptotically normal. Such a conditional likelihood approach does not work for the probit model, since we cannot find simple functions for the parameters of interest that are independent of the nuisance parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16794.gif). However, it is possible to obtain an estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16795.gif) for the probit specification under a random effects framework. Suppose that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16796.gif) is an unobservable random variable, and assume that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16797.gif). Hence, the log-likelihood function for the full sample can be computed and maximized with respect to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16802.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16803.gif) to obtain ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16804.gif) -consistent asymptotically normal estimators. # 26.12 Unbalanced panels

Until now we have focused on cases where observations on a cross-section of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16805.gif) individuals, families, firms, school districts, are available over the same time periods, denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16806.gif). Such data sets are usually called balanced panels because the same time periods are available for all cross-sectional units. A panel is said to be *unbalanced* or *incomplete* if the observations on different groups do not cover the same time periods. Unbalanced panels can arise for various reasons. For example, a variable is unobserved in certain time periods for a subset of cross-sectional units, or the survey design may rotate individuals out of the sample, according to some pre-specified rules; individuals initially participating in the panel may not be willing or able to participate in some waves. The way unbalanced panels are treated critically depends on whether the cause of missing observations on individual cross-sectional units is random or systematic.

Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16807.gif) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16808.gif) is observed and zero otherwise. Then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16809.gif) is an indicator variable telling us which time periods are missing for each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16810.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16811.gif) can be treated as a random sample from the population. If the indicator variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16812.gif), is independent of the error term ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16813.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16814.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16815.gif) (although it may be possibly correlated with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16816.gif) and/or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16817.gif) ), then FE on the unbalanced panel remains consistent and asymptotically normal. A similar approach can be utilized for pooled *OLS* and RE estimators. The pooled *OLS* estimator will be given by

For RE specification, the relevant quasi-demeaned observations for the unbalanced panel are

where
