To remain consistent and asymptotically normal, this estimator requires the stronger condition that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16846.gif) is independent of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16847.gif), as well as of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16848.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16849.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16850.gif).

Sample selection is likely to be a problem and could induce a bias when selection is related to the idiosyncratic errors. One possible way to test for sample selection bias is to compare estimates of the regression equation based on the balanced sub-panel of complete observations only, with estimates from the unbalanced panel by the means of a Hausman test. Significant differences between the estimates should be caused by a non-random response problem. However, note that, since both estimators are inconsistent under the alternative, the power of this test may be limited. As an alternative, a simple test of selection bias has been suggested by Nijman and Verbeek ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-734)). It consists of augmenting the regression equation with the lagged selection indicator, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16851.gif), estimating the model, and performing a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16852.gif) -test for the significance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16853.gif). Under the null hypothesis, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16854.gif) is uncorrelated with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16855.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16856.gif), and selection in the previous time period should not be significant in the equation at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16857.gif).

See Nijman and Verbeek ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-734)) and Wooldridge ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-986)) for further discussion.

# 26.13 Further reading

Early contributions to the methods and applications of panel data econometrics include the works carried during the 1950s and 1960s by Hildreth ([1950](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-508)), Tobin ([1950](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-944)), Mundlak ([1961](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-710)), Balestra and Nerlove ([1966](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-69)) and Maddala ([1971](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-662)). A review of these works, as well as an historical essay on the development of panel data models can be found in Nerlove ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-724)). Comprehensive textbook treatments of panel data methods can be found in Hsiao ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-523)) and its latest edition Hsiao ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-524)), Wooldridge ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-986)), Arellano ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-47)) and Baltagi ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-70)).

# 27.1 Introduction

So far we have considered panels with strictly exogenous regressors, but often we also wish to estimate economic relationships that are dynamic in nature, namely, for which the data generating process is a panel containing lagged dependent variables. If lagged dependent variables appear as explanatory variables, strict exogeneity of the regressors does not hold, and the maximum-likelihood estimator or the within estimator under the fixed-effects specification is no longer consistent in the case of panel data models where the number of cross-section units, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16901.gif), is large and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16902.gif), the number of time periods, is small. This is due to the presence of the incidental parameters problem discussed earlier (see Section 26.4). In addition, the treatment of initial observations in a dynamic process raise a number of theoretical and practical problems. As we shall see in this chapter, the assumption about initial observations plays a crucial role in interpreting the model and formulating consistent estimators. Solving the initial value problem is even more difficult in nonlinear panels, where misspecification in the distribution of initial values can lead to serious bias in the parameter estimates.

# 27.2 Dynamic panels with short *T* and large *N*

Consider the following ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16903.gif) model[¹](#042_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27-note-147)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16904.gif)(27.1)

where the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16905.gif) -dimensional vector of regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16906.gif), is assumed to be strictly exogenous, namely ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16907.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16908.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16909.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16910.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16911.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16912.gif) are the unit-specific effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16913.gif) is a scalar coefficient of the lagged dependent variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16914.gif) is a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16915.gif) -dimensional coefficient vector. The dynamic process of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16916.gif) (conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16917.gif) ) is stable when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16918.gif). As in the case of panels with strictly exogenous regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16919.gif) can be treated as fixed or random. As compared with the static models considered in [Chapter 26](#041_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-26), the presence of lagged values of the dependent variable amongst the regressors, creates two complications. First, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16920.gif) can no longer be viewed as a strictly exogenous regressor. By construction, the lagged dependent variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16921.gif), will be correlated with the unit-specific effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16922.gif), whether they are fixed or random, and with lagged ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16923.gif). The second complication arises due the non-vanishing effects of the initial values, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16924.gif), on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16925.gif), in small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16926.gif) panels. More explicitly, using (27.1) to solve for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16927.gif) recursively from the initial states, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16928.gif), we obtain

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16929.gif)(27.2)

Each observation on the dependent variable can thus be written as the sum of four components: a term depending on initial observations, a component depending on current and past values of the exogenous variables, a modified intercept term that depends on the unit-specific effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16930.gif), and a moving average term in past values of the disturbances. It is firstly clear that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16931.gif) depends on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16932.gif) and the initial values, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16933.gif), and the effects of the latter do not vanish when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16934.gif) is small or when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16935.gif) is close to unity. In such cases, assumptions on initial observations play an important role in determining the properties of the various estimators proposed in the literature (see Nerlove and Balestra ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-725))). At one extreme it can be assumed that the initial observations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16936.gif), are fixed constants specified independently of the parameters of the model. Under this specification there are no unit-specific effects at the initial period, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16937.gif), which considerably simplifies the analysis. However, as pointed out by Nerlove and Balestra ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-725)), unless there is a specific argument in favour of treating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16938.gif) as fixed (see, e.g., the application in Balestra and Nerlove ([1966](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-69))), in general such an assumption is not justified and can lead to biased estimates. Alternatively, the initial values can be assumed to be random draws from a distribution with a common mean

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16939.gif)(27.3)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16940.gif) is assumed to be independent of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16941.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16942.gif). In this case, starting values may be seen as representing the initial individual endowments, and their impact on current observations gradually diminishes and eventually vanishes with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16943.gif). Finally, in the more general case, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16944.gif), could be specified to depend on the unit-specific effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16945.gif), and time averages of the regressors. For example,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16946.gif)(27.4)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16947.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16948.gif) is independent of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16949.gif). This specification is sufficiently general and encompasses a number of other specifications of the initial values considered in the literature as special cases.

According to Nerlove and Balestra ([1992](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-725)), the data generating process of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16950.gif) should be quite similar, if not identical, to the process generating subsequent observations. For further discussion on assumptions concerning initial values, the reader is referred to Anderson and Hsiao ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-29)) (see, in particular, Table 1 in Anderson and Hsiao ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-29))), who show the sensitivity of maximum likelihood estimators to alternative assumptions about initial conditions, and Bhargava and Sargan ([1983](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-112)).

# 27.3 Bias of the *FE* and *RE* estimators

When ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16951.gif) is small, both the fixed-effects (*FE*) and random effects (*RE*) estimators of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16952.gif) introduced in [Chapter 26](#041_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-26) are biased. To understand the source of this bias, recall that both the *FE* and *RE* estimators involve (quasi-) deviation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16953.gif) from its individual-specific time average, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-16954.gif). Kiviet ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-598)) derives an approximation for the bias of the FE estimator in a dynamic panel data model with exogenous regressors, and suggests a bias-corrected FE estimator that subtracts a consistent estimator of this bias from the original FE estimator.

Even when no lagged dependent variable is present in the model, weak exogeneity will render the FE estimator inconsistent for a fixed ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17038.gif).

# 27.4 Instrumental variables and generalized method of moments

Ample literature has been developed on instrumental variables (IV) and the generalized method of moments (*GMM*) estimation of dynamic panel data models. In the following, we discuss the developments of this literature, and refer to [Chapter 10](#021_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-10) for details on the econometric theory underpinning *GMM*.

In the absence of any additional knowledge about initial conditions for the dynamic processes, the estimator (27.34) with weighting matrix (27.35) is asymptotically normal and is efficient in the class of estimators based on the linear moment conditions (Hansen ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-472)), Chamberlain ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-197))). However, as shown in Blundell and Bond ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-128)) and Binder, Hsiao, and Pesaran ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-118)), the performance of the IV and of the one-step and two-step *GMM* estimators deteriorates as the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17124.gif) increases relative to the variance of the idiosyncratic error, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17125.gif) or when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17126.gif) is close to 1. Indeed, in these cases it is possible to show that the instruments ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17127.gif) are only weakly related with the differences ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17128.gif). A further complication with *GMM* arises when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17129.gif) is not small. As ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17130.gif), the number of *GMM* orthogonality conditions ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17131.gif) also tend to infinity. In this case, Alvarez and Arellano ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-13)) show that the *GMM* remains asymptotically normal, but, unless ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17132.gif), it exhibits a bias of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17133.gif). Koenker and Machado ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-604)) finds conditions on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17134.gif) for the limiting distribution of the *GMM* estimator to remain valid.

Another important point to note is that consistency of the *GMM* estimator relies upon the fact that errors are serially uncorrelated, i.e., that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17135.gif). In the case of serially correlated errors, the *GMM* estimator would lose its consistency. Hence, Arellano and Bond ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-48)) suggest testing the hypothesis that the second-order autocovariances for all periods in the sample are zero, based on residuals from first difference equations. See Arellano and Bond ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-48), p. 282).

**Example 61** (Intertemporal dependency in alcohol and tobacco consumption) *In a* *recent paper, Browning and Collado (*[*2007*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-162)*) study the temporal patterns of consumption for a number of goods categories, using quarterly data on expenditure, income and other characteristic for a set of 3,200 Spanish households over the period 1985Q1 to 1996Q4. The authors distinguish between habits (state-dependence) from correlated heterogeneity in consumption behaviour, by adopting the following dynamic panel with random group effects*

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17182.gif)

Table 27.1 Arellano-Bover *GMM* estimates of budget shares determinants

![Table_Image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27-table-48.jpg)

*where* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17183.gif) *is the budget share for good i, by household h, at time* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17184.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17185.gif) *is total expenditure deflated by a price index,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17186.gif) *is a list of demographics and time and seasonal dummies, and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17187.gif) *is a possibly autocorrelated error term. In the above specification, the random group effect,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17188.gif), *allows for persistent individual heterogeneity, while the coefficient* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17189.gif) *captures the state-dependence present in the data. The Arellano and Bover (*[*1995*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-50)*) approach is then adopted to estimate the above model. Results, reported on Table* [*27.1*](#042_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27-tableGroup-48)*, show that lagged budget shares are significant for food-out, alcohol and tobacco, clothing and small durables, whereas for food-in and non-durables and services there is no evidence of state dependence once they control for unobserved heterogeneity. The positive coefficient of the lagged budget shares for food-out and alcohol and tobacco is consistent with habit formation in those commodities, while the negative sign for clothing and for small durables reflects the durability of these two goods. The estimated elasticities show that, as expected, food-in and alcohol and tobacco are necessities, whereas food-out, clothing and* *small durables are luxuries. See Browning and Collado (*[*2007*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-162)*) for further details.*

In particular, Blundell and Bond ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-128)) consider the following general process for the initial observations in a pure dynamic panel data model with no exogenous variables

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17194.gif)(27.37)

The above condition states that deviations of the initial conditions from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17196.gif) are uncorrelated with the level of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17197.gif) itself. To guarantee this, it may be assumed that

If (27.38) holds in addition to other standard assumptions, then the following ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17199.gif) additional moment conditions are available

Hence, calculation of the one-step and two-step *GMM* estimators proceeds as described above, adding ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17201.gif) columns to the matrix of instruments (27.27). This estimator is known as system *GMM*. Blundell and Bond ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-128)) show that the above moment conditions remain informative when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17202.gif) is close to unity or when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17203.gif) is large. A Monte Carlo exercise provided in Blundell, Bond, and Windmeijer ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-130)) shows that the use of these additional moment conditions yields substantial gains in terms of the properties of the 2-step *GMM* estimators, especially in the ‘weak instrument’ case. But when using this estimator it is important to bear in mind that its validity critically depends on assumption (27.38).

## 27.4.6 Testing for overidentifying restrictions

The validity of the moment conditions implied by the dynamic panel data model can be tested using the conventional *GMM* test of over-identifying restrictions (see Section 10.7, Sargan ([1958](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-884)), and Hansen ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-472)))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17265.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17266.gif) (assumed to be greater than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17267.gif) ) refers to the number of columns of the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17268.gif), containing the instruments, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17269.gif) denotes the residuals from the two-step estimation. In a Monte Carlo study, Bowsher ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-140)) shows that, when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17270.gif) is large, using too many moment conditions causes the above test to have extremely low power.

# 27.6 Transformed likelihood approach

The literature discussed so far has mostly focused on *GMM* as a general method for the estimation of dynamic panel data models, and has by and large neglected the maximum likelihood approach. Indeed, the incidental parameters issue and the initial values problem lead to violations in the standard regularity conditions for the *ML* estimators of the structural parameters. Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-529)) develop a transformed likelihood approach to overcome the incidental parameters problem. Consider a dynamic panel data model with group-specific effects assumed to be fixed unknown parameters. To simplify the analysis, abstract from exogenous regressors and take first differences of (27.5) to obtain

However, the transformed *ML* is based on a number of strong distributional assumptions on the disturbances. Using Monte Carlo simulations, it is shown that the transformed likelihood estimator outperforms the *GMM* estimators in almost all cases when the model contains an exogenous regressor, and in many cases if we consider pure autoregressive panels. The transformed *ML* approach has also been extended to panel *VAR* (*PVAR*) models by Binder, Hsiao, and Pesaran ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-118)) and to simultaneous equations models by Hsiao and Zhou ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-531)).

# 27.7 Short dynamic panels with unobserved factor error structure

Estimation methods reviewed so far assume that the errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17382.gif), in (27.1) are distributed independently across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17383.gif), a cross-sectional error independence assumption which might not hold in many applications where cross-section units are subject to common unobserved effects, or have spatial or network patterns where the error cross dependence could be local. Ignoring cross-sectional dependence can have important consequences for conventional estimators of dynamic panels. Phillips and Sul ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-841)) study the impact of cross-sectional dependence modelled as a factor structure on the inconsistency of the pooled least squares estimate of a short dynamic panel regression.[²](#042_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-27-note-150) Sarafidis, Yamagata, and Robertson ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-883)) investigate the properties of a number of standard widely used *GMM* estimators under cross-sectional dependence, and show that such estimators are inconsistent.

In applications where spatial patterns are important and can be characterized by known spatial weight matrices, error cross-sectional dependence is typically modelled as spatial autoregressions and estimated jointly with the other parameters of the dynamic panel data model. Lee and Yu ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-626)) provide a review. For small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17384.gif), Elhorst ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-321)) and Su and Yang ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-933)) consider random effects as well as fixed-effects specifications. In the latter case they apply the first-differencing operator to eliminate the fixed-effects and then use the transformed likelihood approach of Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-529)) to deal with the initial value problem. The treatment of the initial values in spatial dynamic panel data models poses additional difficulties and requires further investigation.

In addition to spatial effects, it is also likely that the error cross-sectional dependence could be due to omitted unobserved common factor(s). This class of models is referred to as multi-factor error panel data models and is reviewed in Section 29.5 in the case where both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17385.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17386.gif) are large. The case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17387.gif) is short and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17388.gif) large (which is the concern of this chapter) is less intensively researched. An early contribution is due to Holtz-Eakin, Newey, and Rosen ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-517)) and Ahn, Lee, and Schmidt ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-4)) who employ a quasi-differencing approach (originally proposed by Chamberlain ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-196))) to purge the panel data model from the factor structure and then use *GMM* to consistently estimate the model parameters. Nauges and Thomas ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-719)) follow this approach in addition to prior first-differencing to eliminate the fixed effect, which they consider separately from the single common factor structure assumed for the errors. Ahn, Lee, and Schmidt ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-6)) extend this approach to the more general case of a multifactor error structure. Robertson and Sarafidis (2013) propose an instrumental variable estimation procedure that introduces new parameters to represent the unobserved covariances between the instruments and the factor component of the errors. They show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically more efficient than the *GMM* estimator based on quasi-differencing as it exploits extra restrictions implied by the model. Elhorst ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-322)) considers a fixed-effects dynamic panel with contemporaneous endogenous interaction effects under small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17389.gif). For estimation purposes, he adopts both the maximum likelihood estimator of Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-529)) and the *GMM* estimator of Arellano and Bond ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-48)) reviewed above (see Section 27.4.2). Bai ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-54)) suggests a quasi-maximum likelihood (*ML*) approach applied to the original dynamic panel without differencing (simple or quasi), and uses the approach of Mundlak ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-711)) and Chamberlain ([1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-194)) to deal with the correlation between the factor loadings and the regressors, but continues to assume that all factor loadings (including the one associated with the intercepts) are uncorrelated with the errors. Hayakawa, Pesaran, and Smith ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-493)), using the transformed *ML* approach of Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-529)), propose an alternative quasi-*ML* approach applied to the panel data model after first-differencing. The proposed estimation procedure includes the transformed likelihood procedure of Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-529)) as a special case. It allows for both fixed and interactive effects (the latter based on a random coefficient specification), and can be used to test the validity of the fixed-effects specification against the more general model with interactive effects.

In what follows, we give a summary account of the quasi-differencing and the transformed *MLE* approaches, as they represent quite different ways of dealing with the unobserved factors when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17390.gif) is short and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17391.gif) large. Also, to simplify the exposition, we consider a factor error structure with only a single unobserved factor. To this end suppose that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17392.gif) in the dynamic panel data model, (27.1), is given by the following unobserved factor error structure,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17393.gif)(27.53)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17394.gif) is the unobserved common factor, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17395.gif) is the factor loading of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17396.gif) unit and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17397.gif) ’s are cross-sectionally independent innovations. # 27.8 Dynamic, nonlinear unobserved effects panel data models

Consider the following dynamic panel specification for the latent (unobserved) variable

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17468.gif)(27.66)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17469.gif) is a latent variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17470.gif) is the discrete observed dependent variable that takes the value of unity if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17471.gif) and zero otherwise, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17472.gif) is a threshold value, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17473.gif) is a vector of strictly exogenous regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17474.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17475.gif). We are interested in modelling

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17476.gif)(27.67)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17477.gif) is typically chosen to be logit or the probit functions. Under the above specification the probability of success at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17478.gif) is allowed to depend on the outcome in the previous period, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17479.gif), as well as on unobserved heterogeneity, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17480.gif). Of particular interest is testing the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17481.gif). Under this hypothesis, the response probability at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17482.gif) does not depend on past outcomes once controlled for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17483.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17484.gif). As with the linear models specification of the initial values plays an important role in the estimation and inference. A simple approach would be to treat ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17485.gif) as non-stochastics, and assume that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17486.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17487.gif) are random and independent of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17488.gif). In such a setting, the density of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17489.gif) given ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17490.gif) can be obtained by integrating out ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17491.gif) ’s, following a Bayesian approach, along similar lines as those described in Section 26.11. Although treating the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17492.gif) as nonrandom simplifies estimation, it is undesirable because it implies that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17493.gif) is independent of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17494.gif) and of any of the exogenous variables, which is a strong assumption. In a recent paper, using a set of Monte Carlo experiments, Akay ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-9)) shows that the exogenous initial values assumption, if incorrect, can lead to serious overestimation of the true state dependence and serious underestimation of the variance of unobserved group effects, when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17495.gif) is small. An alternative approach would be to allow the initial condition to be random, and then to use the joint distribution of all outcomes on the responses—including that in the initial time period—conditional on unobserved heterogeneity and observed strictly exogenous explanatory variables. However, as shown by Wooldridge ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-985)), the main complication with this approach is in specifying the distribution of the initial values given ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17496.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17497.gif). For the dynamic probit specification, Wooldridge ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-985)) proposes a very simple approach, which consists of specifying a distribution for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17498.gif) conditional on the initial values and on the time averages of the exogenous variables

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17499.gif)(27.68)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17500.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17501.gif) is an unobserved individual-effects, such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17502.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17503.gif). Plugging (27.68) into (27.66), under the probit specification, it is possible to derive the joint distribution of outcomes conditional on the initial values and the strictly exogenous variables. Such a likelihood has exactly the same structure as the standard random effects probit model, except for the regressors, which is now given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17504.gif). Hence, with this approach it is possible to add ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17505.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17506.gif) as additional explanatory variables in each time period and use standard random effects probit software to estimate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17507.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17508.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17509.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17510.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17511.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17512.gif).

Al-Sadoon, Li, and Pesaran ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-778)) introduce a binary choice panel data model where the idiosyncratic error term follows an exponential distribution, and derive moment conditions that eliminate the fixed-effect term and at the same time identify the parameters of the model. Appropriate moment conditions are derived both for identification of the state dependent parameter, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17513.gif), as well as the coefficients of the exogenous covariates, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17514.gif). It is shown that the resultant *GMM* estimators are consistent and asymptotically normally distributed at the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17515.gif) rate.

We refer to Hsiao ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-523), Section 7.5.2), and Wooldridge ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-985)) for further discussion on the initial conditions problem and on estimation of dynamic nonlinear models. Arellano and Bonhomme ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-49)) provide a review of recent developments in the econometric analysis of non-linear panel data models.

# 27.9 Further reading

Textbook treatment of this topic can be found in Arellano ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-47)) and Hsiao ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-523)). In particular, Arellano ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-47)) offers an exhaustive overview of *GMM* techniques proposed for estimating dynamic panels, while Hsiao ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-523)) (see, in particular, Ch. 4) provides a discussion of estimation of dynamic models under various assumptions on the distribution of initial values. See also the third edition of Hsiao’s pioneering text, Hsiao ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-524)). For further information on nonlinear dynamic panels, see Chs 15–16 in Wooldridge ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-985)).

# 28.1 Introduction

Panel data models introduced in the previous two chapters, 26 and 27, deal with panels where the time dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17542.gif)) is fixed, and assumes that conditional on a number of observable characteristics, any remaining heterogeneity over the cross-sectional units can be modelled through an additive intercept (assuming either fixed or random), and possibly heteroskedastic errors. This chapter extends the analysis of panels to linear panel data models with slope heterogeneity. It discusses how neglecting such heterogeneities affects the consistency of the estimates and inferences based upon them, and introduces models that explicitly allow for slope heterogeneity both in the case of static and dynamic panel data models. To deal with slope heterogeneity, particularly in the case of dynamic models, it is often necessary to assume that the number of time series observations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17543.gif), is relatively large, so that individual equations can be estimated for each unit separately. Models, estimation and inference procedures developed in this and subsequent chapters are more suited to large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17544.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17545.gif) panels. Such panel data sets are becoming increasingly available and cover countries, regions, industries, and markets over relatively long time periods.

Despite the slope heterogeneity, the cross-sectional units could nevertheless share common features of interest. For example, it is possible for different countries or geographical regions to have different dynamics of adjustments towards equilibrium, due to their historical and cultural differences, but they could all converge to the same economic equilibrium in the very long run, due to forces of arbitrage and interconnections through international trade and cultural exchanges. Other examples include cases where slope coefficients can be viewed as random draws from a distribution with a number of parameters that are bounded in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17546.gif). Large number of panel data sets fit within this setup, where the cross-sectional units might be industries, regions, or countries, and we wish to identify common patterns of responses across otherwise heterogeneous units. The parameters of interest may be intercepts, short-run coefficients, long-run coefficients or error variances.

This chapter deals with panels with stationary variables. The econometric analyses of panels with unit roots and cointegration is covered in [Chapter 31](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31).

# 28.2 Heterogeneous panels with strictly exogenous regressors

Suppose that the variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17547.gif) for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17548.gif) unit at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17549.gif) is specified as a linear function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17550.gif) strictly exogenous variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17551.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17552.gif), in the form

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17553.gif)(28.1)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17555.gif) denotes the random error term, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17556.gif) is a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17557.gif) vector of exogenous variables and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17558.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17559.gif) vector of coefficients. The above specification is very general and allows the coefficients to vary both across time and over individual units. As it is specified it is too general. It simply states that each individual unit has its own coefficients that are specific to each time period. However, as pointed out by Balestra ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-68)), this general formulation is, at most, descriptive. It lacks any explanatory power and it is not useful for prediction. Furthermore, it is not estimable, as the number of parameters to be estimated exceeds the number of observations. For a model to become interesting and to acquire explanatory and predictive power, it is essential that some structure is imposed on its parameters.

One way to reduce the number of parameters in ([28.1](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3249)) is to adopt a random coefficient approach, which assumes that the coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17560.gif) are draws from probability distributions with a fixed number of parameters that do not vary with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17561.gif) and/or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17562.gif) Depending on the type of assumption about the parameter variation, we can further classify the models into one of two categories: stationary and non-stationary random-coefficient models.

The stationary random-coefficient models view the coefficients as having constant means and variance-covariances. Namely, the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17563.gif) vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17564.gif) is specified as

One widely used random coefficient specification is the Swamy ([1970](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-936)) model, which assumes that the randomness is time-invariant

In this chapter we focus on models with time-invariant slope coefficients that vary randomly or freely over the cross-sectional units. We begin by considering the implications of neglecting such heterogeneity on the consistency and efficiency of the homogenous slope type estimators such as fixed and random effects models.

1. The FE estimators, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17705.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17706.gif), are both consistent if

2. 3. In general, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17725.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17726.gif) and/or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17727.gif), the fixed-effects estimators, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17728.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17729.gif), are both inconsistent.

In short, if the slope coefficients are fixed but vary systematically across the groups, the application of the general-to-specific methodology to standard panel data models can lead to misleading results (spurious inference). An important example is provided by the case when attempts are made to check for the presence of nonlinearities by testing the significance of quadratic terms in static panel data models using fixed-effects estimators. In the context of our simple specification, this would involve setting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17730.gif), and a test of the significance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17731.gif) in ([28.14](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3264)) will yield sensible results only if the conditions defined by ([28.29](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3286)) are met. In general, it is possible to falsely reject the linearity hypothesis when there are systematic relations between the slope coefficients and the cross-sectional distribution of the regressors. Therefore, results from nonlinearity tests in panel data models should be interpreted with care. The linearity hypothesis may be rejected not because of the existence of a genuine nonlinear relationship between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17732.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17733.gif), but due to slope heterogeneity.

Finally, it is worth noting that since the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17734.gif) ’s are fixed for each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17735.gif), the nonlinear specification

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17736.gif)(28.30)

cannot be reconciled with ([28.29](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3286)), unless it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17737.gif) varies proportionately with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17738.gif). Clearly, it is possible to allow the slopes, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17739.gif), to vary systematically with some aspect of the cross-sectional distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17740.gif) without requiring ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17741.gif) to be proportional to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-17742.gif), and hence time-varying. However, the validity of these estimates and the inferences based on them critically depend on the extent to which slope coefficients differ across countries, and in the case of static models, whether these differences are systematic. The presence of residual serial correlation could be due to a host of factors: omitted variables, neglected slope heterogeneity in the case of serially correlated regressors, and of course neglected dynamics. The diagnostic statistics provided in the second part of* *Table* [*28.3*](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-52)*, within Example 64, show statistically significant evidence of residual serial* correlation in the case of eight of the twenty countries.[^(*6*)](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-note-160) *It is clear that, even when the slope coefficients are allowed to be estimated freely across countries, residual serial correlation still continues to be a problem, at least in the case of some, if not* all, the countries.[*⁷*](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-note-161) *The usual time series technique for dealing with dynamic misspecification is to estimate error correction models based on ARDL models. ## 28.8.1 Small sample bias

The MG estimator in the case of dynamic panels is biased when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18270.gif) is small, due to the presence of the lagged dependent variable in the model which biases the *OLS* estimator of the short-run coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18271.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18272.gif). Pesaran, Smith, and Im ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-811)) investigate the small sample properties of various estimators of the long-run coefficients for a dynamic heterogeneous panel data model. They find that when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18273.gif) is small the MG estimator can be seriously biased, particularly when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18274.gif) is large relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18275.gif). In particular, for finite ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18276.gif), as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18277.gif) (under the usual panel assumption of independence across groups), the MG estimator still converges to a normal distribution, but with a mean which is not the same as the true value of the parameter under consideration, if the underlying equations contain lagged dependent variables or weakly exogenous regressors. To see this, first note that, for a finite ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18278.gif),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18279.gif)(28.63)

It is easy to see that, due to the presence of lagged dependent variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18280.gif) is not sufficient for eliminating the second term. One needs large enough ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18281.gif) for the bias to disappear. In practice, when the model contains lagged dependent variables, we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18282.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18283.gif) is bounded in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18284.gif) and a function of the unknown underlying parameters. Hence

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18285.gif)

Pesaran and Zhao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-825)) propose a number of bias reduction techniques for the MG estimator of the long-run coefficients in dynamic models. Estimation of such coefficients poses additional difficulties due to the nonlinearity of long-run coefficients in terms of the underlying short-run parameters is an additional source of bias for the MG estimation of dynamic models. In a set of Monte Carlo experiments, Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-528)) showed that the MG estimator is unlikely to be a good estimator when either ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18286.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18287.gif) is small.

Under the assumption that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18288.gif) are fixed and known and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18289.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18290.gif) are independently normally distributed, we can implement the Bayes estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18291.gif) conditional on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18292.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18293.gif), namely

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18294.gif)(28.64)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18295.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18296.gif) This Bayes estimator is a weighted average of the least squares estimator of individual units with the weights being inversely proportional to individual variances. When ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18297.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18298.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18299.gif) the Bayes estimator is asymptotically equivalent to the MG estimator ([28.62](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3372)) (Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-528))).

In practice, the variance components, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18300.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18301.gif) are rarely known. The Monte Carlo studies conducted by Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-528)) show that, following the approach of Lindley and Smith ([1972](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-637)) in assuming that the prior-distributions of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18302.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18303.gif) are independent and are distributed as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18304.gif)(28.65)

yields a Bayes estimator almost as good as the Bayes estimator with known ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18305.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18306.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18307.gif) represents the Wishart distribution with scale matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18308.gif) and degrees of freedom ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18309.gif).

The Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-528)) Bayes estimator is derived under the assumption that the initial observation ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18310.gif) are fixed constants. As discussed in Anderson and Hsiao ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-29), [1982](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-30)), this assumption is clearly unjustifiable for a panel with finite ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18311.gif). However, contrary to the sampling approach where the correct modelling of initial observations is quite important, the Hsiao, Pesaran, and Tahmiscioglu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-528)) Bayesian approach appears to perform fairly well in the estimation of the mean coefficients for dynamic random coefficient models as demonstrated in their Monte Carlo studies.

These *ML* estimators are termed pooled mean group (PMG) estimators in order to highlight the pooling effect of the homogeneity restrictions on the estimates of the long-run coefficients, and the fact that averages across groups are used to obtain group-wide mean estimates of the error-correction coefficients and the other short-run parameters of the model.

Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-799)) propose two different likelihood-based algorithms for the computation of the PMG estimators which are computationally less demanding than estimating the pooled regression. The first is a ‘back-substitution’ algorithm that only makes use of the first derivatives of the log-likelihood function

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18344.gif)(28.69)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18345.gif)(28.70)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18346.gif). Starting with an initial estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18347.gif), say ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18348.gif), estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18349.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18350.gif) can be computed using ([28.69](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3389)) and ([28.70](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3390)), which can then be substituted in ([28.68](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-displayMaths-3388)) to obtain a new estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18351.gif), say ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18352.gif), and so on until convergence is achieved. Alternatively, the PMG estimators can be computed using (a variation of) the Newton-Raphson algorithm which makes use of both the first and the second derivatives. An overview of alternative numerical optimization techniques is provided in Section [A.16](#049_BM_appendixGroupa.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1-div1-395) of Appendix A.

Note that, for small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18353.gif), the PMG estimator (as well as the group-specific estimator) will be subject to the familiar downward bias on the coefficient of the lagged dependent variable. Because the bias is in the same direction for each group, averaging or pooling does not reduce this bias. Bias corrections are available in the literature (e.g., Kiviet and Phillips ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-600))), but these apply to the short-run coefficients. Because the long-run coefficient is a nonlinear function of the short-run coefficients, procedures that remove the bias in the short-run coefficients can leave the long-run coefficient biased. Pesaran and Zhao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-825)) discuss how the bias in the long-run coefficients can be reduced.

**Example 66** *Continuing from Example 65,* *Haque, Pesaran, and Sharma (*[*2000*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-476)*) then allowed for both unrestricted short-run slope heterogeneity and dynamics. To this end, they estimate individual country regressions containing first-order lagged values of the savings rates,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18354.gif). *The MG and pooled mean group (PMG) estimates of the long-run coefficients based on these dynamic individual country regressions are given in* *Table* [*28.5*](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-56). *For ease of comparison, the MG estimator based on a static version of these regressions, as well as the corresponding FE estimates, are reported. Unlike the FE estimates, the consequences of allowing for dynamics on the MG estimates are rather limited. Once again only the coefficients of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18355.gif) *and the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18356.gif) *variables are statistically significant, although the dynamic MG estimates suggest the coefficient of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18357.gif) *variable to be also marginally significant. Finally, the last column of* *Table* [*28.5*](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-56) *provides the pooled mean group estimates of the long-run coefficients, where the short-run dynamics are allowed to differ freely across countries but equality restrictions are imposed on one or more of the long-run coefficients; the rationale being that due to differences in factors such as adjustment costs or the institutional set-up across countries slope homogeneity is more likely to be valid in the long run. The PMG estimates in* *Table* [*28.5*](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-56) *impose the slope homogeneity restrictions only on the long-run coefficients of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18358.gif) *variable. As expected, the PMG estimates are generally more precisely estimated and confirm that, amongst the various determinants of private savings considered by MBS, only the effects of the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18359.gif) *and the* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18360.gif) *variables seem to be reasonably robust to the presence of slope heterogeneity and yield plausible estimates for the offsetting effects of government budget surpluses and government consumption expenditures on private savings across OECD countries.*

There are a number of procedures that can be used to test ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18376.gif), the most familiar of which is the standard ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18377.gif)-test defined by

This problem turns out to be much more serious in the application of the Hausman procedure to the testing problem that concerns us here. ## 28.11.3 *G*-test of Phillips and Sul

Phillips and Sul ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-840)) propose a different type of Hausman test where, instead of comparing two different pooled estimators of the regression coefficients (as discussed in Section [28.11.2](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div2-294)), they propose basing the test of slope homogeneity on the difference between the individual estimates and a suitably defined pooled estimator. ## 28.11.4 Swamy’s test

One possible way of improving on the asymptotic test developed for the *AR* models would be to follow the recent literature and use bootstrap techniques.[¹⁰](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-note-166) Here we make use of a bias-corrected version of the recursive bootstrap procedure.[¹¹](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-note-167)
