## 28.11.8 Application: testing slope homogeneity in earnings dynamics

In this section we examine the slope homogeneity of the dynamic earnings equations with the panel study of income dynamics (*PSID*) data set used in Meghir and Pistaferri ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-686)). Briefly, these authors select male heads aged 25 to 55 with at least nine years of usable earnings data. The selection process leads to a sample of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18646.gif) individuals and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18647.gif) individual-year observations. To obtain a panel data set with a larger ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18648.gif), only individuals with at least 15 time series observations are included in the panel. This leaves us with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18649.gif) individuals and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18650.gif) individual-year observations. Following Meghir and Pistaferri ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-686)), the individuals are categorized into three education groups: High School Dropouts (HSD, those with less than 12 grades of schooling), High School Graduates (HSG, those with at least a high school diploma, but no college degree), and College Graduates (CLG, those with a college degree or more). In what follows, the earning equations for the different educational backgrounds, HSD, HSG, and CLG, are denoted by the superscripts ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18651.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18652.gif), and for the pooled sample by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18653.gif). The numbers of individuals in the three categories are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18654.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18655.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18656.gif). The panel is unbalanced with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18657.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18658.gif), and an average time period of around ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18659.gif) years.

In the research on earnings dynamics, it is standard to adopt a two-step procedure where in the first stage the log of real earnings is regressed on a number of control variables such as age, race and year dummies. The dynamics are then modelled based on the residuals from this first stage regression. The use of the control variables and the grouping of the individuals by educational backgrounds is aimed at eliminating (minimizing) the effects of individual heterogeneities at the second stage.

It is, therefore, of interest to examine the extent to which the two-step strategy has been successful in dealing with the heterogeneity problem. With this in mind we follow closely the two-step procedure adopted by Meghir and Pistaferri ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-686)) and first run regressions of log real earnings, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18660.gif), on the control variables: a square of “age” ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18661.gif), race (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18662.gif)), year dummies (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18663.gif)), region of residence (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18664.gif), and residence in a standard metropolitan statistical area ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18665.gif), for each education group ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18666.gif), separately.[¹³](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-note-169) The residuals from these regressions, which we denote by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18667.gif), are then used in the second stage to estimate dynamics of the earnings process.

Specifically,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18668.gif)

where within each education group ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18669.gif) is assumed to be homogeneous across the different individuals. Our interest is to test the hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18670.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18671.gif) in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18672.gif).

The test results are given in the first panel of [Table 28.6](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-56). The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18673.gif) statistics and the associated bootstrapped ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18674.gif) values by education groups all lead to strong rejections of the homogeneity hypothesis. Judging by the size of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18675.gif) statistics, the rejection is stronger for the pooled sample as compared with the sub-samples, confirming the importance of education as a discriminatory factor in the characterizations of heterogeneity of earnings dynamics across individuals. The test results also indicate the possibility of other statistically significant sources of heterogeneity within each of the education groups, and casts some doubt on the two-step estimation procedure adopted in the literature for dealing with heterogeneity, a point recently emphasized by Browning, Ejrns, and Alvarez ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-163)).

In [Table 28.6](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-tableGroup-56) we also provide a number of different *FE* estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18676.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18677.gif), on the assumption of within group slope homogeneity. Given the relatively small number of time series observations available (on average 18), the bias corrections to the *FE* estimates are quite large. The cross-section error variance heterogeneity also plays an important role in this application, as can be seen from a comparison of *FE* and *WFE* estimates with the latter being larger. Focusing on the bias-corrected *WFE* estimates, we also observe that the persistence of earnings dynamics rises systematically from 0.52 in the case of the school drop outs to 0.72 for the college graduates. This seems sensible, and partly reflects the more reliable job prospects that are usually open to individuals with a higher level of education.

The homogeneity test results suggest that further efforts are needed also to take account of within group heterogeneity. One possibility would be to adopt a Bayesian approach, assuming that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18678.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18679.gif) are draws from a common probability distribution and focus attention on the whole posterior density function of the persistent coefficients, rather than the average estimates that tend to divert attention from the heterogeneity problem. Another possibility would be to follow Browning, Ejrns, and Alvarez ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-163)) and consider particular parametric functions, relating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18680.gif) to individual characteristics as a way of capturing within group heterogeneity. Finally, one could consider a finer categorization of the individuals in the panel; say by further splitting of the education groups or by introducing new categories such as occupational classifications. The slope homogeneity tests provide an indication of the statistical importance of the heterogeneity problem, but are silent as how best to deal with the problem.

| [29](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29) | [Cross-Sectional Dependence in Panels](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29) |

# 29.1 Introduction

This chapter reviews econometric methods for large linear panel data models subject to error cross-sectional dependence. Early panel data literature assumed cross-sectionally independent errors and homogeneous slopes. Heterogeneity across units was confined to unit-specific intercepts, treated as fixed or random (see, e.g., the survey by Chamberlain ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-196))). Dependence of errors was only considered in spatial models, but not in standard panels. However, with an increasing availability of data (across countries, regions, or industries), the panel literature moved from predominantly micro panels, where the cross dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18828.gif)) is large and the time series dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18829.gif)) is small, to models with both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18830.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18831.gif) large, and it has been recognized that, even after conditioning on unit-specific regressors, individual units, in general, need not be cross-sectionally independent.

Ignoring cross-sectional dependence of errors can have serious consequences, and the presence of some form of cross-section correlation of errors in panel data applications in economics is likely to be the rule rather than the exception. Cross correlations of errors could be due to omitted common effects, spatial effects, or could arise as a result of interactions within socioeconomic networks. Conventional panel estimators such as fixed or random effects can result in misleading inference and even inconsistent estimators, depending on the extent of cross-sectional dependence and on whether the source generating the cross-sectional dependence (such as an unobserved common shock) is correlated with regressors (Phillips and Sul ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-840)), Andrews ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-35)), and Sarafidis and Robertson ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-881))). Correlation across units in panels may also have serious drawbacks on commonly used panel unit root tests, since several of the existing tests assume independence. As a result, when applied to cross-sectionally dependent panels, such unit root tests can have substantial size distortions (O’Connell ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-736))). This potential problem has recently given major impetus to the research on panel unit root tests that allow for cross unit correlations. These and other related developments are reviewed in [Chapter 31](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31). If, however, the extent of cross-sectional dependence of errors is sufficiently weak, or limited to a sufficiently small number of cross-sectional units, then its consequences might be unimportant. Consistency of conventional estimators can be affected only when the factors behind cross-correlations are themselves correlated with regressors. The problem of testing for the extent of cross-section correlation of panel residuals and modelling the cross-sectional dependence of errors are therefore important issues.

In the case of panel data models where the cross-section dimension is short and the time series dimension is long, the standard approach to cross-sectional dependence is to consider the equations from different cross-sectional units as a system of seemingly unrelated regression equations (*SURE*), and then estimate it by the generalized least squares techniques (see [Chapter 19](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19) and Zellner ([1962](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-997))). This approach assumes that the factors generating the cross-sectional dependence are not correlated with the regressors, an assumption which is required for the consistency of the *SURE* estimator. Also, if the time series dimension is not sufficiently large, and in particular if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18832.gif), the *SURE* approach is not feasible either.

Currently, there are two main strands in the literature for dealing with error cross-sectional dependence in panels where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18833.gif) is large, namely the spatial econometric and the residual multifactor approaches. The spatial econometric approach assumes that the structure of cross-sectional correlation is related to location and distance among units, defined according to a pre-specified metric given by a ‘connection or spatial’ matrix that characterizes the pattern of spatial dependence according to pre-specified rules. Hence, cross-sectional correlation is represented by means of a spatial process, which explicitly relates each unit to its neighbours (see Whittle ([1954](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-976)), Moran ([1948](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-701)), Cliff and Ord ([1973](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-235), [1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-236)), Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40), [2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-41)), Haining ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-456), [Chapter 7](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7)), and the recent survey by Lee and Yu ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-627))). This approach, however, typically does not allow for slope heterogeneity across the units and requires *a priori* knowledge of the weight matrix. Spatial econometric literature is reviewed in [Chapter 30](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30).

The residual multifactor approach assumes that the cross dependence can be characterized by a small number of unobserved common factors, possibly due to economy-wide shocks that affect all units, albeit with different intensities (see [Chapter 19](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19) for an introduction to common factor models). Geweke ([1977](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-393)) and Sargent and Sims ([1977](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-890)) introduced dynamic factor models, which have more recently been generalized to allow for weak cross-sectional dependence by Forni and Lippi ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-368)), Forni et al. ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-365), [2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-366)). This approach does not require any prior knowledge regarding the ordering of individual cross-sectional units or a weight matrix used in the spatial econometric literature.

The main focus of this chapter is on estimation and inference in the case of large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18834.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18835.gif) panel data models with a common factor error structure. We provide a synthesis of the alternative approaches proposed in the literature (such as principal components and common correlated effects approaches), with particular focus on key assumptions and their consequences from the practitioner’s view point. In particular, we discuss robustness of estimators to cross-sectional dependence of errors, the consequences of coefficient heterogeneity, panels with strictly or weakly exogenous regressors, including panels with a lagged dependent variable, and highlight how to test for residual cross-sectional dependence.

The outline of the chapter is as follows: an overview of the different types of cross-sectional dependence is provided in Section [29.2](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-323). The analysis of cross-sectional dependence using a factor error structure is presented in Section [29.3](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-324). A review of estimation and inference in the case of large panels with a multifactor error structure and strictly exogenous regressors is provided in Section [29.4](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-325), and its extension to models with lagged dependent variables and weakly exogenous regressors is given in Section [29.5](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-326). A review of tests of error cross-sectional dependence in static and dynamics panels is presented in Section [29.7](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-328), and Section [29.8](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-329) discusses the application of common correlated effects estimators and tests of error cross-sectional dependence to unbalanced panels.

# 29.2 Weak and strong cross-sectional dependence in large panels

A better understanding of the extent and nature of cross-sectional dependence is an important issue in the analysis of large panels. This section defines and discusses the notions of weak and strong cross-sectional dependence and considers the measurement of the degree of cross-sectional dependence using the exponent of cross-sectional dependence introduced in (Bailey, Kapetanios, and Pesaran [2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-779)).

Chudik, Pesaran, and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-225)) define the concepts of weak and strong cross-sectional dependence based on the limiting behaviour of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18894.gif) at a given point in time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18895.gif), as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18896.gif).

The above concepts can also be defined conditional on a given information set, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18909.gif). The choice of the conditioning set largely depends on the nature of the underlying processes and the purpose of the analysis. For example, in the case of dynamic stationary models, the information set could contain all lagged realizations of the process ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18910.gif), that is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18911.gif), whilst for dynamic non-stationary models, such as unit root processes, the information included in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18912.gif), could start from a finite past. The conditioning information set could also contain contemporaneous realizations, which might be useful in applications where a particular unit has a dominant influence on the rest of the units in the system. For further details, see Chudik and Pesaran ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-222)).

A particular form of a CWD process arises when pair-wise correlations take non-zero values only across finite subsets of units that do not spread widely as the sample size increases. As we shall see in [Chapter 30](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30), a similar situation arises in the case of spatial processes, where direct dependence exists only amongst adjacent observations, and indirect dependence is assumed to decay with distance.

Since ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18960.gif), it follows from ([29.5](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3471)) that both the spectral radius and the column norm of the covariance matrix of a CSD process will be increasing at the rate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18961.gif). Similar situations also arise in the case of time series processes with long memory or strong temporal dependence where autocorrelation coefficients are not absolutely summable. Along the cross-sectional dimension, common factor models represent examples of strong cross-sectional dependence.

The common factors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18978.gif), simultaneously affect all cross-sectional units, albeit with different degrees as measured by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-18979.gif). Examples of observed common factors that tend to affect all households’ and firms’ consumption and investment decisions include interest rates and oil prices. Aggregate demand and supply shocks represent examples of common unobserved factors. In multifactor models, interdependence arises from reaction of units to some external events. Further, according to this representation, correlation between any pair of units does not depend on how far these observations are apart, and violates the distance decay effect that underlies the spatial interaction model.

The relationship between the notions of CSD and CWD and the definitions of weak and strong factors are explored in the following theorem.

**Theorem 47** *Consider the factor model* *(*[29.8](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3475)*)* *and suppose that Assumptions CF.1-CF.2 hold, and there exists a positive constant* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19097.gif) *in the range* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19098.gif) *such that condition* *(*[*29.13*](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3482)) *is met for any* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19099.gif). *Then the following statements hold:*

*(i)* *The process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19100.gif) *is cross-sectionally weakly dependent at a given point in time* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19101.gif), *if* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19102.gif), *which includes cases of weak, semi-weak or semi-strong factors,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19103.gif) *for* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19104.gif).

*(ii)* *The process* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19105.gif) *is cross-sectionally strongly dependent at a given point in time* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19106.gif), *if and only if there exists at least one strong factor.*

Proof is provided in Chudik, Pesaran, and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-225)).

Weak, strong and semi-strong common factors may be used to represent very general forms of cross-sectional dependence. For example, as we will see in [Chapter 30](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30), a factor process with an infinite number of weak factors, and no idiosyncratic errors can be used to represent spatial processes. In particular, the spatial model ([29.9](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3477)) can be represented by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19171.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19172.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19173.gif). Strong factors can be used to represent the effect of the cross-sectional units that are “dominant” or pervasive, in the sense that they impact all the other units in the sample and their effect does not vanish as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19174.gif) tends to infinity (Chudik and Pesaran ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-222))). As outlined in Example 70 below, a large city may play a dominant role in determining house prices nationally (Holly, Pesaran, and Yamagata ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-515))). Semi-strong factors may exist if there is a cross-sectional unit or an unobserved common factor that affects only a subset of the units and the number of affected units rise more slowly than the total number of units. Estimates of the exponent of cross-sectional dependence reported by Bailey, Kapetanios, and Pesaran ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-779)) suggest that for typical large macroeconomic data sets the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19175.gif) fall in the range of 0.77–0.92, which fall short of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19176.gif) assumed in the factor literature. For cross-country quarterly real GDP growth, inflation and real equity prices the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19177.gif) are much closer to unity and tend to be around 0.97.

**Example 70** (The diffusion of UK house prices) *Holly, Pesaran, and Yamagata (*[*2011*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-515)*) study the diffusion of (log) of quarterly house prices,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19178.gif) *, over time and across London and 11 UK regions in the years from 1973q4 to 2008q2. The authors assume that one of the regions, the London area, to be denoted as region* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19179.gif) *, is dominant in the sense that shocks to it propagate to other regions simultaneously and over time. Conversely, shocks to the remaining regions are assumed to have little immediate impact on region* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19180.gif) *—although there may be some lagged effects of shocks from the other regions onto region* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19181.gif). *Hence, the following first-order linear error correction specification for region* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19182.gif) *is specified by*

*While for the remaining regions the price equation is specified to be*

*In the above equations,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19186.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19187.gif) *are the spatial lags of prices defined as*

At the same time, prices in other regions are allowed to cointegrate with London as well as with their neighbouring regions. The assumption that* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19194.gif) *is weakly exogenous in the equations for* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19195.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19196.gif), *can be tested using the procedure advanced by Wu (*[*1973*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-989)*). OLS estimation of* *equations (*[*29.24)–(29.25*](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3503))*, and the* *Wu (*[*1973*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-989)*)* *statistic are reported in Table*[*29.1*](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-tableGroup-57). *The error correction term measured relative to London is statistically significant in five regions (East Anglia, East Midlands, West Midlands, South West, and North), while the error correction term measured relative to neighboring regions is statistically significant only in the price equation for Scotland. The estimates of short-term dynamics show a considerable degree of heterogeneity in lag lengths and short-term dynamics. Surprisingly, the own lag effect (*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19197.gif) *) is rather weak and generally statistically insignificant, except for the region ‘North’. Finally, the contemporaneous effect of London house prices (*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19198.gif) *) is* *sizeable and statistically significant in all regions. Figure*[*29.1*](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-figureGroup-20) *shows the effect of a unit shock to London house prices on London over time, compared to the impact effects of the same shock on regions ordered by their distance from London, for different horizons,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19199.gif). *This figure clearly shows the levelling off of the effect of shocks over time and across regions, indicating that the decay along the geographical dimension* *seems to be slower as compared with the decay along the time dimension. The effects of a shock to London on itself, die away and are largely dissipated after two years. By contrast, the effects of the same shock on other regions takes much longer to dissipate, the further the region is from London. This finding is in line with other empirical evidence on the rate of spatial as compared to temporal decay discussed* *in Whittle (*[*1954*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-976)*). For further details see* *Holly, Pesaran, and Yamagata (*[*2011*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-515)*).*

The number of factors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19325.gif), is assumed to be fixed relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19326.gif), and in particular ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19327.gif). The idiosyncratic errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19328.gif), could be CWD, for example, being generated by a spatial process, or, more generally, by a weak factor structure. For estimation purposes, as in the case of panels with group effects, the factor loadings, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19329.gif), could be either random or fixed unknown coefficients. We distinguish between the homogeneous coefficient case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19330.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19331.gif), and the heterogeneous case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19332.gif) are random draws from a given distribution. In the latter case, we assume that the object of interest is the mean coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19333.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19334.gif). When the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19335.gif), are strictly exogenous and the deviations ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19336.gif) are distributed independently of the errors and the regressors, the mean coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19337.gif) can be consistently estimated using pooled as well as mean group estimation procedures. But only mean group estimation will be consistent if the regressors are weakly exogenous and/or if the deviations are correlated with the regressors/errors.[⁵](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-178)

The assumption of slope homogeneity is also crucially important for the derivation of the asymptotic distribution of the pooled or the mean group estimators of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19338.gif). Under slope homogeneity, the asymptotic distribution of the estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19339.gif) typically converges at the rate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19340.gif), whilst under slope heterogeneity the rate is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19341.gif). In view of the uncertainty regarding the assumption of slope heterogeneity, non-parametric estimators of the variance matrix of the pooled and mean group estimators are proposed.[⁶](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-179) In the following sub-sections we review a number of different estimators of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19342.gif) proposed in the literature.

## 29.4.1 Principal components estimators

The principal components (*PC*) approach proposed by Coakley, Fuertes, and Smith ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-238)) and Bai ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-53)), by requiring that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19347.gif) tends to a positive definite matrix, implicitly assumes that all the unobserved common factors in ([29.27](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3507)) are strong. Coakley, Fuertes, and Smith ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-238)) consider the panel data model with strictly exogenous regressors and homogeneous slopes (i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19348.gif)), and propose a two-stage estimation procedure. In the first stage, *PC*s are extracted from the *OLS* residuals as proxies for the unobserved variables, and in the second step the estimated factors are treated as observable and the following augmented regression is estimated

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19349.gif)(29.28)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19350.gif) is an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19351.gif) vector of principal components of the residuals computed in the first stage. The resultant estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19352.gif) is consistent for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19353.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19354.gif) large, so long as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19355.gif) and the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19356.gif), are uncorrelated. However, if the factors and the regressors are correlated, as is likely to be the case in practice, the two-stage estimator becomes inconsistent (Pesaran ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-774))).

Building on Coakley, Fuertes, and Smith ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-238)), Bai ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-53)) has proposed an iterative method which consists of alternating the PC method applied to *OLS* residuals and the least squares estimation of ([29.28](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3508)), until convergence. In particular, to simplify the exposition suppose ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19357.gif). Bai ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-53)) shows that such an estimator is consistent even if common factors are correlated with the explanatory variables. Specifically, the least square estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19375.gif) obtained from the above procedure, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19376.gif), is consistent if both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19377.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19378.gif) tend to infinity, without any restrictions on the ratio ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19379.gif). When in addition ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19380.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19381.gif) converges at the rate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19382.gif), but the limiting distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19383.gif) does not necessarily have a zero mean. Nevertheless, Bai shows that the asymptotic bias can be consistently estimated and proposes a bias corrected estimator.

It is important to bear in mind that PC-based estimators generally require the determination of the unknown number of strong factors (PCs), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19384.gif), to be included in the second stage of estimation, and this can introduce some degree of sampling uncertainty into the analysis. There is now an extensive literature that considers the estimation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19385.gif), assuming all the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19386.gif) factors to be strong. See, for example, Bai and Ng ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-57), [2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-59)), Kapetanios ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-566), [2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-568)), Amengual and Watson ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-19)), Hallin and Liska ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-461)), Onatski ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-738), [2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-739)), Ahn and Horenstein ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-3)), Breitung and Pigorsch ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-155)), Choi and Jeong ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-213)), and Harding ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-478)). There are also a number of useful surveys by Bai and Ng ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-60)), Stock and Watson ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-927)), and Breitung and Choi ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-150)), amongst others, that can be consulted for detailed discussions of these methods and additional references. An extensive Monte Carlo investigation into the small sample performance of different selection/estimation methods is provided in Choi and Jeong ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-213)). See also Section [19.5.2](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19-div2-187).

## 29.4.2 Common correlated effects estimator

Pesaran ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-774)) suggests the common correlated effects (*CCE*) estimation procedure that consists of approximating the linear combinations of the unobserved factors by cross-section averages of the dependent and explanatory variables, and then running standard panel regressions augmented with these cross-section averages. Both pooled and mean group versions are proposed, depending on the assumption regarding the slope homogeneity.

The advantage of the non-parametric estimators ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19469.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19470.gif) is that they do not require knowledge of the form of weak cross-sectional dependence of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19471.gif), nor the knowledge of serial correlation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19472.gif). An important question is whether the non-parametric variance estimators ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19473.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19474.gif) can be used in both cases of homogeneous and heterogeneous slopes. As established in Pesaran and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-820)), the asymptotic distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19475.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19476.gif) depends on nuisance parameters when slopes are homogeneous (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19477.gif)), including the nature of cross-section correlations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19478.gif) and their serial correlation structure. However, it can be shown that the robust non-parametric estimators ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19479.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19480.gif) are consistent when the regressor-specific components, **v**![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19481.gif), are independently distributed across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19482.gif).

The *CCE* continues to be applicable even if the rank condition ([29.31](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3517)) is not satisfied. Failure of the rank condition can occur if there is an unobserved factor for which the average of the loadings in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19483.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19484.gif) equations tends to a zero vector. This could happen if, for example, the factor in question is weak, in the sense defined above. Another possible reason for failure of the rank condition is if the number of unobservable factors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19485.gif), is larger than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19486.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19487.gif) is the number of the unit-specific regressors included in the model. In such cases, common factors cannot be estimated from cross-section averages. However, it is possible to show that the cross-section means of the slope coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19488.gif), can still be consistently estimated, under the additional assumption that the unobserved factor loadings, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19489.gif), in equation ([29.27](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3507)) are independently and identically distributed across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19490.gif), and of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19491.gif), **v**![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19492.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19493.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19494.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19495.gif), are uncorrelated with the loadings attached to the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19496.gif). The consequences of the correlation between loadings ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19497.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19498.gif) for the performance of CCE estimators in the rank deficient case are documented in Sarafidis and Wansbeek ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-882)). The following example illustrates the implications of such correlations.

In economic applications such non-stochastic limits do not seem plausible. For example, when factor loadings have zero means, then variances of per capita consumption, output, and investment will all tend to zero, which seems unlikely. Similarly, in the case of capital asset pricing models,* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19568.gif) *, the assumption that* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19569.gif) *have a zero mean is equivalent to saying that there exist risk free portfolios that have positive excess returns—again a very unlikely scenario.*

An advantage of the *CCE* approach is that it yields consistent estimates under a variety of situations. Kapetanios, Pesaran, and Yamagata ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-570)) consider the case where the unobservable common factors follow unit root processes and could be cointegrated. They show that the asymptotic distribution of panel estimators in the case of *I(1)* factors is similar to that in the stationary case. Pesaran and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-820)) prove consistency and asymptotic normality for *CCE* estimators when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19570.gif) are generated by a spatial process. Chudik, Pesaran, and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-225)) prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the *CCE* estimators when errors are subject to a finite number of unobserved strong factors and an infinite number of weak and/or semi-strong unobserved common factors as in ([29.20)–(29.21](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3493)), provided that certain conditions on the loadings of the infinite factor structure are satisfied. A further advantage of the CCE approach is that it does not require an *a priori* knowledge of the number of unobserved common factors.

In a Monte Carlo (MC) study, Coakley, Fuertes, and Smith ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-239)) compare ten alternative estimators for the mean slope coefficient in a linear heterogeneous panel regression with strictly exogenous regressors and unobserved common (correlated) factors. Their results show that, overall, the mean group version of the *CCE* estimator stands out as the most efficient and robust. These conclusions are in line with those in Kapetanios and Pesaran ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-569)) and Chudik, Pesaran, and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-225)), who investigate the small sample properties of *CCE* estimators and the estimators based on principal components. The *MC* results show that *PC* augmented methods do not perform as well as the *CCE* approach, and can lead to substantial size distortions, due, in part, to the small sample errors in the number of factors selection procedure. In a theoretical study, Westerlund and Urbain ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-970)) investigate the merits of the *CCE* and *PC* estimators in the case of homogeneous slopes and known number of unobserved common factors and find that, although the PC estimates of factors are more efficient than the cross-sectional averages, the CCE estimators of slope coefficients generally perform the best.

**Example 72** *There exists extensive literature on the relationship between long-run economic growth and investment in physical capital. Simple exogenous growth theories, such as the Solow model, predict a positive association between investment and the level of per capita GDP, but no relation between investment* *and steady-state growth rates (Barro and Sala-i-Martin (*[*2003*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-91)*)). This conclusion has been supported by a number of empirical studies (see, e.g., the review of* *empirical literature in Easterly and Levine (*[*2001*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-312)*)).* *Bond, Leblebicioglu, and Schiantarelli (*[*2010*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-134)*) reconsider this problem, using data for seventy-five economies over the period 1960–2005, distinguishing between OECD and non-OECD countries. Results show that investment as a share of GDP has a large and statistically significant effect on long-run growth rates, using the full sample of seventy-five countries and sub-sample of non-OECD countries. However, this evidence is weaker for OECD countries, for which the estimated coefficient* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19606.gif) *is not statistically significant. This result may reflect important differences across countries in the growth process.*

# 29.5 Dynamic panel data models with a factor error structure

The problem of estimation of panels subject to cross-section error dependence becomes much more complicated once the assumption of strict exogeneity of the unit-specific regressors is relaxed. One important example is the panel data model with lagged dependent variables and unobserved common factors (possibly correlated with the regressors)[⁹](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-182)

for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19613.gif). It is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19614.gif), and the dynamic processes have started a long time in the past. As in Section [29.4](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-325), we distinguish between the case of homogeneous coefficients, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19615.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19616.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19617.gif), and the heterogeneous case, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19618.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19619.gif) are randomly distributed across units and the object of interest are the mean coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19620.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19621.gif). This distinction is more important for dynamic panels, since not only is the rate of convergence affected by the presence of coefficient heterogeneity, but, as shown by Pesaran and Smith ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-808)), pooled least squares estimators are no longer consistent in the case of dynamic panel data models with heterogeneous coefficients. See also Section [28.6](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div1-314).

The *QMLE* of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19629.gif) is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19630.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19631.gif) is a compact set assumed to contain the true parameter values, and

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19632.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19633.gif),

Both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19635.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19636.gif) minimize the same objective function and therefore, when the same set of regressors is considered, these two estimators are numerically the same. But there are important differences in their bias-corrected versions also considered in Bai ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-53)) and Moon and Weidner ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-700)). The latter paper allows for more general assumptions on regressors, including the possibility of weak exogeneity, and adopts a quadratic approximation of the profile likelihood function, which allows the authors to work out the asymptotic distribution and to conduct inference on the coefficients.

Moon and Weidner (MW) show that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19637.gif) is a consistent estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19638.gif), as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19639.gif) without any restrictions on the ratio ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19640.gif). To derive the asymptotic distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19641.gif), MW require ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19642.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19643.gif) as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19644.gif), and assume that the idiosyncratic errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19645.gif) are cross-sectionally independent. Under certain high level assumptions, they show that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19646.gif) converges to a normal distribution with a non-zero mean, which is due to two types of asymptotic bias. The first follows from the heteroskedasticity of the error terms, as in Bai ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-53)), and the second is due to the presence of weakly exogenous regressors. The authors provide consistent estimators of these two components, and propose a bias-corrected *QMLE*.

There are two important considerations that should be borne in mind when using the *QMLE* proposed by MW. First, it is developed for the case of slope homogeneity, namely under ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19647.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19648.gif) This assumption, for example, rules out the inclusion of fixed-effects into the model, which can be quite restrictive in practice, although the unobserved factor component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19649.gif), does in principle allow for fixed-effects if the first element of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19650.gif) can be constrained to be unity at the estimation stage. A second consideration is the small sample properties of *QMLE* in the case of models with fixed-effects, which are of primary interest in empirical applications. Simulations reported in Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)) suggest that the bias correction does not go far enough and the *QMLE* procedure could yield tests which are grossly over-sized. To check the robustness of the *QMLE* to the presence of fixed-effects, we carried out a small Monte Carlo experiment in the case of a homogeneous AR(1) panel data model with fixed-effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19651.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19652.gif). Using ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19653.gif) replications, the bias of the bias-corrected *QMLE*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19654.gif), turned out to be ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19655.gif), and tests based on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19656.gif) were grossly oversized with size exceeding 60 per cent.

## 29.5.3 Dynamic *CCE* estimators

The *CCE* approach as it was originally proposed in Pesaran ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-774)) does not cover the case where the panel includes a lagged dependent variable or weakly exogenous regressors.[¹⁰](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-183) Extension of the *CCE* approach to dynamic panels with heterogeneous coefficients and weakly exogenous regressors is proposed by Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)). In what follows we refer to this extension as ‘dynamic *CCE*’.

The inclusion of a lagged dependent variable amongst the regressors has three main consequences for the estimation of the mean coefficients. The first is the well-known time series bias, which affects the individual specific estimates and is of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19679.gif). The second consequence is that the full rank condition becomes necessary for consistent estimation of the mean coefficients unless the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19680.gif) is serially uncorrelated. The third complication arises from the interaction of dynamics and coefficient heterogeneity, which leads to infinite lag-order relationships between unobserved common factors and cross-section averages of the observables when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19681.gif) is large. This issue also arises in cross-sectional aggregation of heterogeneous dynamic models. See Section [15.8](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-div1-159) and [Chapter 32](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32) and references cited therein.

To illustrate these complications, using ([29.49](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3541)) and recalling assumption ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19682.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19683.gif), then we have

The rank condition is necessary for the consistency of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19771.gif) because the unobserved factors are allowed to be correlated with the regressors. If the unobserved common factors were serially uncorrelated (but still correlated with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19772.gif)), then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19773.gif) is consistent also in the rank deficient case, despite the inconsistency of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19774.gif), so long as factor loadings are independently, identically distributed across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19775.gif). The convergence rate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19776.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19777.gif) due to the heterogeneity of the slope coefficients. Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)) show that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19778.gif) converges to a normal distribution as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19779.gif) such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19780.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19781.gif) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19782.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19783.gif). The ratio ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19784.gif) needs to be restricted for conducting inference, due to the presence of small time series bias. In the full rank case, the asymptotic variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19785.gif) is given by the variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19786.gif) alone. When the rank condition does not hold, but factors are serially uncorrelated, then the asymptotic variance depends also on other parameters, including the variance of factor loadings. In both cases the asymptotic variance can be consistently estimated non-parametrically, as in ([29.40](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3526)).

Monte Carlo experiments in Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)) show that the dynamic *CCE* approach performs reasonably well (in terms of bias, RMSE, size and power). This is particularly the case when the parameter of interest is the average slope of the regressors (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19787.gif)), where the small sample results are quite satisfactory even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19788.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19789.gif) are relatively small (around ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19790.gif)). But the situation is different if the parameter of interest is the mean coefficient of the lagged dependent variable (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19791.gif)). In the case of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19792.gif) the *CCEMG* estimator suffers from the well known time series bias and tests based on it tend to be over-sized, unless ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19793.gif) is sufficiently large. To reduce this bias, Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)) consider application of the half-panel jackknife procedure (Dhaene and Jochmans ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-285))), and the recursive mean adjustment procedure (So and Shin ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-918))), both of which are easy to implement.[¹⁴](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-187) The proposed jackknife bias-corrected *CCEMG* estimator is found to be more effective in mitigating the time series bias, but it cannot deal fully with the size distortion when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19794.gif) is relatively small. Improving the small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19795.gif) sample properties of the CCEMG estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19796.gif) in the heterogeneous panel data models still remains a challenge.

The application of the *CCE* approach to static panels with weakly exogenous regressors (namely without lagged dependent variables) has not yet been investigated in the literature. In order to investigate whether the standard *CCE* mean group and pooled estimators could be applied in this setting, we conducted some additional Monte Carlo experiments. We used the following data generating process

The rank condition in these experiment does not hold, but this does not seem to cause any major problems for the *CCE* mean group estimator, which performs very well (in terms of bias and *RMSE*) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19853.gif) and for all values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19854.gif). # 29.6 Estimating long-run coefficients in dynamic panel data models with a factor error structure

The previous section focused on the estimation of short-run coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19857.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19858.gif) in the dynamic panel data model ([29.49](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3541))–([29.50](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3542)). However, in many empirical applications the objective of interest is often the long-run coefficients defined by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19859.gif)(29.63)

Long-run relationships are of great importance in economics. The concept of ‘long-run relations’ is typically associated with the steady-state solution of a structural macroeconomic model. Often the same long-run relations can also be obtained from arbitrage conditions within and across markets. As a result, many long-run relationships in economics are free of particular model assumptions; examples include purchasing power parity, uncovered interest parity and the Fisher inflation parity.

Table 29.3. Small sample properties of *CCEMG* and *CCEP* estimators of mean slope coefficients in panel data models with weakly and strictly exogenous regressors

![Table_Image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-table-59.jpg) ![Table_Image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-table-60.jpg)

Estimation of long-run relations in the case of pure time series models has been discussed in Section [6.5](#016_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-6-div1-70), and for dynamic panel data models without cross-sectional dependence has been considered in [Chapter 28](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28) (Sections [28.6](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div1-314)–[28.10](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div1-318)). This section extends the estimation of long-run effects to dynamic panels with multifactor error structure.

There are two approaches to estimating long-run coefficients. One approach, is to estimate the individual short-run coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19860.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19861.gif) in the *ARDL* relation ([29.49](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3541)) and then compute the estimates of long-run effects using formula ([29.63](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3562)) with the short-run coefficients replaced by their estimates (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19862.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19863.gif)) discussed in Section [29.5](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-326). This is the ‘*ARDL* approach to the estimation of long-run effects.’ This approach is consistent irrespective of whether the underlying variables are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19864.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19865.gif), and whether the regressors in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19866.gif) are strictly or weakly exogenous. These robustness properties are clearly important in empirical research. However, the *ARDL* approach also has its own drawbacks. Most importantly, the sampling uncertainty could be large, especially when the speed of convergence towards the long-run relation is rather slow and the time dimension is not sufficiently long. This is readily apparent from ([29.63](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3562)), since even a small change to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19867.gif) could have a large impact on the estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19868.gif), when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19869.gif) is close to unity. In this respect, a correct specification of lag-orders could be quite important for the performance of the *ARDL* estimates. Moreover, the estimates of the short-run coefficients are subject to small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19870.gif) bias.

An alternative approach, proposed by Chudik et al. ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-220)), is to estimate the long-run coefficients ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19871.gif) *directly,* without first estimating the short run coefficients. This is possible by observing that the *ARDL* model ([29.49](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3541)) can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19872.gif)(29.64)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19873.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19874.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19875.gif). We shall refer to the direct estimation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19876.gif) based on the distributed lag (DL) representation ([29.64](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-displayMaths-3563)) as the ‘DL approach to the estimation of long-run effects’.
