The advantage of the DL approach is its robustness to residual serial correlation, breaks in error processes, and dynamic misspecifications. However, unlike the *ARDL* approach, the DL procedure could be subject to simultaneity bias (when there are feedbacks from lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19914.gif) to the regressors in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19915.gif)). Nevertheless, the extensive Monte Carlo experiments reported in Chudik et al. ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-220)) suggest that the endogeneity bias of the DL approach is more than compensated for by its better small sample performance as compared with the *ARDL* procedure when the time dimension is not very large. *ARDL* seems to dominate DL only if the time dimension is sufficiently large and the underlying *ARDL* model is correctly specified.

# 29.7 Testing for error cross-sectional dependence

In this section we provide an overview of alternative approaches to testing cross-sectional independence or weak dependence of the errors in the following panel data model[¹⁵](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-189)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19929.gif)(29.69)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19930.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19931.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19932.gif), are assumed to be fixed unknown coefficients, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19933.gif) is a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19934.gif)-dimensional vector of regressors. We consider both cases where the regressors are strictly and weakly exogenous, as well as when they include lagged values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19935.gif).

The literature on testing for error cross-sectional dependence in large panels follows two separate strands, depending on whether the cross-sectional units are ordered or not. In the case of ordered data sets (which could arise when observations are spatial or belong to given economic or social networks) tests of cross-sectional independence that have high power with respect to such ordered alternatives have been proposed in the spatial econometrics literature. A prominent example of such tests is Moran’s I test. See Moran ([1948](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-701)) with further developments by Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40)), Anselin and Bera ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-42)), Haining ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-456)), and Baltagi, Song, and Koh ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-81)).

In the case of cross-section observations that do not admit an ordering, tests of cross-sectional dependence are typically based on estimates of pair-wise error correlations (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19936.gif)) and are applicable when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19937.gif) is sufficiently large so that relatively reliable estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19938.gif) can be obtained. An early test of this type is the Lagrange multiplier (*LM*) test of Breusch and Pagan ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-159)) which tests the null hypothesis that *all* pair-wise correlations are zero, namely that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19939.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19940.gif). This test is based on the average of the *squared* estimates of pair-wise correlations, and under standard regularity conditions it is shown to be asymptotically (as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19941.gif)) distributed as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19942.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19943.gif) degrees of freedom. The *LM* test tends to be highly over-sized in the case of panels with relatively large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19944.gif).

In what follows, we review the various attempts made in the literature to develop tests of cross-sectional independence when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19945.gif) is large and the cross-sectional units are unordered. But before proceeding further, we first need to consider the appropriateness of the null hypothesis of cross-sectional ‘independence’ or ‘uncorrelatedness’, that underlies the *LM* test of Breusch and Pagan ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-159)), namely that all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19946.gif) are zero for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19947.gif), when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19948.gif) is large. The null that underlies the *LM* test is sensible when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19949.gif) is small and fixed as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19950.gif). But when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19951.gif) is relatively large and rising with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19952.gif), it is unlikely to matter if, out of the total ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-19953.gif) pair-wise correlations, only a few are non-zero. Accordingly, Pesaran ([2015](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-779)) argues that the null of cross-sectionally uncorrelated errors, defined by

The rejection of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20071.gif) could be caused by cross-sectional dependence, heteroskedasticity, slope heterogeneity, and/or non-normal errors. Simulation results reported in Baltagi, Feng, and Kao ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-75)) show that this test performs well in the case of homoskedastic, normal errors, strictly exogenous regressors, and homogeneous slopes, although it is oversized for panels with large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20072.gif) and small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20073.gif), and is sensitive to non-normality of disturbances. Joint assumption of homoskedastic errors and homogeneous slopes is quite restrictive in applied work, and therefore the use of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20074.gif) statistics as a test of cross-sectional dependence should be approached with care.

However, the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20085.gif) test can lead to severe over-rejection when the slopes are in fact heterogeneous and the fixed-effects estimators are used. The problem of testing for cross-sectional dependence in limited dependent variable panel data models with strictly exogenous covariates has also been investigated by Hsiao, Pesaran, and Pick ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-527)). In this paper the authors derive an *LM* test and show that in terms of the generalized residuals of Gourieroux et al. ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-413)), the test reduces to the *LM* test of Breusch and Pagan ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-159)). However, not surprisingly as with the linear panel data models, the *LM* test based on generalized residuals tends to over-reject in panels with large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20090.gif). They then develop a *CD* type test based on a number of different residuals, and using Monte Carlo experiments they find that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20091.gif) test preforms well for most combinations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20092.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20093.gif).

The existing literature on testing for error cross-sectional dependence, with the exception of Sarafidis et al. ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-883)), has mostly focused on the case of strictly exogenous regressors. # 29.8 Application of *CCE* estimators and *CD* tests to unbalanced panels

*CCE* estimators can be readily extended to unbalanced panels, a situation which frequently arises in practice. Denote the set of cross-sectional units with the available data on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20221.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20222.gif) in period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20223.gif) as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20224.gif) and the number of elements in the set by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20225.gif). Initially, we suppose that data coverage for the dependent variables and regressors is the same and later we relax this assumption. The main complication of applying *CCE* estimator to the case of unbalanced panels is the inclusion of cross-section averages in the individual regressions. There are two possibilities regarding the units to include in the computation of cross-section averages, either based on the same number of units or based on a varying number of units. In both cases, cross-section averages should be constructed using at least a minimum number of units (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20226.gif) If the same units are used, we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20227.gif)

for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20228.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20229.gif) and the starting and ending points of the sample ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20230.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20231.gif) are chosen to maximize the use of data subject to the constraint ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20232.gif).[¹⁹](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-note-196) The second possibility utilizes data in a more efficient way,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20233.gif)

for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20234.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20235.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20236.gif) are chosen such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20237.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20238.gif). Both procedures are likely to perform similarly when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20239.gif) is reasonably large, and the occurrence of missing observations is random. In cases where new cross-sectional units are added to the panel over time and such additions can have systematic influences on the estimation outcomes, it might be advisable to de-mean or de-trend the observations for individual cross-sectional units before computing the cross-section averages to be used in the *CCE* regressions.

Now suppose that the cross-section coverage differs for each variable. For example, the dependent variable can be available only for *OECD* countries, whereas some of the regressors could be available for a larger set of countries. Then it is preferable to utilize also data on non-*OECD* countries to maximize the number of units for the computation of cross-section averages for each of the individual variables.

The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20240.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20241.gif) tests can also be readily extended to unbalanced panels. Denote by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20242.gif), the set of dates over which time series observations on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20243.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20244.gif) are available for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20245.gif) individual, and denote the number of elements in the set by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20246.gif). For each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20247.gif) compute the *OLS* residuals based on the full set of available time series observations. # 30.1 Introduction

This chapter reviews econometric methods for linear panel data models that exhibit spatial dependence. Spatial dependence may arise from local interaction of individuals, or from unobserved characteristics that show persistence across space or over a network. In order to measure spatial correlation, we need to specify the modalities of how agents interact and define a metric of distance between individuals. ‘Local’ does not need to be specified in terms of physical space, but can be related to other types of metrics, such as the economic, policy, or social distance.

A sizeable literature has analysed the role of interactions and externalities in several different branches of economics, both at a theoretical and at an empirical level. For instance, a rich literature in microeconomics explores the decision-making process of an agent embedded in a system of social relations, where he/she can watch other agents’ actions (Bala and Goyal ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-67)), Brock and Durlauf ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-160))). A key finding is that local interaction may allow some forms of behaviour to propagate to the entire population (Ellison ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-328))). Recent studies in macroeconomics have theorized the existence of strategic complementaritis that produce aggregate fluctuations in industrial market economies (Cooper and Haltiwanger ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-250)); Binder and Pesaran ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-121))). Factors such as input–output linkages, demand complementarities and human capital spillovers have been used to explain observed comovements not attributable to aggregate shocks (Aoki ([1996](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-44))). Finally, literature on endogenous growth has emphasized the importance of linkages between countries in the analysis of regional income growth (Rivera-Batiz and Romer ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-858)); Barro and Sala-i-Martin ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-91)); Arbia ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-45))). According to this literature, relations established with neighbouring regions, in the form of demand linkages, interacting labour markets and knowledge spillovers, also due to the increased economic integration between developed economies, are determinants of regional economic growth.

Spatial correlation can also be caused by a variety of measurement problems often encountered in applied work, or by the particular sampling scheme used to select units. An example is the lack of concordance between the delineation of observed spatial units, such as the region or the country, and the spatial scope of the phenomenon under study (Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40))). When the sampling scheme is clustered, potential correlation may also arise between respondents belonging to the same cluster. Indeed, units sharing observable characteristics such as location or industry, may also have similar unobservable characteristics that would cause the regression disturbances to be correlated (Moulton ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-706)), Pepper ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-759))).

This chapter provides a survey of econometric methods proposed to deal with spatial dependence in the context of linear panel data regression models.

# 30.2 Spatial weights and the spatial lag operator

In spatial econometrics, neighbourhood effects are typically characterized by means of a non-negative *spatial weights matrix*. The rows and columns of this matrix, often denoted by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20309.gif), correspond to the cross-section observations (e.g., individuals, regions, or countries), and the generic element, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20310.gif), can be interpreted as the strength of potential interaction between units ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20311.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20312.gif). The specification of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20313.gif) is typically based on some measure of distance between units, using for example contiguity or geographic proximity, or more general metrics, such as economic (Conley ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-247)), Pesaran, Schuermann, and Weiner ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-794))), political (Baicker ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-63))), or social distance (Conley and Topa ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-248))). The weights, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20314.gif), are set exogenously, although there are some recent attempts at endogenizing the determination of the weights. By convention, the diagonal elements of the weighting matrix are set to zero, implying that an observation is not a neighbour to itself. To facilitate the interpretation of the estimates, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20315.gif) is typically row-standardized so that the sum of the weights for each row is one, ensuring that all the weights are between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20316.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20317.gif). Finally, although most empirical works assume that weights are time-invariant, these can vary over time (see, for example, Druska and Horrace ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-302)) and Cesa-Bianchi et al. ([2012)](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-193)).

An important role in spatial econometrics is played by the notion of *spatial lag operator*. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20318.gif) be a time-invariant ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20319.gif) spatial weights matrix. The spatial lag of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20320.gif) is defined by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20321.gif), with generic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20322.gif) element given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20323.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20324.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20325.gif) row of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20326.gif). Hence, a spatial lag operator constructs a new variable that is a weighted average of neighbouring observations, with weights reflecting distance among units. The incorporation of these spatial lags into a regression equation is considered in the next section.

# 30.3 Spatial dependence in panels

## 30.3.2 Spatial error models

Another way to include spatial dependence in the regression equation is to allow the disturbances to be spatially correlated. Consider the simple linear regression in stacked form

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20404.gif)(30.3)

where the notation is as above. There exist few main approaches to assign a spatial structure to the error term, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20405.gif) ;[²](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30-note-198) the intent is to represent the covariance as a simpler, lower dimensional matrix than the unconstrained version

One way is to define the covariance between two observations directly as a function of the distance between them. Accordingly, the covariance matrix for the cross-section at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20406.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20407.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20408.gif) is a parameter vector, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20409.gif) is a suitable distance decay function, such as the negative exponential (Dubin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-303)), Cressie ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-255)); see also Example 75). The decaying function suggests that the disturbances should become uncorrelated when the distance separating the observations is sufficiently large. One shortcoming of this method is that it requires the specification of a functional form for the distance decay, which is subject to a degree of arbitrariness.

An alternative strategy consists of specifying a spatial process for the error term, which relates each unit to its neighbours through ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20410.gif). The most widely used model is the spatial autoregressive (SAR) specification. Proposed by Cliff and Ord ([1969](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-234)) and Cliff and Ord ([1981](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-236)), the SAR process is a variant of the model introduced by Whittle ([1954](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-976))

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20411.gif)(30.4)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20412.gif) is a scalar parameter, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20413.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20414.gif). Assuming that the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20415.gif) is invertible, (30.4) can be rewritten in reduced form as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20416.gif)

Other spatial processes suggested to model spatial error dependence, although less used in the empirical literature, are the spatial moving average (*SMA*) and the spatial error component (*SEC*) specifications. The first, proposed by Haining ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-455)) (see also Huang ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-532))), assumes that

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20420.gif) is as above. Its covariance matrix is

According to the SEC specification, introduced by Kelejian and Robinson ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-583)),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20422.gif)(30.6)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20423.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20424.gif). The covariance matrix induced by this model is

A major distinction between the *SAR* and the other two specifications is that under *SAR* there is an inverse involved in the covariance matrix. This has important consequences on the range of dependence implied by its covariance matrix. Indeed, even if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20426.gif) contains few non-zero elements, the covariance structure induced by the *SAR* is not sparse, linking all the units in the system to each other, so that a perturbation in the error term of one unit will be ultimately transmitted to all other units. Conversely, for the *SMA* and *SEC*, the off-diagonal non-zero elements of the covariance matrix are those corresponding to the non-zero elements in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20427.gif).

Conventional panel estimators introduced in [Chapter 26](#041_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-26), such as the fixed-effects (*FE*) or random effects (*RE*) estimators of slope coefficients in equation (30.3) with spatially dependent errors, are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20428.gif) -consistent under broad regularity conditions and strictly exogenous regressors. However, these estimators are in general not efficient since the covariance of errors is non-diagonal and the elements along its main diagonal are in general not constant.

In the case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20449.gif) is row and column standardized the latter condition reduces to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20450.gif).

It is also interesting to observe that, under these conditions, the above process can be represented by a factor process with an infinite number of weak factors, and no idiosyncratic error, by setting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20451.gif) where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20452.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20453.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20454.gif). Under the bounded column and row norms of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20455.gif), the loadings in the above factor structure satisfy condition (29.12) in [Chapter 29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29), and hence ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20456.gif) will be a cross-sectionally weakly dependent (CWD) process.

# 30.4 Estimation

## 30.4.1 Maximum likelihood estimator

The theoretical properties of quasi-maximum likelihood (*ML*) estimator in a single cross- sectional framework have been studied by Ord ([1975](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-742)), Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40)), and Lee ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-619)), among others. More recently, considerable work has been undertaken to investigate the properties of *ML* estimators in panel data contexts, in the presence of spatial dependence and unobserved, time-invariant heterogeneity (Elhorst ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-320)); Baltagi, Song, and Koh ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-81)); Baltagi, Egger, and Pfaffermayr ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-74)); and Lee and Yu ([2010a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-623))).

A set of joint and conditional specification Lagrange multiplier (*LM*) tests for spatial effects within the *RE* framework are proposed by Baltagi, Egger, and Pfaffermayr ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-74)). These statistics allow for testing of the model (30.13)–(30.16) against its restricted counterparts: the Anselin model, the Kapoor, Kelejian, and Prucha model, and the random effects model without spatial correlation (see also Baltagi, Song, and Koh ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-81)); Baltagi and Liu ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-79)); and Baltagi and Yang ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-82))).

As in the non-spatial case, the choice between the *FE* spatial model and its *RE* counterpart can be based on the Hausman test. The properties of a Hausman type specification test and an *LM* statistic for testing the *FE* versus *RE* specification are studied by Lee and Yu ([2010c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-625)).

## 30.4.4 Instrumental variables and *GMM*

In the presence of heteroskedastic disturbances, the *ML* estimator for spatial models under the assumption of homoskedastic innovations is generally inconsistent (Lin and Lee ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-636))). As an alternative, instrumental variables (*IV* ) and generalized method of moments (*GMM*) techniques have been suggested.

In a single cross-sectional setting, Kelejian and Robinson ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-582)) and Kelejian and Prucha ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-577)) propose a simple IV strategy to deal with the endogeneity of the spatially lagged dependent variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20603.gif), that consists of using as instruments the spatially lagged (exogenous) explanatory variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20604.gif) (see Section [10.8](#021_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-10-div1-114) and the example therein). As shown by Mutl and Pfaffermayr ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-716)), the *IV* approach can be easily adapted to spatial panel data either with fixed or random effects (Wooldridge ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-984))). The reader is also referred to Lee ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-618)) for a discussion on the choice of optimal instruments.

*GMM* estimation of spatial regression models in a single cross-sectional setting was originally advanced by Kelejian and Prucha ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-578)). The authors focus on a regression equation with SAR disturbances, and suggest the use of three moment conditions that exploit the properties of disturbances implied by a standard set of assumptions. Estimation consists of solving a nonlinear optimization problem, which yields a consistent estimator under a number of regularity conditions. Considerable work has been carried to extend this procedure in various directions. Liu, Lee, and Bollinger ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-642)) and Lee and Liu ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-621)) suggest a set of moments that encompass Kelejian and Prucha conditions as special cases. They focus on a spatial lag model with SAR disturbances (30.4) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20605.gif), and consider a vector of linear and quadratic conditions in the error term, where the matrices appearing in the quadratic forms have bounded row and column norms (see also Lee ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-620))). In panel (30.3), assuming ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20606.gif) are fixed parameters, consider ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20607.gif) quadratic moments of the type

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20608.gif)(30.25)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20609.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20610.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20611.gif) are non-stochastic matrices having bounded row and column sum matrix norms. Lee and Liu ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-621)) note that the matrices ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20612.gif) have zero diagonal elements, so that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20613.gif). Interestingly, this assumption renders the *GMM* procedure robust to unknown, cross-sectional heteroskedasticity. The empirical counterpart of (30.25) is obtained by dropping the expectation operator, replacing ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20614.gif) by a consistent estimator (e.g., the IV estimator).

Lee and Liu ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-621)) focus on the problem of selecting the matrices appearing in the vector of linear and quadratic moment conditions, in order to obtain the lowest variance for the *GMM* estimator. Lee and Liu ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-622)) extend this framework to estimate the *SAR* model with higher-order spatial lags. Kelejian and Prucha ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-581)) generalize their original work to include spatial lags in the dependent variable and allow for heteroskedastic disturbances. This setting is extended by Kapoor, Kelejian, and Prucha ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-572)) to estimate a spatial panel regression model with group error components, and by Moscone and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-705)) for a panel with fixed-effects. Druska and Horrace ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-302)) have introduced the Keleijan and Prucha *GMM* within the framework of a panel with SAR disturbances, time dummies and time varying spatial weights, while Fingleton ([2008a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-359), [2008b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-360)) has extended it to the case of a regression with spatial moving average disturbances. Egger, Larch, Pfaffermayr, and Walde ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-314)) compare the small sample properties of *ML* and *GMM* estimators, observing that they perform similarly under the assumption of normally and non-normally distributed homoskedastic disturbances. However, one advantage of the *GMM* procedure over *ML* is that it is computationally simpler, especially when dealing with unbalanced panels (Egger, Pfaffermayr, and Winner ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-315))).

# 30.5 Dynamic panels with spatial dependence

Considerable work has been undertaken on estimation of panel data models that feature both spatial dependence and temporal dynamics. A variety of spatiotemporal models have been proposed in the literature (see, for example, Anselin, Le Gallo, and Jayet ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-43)) and Lee and Yu ([2010b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-624))), most of which can be cast as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20662.gif)(30.27)

This model is stable if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20663.gif) assuming that the spatial weight matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20664.gif), is row and column standardized. Yu, de Jong, and Lee ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-992)) derive *ML* estimators for the fixed-effects specification of the above model and show that when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20665.gif) is large relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20666.gif), the *ML* estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal. But if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20667.gif), the limit distribution of the *ML* estimators is not centered around ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20668.gif), in which case the authors propose a bias corrected estimator. See Yu, de Jong, and Lee ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-992)); and Lee and Yu ([2010b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-624)) for further details. IV and *GMM* estimation of a stationary spatiotemporal model is considered in Kukenova and Monteiro ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-610)).

## 30.6.1 Temporal heterogeneity

Temporal heterogeneity may be incorporated in a spatial version of the seemingly unrelated regression equations (*SURE*) approach, as suggested by Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40)). See also Mur, Lpez, and Herrera ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-712)). # 30.7 Non-parametric approaches

Non-parametric regression techniques based on certain mixing conditions applied to space and time have also been considered in the literature, as robust alternatives to *ML* and *GMM* estimation techniques. Variants of the Newey and West ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-728)) heteroskedasticity autocorrelation consistent (*HAC*) estimators employed in the time series literature are adapted to spatial models by Conley ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-247)) and Driscoll and Kraay ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-301)) in the context of *GMM* estimators of spatial panel data regression models (see also Pinkse, Slade, and Brett ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-844))).[³](#045_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-30-note-206) More recently, Kelejian and Prucha ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-580)) have proposed a spatial heteroskedasticity autocorrelation consistent (*SHAC*) estimator for a single cross-sectional regression with spatially correlated errors. This approach approximates the true covariance matrix with a weighted average of cross products of regression errors, where each element is weighted by a function of (possible multiple) distances between cross-sectional units. This procedure can be extended for estimation of the covariance of the FE and MG estimators for a panel of type (30.3), with fixed-effects and spatial errors (30.7), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20721.gif) is allowed to be serially correlated. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20722.gif) be an arbitrary scalar function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20723.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20724.gif) the window size for the time series dimension, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20725.gif) a kernel function such that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20726.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20727.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20728.gif) satisfy a set of regularity conditions (see Kelejian and Prucha ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-580))). A Newey-West type *SHAC* estimator of the variance of the classic FE estimator (30.29) is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20729.gif)(30.38)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20730.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20731.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20732.gif), with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20733.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20734.gif). For the MG estimator we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20735.gif)(30.39)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20736.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20737.gif) column of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20738.gif). One shortcoming of this method is that its finite sample properties may be quite poor when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20739.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20740.gif) are not sufficiently large (Pesaran and Tosetti ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-820))). An alternative strategy has been suggested by Bester, Conley, and Hansen ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-108)), who, using results taken from Ibragimov and Mller ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-535)), propose dividing the sample in groups so that group-level averages are approximately independent, and accordingly suggest an *HAC* estimator based on a discrete group-membership metric. However, the validity of this approach relies on the capacity of the researcher to construct groups whose averages are approximately uncorrelated.

Robinson ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-866)) considers smoothed nonparametric kernel regression estimation. Under this approach, rather than employing mixing conditions, it is assumed that regression errors follow a general linear process representation covering both weak (spatial) dependence as well as dependence at longer ranges. Robinson ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-866)) establishes consistency of the Nadaraya-Watson kernel estimate and derives its asymptotic distribution (see also Hallin, Lu, and Tran ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-462))).

Spatial filtering techniques can also be used to control for spatial effects (Tiefelsdorf and Griffith ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-942))). Under this framework, spatial dependence in the regression is proxied by a linear combination of a subset of eigenvectors of a matrix function of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20741.gif). Hence, estimation is carried out by least squares applied to auxiliary regressions where the observed regressors are augmented with these artificial variables. The reader is referred to Tiefelsdorf and Griffith ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-942)) and Griffith ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-435)) for further discussion.

# 30.8 Testing for spatial dependence

Spatial econometrics literature proposes a number of statistics for testing the null hypothesis of spatial independence, i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20742.gif) in model (30.3). Tests of cross-sectional dependence in the absence of ordering (i.e., when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20743.gif) is not known) are reviewed in Section [29.7](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div1-328). The majority of the tests in the spatial literature have been studied only in the case of a single cross-section. One of the most commonly used is the Moran statistic (Moran ([1950](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-702)); Pinkse ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-843)); Kelejian and Prucha ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-579))), which, extended to a panel setup, takes the form

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20744.gif)(30.40)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20745.gif) is a consistent estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20746.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20747.gif) is a consistent estimator of regression errors. The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20748.gif) is asymptotically normally distributed (see Kelejian and Prucha ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-579))), and, for large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20749.gif), is equivalent to the Burridge ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-170)) *LM* statistic. Another test that has attracted considerable interest in the spatial literature is the Geary ([1954](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-386))’s ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20750.gif). This statistic, based on the average squared differences of residuals, shares very similar characteristics with the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20751.gif). See Hepple ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-504)) for a comparison and discussion on the properties of Geary’s ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20752.gif) and Moran’s statistics.

The information on the distance among units can also be used to obtain ‘local’ versions of some statistics proposed in the panel literature to test against generic forms of cross-sectional dependence. For example, the local ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20753.gif) test proposed by Pesaran ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-773)) is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20754.gif)(30.41)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20755.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20756.gif) is the sample pair-wise correlation coefficient computed between fixed-effects residuals of units ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20757.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20758.gif). The ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20759.gif) test is asymptotically normally distributed. Similarly, it is possible to derive local versions of other tests proposed in the panel literature such as the *LM* test given by (29.74). See also Pesaran, Ullah, and Yamagata ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-821)) and Moscone and Tosetti ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-704)).

Robinson ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-867)) has proposed a general class of statistics that, like ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20760.gif), is based on quadratic forms in *OLS* regression residuals, where the matrices appearing in the quadratic forms satisfy certain sparseness conditions. The author shows that these statistics have a limiting chi-square distribution under the null hypothesis of error independence. Special cases of this class of statistics can be interpreted as *ML* tests directed against specific alternative hypotheses.

# 30.9 Further reading

Textbook treatment of the spatial econometrics literature can be found in Anselin ([1988](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-40)); Arbia ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-45)); and LeSage and Pace ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-629)), while a description of recent developments of these techniques can be found in Anselin, Le Gallo, and Jayet ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-43)), Lee and Yu ([2010b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-624)) and Lee and Yu ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-626)). The reader is referred to McMillen ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-685)); Fleming ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-363)); and LeSage and Pace ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-629)) for an extension of spatial techniques to nonlinear regression models.

| [31](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31) | [ Unit Roots and Cointegration in Panels](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31) |

# 31.1 Introduction

This chapter provides a review of the theoretical literature on testing for unit roots and cointegration in panels where the time dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20786.gif) ), and the cross-section dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20787.gif) ) are relatively large. In cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20788.gif) is large (say over 100) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20789.gif) small (less than 50) the analysis can proceed only under restrictive assumptions such as dynamic homogeneity and/or local cross-sectional dependence as in spatial autoregressive or moving average models. In cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20790.gif) is small (say less than ten) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20791.gif) is relatively large, standard time series techniques applied to systems of equations, such as the seemingly unrelated regression equations (SURE), can be used and the panel aspect of the data should not pose new technical difficulties.

One of the primary reasons behind the application of unit root and cointegration tests to a panel of cross-section units was to gain statistical power and to improve on the poor power of their univariate counterparts. This was supported by the application of what might be called the first generation panel unit root tests to real exchange rates, output and inflation. For example, the augmented Dickey–Fuller ([1979](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-289)) test, reviewed in [Chapter 15](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15), is typically not able to reject the hypothesis that the real exchange rate is nonstationary. By contrast, panel unit root tests applied to a collection of industrialized countries generally find that real exchange rates are stationary, thereby lending empirical support to the purchasing power parity hypothesis (e.g., Coakley and Fuertes ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-237)) and Choi ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-209))).

Testing the unit root and cointegration hypotheses by using panel data instead of individual time series involves several additional complications. First, as seen in previous chapters, the analysis of panel data generally involves a substantial amount of unobserved heterogeneity, rendering the parameters of the model cross-section specific. Second, the assumption of cross-sectional independence is inappropriate in many empirical applications, particularly in the analysis of real exchange rates mentioned above. To overcome these difficulties, variants of panel unit root tests are developed that allow for different forms of cross-sectional dependence (see Section [31.4](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-div1-345)). Third, the panel test outcomes are often difficult to interpret if the null of the unit root or cointegration is rejected. The best that can be concluded is that ‘a significant fraction of the cross-section units is stationary or cointegrated’. Conventional panel tests do not provide explicit guidance as to the size of this fraction or the identity of the cross-section units that are stationary or cointegrated. To deal with issue, recent studies have proposed methods for estimating the fraction of non-stationary series in the panel, and for classifying the individual series into stationary and non-stationary sets (see (Pesaran [2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-778))). Fourth, with unobserved ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20792.gif) common factors affecting some or all of the variables in the panel, it is also necessary to consider the possibility of cointegration between the variables across the groups (cross-section cointegration) as well as within group cointegration (see Section [31.5](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-div1-346)). Finally, the asymptotic theory is considerably more complicated due to the fact that the sampling design involves a time as well as a cross-section dimension. For example, applying the usual Dickey–Fuller test to a panel data set introduces a bias that is not present in the case of a univariate test. Furthermore, a proper limit theory has to take account of the relationship between the increasing number of time periods and cross-section units (see Phillips and Moon ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-837))).

In comparison with panel unit root tests, the analysis of cointegration in panels is still at an early stages of its development. So far the focus of the panel cointegration literature has been on residual based approaches, although there has been a number of attempts at the development of system approaches as well. As in the case of panel unit root tests, such tests are developed based on homogenous and heterogeneous alternatives. The residual based tests were developed to ward against the ‘spurious regression’ problem that can also arise in panels when dealing with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20793.gif) variables. Such tests are appropriate when it is known a priori that at most there can be only one within group cointegration in the panel. System approaches are required in more general settings where more than one within group cointegrating relation might be present, and/or there exist unobserved common ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20794.gif) factors.

Having established a cointegration relationship, the long-run parameters can be estimated efficiently using techniques similar to those proposed in the case of single time series models. Specifically, fully-modified OLS procedures, the dynamic OLS estimator and estimators based on a vector error correction representation were adapted to panel data structures. Most approaches employ a homogeneous framework, that is, the cointegration vectors are assumed to be identical for all panel units, whereas the short-run parameters are panel specific. Although such an assumption seems plausible for some economic relationships (like the PPP hypothesis mentioned above) there are other behavioural relationships (like the consumption function or money demand), where a homogeneous framework seems overly restrictive. On the other hand, allowing all parameters to be individual specific would substantially reduce the appeal of a panel data study. It is therefore important to identify parameters that are likely to be similar across panel units whilst at the same time allowing for sufficient heterogeneity of other parameters. This requires the development of appropriate techniques for testing the homogeneity of a sub-set of parameters across the cross-section units. When ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20795.gif) is small relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20796.gif) standard likelihood ratio based statistics can be used. Groen and Kleibergen ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-441)) provide an application. Testing for parameter homogeneity in the case of large panels poses new challenges that require further research (see Section [28.11](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div1-319)).

# 31.2 Model and hypotheses to test

Assume that time series ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20797.gif) on the cross-section units ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20798.gif) are generated for each ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20799.gif) by a simple first-order autoregressive, *AR*(1), process

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20800.gif)(31.1)

where the initial values, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20801.gif), are given, and the errors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20802.gif) are identically, independently distributed across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20803.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20804.gif) with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20805.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20806.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20807.gif). These processes can also be written equivalently as simple Dickey–Fuller (DF) regressions

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20808.gif)(31.2)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20809.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20810.gif). In further developments of the model it is also helpful to write (31.1) or (31.2) in mean-deviations forms ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20811.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20812.gif). The corresponding DF regression in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20813.gif) is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20814.gif)(31.3)

Most panel unit root tests are designed to test the null hypothesis of a unit root for each individual series in a panel. Accordingly, the null hypothesis of interest is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20815.gif)(31.4)

that is, all time series are independent random walks. The formulation of the alternative hypothesis is instead a controversial issue that critically depends on which assumptions one makes about the nature of the homogeneity/heterogeneity of the panel. First, under the assumption that the autoregressive parameter is identical for all cross-section units, we can consider

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20816.gif)

The panel unit root statistics motivated by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20817.gif) pools the observations across the different cross-section units before forming the ‘pooled’ statistic (see, e.g., Harris and Tzavalis ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-480)) and Levin, Lin, and Chu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-630))). One drawback of tests based on such alternative hypotheses is that they tend to have power even if only a few of the units are stationary; hence a rejection of the null hypothesis, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20818.gif), is not convincing evidence that a significant proportion of the series are indeed stationary. In particular, Westerlund and Breitung ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-968)) show that the local power of the Levin, Lin, and Chu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-630)) test is greater than that of the Im, Pesaran, and Shin ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-537)) test, based on a less restrictive alternative, also when not all individual series are stationary. A further drawback in using ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20819.gif) is that this is likely to be unduly restrictive, particularly for cross-country studies involving differing short-run dynamics. For example, such a homogeneous alternative seems particularly inappropriate in the case of the PPP hypothesis, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20820.gif) is taken to be the real exchange rate. There are no theoretical grounds for the imposition of the homogeneity hypothesis, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20821.gif), under PPP. At the other extreme, there is the alternative hypothesis stating that at least one of the series in the panel is generated by a stationary process

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20822.gif)

Such an alternative hypothesis is at the basis of panel unit root tests proposed by Chang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-201)) and Chang ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-202)). We observe that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20823.gif) is only appropriate when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20824.gif) is finite, namely within the multivariate model with a fixed number of variables analyzed in the time series literature. On the contrary, in the case of large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20825.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20826.gif), panel unit root tests will lack power if the alternative, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20827.gif), is adopted. For large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20828.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20829.gif) panels it is reasonable to entertain alternatives that lie somewhere between the two extremes of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20830.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20831.gif). In this context, a more appropriate alternative is given by the heterogeneous alternative

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20832.gif)(31.5)

such that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20833.gif)(31.6)

Using the above specification the null hypothesis is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20834.gif) while ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20835.gif) can be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20836.gif)

In other words, rejection of the unit root null hypothesis can be interpreted as providing evidence in favour of rejecting the unit root hypothesis for a non-zero fraction of panel members as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20837.gif). The tests developed against the above heterogeneous alternatives, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20838.gif), operate directly on the test statistics for the individual cross-section units using (standardized) simple averages of the underlying individual statistics or their suitable transformations such as rejection probabilities (see, among others, Choi ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-209)), Im, Pesaran, and Shin ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-537)), and Pesaran ([2007b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-776))).

**Remark 8** *The heterogeneity of panel data models used in cross-country analysis introduces a new kind of asymmetry in the way the null and the alternative hypotheses are treated, which is not usually present in the univariate time series (or cross-sectional) models. This is because the same null hypothesis is imposed across all* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20839.gif) *but the specification of the alternative hypothesis is allowed to vary with* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20840.gif). *This asymmetry is assumed away in homogeneous panels. However, as demonstrated in* *Pesaran and Smith* ([*1995*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-808)), *neglected heterogeneity (even if purely random) can lead to spurious results in dynamic panels. Therefore, in cross-country analysis where slope heterogeneity is a norm, the asymmetry of the null and the alternative hypotheses has to be taken into account. The appropriate response critically depends on the relative size of* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20841.gif) *and* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20842.gif). *In large* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20843.gif) -*heterogeneous panel data models with small* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20844.gif) (*say around* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20845.gif)) *it is only possible to devise sufficiently powerful unit root tests which are informative in some average sense, namely whether the null of a unit root can be rejected in the case of a significant fraction of the countries in the panel*.[¹](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-note-207) *To identify the exact proportion of the sample for which the null hypothesis is rejected, one requires country-specific data sets with* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20846.gif) *sufficiently large. But if* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20847.gif) *is large enough for reliable country-specific inferences to be made, then there seems little rationale in pooling countries into a panel*.

In the rest of the chapter we will focus on panel unit root tests designed for one of the alternative hypotheses ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20848.gif) or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-20849.gif). However, we observe that, despite the differences in the way the two classes of test view the alternative hypothesis, both types of test can be consistent against both types of the alternative. See, for example, the discussion in Westerlund and Breitung ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-968)).

## 31.3.2 Asymptotic power of tests

It is interesting to compare the asymptotic power of test statistics against the sequence of local alternatives

A similar result is found by Moon, Perron, and Phillips ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-698)) for the test suggested by Breitung ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-146)).
