Westerlund ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-967)) recommends using a parametric estimate of the long-run variance based on an autoregressive representation. This transformation of the lagged dependent variable eliminates the nuisance parameters in the asymptotic distribution of the ADF statistic and, therefore, the correction for the numerator of the corrected ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21128.gif) -statistic of Levin, Lin, and Chu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-630)) is the same as in the case without short-run dynamics.

Pedroni and Vogelsang ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-758)) have proposed a test statistic that avoids the specification of the short-run dynamics by using an autoregressive approximation. Their test statistic is based on the pooled variance ratio statistic

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21129.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21130.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21131.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21132.gif) is the untruncated Bartlett kernel estimator defined as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21133.gif). As has been shown by Kiefer and Vogelsang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-592)) and Breitung ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-147)), the limiting distribution of such ‘non-parametric’ statistics does not depend on nuisance parameters involved by the short run dynamics of the processes. Accordingly, no adjustment for short-run dynamics is necessary.

## 31.3.5 Other approaches to panel unit root testing

An important problem of combining Dickey–Fuller type statistics in a panel unit root test is that they involve a nonstandard limiting distribution. If the panel unit root statistic is based on a standard normally distributed test statistic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21134.gif), then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21135.gif) has a standard normal limiting distribution even for a finite ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21136.gif). In this case no correction terms need to be tabulated to account for the mean and the variance of the test statistic.

Chang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-201)) proposes a nonlinear instrumental variable (IV ) approach, where the transformed variable

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21137.gif)

with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21138.gif) is used as an instrument for estimating ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21139.gif) in the regression ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21140.gif) (which may also include deterministic terms and lagged differences). Since ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21141.gif) tends to zero as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21142.gif) tends to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21143.gif) the trending behaviour of the nonstationary variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21144.gif) is eliminated. Using the results of Chang, Park, and Phillips ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-203)), Chang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-201)) showed that the Wald test of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21145.gif) based on the nonlinear IV estimator possesses a standard normal limiting distribution. Another important property of the test is that the nonlinear transformation also takes account of possible contemporaneous dependence among the cross-sectional units. Accordingly, Chang’s panel unit root test is also robust against cross-sectional dependence.

It should be noted that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21146.gif) with a maximum (minimum) at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21147.gif) ). Therefore, the choice of the parameter ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21149.gif) is crucial for the properties of the test. First, the parameter should be proportional to the inverse of the standard deviations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21150.gif). Chang notes that, if the time dimension is short, the test slightly over-rejects the null and therefore she proposes the use of a larger value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21151.gif) to correct for the size distortion.

An alternative approach to obtain an asymptotically standard normal test statistic is to adjust the given samples in all cross-sections so that they all have sums of squares ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21152.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21153.gif) as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21154.gif). In other words, the panel data set becomes an unbalanced panel with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21155.gif) time periods in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21156.gif) unit. Chang calls this setting the ‘equi-squared sum contour’, whereas the traditional framework is called the ‘equi-sample-size contour’. The nice feature of this approach is that it yields asymptotically standard normal test statistics. An important drawback is, however, that a large number of observations may be discarded by applying this contour which may result in a severe loss of power.

## 31.3.6 Measuring the proportion of cross-units with unit roots

A strand of literature proposes methods for estimating the proportion of stationary units, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21185.gif) (or, equivalently, the fraction of the panel having unit roots, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21186.gif) ) in the panel, rather than looking at the non-stationarity properties of individual series in the panel (see Pesaran ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-778))). In the context of testing for output and growth convergence, Pesaran ([2007a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-775)) suggests using the proportion of unit root tests applied to pairs of log per capita output gaps across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21187.gif) economies, for which the null hypothesis of non-stationarity is rejected at a given significance level, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21188.gif). He shows that, although the underlying individual unit root tests are not cross-sectionally independent, under the null hypothesis of non-stationarity such average rejection statistic converges to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21189.gif), as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21190.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21191.gif) jointly tend to infinity. Similarly, Ng ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-732)) shows that, if a fraction, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21192.gif), of the panel is made of stationary units, with the remaining series having unit roots, the cross-sectional variance of the panel will have a linear trend that increases exactly at rate ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21194.gif). Hence, she suggests a statistic for the proportion of non-stationary units (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21195.gif) ) based on the time average of the sample cross-sectional variance. While these procedures deliver an estimate of the fraction of (non)stationary units, they are not designed to identify which units are stationary. After rejection of the null hypothesis of unit roots for each individual series in a panel, it is often of interest to identify which series can be considered stationary and which can be deemed non-stationary. Kapetanios ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-565)) and Chortareas and Kapetanios ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-214)) propose a sequential panel selection method that consists of applying the Im, Pesaran, and Shin ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-537)) panel unit root test sequentially on progressively smaller fractions of the original data set, where the reduction is carried out by dropping series for which there is evidence of stationarity, signalled by low individual ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21196.gif) -statistics. A similar approach is taken by Smeeks ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-912)), who proposes testing on user-defined fractions of the panel, using panel unit root tests based on order statistics and computing the corresponding critical values by block bootstrap. Hanck ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-466)) and Moon and Perron ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-697)) apply methods from the literature on multiple testing to classify the individual series into stationary and non-stationary sets. In particular, Moon and Perron ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-697)) suggest the use of the so-called false discovery rate (FDR), given by the expected fraction of series classified as I(0) that are in fact I(1), as a useful diagnostic on the aggregate decision. In the computation of the FDR, the authors estimate the fraction of true null hypotheses by applying the Ng ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-732)) approach described above.

The GLS approach cannot be used if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21261.gif) since in this case the estimated covariance matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21262.gif) is singular. Maddala and Wu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-664)) and Chang ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-202)) have suggested a bootstrap procedure that improves the size properties of the GLS test.

An alternative approach based on ‘panel corrected standard errors’ (PCSE) is considered by Jönsson ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-556)) and Breitung and Das ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-151)). In the model with weak dependence, the variance of the OLS estimator ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21265.gif) is consistently estimated by

If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21267.gif) is followed by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21268.gif) the robust ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21269.gif) statistic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21270.gif) is asymptotically standard normally distributed (Breitung and Das ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-151))).

If it is assumed that the cross-correlation is due to common factors, then the largest eigenvalue of the error covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21271.gif), is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21272.gif) and the robust PCSE approach breaks down. Specifically, Breitung and Das ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-152)) show that in this case ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21273.gif) is distributed as the ordinary Dickey–Fuller test applied to the first principal component.

In the case of a single unobserved common factor, Pesaran ([2007b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-776)) suggests a simple modification of the usual test procedure. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21274.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21275.gif). The cross-section augmented Dickey–Fuller (CADF) test is based on the following regression

In this regression the additional variables ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21277.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21278.gif) are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21279.gif) -consistent estimators for the rescaled factors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21280.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21281.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21282.gif). To test the unit root hypothesis in a heterogenous panel, the average of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21285.gif) individual CADF ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21286.gif) -statistics (or suitably truncated version of them) can be used. Coakley, Kellard, and Snaith ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-240)) apply the CADF test to real exchange rates of fifteen OECD countries.

Pesaran, Smith, and Yamagata ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-804)) have extended the cross-sectionally augmented panel unit root test proposed by Pesaran ([2007b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-776)) to the case of a multifactor error structure. They propose utilizing the information contained in a number of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21287.gif) additional variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21288.gif), that together are assumed to share the common factors of the series of interest, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21289.gif). The basic idea is to exploit information regarding the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21290.gif) unobserved factors that are shared by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21291.gif) observed time series (or covariates) in addition to the series under consideration. The requirement of finding such additional variables seems quite plausible in the case of panel data sets from economics and finance where economic agents often face common economic environments. Most macroeconomic theories postulate the presence of the same unobserved common factors (such as shocks to technology, tastes and fiscal policy), and it is therefore natural to expect that many macroeconomic variables, such as interest rates, inflation and output share the same factors. If anything, it would be difficult to find macroeconomic time series that do not share one or more common factors. For example, in testing for unit roots in a panel of real outputs one would expect the unobserved common shocks to output (that originate from technology) to also manifest themselves in employment, consumption and investment. In the case of testing for unit roots in inflation across countries, one would expect the unobserved common factors that correlate inflation rates across countries to also affect short-term and long-term interest rates across markets and economies. The basic idea of using covariates to deal with a multiple factor structure is intuitive and easy to implement—the ADF regression for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21292.gif) is simply augmented with cross-section averages of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21293.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21294.gif).[⁷](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-note-213) Pesaran, Smith, and Yamagata ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-804)) show that the extended version of the Pesaran ([2007b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-776)) test, denoted as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21295.gif), is valid so long as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21296.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21297.gif) is the assumed maximum number of factors. Importantly, the estimation of the true number of factors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21298.gif) is not needed so long as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21299.gif). Furthermore, it is not required that all of the factors be strong. Following Bai and Ng ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-61)), Pesaran, Smith, and Yamagata ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-804)) also consider a panel unit root test based on simple averages of cross-sectionally augmented Sargan-Bhargava-type statistics, denoted as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21300.gif). Monte Carlo simulations reported by these authors suggest that both ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21301.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21302.gif) tests have the correct size across different experiments and with various combinations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21303.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21304.gif) being considered. The experimental results also show that the proposed ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21305.gif) test has satisfactory power, which for some combinations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21306.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21307.gif) tends to be higher than that of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21308.gif) test.

# 31.5 Cross-unit cointegration

As argued by Banerjee, Marcellino, and Osbat ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-88)) panel unit root tests may be severely biased if the panel units are cross-cointegrated, namely if under the null hypothesis (of unit roots) one or more linear combinations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21309.gif) are stationary. This needs to be distinguished from the case where the errors are cross-correlated without necessarily involving cointegration across the cross-section units. Under the former, two or more cross-sectional units must share at least one common stochastic trend. Such a situation is likely to occur if the PPP hypothesis is examined (see Lyhagen ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-655)); Banerjee, Marcellino, and Osbat ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-88)); and Wagner ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-955))).

The tests proposed by Moon and Perron ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-695)) and Pesaran ([2007b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-776)) are based on the model

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21310.gif)(31.37)

Under the unit root hypothesis, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21311.gif), this equation yields

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21312.gif)

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21313.gif)

Clearly, under the null hypothesis all cross-section units are related to the common stochastic component, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21314.gif), albeit with varying effects, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21315.gif). This framework rules out cross-unit cointegration as under the null hypothesis there does not exist a linear combination of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21316.gif) that is stationary. Therefore, tests based on (31.37) are designed to test the joint null hypothesis: ‘All time series are I(1) and not cointegrated’.

To allow for cross-unit cointegration, Bai and Ng ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-58)) propose analyzing the common factors and idiosyncratic components separately. A simple multi-factor example of the Bai and Ng framework is given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21317.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21318.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21319.gif) vector of unobserved components, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21320.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21321.gif) are stationary common and individual specific shocks, respectively. Two different sets of null hypotheses are considered: ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21322.gif) : (testing the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21323.gif) properties of the common factors) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21324.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21325.gif) : (panel unit root tests) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21326.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21327.gif). A test of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21328.gif) is based on common factors estimated by principal components and cointegration tests are used to determine the number of the common trends, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21329.gif). Panel unit root tests are then applied to the idiosyncratic components. The null hypothesis that the time series have a unit root is rejected if either the test of the common factors or the test for the idiosyncratic component reject the null hypothesis of nonstationary components.[⁸](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-note-214) As has been pointed out by Westerlund and Larsson ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-969)), replacing the unobserved idiosyncratic components by estimates introduces an asymptotic bias when pooling the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21330.gif) -statistic (or ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21331.gif) -values) of the panel units, which renders the pooled tests in Bai and Ng ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-58)) asymptotically invalid. Bai and Ng ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-61)) provide an alternative panel unit root test based on Sargan and Bhargava ([1983](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-888)) that has much better small sample properties.

To allow for short-run and long-run dependencies, Chang and Song ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-204)) suggest a non-linear instrument variable test procedure. As the nonlinear instruments suggested by Chang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-201)) are invalid in the case of cross-unit cointegration, panel specific instruments based on the Hermite function of different order are used as nonlinear instruments. Chang and Song ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-204)) show that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21332.gif) -statistic computed from the nonlinear IV statistic are asymptotically standard normally distributed and, therefore, a panel unit root statistics against the heterogeneous alternative ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21333.gif) can be constructed that has an standard normal limiting distribution.

Choi and Chue ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-212)) employ a subsampling procedure to obtain tests that are robust against a wide range of cross-sectional dependence such as weak and strong correlation as well as cross-unit cointegration. To this end, the sample is grouped into a number of overlapping blocks of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21334.gif) time periods. Using all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21335.gif) possible overlapping blocks, the critical value of the test is estimated by the respective quantile of the empirical distribution of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21336.gif) test statistics computed. The advantage of this approach is that the null distribution of the test statistic may depend on unknown nuisance parameters. Whenever the test statistics converge in distribution to some limiting null distribution as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21337.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21338.gif) fixed, the sub-sample critical values converge in probability to the true critical values. Using Monte Carlo simulations Choi and Chue ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-212)) demonstrate that the size of the subsample test is indeed very robust against various forms of cross-sectional dependence. But such tests are only appropriate in the case of panels where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21339.gif) is small relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21340.gif).

# 31.6 Finite sample properties of panel unit root tests

It has become standard to distinguish first generation panel unit root tests that are based on the assumption of independent cross-sectional units and second generation tests that allow for some kind of cross-sectional dependence. Maddala and Wu ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-664)) compared several first generation tests. For the heterogeneous alternative under consideration they found that in most cases the Fisher test (31.18) performs similarly or slightly better than the IPS statistic with respect to size and power. The Levin and Lin statistic (in the version of the 1993 paper) performs substantially worse. Similar results are obtained by Choi ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-209)). Madsen ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-665)) derived the local power function against homogeneous alternatives under different detrending procedures. Her Monte Carlo simulations support her theoretical findings that the test based on estimating the mean under the null hypothesis (i.e., the initial observation is subtracted from the time series) outperforms tests based on alternative demeaning procedures. Similar findings are obtained by Bond, Nauges, and Windmeijer ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-135)).

Moon, Perron, and Phillips ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-699)) compare the finite sample powers of alternative tests against the homogeneous alternative. They find that the point-optimal test of Moon, Perron, and Phillips ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-699)) performs best and show that the power of this test is close to the power envelope. Another important finding from these simulation studies is the observation that the power of the test drops dramatically if a time trend is included. This confirms theoretical results on the local power of panel unit root tests derived by Breitung ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-146)), Ploberger and Phillips ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-846)) and Moon, Perron, and Phillips ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-699)).

Hlouskova and Wagner ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-511)) compare a large number of first generation panel unit root tests applied to processes with MA(1) errors. Not surprisingly, all tests are severely biased as the root of the MA process approaches unity. Overall, the tests of Levin, Lin, and Chu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-630)) and Breitung ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-146)) have the smallest size distortions. These tests also perform best against the homogeneous alternative, where the autoregressive coefficient is the same for all panel units. Of course, this is not surprising as these tests are optimal under homogeneous alternatives. Furthermore, it turns out that the stationarity tests of Hadri ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-452)) perform very poorly in small samples. This may be due to the fact that asymptotic values for the mean and variances of the KPSS statistics are used, whereas Levin, Lin, and Chu ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-630)) and IPS ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-537)) provide values for small ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21341.gif) as well.

The relative performance of several second generation tests has been studied by Gutierrez ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-449)), and Gengenbach, Palm, and Urbain ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-388)), where the cross-sectional dependence is assumed to follow a factor structure. The results very much depend on the underlying model. The simulations carried out by Gengenbach, Palm, and Urbain ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-388)) show that, in general, the mean CADF test has better size properties than the test of Moon and Perron ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-695)), which tends to be conservative in small samples. However the latter test appears to have more power against stationary idiosyncratic components. Since these tests remove the common factors, they will eventually indicate stationary time series in cases where the series are actually nonstationary due to a common stochastic trend. The results of Gengenbach, Palm, and Urbain ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-388)) also suggest that the approach of Bai and Ng ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-58)) is able to cope with this possibility although the power of the unit test applied to the nonstationary component is not very high.

In general, the application of factor models in the case of weak cross sectional dependence does not yield valid test procedures. Alternative unit root tests that allow for weak cross-sectional dependence are considered in Breitung and Das ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-151)). They find that the GLS ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21342.gif) -statistic may have a severe size bias if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21343.gif) is only slightly larger than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21344.gif). In these cases, the Chang ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-202)) bootstrap procedure is able to substantially improve the size properties. The robust OLS ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21345.gif) -statistic performs slightly worse but outperforms the nonlinear IV test of Chang ([2002](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-201)). However, Monte Carlo simulations carried out by Baltagi, Bresson, and Pirotte ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-72)) show that there can be considerable size distortions even in panel unit root tests that allow for weak dependence. Interestingly enough Pesaran’s test, which is not designed for weak cross-sectional dependence, tends to be the most robust to spatial type dependence.

The residual-based tests are appropriate when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21361.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21362.gif) can be partitioned such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21363.gif) with no cointegration amongst the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21364.gif) (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21365.gif) ) variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21366.gif). The system cointegration approaches are much more generally applicable and allow for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21367.gif) and do not require any particular partitioning of the variables in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21368.gif). Another main difference between the two approaches is the way the stationary component of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21369.gif) is treated in the analysis. Most of the residual-based techniques employ non-parametric (spectral density) procedures to model the residual serial correlation in the error correction terms, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21370.gif), whilst vector autoregressions (VAR) are utilized in the development of system approaches.

In panel data models, the analysis of cointegration is further complicated by heterogeneity, unbalanced panels, cross-sectional dependence, cross unit cointegration and the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21371.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21372.gif) asymptotics. But in cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21373.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21374.gif) are small, such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21375.gif) is less than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21376.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21377.gif) is relatively large (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21378.gif) ), as noted by Banerjee, Marcellino, and Osbat ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-87)), many of these problems can be avoided by applying the system cointegration techniques discussed in [Chapter 22](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22) to the pooled vector, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21379.gif). In this setting, cointegration will be defined by the relationships ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21380.gif) that could contain cointegration between variables from different cross-section units as well as cointegration amongst the different variables specific to a particular cross-sectional unit. This framework can also deal with residual cross-sectional dependence since it allows for a general error covariance matrix that covers all the variables in the panel.

Despite its attractive theoretical features, the ‘full’ system approach to panel cointegration is not feasible even in the case of panels with moderate values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21381.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21382.gif). In practice, cross-sectional cointegration can be accommodated using common factors as in the work of Bai and Ng ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-58)), Pesaran ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-774)), Pesaran, Schuermann, and Weiner ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-794)) (PSW) and its subsequent developments in Dées et al. ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-277)) (DdPS). But their setup can be readily generalized so that cointegration within each cross-sectional unit as well as across the units can be considered. The various contributions to the panel cointegration literature will now be reviewed in the context of the above general set up. First-generation literature on panel cointegration tends to ignore the possible effects of global unobserved common factors, or attempts to account for them either by cross-section de-meaning or by using observable common effects such as oil prices or US output. This literature also focusses on residual based approaches where it is often assumed that there exists at most one cointegrating relation in the individual specific models. Notable contributions to this strand of the literature include Kao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-563)), Pedroni ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-754), [2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-756), [2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-757)), and more recently Westerlund ([2005b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-964)). System approaches to panel cointegration that allow for more than one cointegrating relation include the work of Larsson, Lyhagen, and Lothgren ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-615)), Groen and Kleibergen ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-441)) and Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) who generalized the likelihood approach introduced in Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-799)). Like the second generation panel unit root tests, recent contributions to the analysis of panel cointegration have also emphasized the importance of allowing for cross-sectional dependence which, as we have noted above, could be due to the presence of common stationary or non-stationary components or both. The importance of allowing for the latter has been emphasized in Banerjee, Marcellino, and Osbat ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-87)) through the use of Monte Carlo experiments in the case of panels where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21477.gif) is very small, at most ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21478.gif) in their analysis. But to date a general approach that is capable of addressing all the various issues involved does not exist if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21479.gif) is relatively large.

We now consider in some further detail the main contributions, beginning with a brief discussion of the spurious regression problem in panels.

On the other hand, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21512.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21513.gif) are independent random walks, then the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21514.gif) -statistics for the hypothesis that one component of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21515.gif) is zero is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21516.gif) and, therefore, the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21517.gif) -statistic has similar properties as in the time series case. As demonstrated by Entorf ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-339)) and Kao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-563)), the tendency for spuriously finding a relationship among ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21518.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21519.gif) may be even stronger in panel data regressions than in the pure time series case. Therefore, it is important to test whether the errors in a panel data regression such as (31.46) are stationary.

This analysis suggests that, even if house prices deviate from the equilibrating relationship because of state-specific or common shocks, they will eventually revert. If* *of the five states mentioned above, the price-income ratio declined by 1 per cent in Virginia, 2 per cent in Arizona, 0 per cent in District of Columbia*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21593.gif) *per cent in Indiana, and 4 per cent in Ohio. If we calculate the average change in the log ratio of house prices to per capita income for each state over the period 2000–06, and compare it to the average change in the ratio for 2007, it is to be expected that, if a state on average is above its equilibrium before 2006, the average change after 2006 should be negative, and vice versa otherwise. The results are plotted in* *house prices are above equilibrium they will tend to fall relative to income, and vice versa if they are above equilibrium. Of course, because there is heterogeneity across states, a particular state need not be in the same disequilibrium position as other states. But on average the change in the ratio of house prices to per capita incomes should be zero, consistent with a cointegrating relationship, for* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21591.gif) *sufficiently large. In their conclusions*, *Holly, Pesaran, and Yamagata* ([*2010*](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-514)) *also examine the temporal pattern of the differences*, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21592.gif), *since 2003. The process of house price boom that started in the US in early 2000 accelerated during 2003–06 and some have interpreted this as a bubble. Over the period 2000 to 2006 the average (unweighted) rise in US house prices was 46 per cent, as compared with a 25 per cent rise in income per capita. However, the price increases relative to per capita incomes have been quite heterogeneous. While house prices over the period 2000 to 2006 rose by 67 per cent in Virginia, 73 per cent in Arizona and 92 per cent in the District of Columbia, they rose by only 20 per cent in Indiana and 21 per cent in Ohio. These differences were much more pronounced than the rise in income per capita in these states (respectively 26 per cent, 23 per cent, 40 per cent, 20 per cent, and 19 per cent). Individual states can move about the average because the loading of the driving variables differ across states or because the initial disequilibrium is different. The extent of the heterogeneity in the disequilibrium, as measured by the time profile of the logarithm of price-income per capita over the full sample, 1976–2007, for all the 49 states is displayed in* *Figure* [31.1](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-figureGroup-21). *It is interesting that the excess rise in house prices tends to be associated with increased dispersion in the log price-income ratios, which begin to decline with moderation of house price rises relative to incomes. This fits well with the development of house prices in 2007, where prices rose only by 4 per cent as compared with a rise in per capita income of 5 per cent. The range of house price changes across states was also narrowed down substantially. In fact, in the case* [Figure 31.2](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-figureGroup-22), *and show that of 49 states, 32 states have an average rate of price change in 2007 with the opposite sign to the average price changes for 2000–06. Moreover, we note that the correlation coefficient between the change in the price-income ratio in 2007, when the house price boom began to unwind, and the average change in the same ratio over the preceding price boom period, 2000–2006, is negative and quite substantial, around* ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21594.gif).

## 31.8.2 Tests of panel cointegration

As in the pure time series framework, the variables in a regression function can be tested for cointegration by applying unit roots tests of the sort suggested in the previous sections to the residuals of the estimated regression. Unfortunately, panel unit root tests cannot be applied to the residuals in (31.46) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21690.gif) is endogenous, that is, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21691.gif). Letting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21692.gif) followed by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21693.gif), Kao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-563)) shows that the limiting distribution of the DF ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21694.gif) -statistic applied to the residuals of a pooled OLS regression of (31.46) is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21695.gif)(31.50)

where the values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21696.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21697.gif) depend on the kind of deterministics included in the regression, the contemporaneous covariance matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21698.gif) and the long-run covariance matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21699.gif). Kao ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-563)) proposes adjusting ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21700.gif) by using consistent estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21701.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21702.gif), where he assumes that the nuisance parameters are the same for all units in the panel.

Pedroni ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-757)) suggests two different test statistics for the models with heterogeneous cointegration vectors. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21703.gif) denote the OLS residual of the cointegration regression. Pedroni considers two different classes of test statistics: (i) the ‘panel statistic’ that is equivalent to the unit root statistic against homogeneous alternatives and (ii) the ‘Group Mean statistic’ which is analogous to the panel unit root tests against heterogeneous alternatives. The two versions of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21704.gif) statistic are defined as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21705.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21706.gif) is a consistent estimator of the one-sided long run variance ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21707.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21708.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21709.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21710.gif) denotes the estimated variance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21711.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21712.gif). Pedroni presents values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21713.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21714.gif) such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21715.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21716.gif) have standard normal limiting distributions under the null hypothesis.

Other residual-based panel cointegration tests include the recent contribution of Westerlund ([2005b](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-964)) which is based on variance ratio statistics and does not require corrections for the residual serial correlations.

The finite sample properties of some residual based tests for panel cointegration are discussed in Baltagi and Kao ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-76)). Gutierrez ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-449)) compares the power of various panel cointegration test statistics. He shows that in homogeneous panels with a small number of time periods Kao’s tests tend to have higher power than Pedroni’s tests, whereas in panels with large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21717.gif) the latter tests performs best. Both tests outperform the system test suggested by Larsson, Lyhagen, and Lothgren ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-615)). Wagner and Hlouskova ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-956)) compare various panel cointegration tests in a large scale simulation study. They found that the Pedroni ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-757)) test based on ADF regressions performs best, whereas all other tests tend to be severely undersized and have very low power in many cases. Furthermore, the system tests suffer from large small sample distortions and are unreliable tools for finding out the correct cointegration rank. Gengenbach, Palm, and Urbain ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-387)) investigate the performance of Pedroni’s tests in cross-dependent models with a factor structure.

# 31.9 Tests for multiple cointegration

It is also possible to adapt the Johansen ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-469)) multivariate test based on a VAR representation of the variables in a panel context. Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21718.gif) denote the cross-section specific likelihood-ratio (‘trace’) statistic of the hypothesis that there are (at most) ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21719.gif) stationary linear combinations in the cointegrated VAR system given by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21720.gif). Following the unit root test proposed in IPS ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-537)), Larsson, Lyhagen, and Lothgren ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-615)) suggested the standardized LR-bar statistic

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21721.gif)

to test the null hypothesis that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21722.gif) against the alternative that at most ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21723.gif). Using a sequential limit theory it can be shown that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21724.gif) is asymptotically standard normally distributed. Asymptotic values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21725.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21726.gif) are tabulated in Larsson, Lyhagen, and Lothgren ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-615)) for the model without deterministic terms and Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) for models with a constant and a linear time trend. Unlike the residual-based tests, the LR-bar test allows for the possibility of multiple cointegration relations in the panel.

It is also possible to test the null hypothesis that the errors of the cointegration regression are stationary. That is, under the null hypothesis it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21727.gif) are cointegrated with cointegration rank ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21728.gif). McCoskey and Kao ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-681)) suggest a panel version of the Shin ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-904)) cointegration test based on the residuals of a fully modified OLS regression. Westerlund ([2005c](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-965)) suggests a related test procedure based on the CUSUM statistic.

# 31.10 Estimation of cointegrating relations in panels

## 31.10.1 Single equation estimators

First, we consider a single-equation framework where it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21729.gif) and the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21730.gif) vector of regressors ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21731.gif) are ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21732.gif) with at most one cointegrating relation amongst them, namely that there exists a linear relationship of the form (31.46) such that the error ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21733.gif) is stationary. As before, it is assumed that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21734.gif) is independently and identically distributed across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21735.gif), and the regressors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21736.gif) are not cointegrated. We do not explicitly consider deterministic terms like individual specific constants or trends as the asymptotic theory applies to mean- or trend-adjusted variables as well.

It is assumed that the vector of coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21737.gif), is the same for all cross-sectional units, that is, a homogeneous cointegration relationship is assumed. Alternatively, it may be assumed that the cointegration parameters are cross-section specific (heterogenous cointegration).

By applying a sequential limit theory it can be shown that the OLS estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21738.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21739.gif) consistent and, therefore, the time series dimension is more informative on the long-run coefficients than the cross-section dimension. Furthermore, it is important to notice that—as in the time series framework—the OLS estimator is consistent but inefficient in the model with endogenous regressors.

Pedroni ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-757)) and Phillips and Moon ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-837)) propose a ‘fully-modified OLS’ (FM-OLS) approach to obtain an asymptotically efficient estimator for homogeneous cointegration vectors. This estimator adjusts for the effects of endogenous regressors and short-run dynamics of the errors (see Phillips and Hansen ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-836)) and Section [22.3.2](#036_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-22-div2-215)). To correct for the effect of (long-run) endogeneity of the regressors, the dependent variable is adjusted for the part of the error that is correlated with the regressor

A second correction is necessary when computing the OLS estimator

where

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21742.gif)

The nuisance parameters can be estimated consistently using familiar nonparametric procedures.

In practice the infinite sums are truncated at some small numbers of leads and lags (see Kao and Chiang ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-564)), Mark and Sul ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-673))). Westerlund ([2005a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-963)) considers data dependent choices of the truncation lags. Furthermore, the FM-OLS estimator possesses the same asymptotic distribution as the DOLS estimator. In the heterogeneous case ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21751.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21752.gif) are replaced by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21753.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21754.gif), respectively (see Phillips and Moon ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-837))). Again, the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21755.gif) can be estimated consistently (for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21756.gif) ) by using a non-parametric approach.

In many applications the number of time periods is smaller than 20 and, therefore, the kernel based estimators of the nuisance parameters may perform poorly in such small samples. In these cases, the pooled mean group estimator introduced by Pesaran, Shin, and Smith ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-799)) and discussed in Section [28.10](#043_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-28-div1-318) may be used. This method assumes that the long-run parameters are identical across the cross-section units. Economic theory often predicts the same cointegration relation(s) across the cross-section units, although it is often silent on the magnitude of short-run dynamics, across ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21757.gif). For example, the long-run relationships predicted by the PPP, the uncovered interest parity, or the Fisher equation are the same across countries, although the speed of convergence to these long-run relations can differ markedly over countries due to differences in economic and political institutions. For further discussion see, for example, Pesaran ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-771)).

## 31.10.2 System estimators

Single equation estimators have several drawbacks that can be avoided by using a system approach. First, these estimators assume that all regressors are I(1) and not cointegrated. If there is more than one cointegration relationship, then the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21758.gif) is singular and the asymptotic results are no longer valid. Second, the cointegration relationship has to be normalized such that the variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21759.gif) enters with unit coefficient. As has been argued by Boswijk ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-138)), this normalization is problematic if the original coefficient of the variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21760.gif) tends to zero.

In the case of short panels with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21761.gif) fixed and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21762.gif) large, Binder, Hsiao, and Pesaran ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-118)) consider estimation and inference in panel vector autoregressions (*PVARs*) with homogeneous slopes where (i) the individual effects are either random or fixed, (ii) the time-series properties of the model variables are unknown *a priori* and may feature unit roots and cointegrating relations. generalized method of moments (*GMM*) and quasi-maximum likelihood (*QML*) estimators are obtained and compared in terms of their asymptotic and finite sample properties. It is shown that the asymptotic variances of the *GMM* estimators that are based on levels as well as on first differences of the model variables depend on the variance of the individual effects; whereas by construction, the fixed-effects *QML* estimator is not subject to this problem. Monte Carlo evidence is provided showing that the fixed-effects *QML* estimator tends to outperform the various GMM estimators in finite sample under both normal and non-normal errors. The paper also shows how the fixed-effects *QML* estimator can be successfully used for unit root and cointegration tests in short panels.

In the case of panels with large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21763.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21764.gif), Larsson and Lyhagen ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-614)), Groen and Kleibergen ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-441)), and Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) consider the vector error correction model (*VECM*) for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21765.gif) dimensional vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21766.gif) given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21767.gif)(31.55)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21768.gif). Once again we leave out deterministic terms and lagged differences. To be consistent with the approaches considered above, we confine ourselves to the case of homogeneous cointegration, that is, we let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21769.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21770.gif). Larsson and Lyhagen ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-614)) propose an ML estimator, whereas the estimator of Groen and Kleibergen ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-441)) is based on a nonlinear GMM approach.

It is well known that the ML estimator of the cointegration parameters for a single series may behave poorly in small samples. Phillips ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-833)) has shown that the finite sample moments of the estimator do not exist. Using Monte Carlo simulations Hansen, Kim, and Mittnik ([1998](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-471)) and Brüggemann and Lütkepohl ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-166)) found that the ML estimator may produce implausible estimates far away from the true parameter values. Furthermore the asymptotic ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21771.gif) distribution of the likelihood ratio test for restrictions on the cointegration parameters may be a poor guide for small sample inference (e.g., Gredenhoff and Jacobson ([2001](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-429))).

To overcome these problems, Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) proposes a computationally convenient two-step estimator, which is adapted from Ahn and Reinsel ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-8)). This estimator is based on the fact that the Fisher information is block-diagonal with respect to the short- and long-run parameters. Accordingly, an asymptotically efficient estimator can be constructed by estimating the short- and long-run parameters in separate steps. Suppose that the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21772.gif) matrix of cointegrating vectors is ‘normalized’ as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21773.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21774.gif) is the identity matrix of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21775.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21776.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21777.gif) matrix of unknown coefficients.[¹²](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-note-221) Then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21778.gif) is exactly identified and the Gaussian ML estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21779.gif) is equivalent to the OLS estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21780.gif) in

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21781.gif)(31.56)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21782.gif) is the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21783.gif) vector defined by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21784.gif), and

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21785.gif)

The matrices ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21786.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21787.gif) can be replaced by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21788.gif) -consistent estimates without affecting the limiting distribution. Accordingly, these matrices can be estimated for each panel unit separately, for example by using the Johansen ([1991](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-548)) ML estimator. To obtain the same normalization as in (31.56) the estimator for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21789.gif) is multiplied with the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21790.gif) upper block of the ML estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21791.gif).

Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) shows that the limiting distribution of the OLS estimator of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21792.gif) is asymptotically normal. Therefore, tests of restrictions on the cointegration parameters have the standard limiting distributions (i.e. a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21793.gif) distribution for the usual Wald tests).

Some Monte Carlo experiments are performed by Breitung ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-148)) to compare the small sample properties of the two-step estimator with the FM-OLS and DOLS estimators. The results suggest that the latter two tests may be severely biased in small samples, whereas the bias of the two-step estimator is relatively small. Furthermore, the standard errors (and hence the size properties of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21794.gif) -statistics) of the two-step procedure are more reliable than the ones of the semi-parametric estimation procedures. In a large scale simulation study, Wagner and Hlouskova ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-956)) found that the DOLS estimator outperforms all other estimators, whereas the FM-OLS and the two-step estimator perform similarly.

# 31.11 Panel cointegration in the presence of cross-sectional dependence

As discussed in [Chapter 29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29), an important limitation of the econometric approaches discussed so far is that they assume that all cross-sectional units are independent. In many applications based on multi-country data sets this assumption is clearly unrealistic. To accommodate cross-dependence among panel units Mark, Ogaki, and Sul ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-672)) and Moon and Perron ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-696)) propose a dynamic seemingly unrelated regression (DSUR) estimator. Their approach is based on a GLS estimator of the dynamic representation (31.54) when there exists a single cointegrating relation between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21796.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21797.gif), and does not allow for the possibility of cross unit cointegration.
