They suggest an FM-OLS cointegration regression that accounts for the cross-correlation due to the common factors. Bai, Kao, and Ng ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-56)) consider a model with non-stationary factors. Their estimation procedure is based on a sequential minimization of the criterion function

The asymptotic bias of the resulting estimator is corrected for by using an additive bias adjustment term or by using a procedure similar to the FM-OLS estimator suggested by Phillips and Hansen ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-836)).

A common feature of these approaches is that cross-sectional dependence can be represented by a contemporaneous correlation of the errors, and does not allow for the possibility of cross-unit cointegration. In many applications it is more realistic to allow for some form of dynamic cross-sectional dependence. A general model to accommodate cross-section cointegration and dynamic links between panel units is the panel VECM model considered by Groen and Kleibergen ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-441)) and Larsson and Lyhagen ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-614)). As in Section [31.7](#046_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-31-div1-348), let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21821.gif) denote an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21822.gif) -dimensional vector of times series on the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21823.gif) cross-sectional unit. Consider the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21824.gif) vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21825.gif) of all available time series in the panel data set. The VECM representation of this time series vector is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21826.gif)(31.60)

For cointegrated systems ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21827.gif). It is obvious that such systems typically involve a large number of parameters as the number of parameters increases with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21828.gif). Therefore, to obtain reliable estimates of the parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21829.gif) must be considerably larger than ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21830.gif). In many macroeconomic applications, however, the number of time periods is roughly as large as the number of cross-section units. Therefore, a simple structure must be imposed on the matrices ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21831.gif) that yields a reasonable approximation to the underlying dynamic system.

# 31.12 Further reading

Further discussion on unit roots and cointegration in panels can be found in Banerjee ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-85)), Baltagi and Kao ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-76)), and Choi ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-211)).

# 32.1 Introduction

The aggregation problem is an inevitable aspect of applied research in economics. Nearly every study in economics implicitly or explicitly involves aggregation over time, individuals (consumers or firms), products, or space, and usually over most of these dimensions. Naturally, the problem is more pervasive in the case of macroeconomic research, which is primarily concerned with the analysis of the relationships amongst the aggregates. For example, in a typical small open macroeconomic model, the ‘rest of the world’ is aggregated into a single foreign economy, domestic agents such as households are often represented by a single representative counterpart, and, when it comes to estimation and inference, the available macro data, such as gross domestic product, are typically available only in the form of temporally aggregated data at monthly or quarterly frequencies. Aggregation also tends to be present in applied microeconomic analysis. For example, in the case of microeconometric studies of household consumption, the issues of commodity aggregation and the associated index number problem have been the subject of substantial research in the past. See Gorman ([1953](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-411)) and Muellbauer ([1975](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-708)). Similar considerations also arise in the microeconometric analysis of households’ labour supply, firms’ investment and employment decisions, and governments’ expenditure decisions.

Since aggregation is prevalent in economics, it is important that the consequences of aggregation for the analysis of economic problems of interest are adequately understood. It is widely acknowledged that aggregation can be problematic, but its implications for empirical research are often ignored either by resorting to the concept of a ‘representative agent’, or by arguing that ‘aggregation errors’ are of second-order importance. However, there are empirical studies where aggregation errors are shown to be quite important, including the contributions by Hsiao et al. ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-530)), Altissimo et al. ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-12)), and Imbs et al. ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-538)). In addition to the empirical studies, Geweke ([1985](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-394)) develops a theoretical example, where he argues that ignoring the sensitivity of the aggregates to policy changes seems no more compelling than the Lucas critique of ignoring the dependence of expectations on the policy regime.

Aggregation can be broadly divided into two categories: aggregation across time and over cross-sectional units. The concept of cross-sectional units in this chapter is broadly defined, and includes geographical dimensions (e.g., regions or countries), individuals (e.g., firms or households), industries and products (e.g., the consumer price index basket of goods and services). There are two leading examples of aggregation across time: sequential sampling and temporal aggregation. The former method sequentially samples data from a higher frequency to a lower frequency. One example of sequential sampling is market closing prices or end-of-period prices. The latter method, on the other hand, combines the data typically by using period averages, to convert the series from a higher frequency to a lower frequency. Examples of temporally aggregated data are data measuring economic activity (gross domestic product, industrial output, retail sales) or consumer price data, where prices are collected repeatedly over a number of days within a month and then averaged across collection days to obtain monthly price indices for individual goods and/or services.

Aggregation over cross-sectional units (or ‘cross-sectional aggregation’) can also be divided into two categories, depending on the number of units, whether aggregation is carried out across a finite number of units ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21931.gif) and/or over a large number of units (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21932.gif) ). This distinction is important for theoretical analysis, where taking limits (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21933.gif) ) often simplifies the analysis. Large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21934.gif) asymptotics often seem a reasonable approximation when it comes to macroeconomic data, where the number of cross-sectional units (households, products, firms, etc.) can be very large.

The focus of this chapter is predominantly on large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21935.gif) aggregation. It first briefly reviews the main aggregation problems studied in the literature (Section [32.2](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-356)). Then it presents a general framework for micro/disaggregate behavioral relationships (Section [32.3](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-357)) and develops a forecasting approach to derive the optimal aggregate function (Section [32.4](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-358)). This approach is applied to a large cross-section aggregation of panel ARDL models (Section [32.5](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-359)) and to the case of large factor-augmented VAR models in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21936.gif) cross-sectional units, where each micro unit is potentially related to all other micro units, and where micro innovations are allowed to be cross sectionally dependent (Section [32.6](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-360)). The optimal aggregate function is used to examine the relationship between micro and macro parameters to show which distributional features of micro parameters can be identified from the aggregate model (Section [32.7](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-361)). This chapter also derives and contrasts impulse response functions for the aggregate variables, distinguishing between the effects of composite macro and aggregated idiosyncratic shocks (Section [32.8](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-362)). Some of these findings are illustrated by Monte Carlo experiments (Section [32.9](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-363)) and two applications are presented. The first application investigates the aggregation of life-cycle consumption decision rules under habit formation (Section [32.10](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-364)). The second application investigates the sources of persistence of consumer price inflation in Germany, France, and Italy, and re-examines the extent to which ‘observed’ inflation persistence at the aggregate level is due to aggregation and/or common unobserved factors (Section [32.11](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-365)).

# 32.2 Aggregation problems in the literature

There is a number of questions that have been studied in the aggregation literature. Early surveys are provided by Granger ([1990](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-419)) and Stoker ([1993](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-931)). One important question is how aggregation affects time series properties. One key property is the persistence effects of shocks to the aggregate variables. For example, the extent to which real exchange rates or inflation rates react to shocks is of considerable interest in policy making. Both inflation and real exchange rates are aggregates from data on a large number of goods and services.

The problem of aggregating a large number of independent time series processes was first addressed by Robinson ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-863)) and Granger ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-416)). Granger shows that aggregate variables can have fundamentally different time series properties as compared with those of the underlying micro units. Focusing on autoregressive models of order 1, *AR*(1), he shows that aggregation can generate long memory even if the micro units follow stochastic processes with exponentially decaying autocovariances (see also Section [15.8.3](#028_part4_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-15-div2-138)). Consider the following *AR*(1) disaggregate relations,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21937.gif)

for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21938.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21939.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21940.gif). Suppose these relations are independent, and in addition ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21941.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21942.gif) are independently and identically distributed (IID) random draws with the distribution function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21943.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21944.gif) on the range ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21945.gif). Granger’s objective is the memory properties of the aggregate variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21946.gif). The same setup is considered also in an earlier work by Robinson ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-863)), but with a focus on the estimation of the moments of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21947.gif). To study the persistence properties of the aggregates, Granger considers the spectrum of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21948.gif),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21949.gif)

Then assuming that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21950.gif) is type II beta distributed with parameters ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21951.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21952.gif), he shows that for sufficiently large ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21953.gif), the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21954.gif)-order autocovariance of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21955.gif), is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21956.gif), and therefore the aggregate variable behaves as a fractionally integrated process of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21958.gif). In fact the long memory property holds more generally, so long as the support of the distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21959.gif) covers 1. The problem of aggregation of a finite number of independent autoregressive moving average (*ARMA*) processes is considered, for example, by Granger and Morris ([1976](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-423)), Rose ([1977](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-868)), and Lütkepohl ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-650)). Aggregation across time as opposed to cross-sectional units also changes the time series properties. The persistence of temporally aggregated data has been investigated, for instance, by Chambers ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-198)).

A second, closely related problem is derivation of an optimal aggregate function (Theil ([1954](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-938)), Lewbel ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-632)), and Pesaran ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-772))), which we review in more detail in Section [32.4](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-358) below. The optimal aggregate function can be used for various purposes such as to compare parameter values or impulse responses of the effects of shocks (common or unit specific) when aggregate and disaggregated models are used. The original ‘aggregation problem’ discussed by Theil ([1954](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-938)) is concerned with the possibility of deriving a relationship between the parameters of the aggregate model and the parameters of the underlying micro relations. Theil was the first to consider the problem of identification and estimation of micro parameters or some of their distributional features from aggregate relations in the context of static micro relations. Robinson ([1978](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-863)) considers the problem of estimating moments of the distribution of AR(1) micro coefficients. He identifies moments of the cross-section distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21960.gif) in the AR(1) model in terms of the autocovariances ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21961.gif), and establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21962.gif) to have continuous spectral density. He also considers the problem of estimation of the moments of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21963.gif) using disaggregate data, abstracting from cases where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21964.gif) turns out to be a long-memory process. In particular, he requires ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21965.gif) to exist for consistency, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21966.gif) to exist for asymptotic normality of his proposed estimator. See Section [32.7](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-361) for further analysis and discussions of the aggregation problem in the case of long-run effects and estimation of mean lags.

A third issue of importance concerns the role of common factors and cross-sectional dependence in aggregation, which was first highlighted by Granger ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-418)), and further developed and discussed in Forni and Lippi ([1997](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-367)) and Zaffaroni ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-995)). Granger ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-418)) shows that the strength and pattern of cross-sectional dependence plays a central role in aggregation. He considers a simple factor model to illustrate the main issues,

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21967.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21968.gif) is unit-specific explanatory variable, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21969.gif) is a common factor with loadings, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21970.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21971.gif) is the observation for the unit ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21972.gif) at time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21973.gif). Suppose ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21974.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21975.gif) have zero means, bounded variances, and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21976.gif) is independently distributed of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21977.gif) and of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21978.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21979.gif). Consider the variance of the aggregate variable ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21980.gif),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21981.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21982.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21983.gif). The first summand is at most of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21984.gif), denoted as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21985.gif), and, provided that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21986.gif), the second summand is of order ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21987.gif). The second term will therefore generally dominate the aggregate relationship. Granger demonstrates striking implications of this finding in terms of the fit of the aggregate (macro) relationship, where the common factor prevails when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21988.gif) is sufficiently large, and disaggregate (micro) relationships, where the micro regressor could play a leading role. If the common factor was unobserved, then the aggregate relation would have zero fit (for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21989.gif) large) whereas the fit of disaggregate relations could be quite high, being driven by the micro regressor, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21990.gif). On the other hand, if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21991.gif) was observed and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21992.gif) was unobserved then the macro relation would have a perfect fit (for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21993.gif) large), whereas the micro relation may have a very poor fit due to the missing micro regressor, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-21994.gif). Hence variables that may have very good explanatory power at the micro level might be unimportant at the macro level, and *vice versa*. Granger shows that the strength and pattern of cross-sectional dependence thus play a central role in aggregation and components with weaker cross-sectional dependence typically do not matter for the behaviour of aggregate variables.

Aggregation has also been studied from the perspective of forecasting: is it better to forecast using aggregate or disaggregate data, if the primary objective is to forecast the aggregates? Pesaran, Pierse, and Kumar ([1989](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-788)) and Pesaran, Pierse, and Lee ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-787)), building on Grunfeld and Griliches ([1960](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-447)), develop selection criteria for a choice between aggregate and disaggregate specifications. Giacomini and Granger ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-398)) discuss forecasting of aggregates in the context of space-time autoregressive models.

Other contributions to the theory of aggregation include the contributions of Kelejian ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-576)), Stoker ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-929), [1986](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-930)), and Garderen et al. ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-378)), on aggregation of static nonlinear micro models; Pesaran and Smith ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-808)), Phillips and Moon ([1999](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-837)), and Trapani and Urga ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-945)) on the effects of aggregation on cointegration.

# 32.3 A general framework for micro (disaggregate) behavioural relationships

Aggregation of behavioural or technical relations across individuals becomes a problem when there is some form of heterogeneity across individuals’ relations. When individuals are identical in every respect and the associated micro relations are homogeneous, aggregation will not be a problem. In practice, however, this is extremely unlikely to be the case. Sources of heterogeneity include

• input variables (heterogeneous initial endowments)

• micro parameters (heterogeneous coefficients)

• micro functionals (heterogeneous preferences and/or production functions).

Let the micro behavioural relationship be represented as

# 32.4 Alternative notions of aggregate functions

## 32.4.2 A statistical approach to aggregation

The restrictive nature of the deterministic aggregation condition ([32.10](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3813)) arises primarily because it requires the condition to be satisfied for all realizations of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22036.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22037.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22038.gif), no matter how remote the possibility of their occurrence. An alternative and less restrictive approach would be to require that ([32.10](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3813)) holds ‘on average’. More precisely, let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22039.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22040.gif) be the means of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22041.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22042.gif) across individuals at a point in time or over a given period of time (depending on whether the variables are stocks or flows) and define a macro (or aggregate) relation as one that links ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22043.gif) to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22044.gif) at a point in time ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22045.gif). This approach is suggested by Kelejian ([1980](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-576)) and rigorously formalized by Stoker ([1984](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-929)). It treats ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22046.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22047.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22048.gif) across individuals as stochastic, having a joint probability distribution function ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22049.gif) with parameter vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22050.gif) that can vary over time, but not across individuals. This is clearly an improvement over the deterministic approach, but it is still rather removed from direct empirical analysis and does not adequately focus on the inevitably approximate nature of econometric analysis. Moreover, perhaps more importantly, due to its reliance on unconditional means, this approach is not suitable for the analysis of dynamic systems.

## 32.4.3 A forecasting approach to aggregation

Once again, consider the exact aggregation condition ([32.10](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3813)) specified for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22064.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22065.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22066.gif), but now require that conditional on the aggregate information set ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22067.gif),

We now turn to this and other examples and show how a number of results in the literature can be obtained from the optimal aggregator function given by ([32.37](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3845)). In the general case where micro relations are subject to both common and idiosyncratic shocks, the effect of the common shocks on the aggregate forecast, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22220.gif), will dominate as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22221.gif). Hence, for forecasting purposes, the effects of idiosyncratic shocks can be ignored.

The analysis of aggregation of *ARDL* models by Lewbel ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-632)) can also be related to the optimal aggregate function, ([32.37](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3845)). ## 32.6.1 Aggregation of stationary micro relations with random coefficients

But its use in empirical applications is limited as it depends on unobserved initial state, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22355.gif), and the micro variables, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22356.gif). To derive empirically manageable aggregate functions, in what follows we assume that the underlying processes are stationary and the micro parameters, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22357.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22358.gif), are random draws from a common distribution. More specifically, we make the following assumptions:

Assumption A.7: The micro coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22359.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22360.gif), are random draws from common distributions with finite moments such that

Using this result in ([32.48](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3858)) we obtain the optimal aggregate function

which holds for any finite ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22380.gif).

The dynamic properties of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22381.gif) and its persistence to shocks depend on the decay rates of the distributed lag coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22382.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22383.gif). If ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22384.gif) for some strictly positive constant ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22385.gif), then the distributed lagged coefficients, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22386.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22387.gif) decay exponentially fast and the aggregate function will not exhibit long memory features. However, in the case where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22388.gif) are draws from distributions with supports covering -1 and/or 1, the rate of decay of the distributed lagged coefficients will be slower than exponential, and the resultant aggregate function will be subject to long memory effects. This result confirms Granger’s conjecture in the case of large dimensional *VAR* models, and establishes sufficient conditions for its validity.

It is also worth noting that, in general, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22389.gif) has an infinite-order distributed lag representation even if the underlying micro relations have finite lag-orders. This is an important consideration in empirical macro economic analysis where the macro variables under consideration are often constructed as aggregates of observations on a large number of micro units.

# 32.9 A Monte Carlo investigation

We consider a first-order *VAR* model with a single unobserved factor to examine the response of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22583.gif), to the combined aggregate shock, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22584.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22585.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22586.gif). As before, we decompose the effects into the contribution due to a macro shock, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22587.gif), and the aggregated idiosyncratic shock, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22588.gif). Using ([32.66](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3889)), we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22589.gif)(32.70)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22590.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22591.gif) are the respective contributions of the macro and aggregated idiosyncratic shocks, and the weights ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22592.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22593.gif) are defined below ([32.66](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3889)).

Aggregation weights are set equal to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22594.gif) in all simulations. The subscript ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22595.gif) is introduced to highlight the fact that these impulse responses are based on the disaggregate model. We know from theoretical results that, in cases where the optimal aggregate function exists, the common factor is strong (i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22596.gif) ), and the idiosyncratic shocks are weakly correlated (i.e., ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22597.gif) ), then ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22598.gif) converges to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22599.gif) as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22600.gif), for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22601.gif). But it would be of interest to investigate the contributions of macro and aggregated idiosyncratic shocks to the aggregate impulse response functions, when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22602.gif) is finite, as well as when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22603.gif) takes intermediate values between ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22604.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22605.gif).

We also use Monte Carlo experiments to investigate the persistence properties of the aggregate variable. The degree and sources of persistence in macro variables, such as consumer price inflation, output and real exchange rates, have been of considerable interest in economics. We know from the theoretical results that there are two key components affecting the persistence of the aggregate variables: distribution of the eigenvalues of lagged micro coefficients matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22606.gif), which we refer to as dynamic heterogeneity; and the persistence of the common factor itself, which we refer to as the factor persistence. Our aim is to investigate how these two sources of persistence combine and get amplified in the process of aggregation.

Finally, a related issue of practical significance is the effect of estimation uncertainty on the above comparisons. To this end, we estimate disaggregated models using observations on individual micro units, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22607.gif), as well as an aggregate model that only makes use of the aggregate observations, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22608.gif). We denote the estimated impulse responses of the combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22609.gif) when based on the disaggregate model, and by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22610.gif) when based on an aggregate autoregressive model fitted to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22611.gif). It is important to recall that, in general, the effects of macro and aggregated idiosyncratic shocks cannot be identified from the aggregate model.

The remainder of this section is organized as follows. The next sub-section outlines the Monte Carlo design. Section [32.9.2](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div2-341) describes the estimation of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22612.gif) using aggregate and disaggregate data, and the last sub-section discusses the main findings.

# 32.10 Application I: aggregation of life-cycle consumption decision rules under habit formation

In the life-cycle literature, habit formation has been emphasized as a potentially important factor that may help resolve a number of empirical puzzles. Deaton ([1987](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-276)), among others, argues that habit formation could help explain ‘excess smoothness’ and ‘excess sensitivity’ of aggregate consumption expenditures. ‘Excess smoothness’ refers to the situation where, contrary to the prediction of the permanent income hypothesis, changes in aggregate consumption do not vary closely with unanticipated changes in labour income. ‘Excess sensitivity’ refers to the situation where changes in aggregate consumption respond to anticipated changes in labour income, whilst the theory predicts otherwise. For a review of the empirical literature on excess smoothness and excess sensitivity see, for example, Muellbauer and Lattimore ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-709)). Carroll and Weil ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-185)) suggest that the reverse causality between growth and saving often observed in aggregate data could be due to the neglect of habit formation in consumption behaviour. Fuhrer ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-374)) maintains that the dynamics of aggregate consumption decisions as represented by autocovariance functions can be much better understood using a model with habit formation than using a model with standard time-separable preferences. A problem common to all these studies using representative agent frameworks is that the coefficient of habit formation needed to reconcile the model with the data is typically deemed implausibly high. In this section we consider the aggregate implications of allowing for heterogeneity in habit formation coefficients across individuals and investigate the extent to which empirical puzzles observed in aggregate consumption data are due to the aggregation problem. Using stochastic simulations, Pesaran ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-772)) shows that the estimates of the habit persistence coefficient are likely to be seriously biased downward if they are based on analogue aggregate consumption functions, which could partly explain the excess smoothness and excess sensitivity puzzles in terms of neglected heterogeneity.[¹¹](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-note-234)

The optimal aggregate consumption function can therefore be written as

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22917.gif)(32.104)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22184.gif) is the aggregation error and by construction satisfies the orthogonality condition

The aggregation errors are serially uncorrelated with zero means, but in general are not homoskedastic. The above optimal aggregate function is directly comparable to the aggregate model, ([32.98](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3930)), obtained under homogeneous habit formation coefficients. It is easily seen that ([32.104](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3940)) reduces to ([32.98](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3930)) if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22920.gif) for all ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22921.gif). The aggregation errors, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22919.gif) ’s, also vanish if and only if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22923.gif). Finally, unless the habit formation coefficients are homogeneous, the optimal aggregate model cannot be written as a finite-order *ARDL* model in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22924.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22925.gif). See Pesaran ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-772)) for an illustrative numerical result on the extent of the aggregation bias.

# 32.11 Application II: inflation persistence

Persistence of aggregate inflation and its sources have attracted a great deal of attention in the literature. Prices at the micro level are known to be relatively flexible, whereas at the aggregate level the overall rate of inflation seems to be quite persistent. Using individual category price series, Altissimo et al. ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-12)) conclude that ‘the aggregation mechanism explains a significant amount of aggregate inflation persistence.’ (p. 231). Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) investigate the robustness of this conclusion by estimating a factor-augmented high dimensional *VAR* model in disaggregate inflation series, where the relative contribution of aggregation and common factor persistence is evaluated. The analysis is based on the same data set as that used by Altissimo et al. ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-12)), so that the results can be compared more readily. It is found that the persistence due to dynamic heterogeneity alone does not explain the persistence of the aggregate inflation, rather it is the combination of factor persistence and dynamic heterogeneity that is responsible for the high persistence of aggregate inflation as compared to the persistence of the underlying individual inflation series.

## 32.11.1 Data

The inflation series for the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22927.gif) price category is computed as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22928.gif), where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22929.gif) is the seasonally adjusted consumer price index of unit *i* at time *t*.[¹³](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-note-236) Units are individual categories of the consumer price index (e.g. bread, wine, medical services,…) and the time dimension is quarterly covering the period 1985Q1 to 2004Q2; altogether 78 observations per price category. There are 85 categories in Germany, 145 in France, and 168 in Italy. The aggregate inflation measure is computed as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22935.gif), where *N* is the number of price categories and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22937.gif) is the weight of the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22938.gif) category in the consumer price index. Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) conduct their empirical analysis for each of the three countries separately.

## 32.11.2 Micro model of consumer prices

Following Chudik and Pesaran ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-221)), the possibility that there are unobserved factors or neighbourhood effects in the micro relations are investigated. Individual items are categorized into a small sets of products that are close substitutes. For example, spirits, wine and beer are assumed to be ‘neighbours’. A complete list of ‘neighbours’ for Germany is provided in Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)). Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22939.gif) be the index set defining the neighbours of unit *i*, and consider the following local averages

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22941.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22942.gif) is the number of neighbours of unit ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22943.gif), assumed to be small and fixed as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22944.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22945.gif) is the corresponding ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22946.gif) sparse weights vector with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22947.gif) nonzero elements. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22948.gif) represents the local average of unit ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22949.gif). No unit is assumed to be dominant in the sense discussed by Chudik and Pesaran ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-221)).

Following Pesaran ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-774)) and Chudik and Pesaran ([2015a](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-223)), economy wide average, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22950.gif), and the three sectoral averages

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22951.gif)

are used in estimation, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22952.gif) for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22953.gif) defines the set of units belonging to the food and beverages sector (*f*), the goods sector (*g*), and the services sector (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22956.gif) ). ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22957.gif) is the number of units in sector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22958.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22959.gif) is the corresponding vector of sectoral weights. The following cross-section augmented regressions are estimated by least squares for the price category ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22960.gif) belonging to sector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22961.gif) (intercepts are included but not shown)[¹⁴](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-note-237)

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22962.gif)(32.105)

The same equations are also estimated for the energy price category, but without sectoral averages. The estimates are dynamic CCE discussed in Section [29.5.3](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29-div2-307). Impulse response function of the combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable in a disaggregate model is computed in the same way as in Section [32.9](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-363). The lag-orders for the individual price equations are chosen by AIC with the maximum lag-order set to 2. In line with the theoretical derivations, a higher maximum lag-order is selected when estimating the aggregate inflation equations.

## 32.11.3 Estimation results

[Table 32.3](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-tableGroup-71) summarizes the statistical significance of the various coefficients in the price equations, ([32.105](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-displayMaths-3944)), for Germany, France, and Italy. The parameters are grouped into own lagged effects (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22963.gif) ), lagged neighbourhood effects (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22964.gif) ), country effects (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22965.gif) ), and sectoral effects (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22966.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22967.gif) ). All four types of effects are statistically important, although own lagged effects, perhaps not surprisingly, are more important statistically as compared to the other effects. At the 5 per cent significance level, own lagged effects are significant in 90 cases out of 112 in Germany, 111 cases out of 169 in France, and 158 out of 209 cases in Italy. Local and cross-section averages are statistically significant in about 12 and 25 per cent of cases. These results suggest that micro relations that ignore common factors and the neighbourhood effects are most likely misspecified. Idiosyncratic shocks are likely to dominate the micro relations, which could explain the lower rejection rate for the cross-section averages, compared to the own lagged coefficients. The fit is relatively high in most cases. The average ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22968.gif) is 56 per cent in Germany, 48 per cent in France, and 51 per cent in Italy (median values are 61 per cent, 52 per cent, and 54 per cent, respectively).

## 32.11.4 Sources of aggregate inflation persistence

For each of the three countries, Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) compute and report the *GIRF* of a unit combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable, using aggregate and disaggregate models, as explained in Section [32.8](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-div1-362). (see [Figure 32.3](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-figureGroup-25)). They also provide 90 per cent bootstrap confidence bounds together with the bootstrap means. These impulse responses are quite persistent. The estimates based on the disaggregate model show a higher degree of persistence in the case of France and Italy.

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-graphic-027.gif)

Figure 32.3 *GIRF*s of one unit combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable.

Using the estimates of micro lagged coefficients in ([33.36](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-4021)), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22969.gif), Pesaran and Chudik ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-780)) compute eigenvalues of the companion matrix corresponding to the *VAR* polynomial matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22970.gif),

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22971.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22972.gif), ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22973.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22974.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22975.gif) denote estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22976.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22977.gif), respectively. The modulus of the largest eigenvalue is 0.94 for Germany and Italy, and 0.89 for France, and do not cover unity. The authors therefore conclude that it is unlikely that dynamic heterogeneity alone could generate the degree of persistence observed in [Figure 32.3](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-figureGroup-25).

This conclusion is further investigated in [Figure 32.4](#047_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-32-figureGroup-26), which compares the estimates of *GIRF*s for the combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22978.gif) at horizons ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22979.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22980.gif), where the matrix ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22981.gif) is defined by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22982.gif). ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22983.gif) shows the effects of dynamic heterogeneity on the persistence of the aggregate variable, whereas the *GIRF*s of the combined aggregate shock on the aggregate variable is determined by factor persistence as well as dynamic heterogeneity. In the case of all the three countries, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22984.gif) is found to decline with ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22985.gif) much faster when compared to the effects of the combined aggregate shock. It therefore seems that dynamic heterogeneity alone does not sufficiently explain the observed persistence of the aggregate inflation.

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-graphic-028.gif)

Figure 32.4 *GIRF*s of one unit combined aggregate shocks on the aggregate variable (light-grey colour) and estimates of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22987.gif) (dark-grey colour); bootstrap means and 90% confidence bounds, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22988.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-22989.gif).

| [33](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33) | [ Theory and Practice of *GVAR* Modelling](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33) |

# 33.1 Introduction

Individual economies in the global economy are interlinked through many different channels in a complex way. These include sharing scarce resources (such as oil and other commodities), political and technological developments, cross-border trade in financial assets as well as trade in goods and services, labour and capital movement across countries. Even after allowing for such effects, there might still be residual interdependencies due to unobserved interactions and spillover effects not taken properly into account by using the common channels of interaction. Taking account of these channels of interaction poses a major challenge to modelling the global economy and conducting policy simulations and counterfactual scenario analyses.

The global *VAR* (*GVAR*) approach, originally proposed in Pesaran et al. ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-794)), provides a relatively simple yet effective way of modelling complex high-dimensional systems such as the global economy. Although *GVAR* is not the first large global macroeconomic model of the world economy, its methodological contributions lie in dealing with the curse of dimensionality (i.e., the proliferation of parameters as the dimension of the model grows) in a theoretically coherent and statistically consistent manner. Other existing large models are often incomplete and do not present a closed system, which is required for simulation analysis. See Granger and Jeon ([2007](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-421)) for a recent overview of global models.

The *GVAR* approach was developed in the aftermath of the 1997 Asian financial crisis to quantify the effects of macroeconomic developments on the losses of major financial institutions. It was clear then that all major banks are exposed to risk from adverse global or regional shocks, but quantifying these effects required a coherent and simple-to-simulate global macroeconomic model. The *GVAR* approach provides a useful and practical way of building such a model, and, although developed originally as a tool for credit risk analysis, it soon became apparent that it has numerous other applications. This chapter surveys the *GVAR* approach, focusing on the theoretical foundations of the approach as well as its empirical applications.

The *GVAR* can be briefly summarized as a two-step approach. In the first step, small-scale country-specific models are estimated conditional on the rest of the world. These models are represented as augmented *VAR* models, denoted as *VARX*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23078.gif) and feature domestic variables and weighted cross-section averages of foreign variables, also commonly referred to as ‘star variables’, which are treated as weakly exogenous (or long-run forcing). In the second step, individual country *VARX*![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23079.gif) models are stacked and solved simultaneously as one large global *VAR* model. The solution can be used for shock scenario analysis and forecasting as is usually done with standard low-dimensional *VAR* models.

The simplicity and usefulness of this approach has proved to be quite attractive and there are numerous applications of the *GVAR* approach. Individual units need not necessarily be countries, but could be regions, industries, goods categories, banks, municipalities, or sectors of a given economy, just to mention a few notable examples. Mixed cross-section *GVAR* models, for instance linking country data with firm-level data, have also been considered in the literature. The *GVAR* approach is conceptually simple, although it requires some programming skills since it handles large data sets, and it is not yet incorporated in any of the mainstream econometric software packages. Fortunately, an open source toolbox developed by Smith and Galesi ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-915)) together with a global macroeconomic data set, covering the period 1979–2013, can be obtained from the web at \<[https://sites.google.com/site/gvarmodelling/](https://www.sites.google.com/site/gvarmodelling/)\>. This toolbox has greatly facilitated empirical research using *GVAR* methodology.

We start with methodological issues, considering large linear dynamic systems. We suppose that the large set of variables under consideration are all endogenously determined in a factor-augmented high-dimensional *VAR* model. This model allows for a very general pattern of interlinkages among variables, but, as is well known, it cannot be estimated consistently due to the curse of dimensionality when the cross-section dimension (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23080.gif) ) is large. *GVAR* is one of the common solutions to the curse of dimensionality, alongside popular factor-based modelling approaches, large-scale Bayesian *VAR*s and panel *VAR*s. We introduce the *GVAR* approach as originally proposed by Pesaran et al. ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-794)) and then review conditions (on the underlying unobserved high-dimensional *VAR* data generating process) that justify the individual equations estimated in the *GVAR* approach when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23081.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23082.gif) (the time dimension) are large, and of the same order of magnitude. Next, we survey the impulse response analysis, forecasting, analysis of long-run and specification tests in the *GVAR* approach. Last but not least, we review empirical *GVAR* applications. We separate forecasting from non-forecasting applications, and divide the latter group of empirical papers into global applications (featuring countries) and the remaining sectoral/other applications, where cross-section units represent sectors, industries or regions within a given economy.

We abstract from deterministic terms to keep the exposition simple, but such terms can be easily incorporated in the analysis. *GVAR* allows for very general forms of interdependencies across individual variables within a given unit and/or across units, since lags of all *k* variables enter individual equations, and the reduced form errors are allowed to be cross-sectionally dependent. *GVAR* can also be extended to allow for time varying parameters, nonlinearities, or threshold effects. But such extensions are not considered in this Chapter.[¹](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-note-238)

*VAR* models provide a rather general description of linear dynamic systems, but their number of unknown parameters to be estimated grows at a quadratic rate in the dimension of the model, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23117.gif). We are interested in applications where the cross-section dimension, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23118.gif), as well as the time series dimension, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23119.gif), can both be relatively large, while ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23120.gif), for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23121.gif), are small, so that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23122.gif). A prominent example arises in the case of global macroeconomic modelling, where the number of cross-section units is relatively large but the number of variables considered within each cross-sectional unit (such as real output, inflation, stock prices and interest rates) is small. Understanding the transmission of shocks across economies (space) and time is a key question in this example. Clearly, in such settings unrestricted *VAR* models cannot be estimated due to the proliferation of unknown parameters (often referred to as the curse of dimensionality). The main problem is how to impose a plethora of restrictions on the model ([33.1](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3962)) so that the parameters can be consistently estimated as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23123.gif), while still allowing for a general pattern of interdependencies between the individual variables.

There are several approaches developed for modelling data sets with a large number of variables: models that utilize common factors (see [Chapters 19](#033_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-19) and [29](#044_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-29) on factor models), large Bayesian *VAR*s, Panel *VAR*s, and global *VAR*s. Factor models can be interpreted as data shrinkage procedures, where a large set of variables is shrunk into a small set of factors.[²](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-note-239) Estimated factors can be used together with the vector of domestic variables to form a small-scale model, as in factor-augmented *VAR* models (Bernanke, Bovian, and Eliasz ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-105)) and Stock and Watson ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-926))).[³](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-note-240) Large-scale Bayesian *VAR*s, on the other hand, explicitly shrink the parameter space by imposing tight priors on all or a sub-set of parameters. Such models have been explored, among others, by Giacomini and White ([2006](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-399)), De Mol, Giannone, and Reichlin ([2008](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-270)), Carriero, Kapetanios, and Marcellino ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-183)), and Banbura, Giannone, and Reichlin ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-84)). Large Bayesian *VAR*s share many similarities with Panel *VAR*s. The difference between the two is that, while large Bayesian *VAR*s typically treat each variable symmetrically, Panel *VAR*s take account of the structure of the variables, namely the division of the variables into different cross-section groups and variable types. Parameter space is shrunk in the Panel *VAR* literature by assuming that the unknown coefficients can be decomposed into a component that is common across all variables, a cross-section specific component, a variable-specific component, lag-specific component, and idiosyncratic effects; see Canova and Ciccarelli ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-179)) for a survey. Last but not least, the *GVAR* approach solves the dimensionality problem by decomposing the underlying large dimensional *VAR*s into a smaller number of conditional models, which are linked together *via* cross-sectional averages. The *GVAR* approach imposes an intuitive structure on cross-country interlinkages and no restrictions are imposed on the dynamics of the individual country sub-models. In the case where the number of lags is relatively large (compared with the time dimension of the panel) and/or the number of country specific variables is moderately large, it is possible to combine the *GVAR* structure with shrinkage estimation approaches in light of the usual bias-variance trade-offs. Bayesian estimation of country-specific sub-models that feature in the *GVAR* approach have been considered, for instance in Feldkircher et al. ([2014](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-355)).

# 33.3 The *GVAR* solution to the curse of dimensionality

The *GVAR* approach was originally proposed by Pesaran et al. ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-794)) (PSW) as a pragmatic approach to building a coherent global model of the world economy. We follow the exposition of PSW and introduce the *GVAR* approach initially without the inclusion of common variables.

Consider a panel of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23124.gif) cross-section units, each featuring ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23125.gif) variables observed during the time period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23126.gif). Let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23127.gif) denote a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23128.gif) vector of variables specific to cross-sectional unit ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23129.gif) in time period ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23130.gif), and let ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23131.gif) denote a ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23132.gif) vector of all variables in the panel, where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23133.gif). At the core of the *GVAR* approach are small-scale country specific conditional models that can be estimated separately. These individual country models explain the domestic variables of a given economy, collected in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23134.gif) vector ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23135.gif), in terms of the country-specific cross-section averages of foreign variables, collected in the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23136.gif) vector

The assumption of weak exogeneity can be easily tested as outlined in Section [7.1](#017_part1_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-7-div1-76) of *PSW*, and typically is not rejected when the economy under consideration is small relative to the rest of the world and the weights used in the construction of the star variables are granular.

It is clear from ([33.5](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3967)) that country specific models allow for cointegration both amongst domestic variables as well as between domestic and foreign (star) variables.[⁵](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-note-242) In particular, assuming ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23173.gif) is ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23174.gif), the rank of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23175.gif), denoted as ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23176.gif), specifies the number of cointegrating relationships that exist among the domestic and country-specific foreign variables in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23177.gif); and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23178.gif) can be decomposed as

It is well known that this decomposition is not unique and the identification of long-run relationships requires theory-based restrictions (see Sections [23.6](#037_part5_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-23-div1-255) and [33.7](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-div1-374)).

Country models in ([33.3](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3962)) resemble the small open economy (*SOE*) macroeconomic models in the literature, where domestic variables are modelled conditional on the rest of the world. The data shrinkage given by ([33.2](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3963)) solves the dimensionality problem. The conditions under which it is valid to specify ([33.3](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3962)) are reviewed in Section [33.4](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-div1-371). The estimation of country models in ([33.3](#048_part6_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-33-displayMaths-3962)), which allows for cointegration within and across countries (*via* the star variables), is the first step of the *GVAR* approach.

When common variables are present in the country models (![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23274.gif) ), either as observed common factors or as dominant variables as defined in Chudik and Pesaran ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-222)), then the conditional country models need to be augmented by ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-23275.gif) and its lagged values, in addition to the country-specific vector of cross-section averages of the foreign variables, namely
