## [ A.16.1 Grid search methods ](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1-div2-381)

One simple method for obtaining the maximizer, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24331.gif), is to make use of a grid search method. In grid search methods, the procedure is to select many values of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24332.gif) along a grid, compute ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24333.gif) for each of these values, and choose as the estimator the value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24334.gif) that provides the largest value of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24335.gif). This procedure is convenient when the dimension of the unknown parameters is small, say one or two, and the range of variation of these parameters is known *a priori*. The grid search procedure might, however, be very cumbersome when doing Monte Carlo studies or in empirical work where a large number of parameters needs to be estimated. Further, the amount of computations involved when using the search procedure to obtain an estimate of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24336.gif) which is accurate up to three or four significant figures can be considerable.

## [ A.16.2 Gradient methods ](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1-div2-382)

Iterative methods consist of starting from an initial (or ‘guess estimate’) value of the parameters and then updating it according to an iterative formula. Most iterative methods are gradient methods that change in a direction determined by the gradient. The updated formula is a weighted average of the gradient

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24337.gif)

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24338.gif) is a matrix that depends on ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24339.gif), and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24340.gif) is the gradient vector evaluated at ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24341.gif), given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24342.gif)

The choice of the weighting matrix, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24343.gif), leads to different gradient methods. One common modification to gradient methods is to include a ‘damping factor’ to prevent possible overshooting or undershooting, so that

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24344.gif)(A.27)

The iterations need to be started with a guess-estimate, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24345.gif). Iterations usually stops when one or more of the following convergence criteria are satisfied: (i) a small relative change occurs in the objective function, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24346.gif); (ii) a small change occurs in the gradient vector, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24347.gif), relative to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24348.gif); and (iii) a small relative change occurs in the parameter estimates, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24349.gif). Normally, there is a maximum number of iterations that will be attempted, and if such a maximum is reached, then estimates should not be used, unless convergence has been achieved. Note that a poor choice of starting values can lead to exiting at the maximum number of iterations, and general failure of iterative methods.

###  Newton–Raphson method 

The most frequently used method is the Newton–Raphson technique that makes use of the second-order Taylor series expansion. This method works especially well when the function is globally concave in ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24350.gif). The Newton–Raphson iteration is

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24351.gif)(A.28)

for ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24352.gif) where

A modification of the Newton–Raphson technique is the *method of scoring*, which consists of replacing the Hessian matrix in (A.28) by its expected value

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24354.gif)(A.30)

This modification is particularly useful in maximum likelihood estimation, because in this case, by information matrix inequality, ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24355.gif) is positive definite.

See Cameron and Trivedi ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-174) , Ch. 10), for further discussion on gradient methods. See also Boyd and Vandenberghe ([2004](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-143) ) for a textbook treatment of optimization algorithms.

## [ A.16.3 Direct search methods ](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-1-div2-383)

Gradient methods require the objective function to be sufficiently smooth to ensure the existence of the gradient. However, when there is no gradient or when the function has multiple local optima, alternative methods are required. A number of derivative-free methods of searching for a function optimum have been proposed in the literature, such as the simulated annealing or genetic algorithms. These methods are often very effective in problems with many variables in the objective function. However, they usually require far more function evaluations than the methods based on derivatives that were considered above.

###  Simulated annealing 

Suppose we have a value ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24360.gif) at the ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24361.gif) iteration. Hence, the method sets ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24368.gif) if it increases the objective function, or if it does not increase the value of the objective function but does pass the Metropolis criterion that

See Goffe, Ferrier, and Rogers ([1994](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-408) , Ch. 10) and Cameron and Trivedi ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-174) ) for further details of simulated annealing procedure.

# [Appendix B: Probability and Statistics](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2)

This appendix covers key concepts from probability theory and statistics that are used in the book. We refer to Rao ([1973](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-856)), Billingsley ([1995](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-115)), Zwillinger and Kokoska ([2000](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-1001)), Bierens ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-114)) and Durrett ([2010](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-311)) for further details.

A *random variable* is a variable whose value is not known and depends on the outcome of a statistical experiment. ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24625.gif)(B.23)

The excess kurtosis is a measure of the thickness of the tails of a distribution

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24626.gif)(B.24)

In some cases, the degree of excess kurtosis, given by

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24627.gif)(B.25)

is used. In particular, this measure is adopted to characterize departures from the normal distribution, which has excess of zero.

# [ B.10 Useful probability distributions](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2-div1-408)

## [ B.10.1 Discrete probability distributions](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-2-div2-388)

###  Bernoulli

The random variable *X* has a Bernoulli distribution if it takes the value 1 with success probability ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24691.gif) and the value ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24692.gif) with failure probability ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24693.gif). If so we have

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-24694.gif)(B.31)

The Bernoulli distribution is used to describe an experiment, the so-called Bernoulli trial, where the outcome is random and can be either of two possible outcomes, typically a ‘success’ and a ‘failure’. A sequence of Bernoulli trials is referred to as repeated trials.

# [Appendix C: Bayesian Analysis](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3)

# [C.1 Introduction](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3-div1-412)

he statistical approach adopted in this volume is primarily classical, but a Bayesian approach is also considered in the analysis of DSGE models, forecast combination and panel data modelling. This appendix provides an overview of the Bayesian approach and formally introduces the Bayesian concepts and results used in various parts of the book. A full treatment of Bayesian analysis can be found in Geweke ([2005](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-395)), Greenberg ([2013](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-430)), Koop ([2003](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-607)), and Geweke, Koop, and van Dijk ([2011](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-397)).

## [C.3.2 Choice of the priors](#007_FM_contents.xhtml#r_acprof-9780198759980-appendix-3-div2-402)

The choice of the priors can be quite important if ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25176.gif) is not sufficiently large or if one of the parameters is non-identified or weakly identified. As a result there is a large literature on how best to specify priors such that they are least ‘informative’. In cases where the parameters are defined on finite intervals or regions it is reasonable to use uniform priors as characterizations of non-informativeness. But it may not generally be possible to specify non-informative priors. For example, if one of the parameters of interest ranges from ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25177.gif) to![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25178.gif), specification of a uniform prior probability distribution will not be proper in the sense that its integral over ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25179.gif) to![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25180.gif) will be unbounded and cannot be normalized to unity. Such priors that do not integrate to unity are referred to as ‘improper’. In cases where informative priors are used, it is important that the prior distributions cover the true values of the unknown parameters.

Typical choices of proper priors are conjugate priors and hierarchical (or multilevel) priors. Conjugate priors are specified so that to ensure that the posterior and the prior distributions have the same form. For example, in the case of the independent Bernoulli processes

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25181.gif)

the likelihood is given by

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25199.gif) is the posterior probability distribution of ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25200.gif), defined by (C.2). This result can be obtained by application of the following Bayes rule

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25201.gif)

Marginalizing with respect to ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25202.gif)

A similar estimator (known as the ridged estimator) can also be derived using penalized regression with an ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25325.gif) penalty norm. The criterion function for this penalized regression is given by

where ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25327.gif) and ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25328.gif) is a positive constant such that ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25329.gif). The first-order condition for this optimization problem is

which yields

![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25331.gif)C.9)

It is clear that the shrinkage and the ridge estimators coincide when ![image](markdown/Time Series and Panel Data Econometrics/media/images/acprof-9780198759980-math-25332.gif). The main difference between the Bayesian and the penalized regression approaches lies in the way the shrinkage (or penalty) parameter is chosen. Under the Bayesian approach the choice of must be *a priori*, whilst under the penalized regression approach the choice is often made by cross validation. See also Section [11.9](#022_part2_chapter.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-chapter-11-div1-125) and Hastie, Tibshirani, and Friedman ([2009](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-490)) and Buhlmann and van de Geer ([2012](#050_BM_bibliographyGroup.xhtml#acprof-9780198759980-bibliography-1-bibItem-167)).
